Count again. Each oxygen has 2 lone pairs.

q: Aminoacetonitrile, drawn below, has been detected in interstellar gas clouds and can be converted into the amino acid glycine. What is the hybridization of atoms a, b and c?
c: a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp<sup>3</sup>, c: sp
a: sp<sup>2</sup>, b: sp<sup>3</sup>, c: sp
a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp<sup>3</sup>, c: sp<sup>2</sup>
a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp, c: sp
h: Count electron domains on each atom: bonded atoms plus lone pairs, with a double or triple bond counting as one domain. 4 → sp<sup>3</sup>, 3 → sp<sup>2</sup>, 2 → sp.
w: a (N): 3 bonded atoms + 1 lone pair = 4 domains → sp3. b: 4 bonded atoms → sp3. c: only 2 domains (C–C and C≡N) → sp. So a: sp3, b: sp3, c: sp. Choosing sp2 for N forgets that its lone pair is a domain.
x: N's lone pair counts as a domain, so N has 4 (sp³).
Atom c has only 2 domains, so it's sp.
Atom b has 4 single bonds, so it's sp³.

q: Glycine, the simplest amino acid, is drawn below with 90° angles. In the real molecule, around which labeled atom are the bond angles closest to 120°?
h: Bond angles follow electron domains: 4 domains ≈ 109.5°, 3 domains ≈ 120°, 2 domains = 180°. Count lone pairs as domains.
w: a (N) has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4 domains (≈109.5°, a bit less); b has 4 single bonds (≈109.5°); c has 3 domains (C=O, C–O, C–C) → trigonal planar, ≈120°, so c only. The 90° drawing is just a grid, not the real geometry.
x: Atom a has a lone pair and 3 bonds (4 domains), so it's near 109.5°.
Atom b has 4 single bonds, so it's near 109.5°.
Only one labeled atom has 3 domains.

q: Glycine is drawn below with every bond shown. Counting all of its bonds, what are the totals of sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds?
h: Every bond (single, double or triple) contains exactly one σ bond. Each extra bond in a double or triple bond is a π bond.
w: Count bonds: 2 N–H, 1 N–C, 2 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C=O, 1 C–O, 1 O–H = 9 bonds → 9 σ. Only the C=O has a second bond → 1 π. Getting 10 σ counts the double bond as two σ bonds.
x: This counts the double bond as two σ bonds.
There's only one double bond, so only one π bond.
Only the C=O has a π bond.

q: Propyne is used as a fuel for welding torches. How many σ bonds and π bonds are in the molecule shown?
h: A single bond is 1 σ. A double bond is 1 σ + 1 π. A triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π.
w: There are 6 bonds (4 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C≡C), so 6 σ. The triple bond adds 2 π. Counting the triple bond as three π bonds (5 σ, 3 π) forgets that one of its three bonds is σ.
x: One of the triple bond's three bonds is σ.
The triple bond contains 2 π bonds.
Only 2 of the triple bond's bonds are π.

q: Urea, drawn below, is how the body excretes excess nitrogen. The drawing uses 90° angles. What is the actual O=C–N bond angle around the labeled carbon atom a?
h: Count electron domains around atom a. A double bond counts as one domain, and the shape is set by how far apart the domains can get.
w: Atom a has 3 domains (C=O and two C–N) and no lone pairs → trigonal planar, sp2, about 120°. 90° is only how the grid drawing looks; 109.5° would need 4 domains.
x: 109.5° needs 4 domains. Atom a has 3.
180° needs 2 domains. Atom a has 3.
90° is just how the grid drawing looks.

q: Acetic anhydride, drawn below, is used to make aspirin. How many σ bonds and π bonds does one molecule contain?
h: Count every line in the drawing, including the bonds to H. Each line-pair (double bond) contains one σ and one π.
w: Bonds: 6 C–H, 2 C–C, 2 C–O, 2 C=O = 12 bonds → 12 σ; the two C=O bonds each add 1 π → 2 π. 6 σ forgets the six C–H bonds; 14 σ counts each double bond as two σ bonds.
x: This counts each double bond as two σ bonds.
Each C=O has only one π bond.
This forgets the six C–H bonds.

q: For the molecule shown below, how many carbon atoms are sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup> and sp hybridized?
h: For each carbon count its electron domains: 4 single bonds → sp<sup>3</sup>; one double bond → sp<sup>2</sup>; a triple bond or two double bonds → sp.
w: Left to right: CH2= and =CH– each have 3 domains (sp2); the CH2 with 4 single bonds is sp3; the C≡N carbon has 2 domains (sp). sp3: 1, sp2: 2, sp: 1. Calling the CH2 with 4 single bonds sp2, or calling a C=C carbon sp3 or sp, miscounts its domains.
x: Only one carbon has 4 single bonds.
Only the C≡N carbon is sp.
The CH₂ with 4 single bonds is sp³.

q: What are the approximate bond angles around atoms a, b and c in the molecule shown?
h: Find the number of electron domains on each labeled atom: 4 → tetrahedral, 3 → trigonal planar, 2 → linear.
w: a has 4 single bonds → tetrahedral, 109.5°. b has a double bond plus two singles (3 domains) → 120°. c has a single and a triple bond (2 domains) → 180°. a: 109.5°, b: 120°, c: 180°. The 90° value only reflects the drawing grid.
x: Atom b has a double bond and 3 domains, so it's 120°.
Atom a is tetrahedral (109.5°). 90° is just the drawing grid.
Atom c has only 2 domains, so it's 180°.

q: Methyl acrylate (drawn below) is polymerized to make acrylic paints. Give the total number of sigma and pi bonds in a single molecule.
h: One σ bond per line-connection between two atoms (single, double or triple). Extra bonds in multiple bonds are π.
w: There are 12 atoms joined in a chain with no rings, so 11 connections → 11 σ. The C=C and C=O each contribute one extra bond → 2 π. 13 σ counts each double bond as two σ bonds.
x: This counts each double bond as two σ bonds.
Each double bond has only one π bond.
Some bonds were missed. Every pair of bonded atoms, including each C–H pair, is joined by exactly one σ bond.

q: Acetaldehyde, drawn below, forms in the liver when ethanol is broken down. Which orbitals overlap to form the σ bond between atoms a and b?
c: sp<sup>3</sup> on a and sp<sup>2</sup> on b
sp<sup>3</sup> on a and sp<sup>3</sup> on b
sp<sup>2</sup> on a and sp<sup>2</sup> on b
sp<sup>3</sup> on a and p on b
h: Find the hybridization of each carbon first. A σ bond forms from end-on overlap of the hybrid orbitals of the two atoms.
w: a has 4 single bonds (sp3); b has a C=O, C–H and C–C (3 domains, sp2). The a–b σ bond is sp3 on a and sp2 on b. Unhybridized p orbitals form the π bond of C=O, not the C–C σ bond.
x: Atom b has a double bond (3 domains), so it's sp².
Atom a has 4 single bonds, so it's sp³.
The p orbitals form the C=O π bond, not this C–C σ bond.

q: The double bond between atoms a and b in formaldehyde (drawn below) is made of
c: a σ bond from hybrid orbitals and a π bond from p orbitals
two σ bonds, both from overlap of hybrid orbitals
two π bonds, both from side-by-side p orbitals
a σ bond from p orbitals and a π bond from hybrid orbitals
h: The first bond between two atoms is always end-on (σ). Any second bond uses the leftover unhybridized p orbitals overlapping side by side.
w: Each atom is sp2. End-on overlap of sp2 hybrids gives the σ bond; the leftover p orbitals overlap side by side for the π bond: one σ (hybrid) + one π (p). Hybrid orbitals point along the bond axis, so they cannot form π bonds.
x: The second bond of a double bond is π, not σ.
The first bond of a double bond is always σ.
This is reversed. Hybrid orbitals form the σ bond.

q: In the allene molecule drawn below, each terminal CH2 carbon (such as a) shares a double bond with the middle carbon b. Which orbital set does each labeled carbon use?
h: Two double bonds on one atom count as two electron domains, not four.
w: a has C=C, C–H, C–H (3 domains) → sp2. b has two C=C bonds and nothing else (2 domains) → sp, linear. a: sp2, b: sp. Choosing sp2 for b assumes every carbon in a double bond is sp2.
x: Atom b has only 2 domains (two C=C), so it's sp.
Atom a has 3 domains, so it's sp².
Atom a has three domains (one C=C and two C–H), so it cannot be sp. Count the domains on b as well.

q: The molecule drawn below is a small model of one end of the pain reliever acetaminophen. What is the hybridization of carbon atoms a, b and c?
c: a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp<sup>2</sup>, c: sp<sup>3</sup>
a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp<sup>3</sup>, c: sp<sup>3</sup>
a: sp<sup>2</sup>, b: sp<sup>2</sup>, c: sp<sup>2</sup>
a: sp<sup>3</sup>, b: sp<sup>2</sup>, c: sp<sup>2</sup>
h: For each labeled carbon, count the atoms bonded to it (a double bond counts once). Carbon has no lone pairs here.
w: a and c each have 4 single bonds → sp3. b has C=O, C–C and C–N (3 domains) → sp2. a: sp3, b: sp2, c: sp3. Atom c is bonded to N, but that does not change its 4 single bonds.
x: Atom b has a C=O, so it's sp².
Atoms a and c have 4 single bonds, so they're sp³.
Atom c has 4 single bonds. Being bonded to N doesn't change that.

q: Pyruvic acid, drawn below, is the end product of glycolysis. How many of its carbon atoms are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridized?
h: Carbon with one double bond has 3 electron domains (sp<sup>2</sup>). Carbon with four single bonds is sp<sup>3</sup>.
w: The CH3 carbon has 4 single bonds (sp3). The middle carbon and the right carbon each have one C=O and two single bonds → sp2. Answer: 2. Answering 3 also counts the CH3 carbon, which has only single bonds.
x: The CH₃ carbon has 4 single bonds (sp³).
Two carbons have a C=O, not just one.
Some carbons have C=O double bonds.

q: Which structure (I–IV) is the best Lewis structure for carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>?
h: Count the valence electrons each structure shows (CO<sub>2</sub> has 16), check the atom arrangement, then compare formal charges.
w: I has 16 electrons, C in the center, octets everywhere and all formal charges 0. II has charges +1/−1, III puts O in the center (charges −1, +2, −1), and IV shows 18 electrons instead of 16.
x: II has formal charges of +1 and −1. Another structure has all zeros.
III puts O in the center, giving large charges.
IV shows 18 electrons. CO₂ has 16.

q: A student drew four Lewis structures for formaldehyde, CH<sub>2</sub>O, the preservative in biology lab specimens. Which drawing (I–IV) is correct?
h: CH<sub>2</sub>O has 4 + 2(1) + 6 = 12 valence electrons. Carbon goes in the center. Prefer the structure with all formal charges zero.
w: II uses exactly 12 electrons with C central and zero formal charges. I shows 14 electrons instead of 12; III puts an H on oxygen, leaving charges of −1 on C and +1 on O; IV also puts H on O and shows only 10 electrons, with +2 on O.
x: I shows 14 electrons. Formaldehyde has 12.
III puts an H on oxygen, giving charges of −1 and +1.
IV puts H on O and shows only 10 electrons.

q: Nitrosyl chloride, NOCl, forms when aqua regia is mixed. Which structure (I–IV) is its best Lewis structure?
h: Total the valence electrons (7 + 5 + 6 = 18). The least electronegative non-halogen atom usually goes in the center. Then compare formal charges.
w: III (Cl–N=O) has 18 electrons, N in the center and every formal charge 0. I puts a +1 charge on Cl, II puts O in the center (+1 on O, −1 on N), and IV shows 20 electrons.
x: I puts a +1 charge on Cl.
II puts O in the center, giving charges of +1 and −1.
IV shows 20 electrons. NOCl has 18.

q: Nitromethane, drawn below, is a fuel for model racing engines. What is the formal charge on the labeled nitrogen atom a?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − number of bonds (bond order sum).
w: N has 5 valence electrons, no lone pairs and 4 bonds (C–N, N=O, N–O): FC = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Answering 0 assumes N always forms three bonds; here it forms four.
x: N has 4 bonds here, not 3.
The −1 is on the single-bonded O, not N.
Recount: N has no lone pairs, and each bond counts once toward N. How many bonds does N actually have?

q: Methyl isocyanide is drawn below. What is the formal charge on the carbon atom at the right end of the triple bond?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − (lone-pair electrons) − (number of bonds). Count the triple bond as 3.
w: The end carbon: 4 valence − 2 (one lone pair) − 3 (triple bond) = −1. The N next to it is +1, so the molecule is neutral overall. 0 is the usual charge of carbon only when it has four bonds and no lone pairs.
x: This carbon has a lone pair and only 3 bonds.
The sign is wrong. It owns more electrons than a neutral carbon.
This is too negative. One lone pair counts as 2 electrons, and the triple bond counts as 3 bonds.

q: Three Lewis structures for dinitrogen monoxide (laughing gas, N<sub>2</sub>O) are drawn below. Which of them are resonance structures of one another?
h: Resonance structures keep every atom in the same position and differ only in where the electrons (lone pairs and multiple bonds) are placed.
w: I and II both have the N–N–O arrangement and differ only in electron placement, so I and II only are resonance structures. III has N–O–N connectivity, a different arrangement of atoms, so it is not a resonance form of the others.
x: III has the atoms in a different order (N–O–N), so it isn't a resonance form.
III has a different arrangement of atoms.
III has a different arrangement of atoms.

q: One resonance structure of the carbonate ion is drawn below. What is the average carbon–oxygen bond order in the actual ion?
h: Count the equivalent resonance structures. Spread the total number of C–O bonds evenly over the three C–O positions.
w: Three equivalent resonance structures share 4 bonds (one double + two single) over 3 C–O positions: 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. 1.50 is the value for an ion with two equivalent resonance forms, such as nitrite.
x: 1.50 is for an ion with two resonance forms, like nitrite. Carbonate has three.
2.00 treats one drawn bond as the real bond. The double bond is shared over three positions.
1.00 ignores the double bond. Count every bond in one structure, including the double bond, before you average.

q: Propene is drawn below. Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds a–b and b–c is correct?
c: a–b is shorter and stronger than b–c
a–b is longer and weaker than b–c
a–b is shorter but weaker than b–c
a–b and b–c have equal lengths
h: Compare bond orders. More shared electron pairs pull the atoms closer and take more energy to break.
w: a–b is a double bond (order 2) and b–c is a single bond (order 1). Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond. Equal lengths would need resonance, but propene has only one reasonable Lewis structure.
x: This is reversed. The double bond (a–b) is the shorter, stronger one.
A shorter bond is also a stronger bond. They go together.
Equal lengths would need resonance, and propene has only one Lewis structure.

q: Vinegar contains acetic acid; its ion, acetate, has the two resonance forms shown. How do the two carbon–oxygen bonds compare in real acetate ions?
c: equal, between a C–O and a C=O length
the top one is shorter, as drawn in I
the right one is shorter, as drawn in II
they swap lengths as the ion flips forms
h: Resonance structures are not real forms that the ion flips between. The real ion is a blend (hybrid) of them.
w: In the hybrid, the π electrons are spread over both C–O bonds, so each has a bond order of 1.5: the bonds are equal in length, between single and double. The ion does not flip between I and II; neither drawing alone describes it.
x: Neither drawing alone describes the ion. Both bonds are the same.
Neither drawing alone describes the ion. Both bonds are the same.
The ion doesn't flip between forms. It's always a blend.

q: What is the molecular geometry around atoms a and b in glycolonitrile, drawn below?
h: Count electron domains (including lone pairs) for the electron geometry, then name the shape from the atom positions only.
w: a (O): 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains, tetrahedral electron geometry, but with 2 lone pairs the molecular shape is bent. b: a single bond and a triple bond (2 domains) → linear. "Tetrahedral" for O is the electron geometry, not the molecular shape.
x: O has 2 lone pairs, so its shape is bent, not linear.
Tetrahedral is O's electron geometry, not its molecular shape.
Atom b has only 2 domains (a single and a triple bond), so it's linear.

q: Hydrazine, a rocket fuel, is drawn below on a flat grid. What is the actual molecular geometry around nitrogen atom a?
h: Count electron domains on N (bonded atoms + lone pairs). Then describe the shape using only the atoms.
w: N has 3 bonded atoms + 1 lone pair = 4 domains (tetrahedral electron geometry). With one lone pair the shape is trigonal pyramidal, like NH3. "Tetrahedral" ignores that one domain is a lone pair; the flat drawing does not show the 3-D shape.
x: Trigonal planar needs no lone pair. N has one.
Tetrahedral ignores that one of the 4 domains is a lone pair.
T-shaped needs 5 domains. N has 4.

q: Dichloromethane, a paint stripper, is drawn below with its two Cl atoms opposite each other. Is the molecule polar?
c: Polar: it is really tetrahedral, so its dipoles do not cancel
Nonpolar: the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions
Nonpolar: C–Cl and C–H bonds are both nonpolar bonds
Polar: a lone pair on carbon gives it a bent shape
h: A Lewis drawing is flat, but carbon with 4 bonded atoms is tetrahedral in 3-D. Think about where the two C–Cl dipoles really point.
w: Carbon has 4 domains → tetrahedral. In 3-D the two Cl atoms are never 180° apart (about 109.5°), so the C–Cl dipoles add to a net dipole: polar. The "opposite each other" picture is only an artifact of the flat drawing.
x: The "opposite" Cl atoms are just how the flat drawing looks. In 3-D they're about 109.5° apart.
C–Cl bonds are polar because Cl is much more electronegative than C. The C–H bonds are close to nonpolar, but the C–Cl bond dipoles still make the molecule's polarity depend on its 3-D shape.
Carbon has no lone pair here.

q: Four molecules are drawn below on a flat 90° grid. Once their real three-dimensional shapes are considered, which one (I–IV) has no net dipole moment?
h: Find each molecule's real 3-D shape from its electron domains. A molecule is nonpolar only if its bond dipoles cancel.
w: I, BF3: B has 3 domains and no lone pairs → trigonal planar (120°, not the T-shape drawn), so the three equal B–F dipoles cancel. NH3 is pyramidal, CH3Cl has one different bond, and HCN is linear with different ends; all three are polar.
x: NH₃ is pyramidal, so its dipoles don't cancel.
CH₃Cl has one different bond, so its dipoles don't cancel.
HCN is linear but has different ends, so it's polar.

q: In body fluids, glycine exists mostly in the form drawn below. What are the formal charges on the nitrogen atom and on the oxygen atom at the far right?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − number of bonds. Count the bonds and lone pairs on N and on that O.
w: N: 5 − 0 − 4 bonds = +1. Right-hand O: 6 − 6 (three lone pairs) − 1 bond = −1. The charges sum to 0, so the molecule is neutral overall even though each end is charged.
x: N has 4 bonds and no lone pair, and the right O has 3 lone pairs. Neither is zero.
This has the signs reversed.
Recheck the right-hand O: count its lone pairs and its bonds, and compare with a neutral O, which has 2 lone pairs and 2 bonds.

q: Ethylene reacts with chlorine to make 1,2-dichloroethane, the starting material for PVC plastic (all molecules drawn below). Using the average bond enthalpies in the table, what is the estimated enthalpy change?
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: C=C + Cl–Cl = 611 + 243 = 854 kJ. Formed: C–C + 2 C–Cl = 347 + 2(339) = 1025 kJ (the four C–H bonds cancel). ΔH = 854 − 1025 = −171 kJ. +171 kJ subtracts broken from formed; +168 kJ counts only one new C–Cl bond.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This forms only one C–Cl bond. There are two.
This counts only the change from C=C to C–C. The Cl–Cl bond broken and the two C–Cl bonds formed also count.

q: In sunlight, methane reacts with chlorine as drawn below. From the average bond enthalpies in the table, estimate ΔH.
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: one C–H + Cl–Cl = 414 + 243 = 657 kJ. Formed: C–Cl + H–Cl = 339 + 431 = 770 kJ. ΔH = 657 − 770 = −113 kJ. +318 kJ forgets the H–Cl bond formed; +113 kJ is formed − broken.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This forgets the H–Cl bond formed.
This forgets that one C–H bond in methane is broken so the Cl can attach.

q: Natural gas burns as drawn below (×2 marks a coefficient of 2). Use the bond enthalpies in the table to estimate ΔH for the combustion.
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: 4 C–H + 2 O=O = 4(414) + 2(498) = 2652 kJ. Formed: 2 C=O + 4 O–H = 2(799) + 4(464) = 3454 kJ. ΔH = 2652 − 3454 = −802 kJ. −372 kJ ignores both coefficients of 2; −1300 kJ ignores only the 2 in front of O2.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This ignores both coefficients of 2.
This ignores the 2 in front of O₂.

q: Hydrogen and chlorine react as drawn below (×2 means two molecules). Use the average bond enthalpies in the table to estimate ΔH.
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: H–H + Cl–Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Formed: 2 H–Cl = 2(431) = 862 kJ. ΔH = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. +248 kJ forms only one H–Cl bond; +183 kJ subtracts in the wrong order; −1541 kJ adds the two sums.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This forms only one H–Cl. There are two.
This adds the bonds broken and the bonds formed together. The bonds formed must be subtracted from the bonds broken.

q: Electrolysis splits water as drawn below (×2 marks a coefficient of 2). Using the average bond enthalpies in the table, approximately how much energy is absorbed or released?
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: 4 O–H (two in each of 2 H2O) = 4(464) = 1856 kJ. Formed: 2 H–H + O=O = 2(436) + 498 = 1370 kJ. ΔH = 1856 − 1370 = +486 kJ (endothermic). −442 kJ counts only two O–H bonds; −486 kJ is formed − broken.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This breaks only two O–H bonds. Two waters have four.
This forms only one H–H bond. The reaction makes two H₂ molecules, so two H–H bonds form.

q: Industrial ethanol is made by adding water to ethylene (drawn below). Estimate the reaction enthalpy with the average bond enthalpies in the table.
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: C=C + one O–H = 611 + 464 = 1075 kJ. Formed: C–C + C–H + C–O = 347 + 414 + 360 = 1121 kJ. ΔH = 1075 − 1121 = −46 kJ. −510 kJ forgets that an O–H bond in water is broken; +368 kJ forgets the new C–H bond.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This forgets that an O–H bond in water is broken.
This forgets the new C–H bond formed.

q: Adding hydrogen across the triple bond of hydrogen cyanide gives methylamine, as drawn below (×2 marks a coefficient of 2). What ΔH do the average bond enthalpies in the table predict?
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: C≡N + 2 H–H = 891 + 2(436) = 1763 kJ (the original C–H stays). Formed: C–N + 2 C–H + 2 N–H = 293 + 828 + 778 = 1899 kJ. ΔH = 1763 − 1899 = −136 kJ. −572 kJ breaks only one H–H; +642 kJ leaves out the two N–H bonds formed.
x: This is formed − broken. ΔH = broken − formed.
This breaks only one H–H. There are two.
This leaves out the two N–H bonds formed.

q: Acetone, the solvent in nail-polish remover, is drawn below. What is the strongest type of attraction between acetone molecules in the liquid?
h: Hydrogen bonding needs an H bonded directly to N, O or F. Check where each H atom is attached, then decide whether the molecule is polar.
w: Acetone has a polar C=O bond and is polar, so it has dipole–dipole forces (plus dispersion). Every H is bonded to carbon, not oxygen, so acetone cannot hydrogen-bond with itself. There are no ions, so ion–dipole is impossible.
x: Every H is on carbon, so acetone can't hydrogen bond with itself.
Acetone is polar, so it has more than dispersion forces.
Ion–dipole forces need ions, but acetone is a neutral molecule with no charged particles. Only forces between neutral molecules apply to pure liquid acetone.

q: Look at where the hydrogen atoms are attached in structures I–IV. Molecules of which one can act as both the donor and the acceptor of a hydrogen bond to each other?
h: A hydrogen bond needs an H atom that is covalently bonded to N, O or F in one molecule.
w: Only III (CH3NH2) has H atoms bonded directly to N. In I, II and IV the F or O atoms can accept a hydrogen bond, but every H is on carbon, so these molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other.
x: In I, every H is on carbon.
In II, every H is on carbon.
In IV, every H is on carbon.

q: The three substances drawn below have nearly the same molar mass (44–46 g mol⁻¹). Rank them by increasing boiling point.
h: With similar molar masses, dispersion forces are similar. Compare the other forces: nonpolar, polar, or able to hydrogen-bond.
w: II (propane) is nonpolar (dispersion only); III (dimethyl ether) is polar (dipole–dipole); I (ethanol) has an O–H and hydrogen-bonds. Increasing boiling point: II < III < I. III cannot hydrogen-bond because none of its H atoms is on O.
x: III is polar, so it boils above nonpolar II.
I hydrogen bonds, so it boils highest.
I hydrogen bonds, so it boils above III.

q: Which intermolecular force holds liquid carbon tetrachloride (structure below) together most strongly?
h: Decide first whether the molecule is polar: find its real 3-D shape and see whether its four bond dipoles cancel.
w: CCl4 is tetrahedral with four identical C–Cl bonds, so the bond dipoles cancel and the molecule is nonpolar: only London dispersion forces (strong ones, because Cl atoms are large and polarizable). Polar bonds alone do not make a molecule polar.
x: CCl₄'s four dipoles cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.
CCl₄ has no H atoms at all. Hydrogen bonding needs an H bonded directly to N, O or F, so it is impossible here.
Ion–dipole forces need ions, but CCl₄ is a neutral molecule with no charged particles. Only forces between neutral molecules apply to this pure liquid.

q: Structure III is the main ingredient of car antifreeze; I and II are two other compounds of similar molar mass (58–62 g mol⁻¹). Which order lists their boiling points from lowest to highest?
h: Molar masses are close, so look at hydrogen bonding. Count how many O–H groups each molecule has.
w: I (butane) has dispersion forces only. II has one O–H group for hydrogen bonding; III (ethylene glycol, antifreeze) has two O–H groups and forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule. I < II < III.
x: I (butane) has only dispersion forces, so it boils lowest.
III has two O–H groups, so it boils highest.
This is reversed: it puts the substance with the most hydrogen bonding lowest. Stronger attractions mean a higher boiling point, so more O–H groups per molecule means boiling later, not earlier.

q: The pictures show four molecular orbitals formed from the valence orbitals of two identical atoms (shaded and white lobes have opposite phases; dashed lines are nodes). Which picture is a π* (pi antibonding) orbital?
h: A π orbital comes from side-by-side p orbitals, with lobes above and below the bond axis. Antibonding = phase change and a node between the nuclei.
w: II and IV are side-on (π type) overlaps; II has one continuous lobe above and below the axis (bonding π), while IV also has a node cutting between the nuclei, so it is π*. III is σ*2p: it also has a node between the nuclei, but its lobes point along the bond axis (end-on), so it is σ type.
x: II has no node between the nuclei, so it's bonding π.
III's lobes point along the axis, so it's σ*, not π*.
I is a bonding σ orbital.

q: Which pictured molecular orbital has a nodal plane between the two nuclei, perpendicular to the bond axis?
h: A node that cuts between the nuclei is the signature of an antibonding orbital. A node that contains the bond axis is a π feature.
w: II (σ*1s/σ*2s type) has a node slicing between the nuclei, perpendicular to the bond axis, so electron density is pushed away from the bonding region. IV (bonding π) also has a node, but it lies along the bond axis, not between the nuclei; I and III (σ bonding) have no node between the nuclei.
x: IV's node lies along the bond axis, not between the nuclei.
I has no node between the nuclei.
III is bonding, with no node between the nuclei.

q: The molecular orbital shown forms when two atoms bond along a horizontal axis. Which combination of atomic orbitals produces it?
c: two p orbitals overlapping side by side, in phase
two p orbitals overlapping end to end, in phase
two s orbitals overlapping in phase
two p orbitals overlapping side by side, out of phase
h: Look at where the electron density is: on the bond axis (σ) or above and below it (π)? Is there a node between the nuclei?
w: The density sits above and below the bond axis with a nodal plane containing the axis: that is a π orbital, made by side-by-side overlap of two p orbitals in phase. Out-of-phase side-by-side overlap would give π*, which adds a second node cutting between the nuclei; end-to-end overlap gives σ2p.
x: End-to-end overlap gives a σ orbital.
s orbitals give σ orbitals.
Out-of-phase overlap gives π*, with an extra node between the nuclei.

q: Which molecular orbital is shown? (The two dots are the nuclei; shaded and white lobes have opposite phases.)
h: Do the lobes point along the bond axis or stick out above and below it? Is there a node between the nuclei?
w: The lobes point along the bond axis (σ type), each atom contributes a two-lobed p orbital, and the phases are opposite where the orbitals meet, leaving a node between the nuclei. That is σ*2p. σ*2s also has that node but is built from round s orbitals; π*2p has lobes above and below the axis.
x: σ₂p is bonding, with no node between the nuclei.
π* has lobes above and below the axis.
σ*₂s is built from round s orbitals.

q: Two atoms approach each other along a horizontal axis. Each brings the 2p orbital shown, oriented perpendicular to that axis. Which pair of molecular orbitals can these two atomic orbitals form?
h: Two atomic orbitals always combine into one bonding and one antibonding MO. Perpendicular p orbitals overlap side by side.
w: Two AOs give two MOs. Parallel p orbitals standing perpendicular to the bond axis overlap side by side, giving the bonding π2p (in phase) and the antibonding π*2p (out of phase). σ2p/σ*2p need p orbitals pointing along the axis (end to end).
x: σ orbitals need p orbitals pointing along the axis.
These are 2p orbitals, not 2s.
Side-by-side overlap gives only the π pair.

q: The four molecular orbitals pictured are among the valence MOs of a second-row diatomic molecule such as O<sub>2</sub>. Which one is HIGHEST in energy?
h: Antibonding is above bonding. Among the 2p-derived antibonding MOs, which one has the most head-on out-of-phase overlap?
w: I (σ2s) and III (σ2p) are bonding. II is π*2p and IV is σ*2p; both are antibonding, but head-on (σ) overlap is stronger than side-on overlap, so σ*2p is destabilized the most. IV is highest for every second-row diatomic.
x: π*₂p is antibonding, but σ*₂p is raised even higher.
III is a bonding orbital, so it's low in energy.
I is the lowest-energy orbital of these.

q: The valence molecular orbital diagram of O<sub>2</sub> is shown. What does it predict about the magnetic behavior of O<sub>2</sub>?
c: paramagnetic, with 2 unpaired electrons in π*<sub>2p</sub>
paramagnetic, with 2 unpaired electrons in π<sub>2p</sub>
paramagnetic, with 1 unpaired electron in σ*<sub>2p</sub>
h: Look at the highest occupied level. Hund's rule: electrons in degenerate orbitals spread out with parallel spins before pairing.
w: O2 has 12 valence electrons; the last 2 go into the two degenerate π*2p orbitals, one in each with parallel spins. So O2 is paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons in π*2p (it is attracted into a magnet, as liquid O2 shows). A Lewis structure, with all electrons paired, wrongly suggests diamagnetism.
x: O₂'s last two electrons are unpaired in π*₂p.
The π₂p orbitals are full and paired.
σ*₂p is empty in O₂: it is the highest-energy valence orbital, and O₂'s 12 valence electrons run out before reaching it. The last electrons go into the orbitals just below it.

q: The diagram shows the valence molecular orbitals of C<sub>2</sub>, a species found in flames and comets. What are its bond order and magnetic behavior?
h: Bond order = ½(bonding e⁻ − antibonding e⁻). Paramagnetic means at least one unpaired electron.
w: Bonding: σ2s (2) + π2p (4) = 6; antibonding: σ*2s (2). Bond order = ½(6 − 2) = 2, and the π2p set is completely filled, so all electrons are paired: diamagnetic. Bond order 4 comes from adding the σ*2s electrons to the bonding count instead of subtracting them.
x: The π₂p set is completely full, so every electron is paired.
This counts the σ*₂s electrons as bonding. Antibonding electrons are subtracted, not added.
Subtract the antibonding electrons before halving, then check whether the π₂p set is full or only half full.

q: The valence MO diagram of F2 is shown. If one electron is removed to make F+2, how do the bond order and bond length change?
c: bond order rises from 1 to 1.5; the bond gets shorter
bond order falls from 1 to 0.5; the bond gets longer
bond order rises from 1 to 1.5; the bond gets longer
bond order stays 1; the bond length does not change
h: Which orbital does the removed electron come from: bonding or antibonding? Higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond.
w: The electron leaves the highest occupied MO, π*2p, which is antibonding. Bond order: F2 ½(8 − 6) = 1 → F+2 ½(8 − 5) = 1.5. Bond order rises to 1.5 and the bond gets shorter. Assuming the electron comes from a bonding orbital gives the 0.5 answer.
x: The electron leaves an antibonding orbital, so the bond order goes up.
A higher bond order makes the bond shorter.
Removing an electron changes the bond order.

q: The valence MO diagram of N2 is shown. An electron is added to form N−2. Into which orbital does it go, and what is the new bond order?
h: Fill the next empty level above the highest occupied one. Is that level bonding or antibonding?
w: N2 fills through σ2p (10 e⁻, bond order 3). The next level is the antibonding π*2p, so N−2 has bonding 8, antibonding 3: ½(8 − 3) = 2.5, with the electron in π*2p. σ*2p is the highest MO and fills last.
x: σ*₂p is the highest orbital, so it fills last.
An electron added to an antibonding orbital lowers the bond order.
σ₂p is already full in N₂.

q: In the empty valence MO diagram shown, the π<sub>2p</sub> orbitals lie BELOW σ<sub>2p</sub>. For which homonuclear diatomic molecules is this ordering the one used?
c: all second-row diatomics, Li<sub>2</sub> through Ne<sub>2</sub>
h: The switch depends on how strongly 2s and 2p mix, which is large when the 2s–2p energy gap is small (early in the period).
w: For the lighter atoms, the 2s and 2p energies are close, so s–p mixing pushes σ2p above π2p: this is the order for B2, C2 and N2 (and Li2, Be2). For O2 and F2 the gap is large and σ2p drops below π2p.
x: O₂ and F₂ use the other order (σ₂p below π₂p).
Not all of them. O₂ and F₂ are different.
This is reversed. O₂ and F₂ use the other order.

q: The MO diagram shows the valence electrons of a diatomic species. Which species is it, and what is its bond order?
h: Count the arrows to get the number of valence electrons, then match it to a species. O has 6 valence electrons, F has 7.
w: There are 11 valence electrons: O2 has 12, so this is O+2. Bonding = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8, antibonding = 2 + 1 = 3, bond order = ½(8 − 3) = 2.5. O−2 and F+2 would both show 13 electrons.
x: O₂⁻ would show 13 electrons.
O₂ has 12 electrons. Count again.
F₂⁺ would show 13 electrons.

q: The graph shows the distribution of molecular speeds for four gases, He, Ne, Ar and Kr, all at 300 K. Which curve represents argon?
h: At the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, so heavier atoms move more slowly. Rank the gases by molar mass.
w: Lower molar mass → higher most-probable speed → broader, flatter curve. Ranking by peak speed: Kr (2) < Ar (curve 4) < Ne (1) < He (3). Curve 2 (the tallest, slowest) is Kr, the heaviest; argon is the second heaviest.
x: Curve 2 is the slowest, so it's Kr, the heaviest.
Curve 1 is faster than argon's. It's Ne.
Curve 3 is the fastest, so it's He, the lightest.

q: The curves show the speed distribution of the same N<sub>2</sub> sample at 100 K, 300 K, 600 K and 1200 K (not in order). Which curve corresponds to 300 K?
h: Raising T raises the average speed: the peak moves right, and because the area stays the same the curve gets lower and broader.
w: Order the curves by peak speed (or by height, tallest = coldest): 3 (100 K) → 1 (300 K) → 4 (600 K) → 2 (1200 K). Curve 3 is the coldest; picking it confuses 300 K with the lowest temperature on the list.
x: Curve 3 is the coldest (100 K).
Curve 4 is 600 K: its peak is at a higher speed and lower height than the 300 K curve. Rank the curves by peak speed, slowest peak for the coldest, then pick the second-coldest.
Curve 2 is the hottest (1200 K).

q: Curve 1 is the speed distribution of O<sub>2</sub> at 300 K; its peak is at about 400 m s<sup>−1</sup>. Which sample could give curve 2?
h: The most probable speed is proportional to √(T/M). Read the peak of curve 2 and compare it with curve 1.
w: Curve 2 peaks near 800 m s−1, twice the speed of curve 1. Since speed ∝ √(T/M), doubling the speed of the same gas needs 4× the Kelvin temperature: O2 at 1200 K. Doubling T (600 K) only raises the speed by √2 ≈ 1.4×; SO2 at 300 K would be slower than curve 1.
x: Doubling T raises the speed by only √2.
A colder gas would be slower, not faster.
SO₂ is heavier, so it would be slower.

q: The graph shows pressure vs. volume for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature. Predict the pressure if the gas is expanded to 10.0 L.
h: Boyle's law: P × V is the same for every point. Get the constant from any dot on the graph.
w: From any point, PV = (1.00 atm)(4.00 L) = 4.00 L·atm. At 10.0 L: P = 4.00 L·atm / 10.0 L = 0.400 atm. 40.0 atm comes from multiplying instead of dividing; 0.500 atm just reads the last point on the graph.
x: This reads the last point on the graph. Use PV = constant.
This flips the ratio. Expanding lowers the pressure.
This multiplies instead of dividing.

q: A student measured the volume of a gas sample at constant pressure (dots) and extended the best-fit line until it reached zero volume at point X. What is the temperature at X, and what does it represent?
c: −200 °C; the temperature at which the gas liquefies
h: Charles's law says V is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. Where would V be zero on the Kelvin scale?
w: V ∝ T(K), so the line hits V = 0 at T = 0 K, which is −273 °C (absolute zero). The value on this axis is in °C, so writing −273 K is wrong (that is impossible: nothing is below 0 K). A real gas would liquefy before reaching X, which is why the line is extrapolated.
x: Nothing can be below 0 K, and the axis is in °C.
At 0 °C, the gas still has volume.
The line is extended past the real data. It isn't a liquefaction point.

q: The box shows a gas mixture of helium, nitrogen and oxygen. The total pressure is 1.20 atm. What is the partial pressure of N<sub>2</sub>?
h: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure. Count molecules (not atoms) of each gas.
w: There are 5 He + 3 N2 + 2 O2 = 10 molecules. χ(N2) = 3/10, so P(N2) = (3/10)(1.20 atm) = 0.360 atm. Counting atoms instead (6 N of 15 atoms) gives 0.480 atm; 0.600 atm is the partial pressure of He.
x: This counts atoms. Count molecules.
This counts the N atoms as if they were molecules.
0.600 atm is helium's partial pressure.

q: Four rigid containers of the SAME volume at the SAME temperature hold the gas mixtures shown. In which container is the partial pressure of O<sub>2</sub> the greatest?
h: At fixed V and T, a gas's partial pressure depends only on how many of ITS molecules are present: P = nRT/V.
w: P(O2) = n(O2)RT/V, so the container with the most O2 molecules wins: II (5 O2). Container I has the highest mole fraction of O2 (1.0), but only 4 O2 molecules, so its O2 pressure is lower. The N2 molecules don't change the O2 partial pressure.
x: I has the highest O₂ fraction, but fewer O₂ molecules.
III has fewer O₂ molecules.
IV has fewer O₂ molecules.

q: A container starts with 8 He atoms and 8 Ar atoms (Start). A pinhole lets gas effuse out until 8 atoms in total have escaped. Which box best shows the 8 atoms that remain?
h: Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M. Which atom escapes faster, and by about how much?
w: rate(He)/rate(Ar) = √(39.95/4.003) ≈ 3.2, so He atoms escape about three times as fast: of the 8 atoms that leave, most (about 5–6) are He and only 2–3 are Ar. The remaining 8 are mostly Ar, best shown by box II (2 He, 6 Ar). Box IV assumes only He escapes, but Ar also effuses, just more slowly; box I reverses Graham's law.
x: Box I reverses Graham's law. The lighter He escapes faster.
He escapes about 3 times faster, so most of the atoms that leave are He.
Ar also escapes, just more slowly.

q: The graph shows P vs. V for the same sample of gas (same number of moles) at two different temperatures. Which curve is at the higher temperature, and how do the two Kelvin temperatures compare?
c: curve 2; its Kelvin temperature is twice that of curve 1
curve 1; its Kelvin temperature is twice that of curve 2
curve 2; its Kelvin temperature is four times that of curve 1
curve 1; its Kelvin temperature is four times that of curve 2
h: For each curve PV = nRT is constant. Compare the PV products at the same volume.
w: At V = 2 L, curve 1 has P = 1 atm (PV = 2 L·atm) and curve 2 has P = 2 atm (PV = 4 L·atm). With n fixed, PV ∝ T, so curve 2 is hotter, at twice the Kelvin temperature. Squaring the ratio (4×) is a common slip; the pressure doubles, not quadruples. Curve 1 lies below curve 2 at every volume, so it is the colder sample.
x: Curve 1 has the lower pressure at the same volume, so it's colder.
Compare the PV products of the two curves at the same volume. T changes by the same factor as PV, not by its square.
Curve 1 is the colder sample.

q: The boxes show a reaction mixture before and after reaction. Which balanced equation best represents the reaction?
h: Cross out anything that appears unchanged on both sides, then count what was used and made. Reduce to the smallest whole numbers.
w: 4 NO and 2 O2 were used to make 4 NO2; two O2 are left over and are not part of the reaction. 4:2:4 reduces to 2 NO + O2 → 2 NO2. Writing the leftover O2 into the equation (choice with 4 NO + 4 O2) describes the box, not the reaction.
x: This includes the leftover O₂, which didn't react.
No NO₃ forms. The product is NO₂.
No NO₃ forms. The product is NO₂.

q: The box shows a mixture of H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> molecules that react completely. Which reactant is limiting, and how many molecules of the other reactant are left over?
c: H<sub>2</sub> is limiting; 2 O<sub>2</sub> left over
O<sub>2</sub> is limiting; 1 H<sub>2</sub> left over
H<sub>2</sub> is limiting; 3 O<sub>2</sub> left over
O<sub>2</sub> is limiting; 4 H<sub>2</sub> left over
h: Write the balanced equation first. Then ask how much O<sub>2</sub> the H<sub>2</sub> in the box needs.
w: 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. The 6 H2 need 3 O2, and 5 are present, so H2 is limiting and 5 − 3 = 2 O2 are left over. Picking O2 because there are fewer O2 molecules ignores the 2:1 mole ratio.
x: Fewer O₂ molecules doesn't make O₂ limiting. Use the 2:1 ratio.
H₂ is limiting, but recount how many O₂ the 6 H₂ consume using the 2 : 1 ratio.
O₂ isn't limiting. H₂ runs out first.

q: Carbon monoxide burns according to the equation shown. The box labeled Before shows the mixture before reaction. Which box (I–IV) shows the contents after the reaction goes to completion?
h: Find the limiting reactant from the mole ratio, then remember that leftover excess reactant stays in the box. Atoms must be conserved.
w: 4 CO need only 2 O2, so CO is limiting: 4 CO2 form and 3 − 2 = 1 O2 is left: box III. Box I loses the leftover O2 (oxygen atoms disappear); box II adds an extra O2; box IV stops before the limiting CO is used up even though O2 remains.
x: Box I loses the leftover O₂. Atoms can't disappear.
Box II adds an extra O₂, so it has more oxygen atoms than the Before box. Atoms are conserved: count the atoms of each element before and after the reaction.
Box IV stops before the limiting CO is used up.

q: Which box best represents an aqueous solution of sodium sulfate, Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq)? (Water molecules are not shown.)
h: A soluble ionic compound dissociates completely into its ions. How many Na<sup>+</sup> ions does each formula unit give? Polyatomic ions stay together.
w: Na2SO4 is a strong electrolyte: each unit gives 2 Na+ + 1 SO2−4, separated in water, and the charges balance (6 × +1 + 3 × −2 = 0). That is box II. Box III shows intact, undissociated units; I and IV have the wrong 2:1 ratio.
x: Box I has the wrong ratio. Na₂SO₄ gives 2 Na⁺ per SO₄²⁻.
Box III shows intact units. A strong electrolyte separates into ions.
Box IV has more SO₄²⁻ than Na⁺, so its charges do not balance. Each Na₂SO₄ gives 2 Na⁺ for every SO₄²⁻.

q: Hydrofluoric acid, HF, is a weak acid. Which box best represents HF(aq)? (Water molecules other than those in H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> are not shown.)
h: A weak acid only partly ionizes. Most of the acid should still be intact molecules, with a few ions.
w: In a weak acid only a small fraction of HF molecules transfer H+ to water: mostly HF with a few H3O+ and F− ions, box IV. Box I (complete ionization) is a strong acid such as HCl; box II (no ions) is a nonelectrolyte; box III is not electrically neutral.
x: Complete ionization is a strong acid, like HCl.
No ions at all is a nonelectrolyte.
Box III isn't electrically neutral.

q: Each box represents an aqueous solution of a different solute (water not shown). Which box represents a solution of glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>?
h: Is glucose ionic or molecular? Does it produce ions (conduct electricity) when it dissolves?
w: Glucose is a molecular nonelectrolyte: it dissolves as intact, neutral molecules and makes no ions, box I. Box III (a few ions) is a weak electrolyte such as acetic acid; II is a 1:1 salt like NaCl and IV a 1:2 salt like MgCl2. Dissolving does not break covalent bonds in glucose.
x: A few ions is a weak electrolyte.
Box II is a 1:1 salt like NaCl.
Box IV is a 1:2 salt like MgCl₂.

q: Solutions of Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and KI, shown as ions, are mixed. Yellow PbI<sub>2</sub>(s) precipitates. Which ions remain dissolved in the mixture after the reaction is complete?
h: Net ionic equation: Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2 I<sup>−</sup> → PbI<sub>2</sub>(s). Which ions are spectators, and is any Pb<sup>2+</sup> or I<sup>−</sup> left over?
w: 3 Pb2+ combine with exactly 6 I− to make 3 PbI2(s), so neither is left over. The spectator ions stay in solution: 6 K+ and 6 NO−3. Choosing Pb2+ and I− confuses the ions that precipitate with the ones that stay dissolved.
x: Pb²⁺ and I⁻ form the precipitate, so they aren't dissolved.
Pb²⁺ and I⁻ leave as the solid.
Spectator ions are not used up. Recount the K⁺ and NO₃⁻ in the two starting boxes.

q: The two solutions shown are mixed, and BaSO<sub>4</sub>(s) precipitates. Which box (I–IV) shows the ions still dissolved after the reaction is complete? (The solid is not shown.)
h: Net ionic: Ba2+ + SO2−4 → BaSO4(s). Which of those two ions runs out first? Spectator ions all stay.
w: 3 Ba2+ and 2 SO2−4 are present, so SO2−4 is limiting: 2 BaSO4(s) form and 1 Ba2+ remains with the spectators 6 Cl− and 4 Na+: box III (charges balance: +2 − 6 + 4 = 0). Box I forgets the excess Ba2+; box II treats NaCl as the precipitate.
x: This forgets the extra Ba²⁺. SO₄²⁻ runs out first.
NaCl is soluble, so it doesn't precipitate.
Box IV keeps a sulfate ion and has lost some Cl⁻. Recheck which of Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ runs out first, and keep every spectator ion.

q: The box represents a 1.0 mL portion of a solution. The solution is diluted by adding water until its total volume is four times the original. Which box (I–IV) best represents a 1.0 mL portion of the diluted solution?
h: Diluting doesn't change the number of solute particles, only the volume they spread through. M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.
w: The volume is 4× larger, so the concentration is ¼ as large: 8 particles per mL → 8/4 = 2 particles per mL, box II. Box I (4 particles) is only a 2× dilution, box III an 8× dilution, and box IV (8 particles) is the original concentration.
x: 4 particles per mL is only a 2× dilution.
1 particle per mL is an 8× dilution.
8 particles per mL is the original concentration.

q: Each box shows the solute particles in a sample of a sugar solution; the volume of each sample is given under the box. Which solution has the greatest molarity?
h: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution. Compare particles per liter, not total particles.
w: Particles per liter: I 6/1.0 = 6, II 4/0.50 = 8, III 9/2.0 = 4.5, IV 3/0.25 = 12. IV is the most concentrated even though it holds the fewest particles. Box III has the most particles but is spread through the largest volume.
x: III has the most particles, but they're spread through 2.0 L.
I has 6 particles per liter, which is less than another sample. Molarity is particles divided by volume, so a sample with fewer particles in a much smaller volume can be more concentrated.
II has 8 particles per liter, which is not the highest. Molarity is particles divided by volume, so check the samples with small volumes: fewer particles in less space can be more concentrated.

q: The box shows molecules of a gaseous compound of sulfur and oxygen. What is the mass percent of sulfur in this compound?
h: Get the formula from one molecule, then use molar masses: mass % = (mass of S in 1 mol ÷ molar mass) × 100.
w: Each molecule is SO3. %S = 32.06 / (32.06 + 3 × 16.00) × 100 = 32.06/80.06 × 100 = 40.0%. 25.0% is the percent of ATOMS that are S (1 of 4), not the mass percent; 50.0% would be SO2.
x: 25% is the fraction of atoms that are S, not the mass percent.
50% would be SO₂, where S (32.06) is about half of 64.06 g/mol. Count the O atoms in each molecule in the box; with more oxygen, sulfur is a smaller share of the mass.
66.7% is not a mass percent. Use the molar mass of S and of the whole molecule.

q: The box represents 0.500 L of a potassium sulfate solution, K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq). Each drawn ion stands for 0.010 mol of that ion. What is the molarity of K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Each formula unit of K2SO4 gives one SO2−4. Find moles of K2SO4, then divide by liters.
w: 4 SO2−4 × 0.010 mol = 0.040 mol K2SO4; 0.040 mol / 0.500 L = 0.080 M. Counting all 12 ions gives 0.24 M (that is the total ion concentration); counting K+ gives 0.16 M, which is [K+]; 0.040 forgets to divide by the volume.
x: This counts all 12 ions. That's the total ion concentration.
This counts K⁺. That's [K⁺], not [K₂SO₄].
This forgets to divide by the 0.500 L volume.

q: What volume should be recorded for the liquid in this graduated cylinder?
h: Read at the bottom of the meniscus. Record every certain digit plus ONE estimated digit beyond the smallest marked division.
w: The marks are every 1 mL, so the reading is certain to the ones place and estimated to the tenths place. The bottom of the meniscus is a bit less than halfway from 26 to 27: 26.4 mL. 26 mL drops the estimated digit, 26.40 mL claims a precision the scale can't give, and 26.8 mL reads the edge of the meniscus.
x: This drops the estimated digit.
This adds a digit the 1 mL marks can't support.
This reads the edge of the meniscus. Read the bottom.

q: The scale on this small graduated cylinder is marked every 0.2 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is exactly halfway between two marks. Which reading is recorded correctly?
h: One estimated digit beyond the smallest division: marks every 0.2 mL let you estimate to the hundredths place.
w: The meniscus is halfway between the 7.4 and 7.6 mL marks, so the value is 7.5 with the hundredths place estimated: 7.50 mL. Writing 7.5 mL would imply only tenths could be read; on this scale the trailing zero is a measured (estimated) digit.
x: 7.5 implies only tenths could be read. With 0.2 mL marks, estimate hundredths.
This adds a digit the scale can't support.
7.6 is the next mark. The meniscus is halfway, not on it.

q: A buret is marked every 0.1 mL; its numbers increase downward. What reading should be recorded?
h: Read the bottom of the meniscus, remembering a buret scale increases DOWNWARD. Estimate one digit past the 0.1 mL marks.
w: The meniscus bottom is below the 19.3 mark and a little past halfway to 19.4, so the reading is 19.36 mL (hundredths estimated). 19.4 mL drops the estimated digit; 19.360 mL claims too much precision; 20.64 mL comes from reading the scale as if it increased upward.
x: This drops the estimated hundredths digit.
This adds a digit the buret can't support.
Buret numbers increase going down. This reads them going up.

q: In a titration the initial buret reading is given in the table, and the final reading is shown in the drawing. What volume of titrant was delivered?
h: Read the final level to the hundredths place (buret numbers increase downward), then subtract the initial reading.
w: Final reading: 23.27 mL (between 23.2 and 23.3, about 7/10 of the way). Volume delivered = 23.27 − 0.52 = 22.75 mL. 23.79 mL adds the readings; 23.27 mL forgets the initial reading; 22.8 mL rounds away a measured digit (subtraction keeps the hundredths place).
x: This rounds away a measured digit. Keep the hundredths.
This adds the readings. Subtract them.
23.27 mL is the final reading. Subtract the initial 0.52 mL.

q: What is the length of the bar, measured with this centimeter ruler (smallest marks every 0.1 cm)?
h: Count the certain digits from the marks, then estimate one more digit between the smallest marks.
w: The end falls between the 3.4 and 3.5 cm marks, about 7/10 of the way: 3.47 cm (the 7 is estimated). 3.5 cm leaves out the estimated digit, 3.470 cm adds a digit that can't be read, and 3.57 cm miscounts the millimeter marks after the 3.5 half-mark.
x: This drops the estimated digit.
This adds a digit the ruler can't support.
This miscounts the marks after the 3.5 half-mark.

q: This ruler is marked only in whole centimeters. Which value is the correctly recorded length of the bar?
h: Marks every 1 cm: the ones digit is certain. How many more digits can you estimate?
w: With marks every 1 cm, the ones place is certain and the tenths place is estimated: the bar ends about 3/10 of the way from 6 to 7, so 6.3 cm. 6.30 cm and 6.25 cm each claim a second digit beyond the marks, which can't be estimated; 6 cm drops the estimated digit.
x: This drops the estimated tenths digit.
This claims hundredths, which a 1 cm ruler can't give.
This claims hundredths, which a 1 cm ruler can't give.

q: A sample of an iron supplement is weighed on the analytical balance shown. How many significant figures are in the reading?
h: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are measured digits.
w: In 0.0450 g, the zeros before the 4 are placeholders and do not count; the 4, 5 and the trailing 0 (after the decimal point) are significant: 3. Answering 5 counts the leading zeros; answering 2 drops the measured trailing zero.
x: This counts too many digits. Leading zeros don't count.
This counts the leading zeros, which are only placeholders.
This drops the trailing zero. After a decimal point, it counts.

q: A 5.00 mL pipet delivers a sample of an organic liquid into a tared beaker on the balance. The display is shown. What is the density of the liquid, to the correct number of significant figures?
h: Density = mass ÷ volume. In division, keep the number of significant figures of the least precise value.
w: d = 4.395 g / 5.00 mL = 0.8790 g mL−1, rounded to 3 sig figs (set by 5.00 mL): 0.879 g mL−1. 0.8790 keeps 4 sig figs; 1.14 inverts the ratio (volume ÷ mass).
x: This keeps 4 sig figs. 5.00 mL has only 3.
This keeps only 2 sig figs. 5.00 mL has 3.
This divides volume by mass (upside down).

q: Each target shows five measurements of the same quantity; the center is the true value. Which target shows results that are accurate but NOT precise?
h: Accuracy = closeness of the average to the true value. Precision = closeness of the measurements to one another.
w: In III the hits are spread widely, but they are scattered evenly around the center, so their average is close to the true value: accurate, not precise. II is a tight cluster away from the center (precise, not accurate); I is a tight cluster on the center; IV is scattered and off-center.
x: Target I is tight and centered: precise and accurate.
Target II is tight but off-center: precise, not accurate.
Target IV is scattered and off-center: neither.

q: A student's balance has a calibration error, so every reading is 0.15 g too high, but her technique is careful and consistent. Which target best represents her measurements?
h: A systematic error shifts every result the same way. Careful, consistent technique keeps the results close together.
w: A systematic (calibration) error moves all the results the same distance off the true value, and consistent technique keeps them tightly grouped: a tight cluster away from the center, target IV (precise, not accurate). III (tight on the center) would need a correct calibration; II and I are spread out, which signals random error.
x: Target II is spread out, which signals random error, not careful technique.
Target I is spread out, which signals random error.
Target III is centered, which would need a correct calibration.

q: Ammonia is drawn below with 90° angles. What is the ACTUAL H–N–H bond angle in an NH<sub>3</sub> molecule?
h: A Lewis drawing on paper is flat. Count electron domains around N (bonds + lone pairs) and remember lone pairs squeeze bond angles.
w: The drawing is flat and does not show the real geometry. N has 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4 domains → tetrahedral electron geometry, trigonal pyramidal shape. The lone pair pushes the bonds closer than 109.5°, giving about 107°. 90° just reads the paper drawing; 120° would need a flat (trigonal planar) molecule with no lone pair.
x: 90° is just the flat drawing.
120° would need a flat molecule with no lone pair.
180° would be linear, which needs only two electron groups on the central atom. N in NH₃ has 3 bonds plus 1 lone pair, so the molecule cannot be a straight line.

q: A student draws water as shown, with the two H atoms on opposite sides of O. What are the actual shape and H–O–H angle of a water molecule?
h: Ignore where the drawing puts the atoms. Count all electron domains on O, including lone pairs, then name the shape from atom positions only.
w: The drawing only shows connections, not angles. O has 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4 domains (tetrahedral electron geometry); with only 2 atoms attached the molecular shape is bent, about 104.5° (two lone pairs compress it below 109.5°). Tetrahedral describes the electron geometry, not the shape.
x: The straight drawing only shows connections. The lone pairs bend the molecule.
Bent is right, but 90° is too small. Four domains start near 109.5°, and the two lone pairs squeeze the angle only a little below that.
Tetrahedral is the electron geometry, not the shape.

q: Dichloromethane is drawn as a flat cross below, with the two Cl atoms opposite each other. Which statement about the real molecule is correct?
c: It is square planar (90°) and nonpolar.
It is square planar (90°) and polar.
h: Four bonding domains on C, no lone pairs. Then ask whether C–Cl bond dipoles can cancel in that 3-D shape.
w: The cross is only a flat drawing: C has 4 domains, so the molecule is tetrahedral with angles of about 109.5°. In a tetrahedron any two positions are 109.5° apart, so the two C–Cl dipoles can never point in opposite directions and do not cancel: the molecule is polar. The nonpolar answer trusts the drawing, where the Cl atoms look 180° apart.
x: This trusts the flat drawing. The real molecule is tetrahedral.
In a tetrahedron, the two C–Cl dipoles can't point opposite each other, so they don't cancel.
The real molecule is tetrahedral, not square planar.

q: The Lewis structure of SF<sub>4</sub> is drawn below on a flat 90° grid. What is the actual molecular shape of SF<sub>4</sub>?
h: Count the domains on S (4 bonds + lone pairs). Five domains start from a trigonal bipyramid; where does the lone pair go?
w: S has 4 bonds + 1 lone pair = 5 domains → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The lone pair takes an equatorial position (more room), leaving the four F atoms in a seesaw shape (axial F–S–F near 180°, equatorial F–S–F near 102°, less than 120°). Square planar just copies the flat drawing; tetrahedral ignores the lone pair.
x: This copies the flat drawing. S has a lone pair.
Tetrahedral ignores sulfur's lone pair.
Trigonal pyramidal is 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. SF₄ has 4 bonds.

q: XeF<sub>4</sub> is drawn below on a flat 90° grid. What is the actual F–Xe–F angle between two ADJACENT fluorine atoms?
h: Count the electron domains on Xe, including both lone pairs. Where do two lone pairs sit in an octahedron?
w: Xe has 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 6 domains → octahedral electron geometry. The two lone pairs sit opposite each other (180° apart), so the four F atoms lie in a plane: square planar, with adjacent F–Xe–F angles of 90°. Here the flat drawing happens to match the real shape, so answering 109.5° (assuming every 4-atom drawing is really tetrahedral) is the trap.
x: This assumes every 4-atom drawing is tetrahedral. Xe has 6 domains.
120° is for 3 groups in a plane.
About 102° is the equatorial angle in SF₄, not XeF₄.

q: One Lewis structure of the nitrate ion is drawn below. Counting this one, how many resonance structures can be drawn in which every atom obeys the octet rule?
h: Keep every atom where it is. In how many different places can the N=O double bond go?
w: Only the double bond moves: it can sit on any of the three equivalent oxygens, giving 3 resonance structures. Answering 1 treats the drawing as the real ion; 4 counts atoms, not positions for the double bond.
x: One drawing doesn't describe the ion. The double bond can move.
4 counts atoms, not places for the double bond.
The double bond can go on any of the 3 oxygens.

q: Limestone and seashells contain the carbonate ion, drawn below in one of its Lewis structures. How many equivalent resonance structures does carbonate have?
h: Resonance forms differ only in where electrons sit. How many oxygens could carry the C=O double bond?
w: The C=O double bond can be on any of the 3 oxygens, and the other two then carry the −1 charges: 3 equivalent structures. Answering 2 counts only the two negatively charged oxygens.
x: This counts only the two oxygens with a negative charge.
Carbonate has resonance: the C=O double bond in the drawing could sit on another oxygen just as well. Count how many oxygens could hold that double bond.
There are only 3 oxygens.

q: Ozone in the upper atmosphere absorbs UV light. One Lewis structure of O<sub>3</sub> is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does ozone have?
h: The central O stays in the middle. Which of the outer oxygens could share the double bond?
w: The double bond can join the central O to either end oxygen, so there are 2 equivalent structures. 3 is the number of atoms; the central O cannot hold the double bond to itself.
x: Ozone has resonance: the double bond in the drawing could join the central O to the other end oxygen instead. Count how many equivalent placements of that double bond exist.
3 counts the atoms. The double bond has only two places to go.
There are only two O–O bonds.

q: Sulfur dioxide is drawn below with an octet on every atom. How many resonance structures of SO<sub>2</sub> can be drawn in which every atom obeys the octet rule?
h: With octets only, S can form just one double bond. How many oxygens could it go to?
w: With octets only, S has one S=O and one S–O (formal charges +1 on S, −1 on the single-bonded O). The double bond can go to either O: 2 structures. A drawing with two S=O bonds gives S 10 electrons, which the question excludes.
x: SO₂ has resonance. The double bond can go to either O.
There are only 2 oxygens.
There are only 2 oxygens.

q: Sulfur trioxide, which forms acid rain, is drawn below with an octet on every atom. How many octet-rule resonance structures does SO<sub>3</sub> have?
h: Octets only: sulfur keeps one S=O double bond. How many oxygens could it go to?
w: In an octet structure S has one S=O and two S–O bonds (formal charge +2 on S). The double bond can be on any of the 3 oxygens: 3 structures. 4 adds the expanded-octet form with three S=O bonds, which the question excludes; 1 treats the drawing as the real molecule.
x: One drawing doesn't describe SO₃. The double bond can move.
This adds the expanded-octet form, which the question excludes.
There are only 3 oxygens.

q: Nitrite, used to cure bacon and ham, is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does the nitrite ion, NO−2, have?
h: The lone pair on N stays put. Count the oxygens that could share the N=O double bond.
w: Either oxygen can hold the N=O double bond (the other O then carries the −1 charge), so there are 2 equivalent resonance structures. The real ion has two identical N–O bonds.
x: Nitrite has resonance: the N=O double bond could be on either oxygen, which is why the real ion has two identical N–O bonds. One drawing alone does not describe it.
3 counts the atoms, not the structures. Only the double bond moves, and it can only go between N and an oxygen; N cannot form a double bond to itself.
There are only 2 oxygens.

q: The bicarbonate ion in blood is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does HCO−3 have?
h: Unlike carbonate, one oxygen holds an H. Can that O share the double bond equally with the other two?
w: The C=O double bond can be on either O that lacks H, giving 2 equivalent forms. 3 copies carbonate: putting the double bond on the O–H oxygen gives a structure with +1 on that O and −1 on the other two, which is not equivalent and contributes far less.
x: Putting the double bond on the O–H oxygen gives a different, much weaker structure.
Bicarbonate has resonance.
Only 2 oxygens can hold the double bond equally.

q: Formate, the ion of formic acid in ant stings, is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does HCOO<sup>−</sup> have?
h: Hydrogen can form only one bond. Which atoms could share the C=O double bond?
w: The double bond can be to either oxygen: 2 equivalent structures, so both C–O bonds are identical (bond order 1.5). Answering 3 treats formate like carbonate, but H can never take part in a double bond.
x: H can't take part in a double bond. Only the two O atoms can.
Formate has resonance: the C=O double bond could be on either oxygen, so both C–O bonds are actually identical. One drawing alone does not describe it.
Only 2 oxygens can hold the double bond.

q: Nitromethane, a racing fuel, is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures can be drawn for CH<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>?
h: The CH<sub>3</sub> group has no lone pairs or double bonds to move. Look only at the NO<sub>2</sub> part.
w: The N=O double bond can be to either oxygen, so there are 2 equivalent structures, each with +1 on N and −1 on the single-bonded O. Answering 1 treats the drawing as the real molecule; the real N–O bonds are identical.
x: One drawing doesn't describe the molecule. The double bond can go to either O.
There are only 2 oxygens to hold the double bond.
There are only 2 oxygens to hold the double bond.

q: Benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, is drawn below as a ring of six carbons, each bonded to one H (not shown). How many equivalent resonance structures does benzene have?
h: Keep the ring atoms fixed. In how many ways can three C=C double bonds alternate around the ring?
w: The three double bonds can sit on either set of alternating C–C bonds, giving 2 equivalent (Kekulé) structures. 3 is the number of double bonds in one structure, and 6 the number of carbons.
x: Benzene has resonance. One Kekulé drawing doesn't describe it.
3 is the number of double bonds, not resonance structures.
6 is the number of carbons, not resonance structures.

q: Which structure is NOT a valid resonance structure of the nitrate ion, NO−3?
h: Resonance structures of one ion keep the same atom positions and the same total number of electrons. Count electrons or check the overall charge.
w: Nitrate has 5 + 3(6) + 1 = 24 valence electrons. The structure with three N–O single bonds and a lone pair on N has 26, so it is a different ion (charge 3−), not a resonance form. The other three only move the N=O double bond, which is exactly what resonance allows.
x: This only moves the N=O double bond, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the wrong electron count.
This only moves the N=O double bond, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the wrong electron count.
This only moves the N=O double bond, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the wrong electron count.

q: Which drawing is NOT a resonance structure of the cyanate ion, OCN<sup>−</sup> (atom order O–C–N)?
h: All four have 16 valence electrons. Resonance can move electrons, but can it change which atom is in the middle?
w: Resonance structures keep every atom in place. The structure with N in the middle (C–N–O) is the fulminate ion, a different ion (an isomer), not a resonance form. The other three have O–C–N and differ only in electron placement; one is poor (−2 on N, +1 on O) but still a valid resonance structure.
x: This keeps the O–C–N order and only moves electrons, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the atoms in a different order.
This keeps the O–C–N order and only moves electrons, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the atoms in a different order.
This keeps the O–C–N order and only moves electrons, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one with the atoms in a different order.

q: The guanidinium ion, C(NH2)+3, is part of the amino acid arginine. Which structure is NOT a resonance structure of guanidinium?
h: Resonance moves only electrons (lone pairs and double bonds). Check whether every N keeps the same number of H atoms.
w: In guanidinium each N has two H. The structure with an NH+3 group and an =NH group has moved an H atom from one N to another, so it is a different species (a tautomer), not a resonance form. The other three only move the C=N double bond and the + charge.
x: This only moves the C=N double bond and the + charge, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one where an H atom moved.
This only moves the C=N double bond and the + charge, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one where an H atom moved.
This only moves the C=N double bond and the + charge, so it's a valid resonance form. Look for one where an H atom moved.

q: One resonance structure of ozone is drawn below. What is the average oxygen–oxygen bond order in the real O<sub>3</sub> molecule?
h: Spread the total number of O–O bonds in one structure evenly over the O–O positions.
w: Each structure has one O=O and one O–O: 3 bonds over 2 positions, 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5. Both bonds are identical, between a single and a double bond. 1.33 applies to three positions, as in nitrate.
x: 1 would mean only single bonds.
2 would mean only double bonds.
1.33 is for three positions, as in nitrate. Ozone has two.

q: Benzene is drawn below in one Kekulé form. A C–C single bond is about 154 pm long and a C=C double bond about 134 pm. Which describes the carbon–carbon bonds in real benzene?
c: All six are equal, about 139 pm
Three are 154 pm and three are 134 pm
All six are equal, about 154 pm
All six are equal, about 134 pm
h: Benzene has two equivalent resonance structures. What bond order does each C–C position have on average?
w: Each C–C bond is single in one Kekulé form and double in the other, so its bond order is 1.5 and all six bonds are equal, between single and double (about 139 pm). Alternating 154/134 pm would be true only if the drawing were the real molecule.
x: That would be true only if one drawing were the real molecule.
154 pm is a pure single bond. Each bond is part single, part double.
134 pm is a pure double bond. Each bond is part single, part double.

q: One Lewis structure of the bicarbonate ion is drawn below. In the real ion, which carbon–oxygen bonds have the same length?
h: Find the equivalent resonance structures. Which oxygens trade the double bond between them?
w: The double bond moves between the two oxygens that lack H (2 equivalent forms), so each of those bonds has order 1.5: the C=O and C–O− bonds become equal. The O–H oxygen stays single-bonded, so its C–O bond is the longest. "All three" would be true for carbonate, not bicarbonate.
x: The O–H oxygen stays single-bonded, so its bond is longer than the other two.
The C–OH bond stays single, so it's longer than the C–O⁻ bond.
The C–OH bond stays single, so it's longer than the C=O bond.

q: One Lewis structure of each species is drawn below. Rank the nitrogen–oxygen bonds from STRONGEST to WEAKEST.
h: Average each bond order over the resonance structures. Higher bond order means a stronger bond.
w: Bond orders: NO+ 3 (triple, no resonance), NO−2 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5, NO−3 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. Strongest to weakest: NO+ > NO−2 > NO−3. Nitrate has the most oxygens, but its one double bond is shared over three positions.
x: This is reversed. Higher bond order means a stronger bond.
Nitrate has the lowest bond order (1.33), so it's the weakest.
NO⁺ has a triple bond (order 3), so it's the strongest.

q: Lewis structures of three carbon–oxygen species are drawn below. Rank their C–O bond lengths from LONGEST to SHORTEST.
h: Average each C–O bond order over the resonance structures. A lower bond order means a longer bond.
w: Average C–O bond orders: CO2−3 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 (one double bond shared by three O), HCOO− 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 (shared by two O), CO2 2 (no resonance). Lower bond order means a longer bond: CO2−3 > HCOO− > CO2. The reversed order ranks bond strength, not length.
x: This ranks bond strength, not length. It's reversed.
Formate (1.5) has a higher bond order than carbonate (1.33), so it's shorter.
CO₂ has true double bonds, so its bonds are the shortest.

q: Thiocyanate, SCN<sup>−</sup>, is used in a blood-red test for Fe<sup>3+</sup>. Which is the best (major) Lewis structure of the thiocyanate ion?
h: Keep formal charges as close to zero as possible, and put any negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
w: Two S–C–N structures have only one −1 charge: on N (S=C=N) or on S (S–C≡N). N is more electronegative than S, so the best is S=C=N with −1 on N. S≡C–N has charges +1 and −2. Putting N in the middle gives C a −2 charge and the wrong skeleton: the least electronegative atom (C) belongs in the center.
x: Check the formal charge on every atom. When two structures have equally small charges, which atom should carry the negative charge?
This has larger formal charges or the wrong skeleton. The best structure has a single −1 charge, on the most electronegative atom.
This has larger formal charges or the wrong skeleton. The best structure has a single −1 charge, on the most electronegative atom.

q: Dinitrogen monoxide (laughing gas, N<sub>2</sub>O) has the atom order N–N–O. Based on formal charges, which is its best Lewis structure?
h: Pick the smallest formal charges. If two structures tie, prefer the one with the negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
w: N≡N–O and N=N=O each have one +1 and one −1. In N≡N–O the −1 is on O, the most electronegative atom, so it is best; N=N=O puts −1 on the end N. N–N≡O has −2 on the end N and +1 on both the middle N and O. The N–O–N drawing has O at +2 and the wrong atom order.
x: Check the formal charge on every atom. When two structures have equally small charges, which atom should carry the negative charge?
This has larger formal charges or the wrong atom order. The best structure keeps charges small and puts the −1 on O.
This has larger formal charges or the wrong atom order. The best structure keeps charges small and puts the −1 on O.

q: Sodium azide in car airbags contains the azide ion, N−3. One of its Lewis structures is drawn below. In the BEST Lewis structure of azide, what are the formal charges (end N, middle N, end N)?
h: Try two N=N double bonds instead of a single plus a triple. Compute each formal charge: valence − lone-pair electrons − bonds.
w: With two N=N bonds, each end N has 2 lone pairs and 2 bonds (5 − 4 − 2 = −1) and the middle N has 4 bonds (5 − 0 − 4 = +1): −1, +1, −1. The drawn form, −2, +1, 0, has a larger −2 charge, so it contributes less. "0, −1, 0" and "−1, 0, 0" cannot be drawn with octets on all three atoms.
x: This has a −2 charge, which is larger than the best structure's charges.
This can't be drawn with octets on all three atoms.
This can't be drawn with octets on all three atoms.

q: Sodium-vapor streetlights glow yellow-orange at 589 nm. What is the frequency of this light?
h: Use c = λν. Put the wavelength in meters before dividing.
w: ν = c/λ = (2.998×108 m s−1) ÷ (589×10−9 m) = 5.09×1014 s−1. 5.09×105 s−1 comes from leaving λ in nm.
x: This leaves λ in nm. Convert to meters.
This divides λ by c (upside down).
This multiplies c by λ. Frequency comes from dividing c by λ.

q: Breaking the Cl–Cl bond requires 242 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the LONGEST wavelength of light whose photons each have enough energy to break one Cl–Cl bond?
h: Convert kJ mol⁻¹ to J per bond (÷ N<sub>A</sub>, × 1000), then λ = hc/E. Longer wavelength means less energy.
w: E per bond = 242,000 J mol⁻¹ ÷ 6.022×1023 mol−1 = 4.02×10−19 J; λ = hc/E = 494 nm. Any longer wavelength carries too little energy. Skipping NA gives the absurd 8.21×10−22 nm. 4.94×10−7 is the wavelength in meters, never converted to nm.
x: This is the wavelength in meters, not converted to nm.
This skips Avogadro's number. Find the energy per bond first.
This uses twice the energy needed. One photon only has to break one Cl–Cl bond, so do not double the bond energy.

q: Compared with photons of red light (700 nm), photons of violet light (400 nm) have
c: a higher speed in a vacuum
h: Shorter wavelength means more waves pass per second. Photon energy is E = hν.
w: λν = c, so the shorter-wavelength violet light has the higher frequency, and E = hν gives it the higher energy. All light travels at the same speed, c, in a vacuum.
x: Higher frequency also means higher energy (E = hν).
Violet light has the higher frequency.
All light travels at the same speed in a vacuum.

q: Hydrogen atoms in a gas sample move between energy levels. For which change must the atom take in light energy?
h: Absorbing energy moves the electron to a higher level; emitting moves it down.
w: Absorption raises the electron's energy, so it must move to a larger n: n = 2 → n = 5. The other three move down and emit light.
x: Moving down to n = 2 releases light.
Moving down to n = 1 releases light.
Moving down to n = 4 releases light.

q: Four possible upward jumps for hydrogen's electron are listed. Which jump needs light of the SHORTEST wavelength?
