h: Shortest wavelength = largest energy gap. Levels crowd together as n increases, so gaps near n = 1 are largest.
w: ΔE ∝ (1/n2i − 1/n2f): 1→3 gives 0.889, 1→2 gives 0.750, 2→6 gives 0.222, 3→7 gives 0.091. The largest ΔE (n = 1 → n = 3) has the shortest λ. A big change in n high up (3→7) spans only a small energy gap.
x: 1 → 2 is a smaller energy gap than 1 → 3.
2 → 6 is a smaller energy gap than jumps that start at n = 1, because levels crowd together higher up. Shortest wavelength means largest energy, so compare ΔE, not the change in n.
3 → 7 spans only a small gap high up in the atom.

q: In the Lyman series, hydrogen's electron falls from the third level to the ground state. What wavelength of light is given off? (E<sub>n</sub> = −2.179×10<sup>−18</sup> J/n<sup>2</sup>)
h: Find the energy difference between the n = 3 and n = 1 levels from the En equation. Then use λ = hc/ΔE.
w: ΔE = 2.179×10−18 J (1 − 1/9) = 1.937×10−18 J; λ = hc/ΔE = 103 nm (ultraviolet). 656 nm is the 3 → 2 Balmer line (wrong final level), 91.2 nm is ionization from n = 1, and 82.0 nm comes from ADDING 1/12 and 1/32.
x: 91.2 nm is the wavelength that removes the electron from n = 1 completely. Here the electron moves between two levels.
656 nm is the 3 → 2 line. This drop ends at n = 1.
This adds the two terms. Subtract them: 1 − 1/9.

q: How much energy is needed to ionize one MOLE of hydrogen atoms whose electrons are in the n = 2 level? (E<sub>n</sub> = −2.179×10<sup>−18</sup> J/n<sup>2</sup>)
h: Ionization from level n means going from E<sub>n</sub> to E = 0. Remember n is squared, and multiply by Avogadro's number.
w: Per atom: 2.179×10−18 J/22 = 5.448×10−19 J; × 6.022×1023 = 328 kJ per mole. 1312 kJ is ionization from n = 1, and 656 kJ forgets to square n.
x: 1312 kJ is ionization from n = 1.
This forgets to square n.
This is the 1 → 2 energy, not ionization from n = 2.

q: Light from glowing hydrogen gas passes through a prism and shows only a few sharp colored lines, not a continuous rainbow. What does this show?
c: The electron in H can have only certain energies.
Hydrogen atoms emit photons of every energy.
Hydrogen absorbs all visible light except a few colors.
Each line comes from a different isotope of hydrogen.
h: A sharp line means one exact photon energy. What does that say about the levels the electron jumps between?
w: Each line is a photon with one exact energy = the gap between two allowed levels. Discrete lines mean the electron's energy is quantized. A continuous spectrum would mean any energy is possible.
x: Every energy would give a continuous rainbow.
This is emission, not absorption.
The lines come from energy levels, not isotopes.

q: An electron has n = 4 and ml = −3. What must its angular-momentum quantum number l be?
h: m<sub>l</sub> runs from −l to +l, and l runs from 0 to n − 1.
w: |ml| ≤ l requires l ≥ 3, and l ≤ n − 1 = 3. So l = 3 (a 4f orbital). l = 4 is not allowed when n = 4, and l is never negative.
x: l can be at most n − 1 = 3.
With l = 2, m_l can only go from −2 to +2.
l is never negative: it can only be 0, 1, 2 … up to n − 1. Only ml can be negative, and its size cannot exceed l.

q: A chemist wants to label an electron sitting in a 4d orbital. Which of these quantum-number lists (n, l, ml, ms) could she use?
h: d means l = 2; the shell number is n. Then check that m<sub>l</sub> fits.
w: 4d → n = 4, l = 2, and ml can be −2…+2: 4, 2, −1, +½. l = 3 is an f orbital; n = 3 is 3d; ml = +3 is impossible for l = 2.
x: l = 3 is an f orbital, not d.
n = 3 would be a 3d orbital.
m_l = +3 is impossible when l = 2.

q: Counting all of its subshells, the third shell (n = 3) can hold at most how many electrons?
h: Count the orbitals in the shell (n²), then put two electrons in each.
w: n = 3 has 3s, 3p and 3d: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 orbitals = n2, holding 2n2 = 18 electrons. 9 is the number of orbitals; 8 is the octet idea, not the shell capacity.
x: 8 is the octet idea, not the shell's capacity.
9 is the number of orbitals. Each holds 2 electrons.
32 is the capacity of n = 4.

q: Quantum numbers n = 4 and l = 1 together label one subshell. At most, how many electrons can it hold?
h: n and l together name one subshell. How many orbitals does that subshell have?
w: n = 4, l = 1 is the 4p subshell: 3 orbitals (ml = −1, 0, +1) × 2 electrons = 6. 3 counts orbitals only.
x: 3 is the number of orbitals. Each holds 2 electrons.
2 is the capacity of one orbital.
8 is the octet idea, not a p subshell's capacity.

q: An element's atoms have their electrons arranged as [Ar]4s<sup>1</sup>3d<sup>10</sup> in the lowest-energy state. Identify the element.
h: Count electrons: 18 + 1 + 10. Watch for elements that move a 4s electron into 3d.
w: 18 + 1 + 10 = 29 electrons → Cu. A full 3d10 is extra stable, so Cu is [Ar]4s13d10 rather than 4s23d9. Zn (30 e⁻) is [Ar]4s23d10.
x: Zn has 30 electrons ([Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰).
Ni has 28 electrons, but [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰ has 18 + 1 + 10 = 29. Add up the electrons in the configuration and match the total to the atomic number.
Ga has 31 electrons, with a 4p electron beyond the full 3d. This configuration has 18 + 1 + 10 = 29 electrons, so match that total to the atomic number.

q: Many enzymes need Mn<sup>2+</sup> ions (Mn, Z = 25). In its ground state, how are this ion's electrons arranged?
h: Write neutral Mn first. Transition metals lose their 4s electrons before 3d.
w: Mn = [Ar]4s23d5. Removing the two 4s electrons gives [Ar]3d5. [Ar]4s23d3 removes from 3d (last in, first out is wrong here); [Ar]4s23d5 is neutral Mn.
x: This removes electrons from 3d. The 4s electrons leave first.
This removes electrons from the wrong subshells.
[Ar] 4s² 3d⁵ is neutral Mn.

q: Exactly one of these atoms or ions is described by [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup> in its lowest-energy state. Which one?
h: Count total electrons (24), and remember that metal cations have empty 4s orbitals.
w: [Ar]3d6 = 24 electrons. Co (27) − 3 = 24, with both 4s electrons removed first: Co3+. Neutral Fe also has 3d6 but keeps 4s2 (26 e⁻). Co2+ is 3d7; Ni2+ is 3d8.
x: Neutral Fe has 3d⁶ but keeps its 4s².
Co²⁺ has 27 − 2 = 25 electrons, so it is [Ar]3d⁷, one d electron too many. Both 4s electrons leave first, and then more must come off to reach 3d⁶.
Ni²⁺ has 28 − 2 = 26 electrons, so it is [Ar]3d⁸ after losing its 4s electrons. That is two d electrons more than 3d⁶.

q: Selenium (Z = 34), an essential trace element, sits in group 16. Which configuration is correct for a neutral Se atom?
h: Count across period 4: 4s, then the 3d block, then 4p. Electrons must total 34.
w: Se: 18 (Ar) + 2 (4s) + 10 (3d) + 4 (4p) = 34 → [Ar]4s23d104p4. Skipping 3d counts only 24 electrons; 4p6 describes Se2− (36 e⁻).
x: This skips 3d and counts only 24 electrons.
4p⁶ is Se²⁻ (36 electrons).
3d holds 10, not 8, before 4p fills.

q: Of the four species listed, which has the greatest number of unpaired electrons in its lowest-energy state?
h: Write each configuration (remember the Cr exception and that cations lose 4s first), then fill orbitals by Hund's rule.
w: Cr = 4s13d5: 6 unpaired. Mn2+ = 3d5: 5; Fe = 4s23d6: 4; V = 4s23d3: 3. Mn2+ is tempting because half-filled d looks like the maximum, but Cr's lone 4s electron adds one more.
x: Mn²⁺ has 5 unpaired. Another choice has one more.
Fe (4s²3d⁶) has 4 unpaired electrons: five d electrons fill each orbital singly, then the sixth pairs up. Another species here has more singly filled orbitals.
V (4s²3d³) has only 3 unpaired electrons, one in each of three d orbitals, with the 4s pair filled. Other species here have more singly occupied orbitals.

q: Which atom would be weakly repelled by a magnet because all of its electrons are paired?
h: Diamagnetic means every electron is paired. Look at the last subshell being filled.
w: Mg = [Ne]3s2: all paired, so diamagnetic. Na (3s1) and Al (3p1) have one unpaired electron; O (2p4) has two, so all three are paramagnetic.
x: Na has one unpaired electron.
Al has one unpaired electron.
O has two unpaired electrons.

q: Nickel(II) ions (Ni, Z = 28) give many solutions a green color. Which description of a ground-state Ni<sup>2+</sup> ion is correct?
h: Remove the 4s electrons first. Then spread the 3d electrons over five orbitals by Hund's rule and look for unpaired ones.
w: Ni = [Ar]4s23d8; the two 4s electrons leave first, giving [Ar]3d8. Eight electrons in five d orbitals leave 2 unpaired, so the ion is paramagnetic. 4s23d6 wrongly removes 3d electrons; '3d8, diamagnetic' ignores Hund's rule.
x: Eight d electrons in five orbitals leave 2 unpaired (Hund's rule).
This removes 3d electrons. The 4s electrons leave first.
This removes the wrong electrons and ignores Hund's rule.

q: Count the nodes of a 3d orbital. How many are radial and how many are angular?
h: Angular nodes = l. Radial nodes = n − l − 1.
w: For 3d, n = 3 and l = 2: angular = l = 2 and radial = 3 − 2 − 1 = 0 → 0 radial, 2 angular (total n − 1 = 2). '2 radial, 0 angular' swaps the two kinds.
x: A 3d orbital has 0 radial nodes (3 − 2 − 1).
This swaps the radial and angular counts.
3 angular nodes would be an f orbital.

q: Which orbital has exactly two radial nodes and two angular nodes?
h: Angular nodes fix l. Then use radial nodes = n − l − 1 to find n.
w: Two angular nodes → l = 2 (a d orbital). n − 2 − 1 = 2 → n = 5: 5d. 4d has one radial node and 6d has three; 4p has two radial nodes but only one angular node.
x: 4d has only 1 radial node.
4p has only 1 angular node.
6d has 3 radial nodes, one too many: radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 6 − 2 − 1. It does have two angular nodes, but the n value is too high.

q: In a hydrogen atom the 2s and 2p orbitals have the same energy, but in a lithium atom 2s is lower than 2p. What is the best explanation?
c: 2s penetrates closer to the nucleus and is shielded less.
The 2s orbital is larger than the 2p orbital in lithium.
The 2p subshell can hold more electrons than the 2s.
The 2s orbital has more angular nodes than the 2p.
h: With more than one electron, think shielding: which orbital lets its electron spend time inside the 1s core?
w: In many-electron atoms the 2s electron penetrates the 1s core more than 2p, feels a larger Zeff, and is lower in energy. 2s has zero angular nodes and 2p has one, so the choice about angular nodes is backwards.
x: Orbital size isn't the reason. It's how close 2s gets to the nucleus.
How many electrons a subshell holds doesn't set its energy.
This is backward. 2s has 0 angular nodes and 2p has 1.

q: Zinc metal has a threshold frequency of 1.04×10<sup>15</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> for the photoelectric effect. Which light will eject electrons from a zinc plate?
h: Find the threshold wavelength with λ = c/ν. Only photons with MORE energy (shorter λ) than that eject electrons.
w: λ0 = c/ν0 = (2.998×108 m s−1)/(1.04×1015 s−1) = 288 nm. Only light shorter than 288 nm works: 254 nm. The longer wavelengths have photons with too little energy, no matter how bright.
x: 312 nm is longer than the threshold wavelength, so its photons carry too little energy. Find the threshold wavelength from c ÷ ν.
365 nm is longer than the threshold wavelength, so its photons carry too little energy. Find the threshold wavelength from c ÷ ν.
405 nm is longer than the threshold wavelength, so its photons carry too little energy. Find the threshold wavelength from c ÷ ν.

q: The threshold wavelength for a metal is 620. nm. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an electron ejected when 350. nm light strikes the metal?
h: KE<sub>max</sub> = E<sub>photon</sub> − work function. Get each from E = hc/λ.
w: Ephoton = hc/350 nm = 5.68×10−19 J; work function = hc/620 nm = 3.20×10−19 J. KE = 2.47×10−19 J. 5.68×10−19 J ignores the energy needed to free the electron.
x: This ignores the energy needed to free the electron.
This is the work function, not the kinetic energy.
This adds the work function. Subtract it.

q: A lamp whose light is above a metal's threshold frequency is knocking electrons out of the metal. The lamp is made twice as bright, same color. What changes?
c: More electrons are ejected; their maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.
The same number of electrons are ejected, each with twice the kinetic energy.
More electrons are ejected, each with greater kinetic energy.
Fewer electrons are ejected because the photons share the energy.
h: Brighter light = more photons, not more energetic photons. One photon ejects one electron.
w: Doubling intensity doubles the NUMBER of photons, so more electrons come off. Each photon still has E = hν, so KEmax = hν − Φ is unchanged. Only a higher frequency raises KE.
x: The energy of each photon doesn't change, so the kinetic energy doesn't double.
Brighter light doesn't raise each photon's energy.
More photons free more electrons, not fewer.

q: Which list puts the atoms F, O, S, and Se from smallest to largest?
h: Radius increases down a group (more shells) and decreases left to right across a period (higher Z<sub>eff</sub>).
w: F is right of O in period 2 (smaller); S and Se add shells down group 16. So F < O < S < Se. The reverse order lists largest first.
x: This is reversed. It lists largest first.
F is to the right of O, so F is smaller.
Se is below S, so Se is larger.

q: Isoelectronic species have identical electron counts. Which ion does NOT belong in a series with neon?
h: Isoelectronic = same number of electrons. Neon has 10.
w: F− (9 + 1), Na+ (11 − 1) and Mg2+ (12 − 2) all have 10 electrons. Cl− has 17 + 1 = 18, like argon.
x: F⁻ has 10 electrons, like neon. Look for the one that doesn't.
Na⁺ has 10 electrons, like neon. Look for the one that doesn't.
Mg²⁺ has 10 electrons, like neon. Look for the one that doesn't.

q: Why is a Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion much smaller than a Mg atom?
c: Mg<sup>2+</sup> has lost its entire n = 3 shell.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> has more protons than Mg.
The nucleus of Mg<sup>2+</sup> has shrunk.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> has gained electrons in a lower shell.
h: Which electrons does Mg lose to form Mg²⁺, and which shell are they in?
w: Mg ([Ne]3s2) loses both 3s electrons, so Mg2+ ([Ne]) has no n = 3 shell left, and the 12 protons pull the 10 remaining electrons closer. The number of protons does not change.
x: The number of protons doesn't change when an ion forms.
The nucleus doesn't shrink.
Mg²⁺ lost electrons. It didn't gain them.

q: The first ionization energy of boron (801 kJ mol⁻¹) is LOWER than that of beryllium (900 kJ mol⁻¹). Which explanation is best?
c: B's electron comes from 2p, which is higher in energy than 2s.
Boron has a smaller nuclear charge than beryllium.
Removing an electron from boron breaks up a paired 2p orbital.
Boron is larger than beryllium because it has more electrons.
h: Compare which subshell the removed electron comes from in Be (2s²) and B (2s²2p¹).
w: B's outermost electron is in 2p, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s pair, so it is easier to remove than Be's 2s electron. B has MORE protons, and its single 2p electron is unpaired (pairing explains the N/O dip, not this one).
x: B has more protons than Be, not fewer.
B's single 2p electron is unpaired.
B is smaller than Be: across a period, added protons pull the electrons closer even as electrons are added. So size cannot explain why boron's ionization energy is lower.

q: Rank the period-2 elements Li, Be, B, and C from lowest to highest first ionization energy.
h: IE₁ generally rises across a period, but watch for the group 2 → group 13 dip.
w: IE1: Li 520, B 801, Be 900, C 1086 kJ mol⁻¹ → Li < B < Be < C. B dips below Be because its electron comes from the higher-energy 2p subshell. Li < Be < B < C ignores that dip.
x: This ignores the dip at B. Its 2p electron is easier to remove.
This is reversed: it ranks lowest to highest backwards. Ionization energy generally increases across a period (left to right) as nuclear charge grows, so Li, on the far left, is lowest.
B's IE is higher than Li's.

q: Nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine are neighbors in period 2. Which order of their first ionization energies, smallest first, is correct?
h: Draw the 2p orbital boxes for N and O. Does removing O's electron relieve anything?
w: O (2p4) has one paired 2p orbital; electron–electron repulsion makes that electron easier to remove than any of N's half-filled 2p3 electrons. So O < N < F; F has the highest Zeff.
x: N is higher than O, because O's paired 2p electron is easier to remove.
This is reversed: it ranks the elements highest to lowest. F, with the greatest nuclear charge of the three, holds its electrons most tightly and has the highest ionization energy.
F has the highest IE of the three.

q: The table gives the first five ionization energies of a period-3 element X. What is the most likely formula of the oxide of X?
h: Find the huge jump: electrons before it are valence electrons. That count gives the ion charge.
w: IE4 is about 4 times IE3, so X has 3 valence electrons (it is Al) and forms X3+. With O2−, charges balance as X2O3. XO would fit a jump after IE2; X3O2 swaps the subscripts.
x: XO would fit a big jump after IE₂.
This swaps the subscripts.
XO₂ would need X to be 4+.

q: For one of these elements, removing a third electron is far harder than removing the second. For which is IE<sub>3</sub> ÷ IE<sub>2</sub> greatest?
h: A very large jump happens once all valence electrons are gone and a core electron must be removed.
w: Ca has 2 valence electrons; its third electron comes from the [Ar] core, so IE3 ≫ IE2. For K the big jump is IE2/IE1; Ga and Sc have 3 valence electrons, so their jump is after IE3.
x: K's big jump is between IE₁ and IE₂.
Ga has 3 valence electrons, so its jump comes after IE₃.
Sc has 3 valence electrons, so its jump comes after IE₃.

q: Which equation represents the first electron affinity of chlorine?
h: Electron affinity: a single gaseous atom gains one electron.
w: Electron affinity is the energy change for Cl(g) + e− → Cl−(g). Cl(g) → Cl+ + e− is ionization; starting from Cl2 would include breaking the Cl–Cl bond.
x: This is ionization (losing an electron).
Starting from Cl₂ also includes breaking the Cl–Cl bond.
This loses an electron. Electron affinity is about gaining one.

q: One of these elements has a positive (endothermic) electron affinity, meaning its gaseous anion is unstable. Which one?
h: Where would an added electron go? A filled subshell forces it into a higher-energy subshell.
w: Mg is [Ne]3s2; an extra electron must enter the higher-energy 3p subshell, so Mg− is not stable (EA > 0). Na adds to its half-filled 3s, and Si and S add to 3p, all releasing energy.
x: Na adds an electron to its half-filled 3s and releases energy.
Si adds to 3p and releases energy.
S adds to 3p and releases energy.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes electronegativity from electron affinity?
c: Electronegativity describes an atom pulling shared electrons in a bond; electron affinity is the energy change when an isolated gas atom gains an electron.
Electronegativity is measured in kJ mol⁻¹; electron affinity is a unitless number.
Electronegativity describes an isolated gas atom gaining an electron; electron affinity describes an atom pulling shared electrons in a bond.
Electronegativity and electron affinity are two names for the same measured energy.
h: One is a measured energy for a lone atom; the other is a relative scale for atoms in bonds.
w: Electronegativity (Pauling scale, unitless) compares how strongly a bonded atom attracts shared electrons; electron affinity is a measured energy (kJ mol⁻¹) for X(g) + e− → X−(g). One wrong choice swaps the units; another swaps the definitions.
x: This swaps the units. Electronegativity is unitless.
This swaps the two definitions.
They are two different ideas.

q: Across period 3 from Na to Cl, atomic radius decreases. What is the main reason?
c: Effective nuclear charge rises while the shell stays the same.
Each element adds one more electron shell than the last.
Added electrons repel each other and push the shell outward.
Atoms on the right gain electrons to form anions.
h: Electrons go into the same n = 3 shell, but the number of protons keeps growing.
w: Each step adds a proton, while the new electron goes into the same shell and shields poorly. Zeff rises, pulling the n = 3 electrons closer. Shells are added going DOWN a group, not across.
x: Shells are added going down a group, not across.
Effective nuclear charge wins out, pulling the electrons closer.
These are neutral atoms, not anions.

q: Sodium fluoride and magnesium chloride contain four different ions. Which ranking of those ions' radii, smallest first, is correct?
h: Mg²⁺, Na⁺ and F⁻ are isoelectronic: more protons → smaller. Cl⁻ has an extra shell.
w: Mg2+, Na+ and F− all have 10 electrons; 12, 11 and 9 protons make them shrink in that order. Cl− has electrons in n = 3, so it is largest: Mg2+ < Na+ < F− < Cl−.
x: Mg²⁺ has more protons than Na⁺, so it's smaller.
This is reversed: it ranks the ions from largest to smallest. Cl⁻ has electrons in a third shell, so it is biggest, and among the 10-electron ions more protons means a smaller ion.
Cl⁻ has electrons in n = 3, so it's the largest.

q: Sodium thiosulfate, Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, is used to remove excess chlorine from water. What is the AVERAGE oxidation number of sulfur in it?
h: Na is +1 and O is −2. The two S atoms share whatever charge is left; divide by 2.
w: 2(+1) + 2x + 3(−2) = 0 → 2x = +4 → x = +2. +4 comes from forgetting to divide by the two S atoms.
x: This forgets to divide by the two S atoms.
+6 is sulfur in sulfate (SO₄²⁻), which has four O atoms. Thiosulfate has two S atoms sharing the charge left over from three O atoms and two Na⁺, so set up the sum and divide by 2.
−2 is sulfur in sulfides.

q: Lithium aluminum hydride, LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, is a strong reducing agent. What are the oxidation numbers of Al and H in this compound?
h: In a hydride of a metal, H is bonded to atoms less electronegative than itself. Li is +1.
w: In metal hydrides H is −1. Then +1 + x + 4(−1) = 0 gives Al = +3. Assuming H = +1 forces Al to −5, which is not reasonable for a metal.
x: In metal hydrides, H is −1, not +1.
Check the math: +1 + x + 4(−1) = 0.
In metal hydrides, H is −1.

q: Sodium peroxide (Na<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is used to regenerate oxygen in submarines. What oxidation state does oxygen have in it?
h: Na is always +1 in compounds. Peroxides contain an O–O bond, so oxygen is not −2 here.
w: 2(+1) + 2x = 0 → x = −1. Peroxides (O2−2, as in H2O2) are the classic exception to O = −2. Using −2 would require Na = +2.
x: Peroxides are the exception to O = −2.
Oxygen is more electronegative than sodium, so it cannot have a positive oxidation number here.
This would need each Na to be +4.

q: In which compound does chlorine have an oxidation number of +5?
h: Set the sum to zero: alkali metal +1, each O −2, solve for Cl.
w: KClO3: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0 → x = +5. KClO4 gives +7, NaClO2 gives +3, and ClO2 gives +4.
x: Cl is +7 in KClO₄: K is +1 and four O give −8, so Cl must be +7 to make the total zero. Count the oxygens carefully.
Cl is +3 in NaClO₂: Na is +1 and two O give −4, so Cl must be +3 to make the total zero. Count the oxygens carefully.
Cl is +4 in ClO₂: there is no metal ion, so Cl must balance two O at −2 each by itself. Don't assume every chlorine oxide needs the same charge as a chlorate salt.

q: Chlorine gas bubbled through potassium bromide solution turns it orange-brown (equation below). Which species acts as the oxidizing agent?
h: The oxidizing agent is the reactant that GAINS electrons (is reduced).
w: Cl goes from 0 in Cl2 to −1 in KCl: Cl2 is reduced, so Cl2 is the oxidizing agent. Br− (−1 → 0) is oxidized, so it is the reducing agent. K+ is a spectator.
x: Br⁻ is oxidized, so it's the reducing agent.
K⁺ is a spectator: it stays +1 and appears unchanged on both sides. A species that does not change oxidation number cannot be an oxidizing or reducing agent.
Br₂ is a product, formed when Br⁻ is oxidized. The oxidizing agent is a reactant that takes electrons and is itself reduced in the reaction.

q: When copper dissolves in nitric acid (equation below), a colorless gas forms. Which description of the electron transfer is correct?
h: Assign oxidation numbers to Cu and to N in HNO₃ and NO. Reduction = oxidation number decreases.
w: N: +5 in HNO3 → +2 in NO, a decrease, so N is reduced. Cu goes 0 → +2 (oxidized, not reduced). No H2 forms, so H stays +1.
x: Cu goes from 0 to +2, which is oxidation, not reduction.
A decrease in oxidation number is reduction, not oxidation.
No H₂ forms, so H stays +1.

q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes as shown. Which statement describes the oxygen atoms?
c: Some O atoms are oxidized and others are reduced.
All O atoms are reduced, from −1 to −2.
All O atoms are oxidized, from −2 to 0.
h: Oxygen in H₂O₂ is a peroxide. Compare it with oxygen in H₂O and in O₂.
w: O is −1 in H2O2. It becomes −2 in H2O (reduced) and 0 in O2 (oxidized): the same element is both oxidized and reduced (disproportionation). Taking O as −2 in H2O2 hides the change.
x: Some O atoms go from −1 to 0 (oxidized).
O is −1 in H₂O₂, not −2, because the two O atoms are bonded to each other. Starting from −1, check where O ends up in each product: H₂O and O₂ give different results.
O changes from −1 to both −2 and 0.

q: Use the activity series in the table. A jeweler wants a metal that will recover silver from AgNO<sub>3</sub> solution but will NOT dissolve in hydrochloric acid. Which metal works?
h: A metal reduces the ions of anything BELOW it in the series. Check each metal against both Ag⁺ and H⁺.
w: Cu is above Ag, so Cu + 2 Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2 Ag, but below H2, so it does not react with H+: Cu. Zn, Fe and Ni also recover silver, but they sit above H2 and dissolve in HCl.

head: Activity series (most active first)
rows: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Ni > Pb > H<sub>2</sub> > Cu > Ag

x: Zn is above H₂, so it dissolves in HCl.
Fe is above H₂, so it dissolves in HCl.
Ni is above H₂, so it dissolves in HCl.

q: Strips of three metals, X, Y and Z, are put in solutions of each other's nitrates, with the results in the table. What is the order of activity (most active first)?
h: A metal that becomes coated with another metal is more active than that metal.
w: X displaces Y, Z displaces Y, but Z cannot displace X. So X > Z and Z > Y: X > Z > Y. Z > X > Y misreads 'no reaction' as Z being the more active metal.
x: No reaction means Z is less active than X.
Y is displaced by both, so it's the least active.
This is reversed: it ranks the metal that displaces the others as least active. A metal that pushes another metal's ion out of solution is the more active one.

q: A chemist needs a salt that will NOT dissolve appreciably in water. Which one should she choose?
h: Nitrates and ammonium or alkali-metal salts are always soluble. Sulfates are soluble with a few exceptions.
w: Sulfates are soluble except with Pb2+, Ba2+, Ca2+ (slightly), Sr2+ and Hg2+2, so PbSO4 is insoluble. Phosphates and sulfides are insoluble EXCEPT with NH+4 or alkali metals.
x: NH₄⁺ compounds are always soluble.
Nitrates are always soluble.
K⁺ compounds are always soluble.

q: Iron(III) nitrate and sodium hydroxide solutions are combined. Which solid settles out?
h: Swap partners, use the ion charges to write formulas, then check the solubility rules.
w: Fe3+ + 3 OH− → Fe(OH)3(s), a rust-brown solid; most hydroxides are insoluble. NaNO3 stays dissolved (nitrates and Na+ salts are soluble). Fe(OH)2 uses the wrong iron charge.
x: NaNO₃ is soluble: all nitrates and all Na⁺ salts dissolve, so Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay in solution as spectators. Look for the ion pair that forms an insoluble compound.
Fe(OH)₂ uses the wrong iron charge. Iron(III) is Fe³⁺.
Fe(OH)₃ is insoluble, so a solid does form.

q: A student mixes the two solutions in each pair. In which case does the mixture stay clear, with no solid forming?
h: Write the two new combinations for each pair and check them against the solubility rules.
w: NH4Br + Ca(NO3)2 could only give NH4NO3 and CaBr2, both soluble: no precipitate. The others form CuS, Hg2Cl2 and Mg(OH)2, all insoluble.
x: CuS is insoluble, so a solid forms.
Hg₂Cl₂ is insoluble, so a solid forms.
Mg(OH)₂ is insoluble, so a solid forms.

q: Baking soda (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) is added to vinegar (acetic acid) and the mixture fizzes. Which gas is produced?
h: Carbonates and hydrogen carbonates react with acids to form H₂CO₃, which falls apart.
w: HCO−3 + H+ → H2CO3 → H2O + CO2(g). H2 forms when an ACTIVE METAL reacts with acid, not a carbonate.
x: H₂ forms when an active metal reacts with acid, not a carbonate.
A carbonate and an acid do not make O₂. The bubbles come from H₂CO₃ breaking apart.
Carbonate + acid gives CO₂, not CO.

q: Solid iron(II) sulfide is dropped into hydrochloric acid, and a gas with a rotten-egg odor forms. What is the gas?
h: In a gas-evolution reaction the acid's H⁺ combines with the anion of the salt.
w: FeS + 2 HCl → FeCl2 + H2S(g): H+ plus sulfide gives hydrogen sulfide. SO2 comes from a SULFITE (SO2−3) with acid, and no element changes oxidation number here, so H2 does not form.
x: SO₂ comes from a sulfite with acid, not a sulfide.
H₂ would need a redox change, which doesn't happen here.
Cl⁻ stays dissolved as a spectator ion. Making Cl₂ would need an oxidizing agent, and none is present.

q: A student warms solid ammonium sulfate with sodium hydroxide solution. A gas forms that turns moist red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
h: OH⁻ takes an H⁺ from the ammonium ion. A gas that turns red litmus blue is basic.
w: NH+4 + OH− → NH3(g) + H2O. Ammonia is a basic gas, so it turns red litmus blue. SO2 is acidic; H2 and N2 do not affect litmus.
x: H₂ doesn't affect litmus.
SO₂ is acidic, so it wouldn't turn litmus blue.
N₂ doesn't affect litmus.

q: Aqueous potassium sulfite and hydrochloric acid are mixed as shown. What are the products?
c: No reaction; all ions stay in solution.
h: Sulfite plus acid gives H₂SO₃, which is unstable, like H₂CO₃. Then check KCl with the solubility rules.
w: 2 H+ + SO2−3 → H2SO3 → SO2(g) + H2O(l), and KCl stays dissolved. KCl(s) is wrong because potassium salts are soluble; SO3 + H2 would require a redox change that does not occur.
x: SO₃ + H₂ would need a redox change, which doesn't happen.
KCl is soluble, so it stays (aq).
A gas (SO₂) does form: H⁺ from the acid combines with sulfite to make H₂SO₃, which breaks down into SO₂ gas and water. Forming a gas removes ions, so a reaction occurs.

q: Calcium hydroxide completely neutralizes phosphoric acid (skeleton equation below). After balancing with the lowest whole numbers, how many H<sub>2</sub>O appear?
h: Products are the salt Ca₃(PO₄)₂ and water. Each H⁺ from the acid meets one OH⁻ to make one H₂O.
w: 2 H3PO4 + 3 Ca(OH)2 → Ca3(PO4)2 + 6 H2O. Six H+ (2 × 3) neutralize six OH− (3 × 2). 3 counts the H in one acid molecule only.
x: 3 counts the H in one acid molecule only.
2 is the coefficient of H₃PO₄.
Balance it fully. Count the H⁺ supplied by all the acid molecules and match each with one OH⁻.

q: Heating potassium chlorate releases oxygen (below). What type of reaction is this?
h: Count reactants and products: what happens to one compound when heated?
w: One reactant breaks into two simpler substances: decomposition (it is also a redox reaction: Cl +5 → −1, O −2 → 0). Combination is the reverse, two or more substances forming one.
x: Combination is the reverse: two substances forming one.
Single displacement needs an element and a compound.
Double displacement swaps partners between two compounds.

q: Each reaction below is paired with a reaction type. Which pairing is right?
c: Zn(s) + CuSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) → ZnSO<sub>4</sub>(aq) + Cu(s): single displacement
h: Single displacement: element + compound. Combination: several → one. Decomposition: one → several.
w: Zn replaces Cu in its compound: single displacement. The HCl/NaOH reaction is neutralization (double displacement); CaO + CO2 is combination; Mg + O2 is combination (and combustion).
x: This is neutralization (a double displacement), not combination.
CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃ is combination.
Mg + O₂ → MgO is combination.

q: Isopropanol (rubbing alcohol) burns completely, as in the skeleton equation. What coefficient does O<sub>2</sub> get with the smallest whole numbers?
h: Balance C, then H, then O last. Don't forget the oxygen atom already in the alcohol.
w: 2 C3H7OH + 9 O2 → 6 CO2 + 8 H2O. Right side has 12 + 8 = 20 O; the alcohol supplies 2, so O2 supplies 18 atoms = 9 molecules. Ignoring the alcohol's O gives 10. 20 counts every O atom on the right without subtracting the alcohol's O or dividing by 2.
x: This ignores the alcohol's own oxygen.
18 is the number of O atoms. Each O₂ carries 2.
This counts all the O on the right without subtracting the alcohol's O.

q: Aluminum metal reacts with sulfuric acid and releases hydrogen gas (skeleton equation below). In the smallest whole-number balanced equation, what number goes in front of H<sub>2</sub>?
h: Balance Al and the sulfate groups first (treat SO₄ as one unit), then balance hydrogen.
w: 2 Al + 3 H2SO4 → Al2(SO4)3 + 3 H2. Three sulfates need 3 H2SO4, which bring 6 H atoms = 3 H2 molecules. 6 counts H atoms instead of H2 molecules.
x: 6 counts H atoms. Count H₂ molecules.
2 is the coefficient of Al.
With 1 H₂, the hydrogens don't balance.

q: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) solution fizzes when excess hydrochloric acid is added. Which net ionic equation describes the change?
h: Write soluble strong electrolytes as ions, then cancel ions that appear unchanged on both sides.
w: Na2CO3 and HCl are fully ionized; Na+ and Cl− are spectators (NaCl is soluble). Net: CO2−3 + 2 H+ → CO2 + H2O. Writing HCl as a molecule ignores that it is a strong acid.
x: Na⁺ is a spectator. Na₂CO₃ should be written as ions and the Na⁺ canceled.
NaCl is soluble, so no solid forms.
HCl is a strong acid. Write it as ions.

q: Which ions are spectator ions in the reaction shown?
h: Spectators are dissolved ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Which ions end up in the solid?
w: Ca2+ and PO3−4 form the solid Ca3(PO4)2. Na+ and Cl− start dissolved and stay dissolved as NaCl(aq), so they are spectators.
x: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ form the solid, so they react.
Ca²⁺ is part of the solid.
PO₄³⁻ is part of the solid.

q: Aqueous ammonia is used to neutralize a hydrochloric acid spill. Which net ionic equation is correct?
h: NH₃ is a weak base: keep it as molecules. HCl is a strong acid: write it as ions. Then cancel spectators.
w: HCl ionizes completely and Cl− is a spectator; NH3 (mostly un-ionized) takes the H+: NH3 + H+ → NH+4. H+ + OH− treats ammonia as a source of free OH−; NH4Cl is soluble; the equation that shows HCl(aq) leaves HCl un-ionized.
x: Aqueous ammonia isn't a source of free OH⁻ here.
NH₄Cl is soluble (ammonium salts always dissolve), so no solid forms. NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ stay dissolved, and Cl⁻ is a spectator that does not belong in a net ionic equation.
HCl ionizes completely. Write it as H⁺.

q: A magnesium ribbon dissolves in hydrochloric acid, releasing bubbles. Choose the net ionic equation.
h: Mg is a solid element (keep it whole). HCl is a strong acid (write as ions). Cancel spectators.
w: Mg is oxidized to Mg2+ and H+ is reduced to H2; Cl− is a spectator: Mg(s) + 2 H+ → Mg2+ + H2. MgCl2 is soluble, so no solid forms.
x: MgCl₂ is soluble, so no solid forms. The H⁺ is what reacts.
This is reversed. Mg metal is oxidized, not formed.
HCl ionizes completely. Write it as H⁺ and cancel the Cl⁻.

q: A blue solid forms when copper(II) nitrate solution is poured into sodium hydroxide solution. Which equation is the net ionic equation?
h: Identify the insoluble product from the solubility rules, then keep only the ions that form it.
w: Copper(II) hydroxide is insoluble; Na+ and NO−3 are spectators: Cu2+ + 2 OH− → Cu(OH)2(s). CuOH ignores the 2+ charge; Cu(NO3)2(aq) should be written as ions.
x: Cu²⁺ needs two OH⁻, not one.
NaNO₃ is soluble, so Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.
Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) should be written as ions, and the nitrate canceled.

q: A flask of helium and a flask of sulfur dioxide are both at 300 K. Which statement compares their particles correctly?
c: Same average kinetic energy; He atoms move faster on average.
Same average speed; SO<sub>2</sub> molecules have more kinetic energy.
He atoms have more kinetic energy and a higher average speed.
SO<sub>2</sub> molecules have more kinetic energy because they are heavier.
h: Average kinetic energy depends only on the Kelvin temperature. With KE = ½mu², how must a lighter particle compare?
w: At the same T every gas has the same average kinetic energy. Since KE = ½mu², the lighter He (4.003 vs 64.07 g mol⁻¹) must move faster: urms ∝ 1/√M, about 4 times faster. Heavier molecules move slower; they do not carry more energy.
x: Their speeds differ. Lighter He moves faster.
At the same temperature, kinetic energy is the same.
Heavier molecules move slower. They don't carry more energy.

q: Under identical conditions, how many times faster does methane (CH<sub>4</sub>, 16.04 g mol⁻¹) effuse than sulfur dioxide (SO<sub>2</sub>, 64.07 g mol⁻¹)?
h: Graham's law: rate₁/rate₂ = √(M₂/M₁). The lighter gas is faster.
w: rate(CH4)/rate(SO2) = √(64.07/16.04) = √3.99 = 2.00. Forgetting the square root gives 3.99; inverting the ratio gives 0.500, which would make the lighter gas slower.
x: This flips the ratio. The lighter gas effuses faster.
This forgets the square root.
This flips the ratio and forgets the square root.

q: A certain volume of N<sub>2</sub> (28.02 g mol⁻¹) effuses through a pinhole in 42.0 s. Under the same conditions, how long does it take the same volume of Cl<sub>2</sub> (70.90 g mol⁻¹) to effuse?
h: Time is inversely proportional to rate, so t ∝ √M. A heavier gas takes longer.
w: t(Cl2) = 42.0 s × √(70.90/28.02) = 42.0 × 1.591 = 66.8 s. 26.4 s treats time like rate (heavier gas would finish first); 106 s forgets the square root.
x: This treats time like rate. The heavier gas takes longer.
This forgets the square root.
This flips the ratio and forgets the square root.

q: The Kelvin temperature of a gas sample is doubled. By what factor does the root-mean-square speed of its molecules change?
c: It increases by a factor of √2.
It increases by a factor of 4.
h: Average kinetic energy ∝ T, and KE = ½mu². How does u depend on T?
w: urms = √(3RT/M) ∝ √T, so doubling T multiplies u by √2 ≈ 1.41. It is the average KINETIC ENERGY that doubles.
x: It's the average kinetic energy that doubles, not the speed.
Speed goes as √T. It doesn't quadruple.
Raising T does change the speed.

q: Which sample has the SAME distribution of molecular speeds as argon (39.95 g mol⁻¹) at 400 K?
h: The Maxwell–Boltzmann speed curve depends only on the ratio T/M.
w: Speeds depend on T/M (u ∝ √(T/M)). Same curve needs T/M equal: T = 400 K × 20.18/39.95 = 202 K for neon. Neon at 400 K is faster (lighter); 792 K comes from inverting the mass ratio.
x: This flips the mass ratio.
Neon is lighter, so at the same T it moves faster.
Krypton is heavier, so it moves slower.

q: Nitrogen in a gas cylinder is compressed to several hundred atmospheres, where PV/nRT is greater than 1. Which factor causes this?
c: The molecules' own volume is a significant part of the space.
Attractions between molecules pull them closer together.
Molecules move much faster at very high pressure.
Collisions between molecules stop being elastic.
h: Ideal gases assume point particles with no attractions. Which assumption fails when the molecules are squeezed close?
w: When the gas is highly compressed, the molecules' own volume takes up a real fraction of the space, so the actual V is larger than ideal and PV/nRT > 1. Attractions push PV/nRT BELOW 1 (they matter most at moderate pressure and low T).
x: Attractions push PV/nRT below 1, not above.
Speed depends on temperature, not pressure.
Ideal and real collisions are both treated as elastic. That isn't the reason.

q: Which gas has the largest van der Waals constant a (the correction for attractions between molecules)?
h: Stronger intermolecular forces mean a larger a. Think polarity and number of electrons.
w: SO2 is polar (dipole–dipole forces) and has the most electrons (greatest dispersion), so its attractions and a are largest. Ne and H2 have very weak dispersion forces only.
x: Ne has only weak dispersion forces.
H₂ has only 2 electrons, so its dispersion forces are very weak and its a value is small.
CH₄ is nonpolar with few electrons.

q: Which statement is NOT part of the kinetic molecular theory of an ideal gas?
c: Gas particles attract each other when they come close together.
Gas particles are in constant, random, straight-line motion.
Collisions between gas particles are elastic.
The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the Kelvin temperature.
h: The ideal model assumes tiny particles that do not interact except by collision.
w: The ideal model assumes no attractions or repulsions between particles; attractions are what make real gases deviate. The other three statements are postulates of the theory.
x: This is part of the kinetic molecular theory. Look for the one the ideal model leaves out.
This is part of the kinetic molecular theory. Look for the one the ideal model leaves out.
This is part of the kinetic molecular theory. Look for the one the ideal model leaves out.

q: A burn from 100 °C steam is usually much worse than a burn from the same mass of 100 °C liquid water. Why?
c: Condensing steam releases extra heat into the skin.
Steam has a higher specific heat than liquid water.
Steam is hotter than liquid water at 100 °C.
Condensing steam absorbs heat from the skin.
h: Both start at the same temperature. What extra process happens when steam touches skin?
w: Steam first condenses, releasing about 2.26 kJ per gram (ΔHvap) into the skin, then cools like the water does. Same temperature means same 'hotness'; condensation RELEASES heat, it does not absorb it.
x: Specific heat isn't the reason. Steam also condenses.
At 100 °C, steam and water are equally hot.
Condensing releases heat. It doesn't absorb it.

q: A cold soda can 'sweats' as water vapor from the air condenses on it. For the water, which is true?
c: q = 0, because the temperature stays constant.
h: Condensation forms attractions between molecules. Does the water gain or lose energy?
w: Condensing water releases heat to the can, so heat leaves the system: q < 0, exothermic. A phase change at constant temperature still transfers heat; it goes into or out of intermolecular attractions.
x: Condensing releases heat, so q is negative.
A negative q means exothermic, not endothermic.
A phase change still transfers heat, even at constant temperature.

q: Of these phase changes, which one requires heat to be absorbed?
h: Endothermic phase changes separate particles: solid → liquid → gas.
w: Sublimation (solid → gas) breaks intermolecular attractions, so it absorbs heat. Freezing, condensation and deposition all bring particles together and release heat.
x: Freezing releases heat: as liquid becomes solid, molecules come closer and form attractions, giving off energy. A change that absorbs heat must pull particles apart instead.
Condensation releases heat.
Deposition releases heat.

q: For which combination of heat (q) and work (w) is ΔE of the system ALWAYS negative?
c: Heat released and work done BY the system
Heat absorbed and work done ON the system
Heat released and work done ON the system
Heat absorbed and work done BY the system
h: ΔE = q + w. Signs are from the system's point of view: energy leaving is negative.
w: Heat released → q < 0; work done BY the system → w < 0. Both negative, so ΔE = q + w is always negative. The mixed-sign cases depend on the sizes of q and w.
x: Both of these are positive, so ΔE is always positive.
The signs are mixed, so it depends on which is bigger.
The signs are mixed, so it depends on which is bigger.

q: The heating curve shows 1 mol of water heated at a steady rate from −20 °C to 120 °C. About how much heat does it take to boil the water at 100 °C?
h: Boiling happens on the flat segment at 100 °C. Read the heat added where that segment starts and where it ends.
w: The 100 °C plateau runs from about 14 kJ to about 55 kJ: 55 − 14 ≈ 41 kJ (ΔHvap = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹). 55 kJ is the total heat added by the end of boiling, 14 kJ is where boiling starts, and about 6 kJ is the melting plateau.
x: 55 kJ is the total heat added by the end of boiling.
14 kJ is where boiling starts. Measure the plateau width.
About 6 kJ is the melting plateau.

q: A gas is taken from the same initial state to the same final state by two different paths. Which quantity must have the same value for both paths?
c: ΔE, the change in internal energy
q, the heat absorbed by the gas
w, the work done on the gas
the temperature change of the surroundings
h: A state function depends only on the starting and ending states, not on how the change happens.
w: ΔE is a state function: it depends only on the initial and final states. q and w depend on the path; different paths split the same ΔE = q + w differently. How much the surroundings warm depends on q, so it is path-dependent too.
x: Heat (q) depends on the path.
Work (w) depends on the path.
The surroundings' temperature change depends on q, which depends on the path.

q: A nitrogen atom's seven electrons have been placed in orbital boxes in four different ways (I–IV). Which arrangement is nitrogen's ground state?
h: Ground state = lowest energy AND obeys every rule: fill 2s before 2p, one electron per 2p box before pairing, opposite spins when paired.
w: Diagram I fills 1s and 2s, then puts one electron with parallel spin in each 2p orbital (Hund's rule). IV is a legal but excited state (a 2s electron was promoted to 2p); II pairs electrons in 2p while a 2p box is empty (Hund violation); III has two same-spin electrons in 2s (Pauli violation).
x: IV has a promoted 2s electron, so it's an excited state.
II pairs electrons in 2p while a box is empty (breaks Hund's rule).
III has two same-spin electrons in one box (breaks Pauli).

q: Arrangements I–IV each hold the eight electrons of an oxygen atom. Which arrangement is forbidden by the Pauli exclusion principle?
h: Pauli: no two electrons in the same orbital can have the same spin. Look for a box with two arrows pointing the same way.
w: Diagram III puts two electrons with the same spin in the single 2s orbital, so they would have identical quantum numbers (n, l, ml, ms) — forbidden. II breaks Hund's rule (pairing in 2p while one 2p box is empty), which is a higher-energy state but not impossible; IV is an allowed excited state; I is the ground state.
x: II breaks Hund's rule, but it's still allowed (just higher in energy).
IV is an allowed excited state.
I is the ground state: it follows Aufbau order, Hund's rule and the Pauli principle. The forbidden arrangement puts two electrons with the same spin in one orbital.

q: Carbon has six electrons. Of arrangements I–IV, which one is an EXCITED state that nevertheless breaks neither the Pauli exclusion principle nor Hund's rule?
h: Excited = not the lowest-energy arrangement. But it must still have no same-spin pairs in one box and no needless pairing in a degenerate set.
w: Diagram I has promoted a 2s electron into 2p (higher energy than the ground state II), yet every box holds at most two opposite-spin electrons and the 2p electrons are spread out with parallel spins. III violates Hund's rule (pairing in 2p while two 2p boxes are empty) and IV violates Pauli (two same-spin electrons in 2s), so neither fits: III is an allowed but higher-energy arrangement that breaks Hund's rule, and IV cannot exist at all.
x: III pairs electrons in 2p while two boxes are empty (breaks Hund's rule).
IV has two same-spin electrons in 2s (breaks Pauli).
II is the ground state, not an excited state.

q: The diagrams show only the valence (4s and 3d) electrons of four possible arrangements for a chromium atom (Z = 24). Which diagram is the experimentally observed ground state?
h: Chromium is one of the exceptions: a half-filled d subshell is extra stable. Count six valence electrons beyond the argon core.
w: Chromium is [Ar]4s13d5: one electron in 4s and one in each 3d orbital, all parallel — diagram I. Diagram II is the 'expected' 4s23d4 that the filling order predicts but Cr does not adopt; III also pairs 3d electrons unnecessarily; IV (3d6) empties 4s, which is not the ground state of the neutral atom.
x: II is what the filling order predicts, but Cr doesn't follow it.
III pairs 3d electrons unnecessarily.
IV empties 4s, which isn't the neutral atom's ground state.

q: Iron (Z = 26) is [Ar]4s<sup>2</sup>3d<sup>6</sup>. The diagrams show four ways to arrange the six remaining valence electrons of an Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion. Which diagram is the ground state of Fe<sup>2+</sup>?
h: Transition metals lose their 4s electrons FIRST when they form cations. Then apply Hund's rule to what is left.
w: Removing two electrons from Fe takes both 4s electrons (they are the outermost), leaving [Ar]3d6: five parallel electrons plus one paired, diagram I (4 unpaired electrons). II and III wrongly remove 3d electrons and keep 4s2; IV has the right 3d6 count but pairs electrons while two 3d orbitals are empty, violating Hund's rule.
x: II keeps 4s². The 4s electrons leave first.
IV has the right count but pairs electrons while boxes are empty (breaks Hund's rule).
III keeps 4s². The 4s electrons leave first.

q: The boxes hold every electron beyond the argon core of a neutral atom in its ground state. Add up the electrons shown and identify the element.
h: Count the electrons in the boxes, add the 18 electrons of the argon core, and that total is the atomic number.
w: The diagram holds 2 + 3 = 5 electrons; 18 + 5 = 23 = vanadium, [Ar]4s23d3. Counting only the 3d electrons (3) gives scandium (Z = 21); manganese would need five 3d electrons; phosphorus has an [Ne] core and no d electrons.
x: This counts only the 3d electrons. Count the 4s too.
Mn would need five 3d electrons.
P has an [Ne] core and no d electrons.

q: Each diagram shows the 3d electrons of a different transition-metal ion in its ground state (the 4s orbital is empty in every ion). Which ion is diamagnetic?
h: Diamagnetic means every electron is paired, so the ion is weakly repelled by a magnet. Paramagnetic ions have at least one unpaired electron.
w: Only diagram I (3d10, e.g., Zn2+) has all ten electrons paired. III has 1 unpaired electron, II has 2, and IV has 5 — all paramagnetic. A common slip is choosing IV because it 'looks balanced', but five single arrows mean five unpaired electrons.
x: III has 1 unpaired electron.
II has 2 unpaired electrons.
IV has 5 unpaired electrons.

q: The visible emission spectrum of hydrogen is shown with the wavelength of each line. Which line is produced by electrons falling from n = 3 to n = 2?
h: All four lines end at n = 2. The 3 → 2 drop is the smallest energy gap, and E = hc/λ links energy to wavelength.
w: The smallest downward jump (3 → 2) releases the least energy, so it has the LONGEST wavelength: 656 nm (red). 1/λ = RH(1/2² − 1/3²) gives 656 nm. Students often pick 410 nm thinking the 'first' line is the shortest wavelength; 410 nm is actually the 6 → 2 line.
x: 410 nm is the 6 → 2 line.
486 nm is the 4 → 2 line.
434 nm is the 5 → 2 line.

q: The diagram shows energy levels n = 2 through n = 5 of a hydrogen atom (the n = 1 level, at −21.8 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J, is far below the bottom of the graph). Arrows A–D are electron transitions. Which arrow represents EMISSION of the photon with the longest wavelength?
h: Emission arrows point down. Longest wavelength = lowest photon energy = smallest gap between the two levels.
w: Arrow D (n = 5 → n = 4) drops only about 0.5 × 10−19 J, the smallest emission gap, so λ = hc/ΔE ≈ 4050 nm (infrared). Arrow A is the longest arrow, but a big energy drop means a SHORT wavelength (434 nm); B is the 656 nm red line; C points up, so it is absorption, not emission.
x: A's big energy drop gives a short wavelength.
B is the 656 nm line, shorter than D's.
C points up, so it's absorption, not emission.

q: The diagram shows the five lowest energy levels of a hypothetical one-electron atom. Arrows A–D show the electron absorbing a photon. Which transition requires light of the highest frequency?
h: E<sub>photon</sub> = hν = E<sub>upper</sub> − E<sub>lower</sub>. Compare the energy gaps, not the number of levels skipped.
w: Gaps: A = 9.0, B = 7.0, C = 13.5, D = 4.5 (×10−19 J). The largest gap, C (n = 1 → n = 3), needs the highest-frequency photon. D also climbs two levels, just like C, but spans only 4.5 units because the upper levels crowd together; A is the biggest single-step jump but still smaller than C.
x: A is a 9.0 gap. Another arrow is bigger.
D spans only 4.5 units because the upper levels crowd together.
B is a 7.0 gap. Another arrow is bigger.

q: The graph shows the maximum kinetic energy of electrons ejected from a metal surface as a function of the frequency of the light shining on it. What is the work function (binding energy) of this metal?
h: KE = hν − Φ. Electrons first appear at the threshold frequency ν<sub>0</sub>, where KE = 0, so Φ = hν<sub>0</sub>.
w: The line leaves the axis at ν0 = 10 × 1014 = 1.00 × 1015 Hz. Φ = hν0 = (6.626 × 10−34 J s)(1.00 × 1015 s−1) = 6.63 × 10−19 J. Using the frequency at the right edge (2.0 × 1015 Hz) gives 1.33 × 10−18 J, which is hν, not Φ; 6.63 × 10−34 J is just Planck's constant with the wrong unit.
x: This uses the frequency at the right edge. That's hν, not the work function.
Read the frequency where the line meets the axis.
This is just Planck's constant.

q: The graph shows photoelectron kinetic energy versus light frequency for two metals, A and B. Which statement is correct?
c: The lines are parallel because both slopes equal Planck's constant.
Metal B has the smaller work function because its line starts farther right.
Doubling the light intensity would double the kinetic energy at every frequency.
Below 5 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz, metal A still ejects electrons but with very low kinetic energy.
h: KE = hν − Φ is a straight line with slope h and x-intercept ν₀ = Φ/h. Intensity changes how MANY electrons, not their energy.
w: KEmax = hν − Φ: the slope is h for every metal, so the lines are parallel; only the intercept (Φ/h) changes. Metal B's higher threshold (8 × 1014 Hz) means a LARGER work function, not smaller. Intensity affects the number of electrons, not their KE, and below the threshold no electrons are ejected at all.
x: A higher threshold means a larger work function, not smaller.
Intensity changes the number of electrons, not their energy.
Below the threshold, no electrons are ejected at all.

q: The table lists the quantum numbers of four electrons in the same atom. Which two electrons occupy the SAME orbital?
h: An orbital is fixed by n, ℓ and m<sub>ℓ</sub>. Two electrons share an orbital only if those three match and their spins differ.
w: Electrons I and II both have (n, ℓ, mℓ) = (2, 1, 0) — the same 2p orbital — and opposite spins, as Pauli requires. I and III are both 2p electrons but in different 2p orbitals (mℓ = 0 vs 1); IV is in the 2s orbital (ℓ = 0). 'Same subshell' is not the same as 'same orbital'.
x: I and III are in different 2p orbitals (m_ℓ = 0 vs 1).
IV is in the 2s orbital (ℓ = 0), while III is a 2p electron (ℓ = 1). Electrons in the same orbital must match in n, ℓ and m<sub>ℓ</sub>, differing only in spin.
II and IV are in different subshells.

q: A gas-discharge tube containing an unknown element gives the emission spectrum labeled '?'. Reference spectra of four elements are shown below it. Which element is in the tube?
h: Every element has its own fingerprint of line wavelengths. Match every line position, not just one.
w: The unknown's lines at about 405, 436, 546 and 579 nm match mercury exactly. Helium (447 nm) and sodium (589 nm) each have a line close to one of the unknown's lines, but a near miss is not a match — all lines must line up.
x: Some helium lines sit close to the unknown's lines, but none of them line up exactly. Every line must match.
Hydrogen's lines don't line up.
Sodium shares only one nearby line. All lines must match.

q: White light passes through cool hydrogen gas and the spectrum below is observed: dark lines on a continuous background. Which electron transition produces the dark line at 486 nm?
h: Dark lines are ABSORPTION: electrons jump UP by taking in photons. The visible lines of hydrogen all involve n = 2.
w: Absorption lines occur where atoms absorb photons, so the electron moves UP: n = 2 → n = 4 (ΔE = hc/λ = 4.09 × 10−19 J matches E4 − E2). n = 4 → n = 2 has the same wavelength but is emission (a bright line). 2 → 3 absorbs 656 nm and 1 → 2 absorbs 122 nm (ultraviolet, off the chart).
x: 4 → 2 has the same wavelength but is emission (a bright line).
2 → 3 absorbs at 656 nm (the red line), not 486 nm. A shorter wavelength means a larger energy gap, so the 486 nm line needs a bigger jump up from n = 2.
1 → 2 absorbs at 122 nm, in the ultraviolet.

q: Four elements are marked on the blank periodic table. Which has the LARGEST atomic radius?
h: Radius grows down a group (more shells) and shrinks across a period (more protons pulling on the same shell).
w: Y is in period 4, group 1: the most shells and the fewest protons of the four, so its valence electron is held farthest out. W (period 2, group 1) is small because it has only two shells; Z is in period 4 but far to the right, where the higher nuclear charge contracts the atom; X is the smallest.
x: W has only two shells, so its valence electron is close to the nucleus and the atom is small. Atomic radius grows going down a group as shells are added.
Z is far to the right, where higher nuclear charge shrinks the atom.
X is the smallest of the four.

q: Positions Q, R, S and T are marked on the outline table with no symbols given. Removing one electron from a gaseous atom takes the MOST energy for the element at which position?
h: Ionization energy increases up a group and to the right across a period (toward the noble gases).
w: R (period 2, group 17 — fluorine's position) is farthest up and to the right of the four, so its valence electrons feel the strongest pull. S is in the same group but one period lower (larger, easier to ionize); Q is in period 2 but farther left; T (period 4, group 2) has the lowest IE.
x: Q is farther left, so its IE is lower.
S is one period lower, so it's easier to ionize.
T has the lowest IE of the four.

q: Positions J–M are marked on the outline table. For the element at which position does a gaseous atom release the MOST energy when it gains one electron?
h: Halogens gain electrons most readily, but the period-2 member is a well-known exception: its tiny size causes extra electron–electron repulsion.
w: K is in chlorine's position (period 3, group 17). Chlorine has the most negative electron affinity of all elements (−349 kJ mol⁻¹), beating fluorine (J, −328 kJ mol⁻¹) because the incoming electron in tiny F feels strong repulsion from the crowded 2p electrons. L (oxygen) is less exothermic than either halogen, and M (sodium) barely attracts an extra electron.
x: Fluorine's position releases slightly less, because tiny F repels the added electron.
Oxygen's position releases less than the halogens.
Sodium's position barely attracts an extra electron.

q: Each of the four marked elements forms an ion that is isoelectronic with neon (10 electrons). Which of these ions has the LARGEST radius?
h: In an isoelectronic series the electron count is the same, so the ion with the FEWEST protons holds its electrons most loosely.
w: All four ions have 10 electrons. G2− (oxygen's position, 8 protons) has the smallest nuclear charge pulling on those 10 electrons, so it is largest: O2− > F− > Na+ > Mg2+. Students often pick D+ because D (sodium) is the biggest ATOM, but as a cation it has lost its outer shell.
x: D⁺ has lost its outer shell and has 11 protons, so it's small.
J⁻ has 9 protons, more than G²⁻'s 8.
E²⁺ has the most protons (12), so it's the smallest.

q: Which pair of the marked elements is most likely to form an IONIC compound?
h: Ionic bonding needs a metal (low ionization energy, far left) and a nonmetal (high electron affinity, far right).
w: A (period 3, group 1 — a reactive metal) gives an electron to B (period 3, group 16 — a nonmetal), forming an ionic compound such as A2B (like Na2S). C and D (carbon and oxygen positions) are both nonmetals and share electrons covalently, as do B–D and B–C.
x: C and D are both nonmetals, so they share electrons.
B and D are both nonmetals, so they share electrons.
B and C are both nonmetals, so they share electrons.

q: The outline table marks four positions. At which position is the element a semiconducting metalloid rather than a true metal or nonmetal?
h: Metalloids sit along the stair-step line between metals and nonmetals, starting at boron and running diagonally down and to the right.
w: K is in silicon's position (period 3, group 14), on the stair-step line — a metalloid used in semiconductors. L (aluminum) lies just left of the line and is a metal; M (selenium, period 4, group 16) is a nonmetal to the right of the line; N (carbon) is a nonmetal even though it sits above silicon.
x: L is aluminum's position, a metal.
M is selenium's position, a nonmetal.
N is carbon's position, a nonmetal.

q: Elements X and Y are marked on the blank periodic table. What is the formula of the compound they form?
h: Find each element's group. Group 1 elements form 1+ ions; group 16 elements form 2− ions. Balance the charges.
w: Y is in group 1 (period 3, sodium's position) and forms Y+; X is in group 16 (period 4, selenium's position) and forms X2−. Two Y+ balance one X2−: Y2X (compare Na2Se, K2S). YX2 reverses the charges, as if the metal were 2+.
x: YX doesn't balance +1 and −2.
This reverses the charges.
Y₂X₃ would fit 3+ and 2− ions.

q: Elements P, Q, R and S sit at the highlighted positions. Which of them has the greatest metallic character, giving up an electron most readily?
h: Metallic character means losing electrons easily: it increases DOWN a group and to the LEFT across a period.
w: P (period 5, group 1 — rubidium's position) is farthest down and to the left, so it has the lowest ionization energy and the most metallic behavior. Q (period 3, group 1) is also an alkali metal but smaller and holds its electron more tightly; R (period 5, group 14, tin) is a metal but less reactive; S (period 2, group 13, boron) is a metalloid.
x: Q is an alkali metal too, but it's smaller and holds its electron tighter.
R is tin, a metal but less reactive.
S is boron, a metalloid, so it does not give up electrons readily. Metallic character increases toward the lower left of the table, and S is near the top right of these positions.

q: The graph shows the first ionization energy of the first 20 elements plotted against atomic number. Four points are labeled P–S. Which labeled point is a noble gas?
h: Noble gases have full valence shells, so they sit at the PEAKS of the ionization-energy pattern; alkali metals sit in the valleys.
w: Point Q (Z = 10, neon) is the top of a peak: removing an electron from a filled n = 2 shell takes the most energy in its period. S (Z = 17, chlorine) is high but one step before the peak; R (Z = 11, sodium) is the valley right after neon — the alkali metal; P (Z = 4, beryllium) is a small bump from its filled 2s subshell.
x: S is chlorine, one step before the peak.
P is beryllium, a small bump.
R is sodium, the valley right after neon.

q: The bars show the first ionization energies of the eight period-2 elements in order of increasing atomic number (bar 1 = Li, bar 8 = Ne). One bar is lower than its left-hand neighbor because the electron removed comes from a p orbital that already holds another electron. Which bar is it?
h: There are two dips. One is where the first p electron is removed (p is higher than s); the other is where the first PAIRED p electron is removed.
w: Bar 6 (oxygen, 2p4) is lower than bar 5 (nitrogen, 2p3) because its fourth 2p electron must share an orbital, and that electron–electron repulsion makes it easier to remove. Bar 3 (boron) is the other dip, but that one is because boron's 2p electron is higher in energy than beryllium's 2s — not because of pairing. Bar 8 is the period's maximum.

x.label: Bar number (left to right across period 2)

x: Bar 3 (boron) is a dip for a different reason: its electron is in a higher-energy 2p.
Bar 5 is nitrogen, which is higher than its neighbor.
Bar 8 is the period's maximum.

q: The bar chart shows the radii of four ions — O<sup>2−</sup>, F<sup>−</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup> — in scrambled order and labeled only I–IV. Which bar is Mg<sup>2+</sup>?
h: All four ions have 10 electrons. More protons → stronger pull → smaller ion. Which ion has the most protons?
w: The ions are isoelectronic (10 electrons each), so size is set by nuclear charge: Mg2+ (12 protons) pulls hardest and is the SMALLEST, bar II (72 pm). Bar III (140 pm) is O2−, I is F− and IV is Na+. Choosing a large bar confuses Mg's large ATOMIC radius with its much smaller ionic radius.
x: III is the largest, so it's O²⁻.
IV is Na⁺. All four ions have 10 electrons, so the one with the most protons (Mg²⁺, 12) pulls hardest and is the smallest bar; Na⁺, with only 11, is larger.
I is F⁻. All four ions have 10 electrons, and F⁻ has only 9 protons to hold them, so it is one of the largest. Mg²⁺, with 12 protons, should be the smallest bar.

q: The phase diagram of a pure substance is shown with its three regions labeled I, II and III. Which region is the LIQUID phase?
c: the gray area beyond the critical point
h: Low pressure and high temperature favor gas; high pressure and low temperature favor solid. The liquid sits between them, above the triple point.
w: Region II lies at high pressure and moderate temperature, bounded by the steep melting line (to the solid, I) and the vaporization curve that ends at the critical point (to the gas, III). Region III, at the bottom, is the gas. The gray area past the critical point is a supercritical fluid, where liquid and gas are no longer distinct — not the liquid phase.
x: Region I is the solid: it lies at low temperature and high pressure, to the left of the steep melting line. The liquid lies between the melting line and the vaporization curve.
Region III is the gas: it lies at low pressure, below the vaporization curve. The liquid region sits above that curve at higher pressure.
Past the critical point is a supercritical fluid, not a liquid.

q: A sample of the substance whose phase diagram is shown is warmed slowly from −10 °C to 120 °C at a constant pressure of 1.0 atm (dashed line). Which sequence of phases does it pass through?
h: Follow the horizontal dashed line left to right and note every curve it crosses. Sublimation happens only BELOW the triple-point pressure.
w: At 1.0 atm the path starts in the solid region, crosses the melting line near 21 °C (solid → liquid), then crosses the vaporization curve near 58 °C (liquid → gas). Because 1.0 atm is above the triple-point pressure (0.5 atm), the sample does not sublime; it would only go solid → gas directly below 0.5 atm.
x: 1.0 atm is above the triple-point pressure, so it melts instead of subliming.
By 120 °C it has also boiled.
It starts as a solid at −10 °C.

q: The phase diagram of water is sketched (not to scale). Which statement is supported by the diagram?
c: Squeezing ice at −2 °C hard enough can turn it into liquid water.
Ice is denser than liquid water, which is why the melting line tilts left.
Ice warmed at 1.0 atm turns directly into vapor without melting.
At the triple point only liquid water and water vapor are present.
h: Look at the SLOPE of the solid–liquid line. Moving straight up (raising pressure) from the solid region, which region do you enter?
w: The solid–liquid line leans to the LEFT (negative slope), so starting in the solid at −2 °C and increasing the pressure crosses into the liquid region: pressure melts ice. That slope exists because ice is LESS dense than liquid water (the opposite of the choice that calls ice denser). At 1.0 atm, well above the triple-point pressure, ice melts rather than sublimes, and the triple point is where all three phases coexist.
x: Ice is less dense than liquid water. That's why the line tilts left.
At 1.0 atm, above the triple-point pressure, ice melts.
At the triple point, all three phases are present.

q: The phase diagram of carbon dioxide is shown. According to the diagram, what is the LOWEST pressure at which liquid CO<sub>2</sub> can exist?
h: Liquid exists only above the triple point. Read the pressure of the point where the three curves meet.
w: The three phase boundaries meet at the triple point, about (−57 °C, 5 atm); below that pressure the liquid region does not exist, which is why dry ice sublimes at 1 atm instead of melting. 73 atm and 31 °C are the critical pressure and temperature (the UPPER end of the liquid–gas curve), not the lower limit for liquid.
x: 1 atm is below the triple point, so liquid CO₂ can't exist there.
73 atm is the critical pressure, the upper end of the curve.
31 is the critical temperature (°C), not a pressure.

q: Vapor-pressure curves for liquids A, B and C are shown. Liquid B is heated in an open beaker at an atmospheric pressure of 760 torr. Which statement describes liquid B at 60 °C?
c: It is still a liquid; its vapor pressure is about 370 torr.
It is boiling, because its vapor pressure has reached 760 torr.
It is still a liquid; its vapor pressure is about 760 torr.
It has entirely become a gas, because 60 °C is above its boiling point.
h: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. Read curve B at 60 °C and compare with 760 torr.
w: At 60 °C curve B reads about 370 torr, well below the 760 torr of the surroundings, so B is a liquid that is evaporating but not boiling. B reaches 760 torr (boils) only near 78 °C. It is liquid A, not B, that boils near 35 °C.
x: At 60 °C, B's vapor pressure is only about 370 torr.
Read curve B at 60 °C. It's well below 760 torr.
60 °C is below B's boiling point.

q: The same three liquids are taken to a mountain laboratory where the atmospheric pressure is 500 torr. At about what temperature does liquid C boil there?
h: Boiling: vapor pressure = external pressure. Find where curve C reaches 500 torr (dashed line) and read the temperature.
w: Curve C crosses the 500 torr line at about 88 °C, so liquid C boils below its normal boiling point of 100 °C at reduced pressure (Clausius–Clapeyron gives 88.5 °C). 100 °C is its NORMAL boiling point (760 torr); 66 °C comes from the false proportion (500/760) × 100 °C; boiling above 100 °C would need a pressure above 760 torr.
x: 100 °C is the normal boiling point (at 760 torr).
This uses a false proportion. Read the curve at 500 torr.
Boiling above 100 °C would need more than 760 torr.

q: A pure substance is heated at a constant rate; its heating curve is shown with segments A–E. During which segment is the sample entirely LIQUID (no solid and no gas present)?
h: Flat segments are phase changes (two phases present). Sloped segments are a single phase warming up: solid, then liquid, then gas.
w: Segment C is the sloped part between the two plateaus: melting is finished (end of B) and boiling has not started (start of D), so only liquid is present and its temperature rises. B contains solid + liquid, D contains liquid + gas, and E is pure gas.
x: Segment B is melting: solid and liquid together.
Segment D is boiling: liquid and gas together.
Segment E is all gas: it comes after boiling is complete, as the vapor heats up. All-liquid heating happens between the melting and boiling plateaus.

q: The heating curve for a 10.0 g sample of a pure substance is plotted against the heat added. What is the heat of vaporization of the substance?
h: Vaporization is the upper flat segment. Heat used = (heat at its end) − (heat at its start), then divide by the mass.
w: The boiling plateau at 110 °C runs from 5.0 kJ to 13.0 kJ: 8.0 kJ ÷ 10.0 g = 0.80 kJ g−1. 0.15 kJ g−1 is the heat of FUSION (the lower plateau, 1.0 → 2.5 kJ); 1.3 kJ g−1 uses 13.0 kJ, the total heat added by the end of boiling, instead of just the plateau width.
x: 0.15 kJ/g is the heat of fusion (the lower plateau).
This uses the total heat added. Measure only the plateau width.
This uses the heat where boiling starts. Use the width of the boiling plateau, its end minus its start.

q: The table gives the normal boiling points of the group 15 hydrides. Which explains why NH<sub>3</sub> does not follow the trend of the other three?
c: NH<sub>3</sub> molecules form hydrogen bonds; the others do not.
NH<sub>3</sub> has the smallest molar mass, so its dispersion forces are strongest.
N–H bonds are stronger than P–H, As–H or Sb–H bonds, so NH<sub>3</sub> is harder to boil.
NH<sub>3</sub> is an ionic compound, while the others are molecular.
h: Boiling point should rise with molar mass (dispersion). The exception needs an extra intermolecular force available only with N–H, O–H or H–F.
w: From PH3 to SbH3 the boiling point rises with molar mass, as dispersion forces predict. NH3 should then be the lowest, but it boils far higher because N–H bonds allow hydrogen bonding between molecules. Smaller molar mass means WEAKER dispersion forces, and boiling breaks intermolecular attractions, not the N–H covalent bonds.
x: A smaller molar mass means weaker dispersion forces, not stronger.
Boiling breaks attractions between molecules, not N–H bonds.
NH₃ is molecular, not ionic.

q: The vapor pressure of a liquid was measured at two temperatures (table). What is the heat of vaporization of the liquid?
h: Clausius–Clapeyron: ln(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>) = (ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R)(1/T<sub>1</sub> − 1/T<sub>2</sub>). Temperatures must be in kelvin.
w: ln(400/100) = 1.386; 1/313.15 K − 1/343.15 K = 2.792 × 10−4 K−1. ΔHvap = (8.314)(1.386)/(2.792 × 10−4) = 4.13 × 104 J mol⁻¹ ≈ 41 kJ mol−1. Using 40 and 70 directly (°C, not K) gives 1.1 kJ mol⁻¹; using log10 instead of ln gives 18 kJ mol⁻¹; 83 kJ mol⁻¹ is double the answer.
x: This uses °C. The equation needs kelvins.
This uses log₁₀ instead of ln.
Recheck each part: ln(P₂/P₁), the difference 1/T₁ − 1/T₂ in kelvin, and R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

q: Four substances are listed with their molar masses and dipole moments. Which one has the HIGHEST normal boiling point?
h: Similar molar masses, so compare the TYPE of intermolecular force: dispersion only, dipole–dipole, or hydrogen bonding (H on N, O or F).
w: CH3OH, SiH4 and CH3F all have molar masses near 32–34 g mol⁻¹, so dispersion forces are similar; the deciding factor is hydrogen bonding in CH3OH (an O–H group), which gives it by far the highest boiling point (65 °C). CH3F has the largest dipole moment but no H bonded to N, O or F, so only dipole–dipole forces (−78 °C); SiH4 and CH4 are nonpolar.
x: CH₃F has no H on N, O or F, so no hydrogen bonding.
SiH₄ is nonpolar, so it has only dispersion forces, which are similar for these molecules of near-equal molar mass. A molecule that can hydrogen-bond (O–H) will boil much higher.
CH₄ is nonpolar and the smallest.

q: Using the solubility curves, classify a solution made by stirring 60 g of KNO<sub>3</sub> into 100 g of water at 50 °C until all of the solid has dissolved.
c: a saturated solution with 25 g of undissolved solid
h: Compare the amount added with the curve's value at that temperature. Below the curve = unsaturated; on it = saturated; above it = supersaturated.
w: At 50 °C the KNO3 curve reads about 85 g per 100 g water, so all 60 g dissolve and about 25 g MORE could still dissolve: the solution is unsaturated. 'Saturated with 25 g undissolved' reverses the comparison (that would need 110 g added). A supersaturated solution holds more than the curve allows, which 60 g is not.
x: Saturated would mean 85 g dissolved. Only 60 g is here.
Supersaturated holds more than the curve allows.
This reverses the comparison. All 60 g dissolves.

q: A saturated solution of KNO<sub>3</sub> in 100 g of water is prepared at 60 °C and then cooled to 20 °C. About how much KNO<sub>3</sub> crystallizes out of solution?
h: Read the solubility at the starting and ending temperatures. The difference is what can no longer stay dissolved.
w: At 60 °C the solution holds about 110 g; at 20 °C only about 32 g can stay dissolved. 110 − 32 ≈ 78 g crystallizes. 32 g is what REMAINS dissolved, 110 g is the starting amount (as if nothing stayed in solution), and 142 g adds the two values instead of subtracting.
x: 32 g is what stays dissolved.
110 g is the starting amount.
This adds the two values. Subtract them.

q: Lines I and II show how the solubility of O<sub>2</sub> in water depends on its partial pressure, measured at two different temperatures. Which statement is correct?
c: Line II was measured at the higher temperature, where O<sub>2</sub> is less soluble.
Line II was measured at the lower temperature, where O<sub>2</sub> is less soluble.
The lines show that gas solubility does not depend on pressure once the solution is saturated.
Line II was measured at the higher temperature, where O<sub>2</sub> is more soluble.
h: Henry's law: S = k<sub>H</sub>P, a straight line through the origin whose slope k<sub>H</sub> gets SMALLER as the water warms.
w: Both lines pass through the origin with solubility proportional to pressure (Henry's law). Line II has the smaller slope, meaning less O2 dissolves at any pressure — exactly what happens at a HIGHER temperature, where gas molecules escape the liquid more easily (why warm water holds less oxygen for fish). The lines are straight, so solubility keeps rising with pressure.
x: A lower temperature dissolves more O₂, not less.
The lines show solubility keeps rising with pressure.
At higher temperature, O₂ is less soluble, not more.

q: The graph shows the solubility of nitrogen gas in water at 25 °C. Air is 78% N<sub>2</sub> by volume, so N<sub>2</sub> has a partial pressure of 0.78 atm at sea level. What mass of N<sub>2</sub> is dissolved in 1.0 L of water open to the air at 25 °C? (N<sub>2</sub>: 28.02 g mol⁻¹)
h: Get the Henry's-law constant from the slope (solubility at 1.0 atm), multiply by 0.78 atm, then convert moles to grams.
w: From the line, S = 6.1 × 10−4 M at 1.0 atm, so kH = 6.1 × 10−4 M/atm. At 0.78 atm: 4.76 × 10−4 mol L⁻¹ × 28.02 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0133 g = 13 mg. Using the full 1.0 atm gives 17 mg; 0.48 mg forgets the molar mass (reports 4.8 × 10−4 as if it were grams).
x: This uses the full 1.0 atm. Use N₂'s 0.78 atm.
This forgets the molar mass.
This divides by 0.78 atm. A gas dissolves less at lower pressure, so multiply the 1.0 atm solubility by 0.78.

q: The graph shows the freezing point of three aqueous solutions as a function of solute molality. The solutes are glucose, NaCl and CaCl<sub>2</sub> (assume complete dissociation). Which line is CaCl<sub>2</sub>?
c: The lines cannot be assigned without knowing K<sub>f</sub>.
h: ΔT<sub>f</sub> = i K<sub>f</sub> m. The slope of each line is −i K<sub>f</sub>, so the solute that makes the most particles per formula unit has the steepest line.
w: CaCl2 → Ca2+ + 2 Cl− gives i = 3, the largest van 't Hoff factor, so its line falls fastest: III (slope −3 × 1.86 = −5.58 °C per m). Line II (i = 2) is NaCl and line I (i = 1) is glucose, a nonelectrolyte. Kf is the same for all three (same solvent), so it is not needed to rank them.
x: Line I falls the least, so it's glucose (i = 1).
Line II falls at a middle rate, which matches i = 2 (NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻). The salt that makes the most particles per formula unit lowers the freezing point fastest.
K_f is the same for all three, so it isn't needed.
