q: An unknown ionic compound is dissolved in water at several molalities and the freezing point of each solution is measured (graph; K<sub>f</sub> = 1.86 °C kg mol<sup>−1</sup>). Assuming complete dissociation, which solute is consistent with the data?
h: Slope = −i K<sub>f</sub>. Read ΔT<sub>f</sub> at one molality, divide by K<sub>f</sub> m, and the result is the number of ions per formula unit.
w: At 0.50 m the freezing point is −1.86 °C, so ΔTf = 1.86 = i (1.86)(0.50) → i = 2: two ions per formula unit, KNO3 (K+ + NO−3). Reading '1.86' and matching it to Kf tempts students toward a nonelectrolyte (i = 1), but that forgets the molality is only 0.50. MgCl2 (i = 3) would reach −2.79 °C and Al(NO3)3 (i = 4) −3.72 °C.
x: MgCl₂ (i = 3) would reach −2.79 °C.
Glucose (i = 1) would reach only −0.93 °C.
Al(NO₃)₃ (i = 4) would reach −3.72 °C.

q: A student draws four particle pictures (water left out) for a dilute solution of potassium bromide, KBr, a strong electrolyte. Which drawing is correct?
h: A strong electrolyte dissociates completely into separate, independent ions. Think about what charges each particle carries.
w: Box I shows separate K+ and Br− ions in a 1 : 1 ratio, each surrounded by (undrawn) water — the correct picture of a dissolved strong electrolyte. Box II keeps K and Br paired as intact 'molecules' (KBr is not molecular and does not stay together in water); box III shows Br2 molecules, which do not form on dissolving; box IV has neutral atoms with no charges, so the solution could not conduct electricity.
x: Box II keeps K and Br paired. KBr separates into ions.
Box III shows Br₂, which doesn't form.
Box IV has neutral atoms, which couldn't conduct.

q: Three aqueous solutions of equal concentration are drawn at the particle level (water not shown; a pair of touching circles with no charge is a neutral molecule). Rank the solutions by electrical conductivity, from HIGHEST to lowest.
h: Conductivity depends on how many free IONS are in solution. Count charged particles, not total particles.
w: Box I has every unit dissociated into ions (strong electrolyte); box III has mostly intact molecules with one dissociated pair (weak electrolyte); box II has only neutral molecules (nonelectrolyte — no ions, no current). So I > III > II. Counting total particles instead of ions gives the wrong idea that II conducts, since it has nearly as many particles as III.
x: Box II has no ions, so it conducts the least.
Box II has no ions, so it's last.
Box I has the most ions, so it's first.

q: The graph shows the vapor pressure of a solvent at 25 °C as a nonvolatile, nonelectrolyte solute is added. What is the vapor pressure of a solution made from 1.00 mol of this solute and 4.00 mol of the solvent?
h: Raoult's law: P = χ<sub>solvent</sub> P°. First find the mole FRACTION of solute (moles solute ÷ TOTAL moles), then read or compute.
w: χsolute = 1.00/(1.00 + 4.00) = 0.200, so χsolvent = 0.800 and P = 0.800 × 200 torr = 160 torr, matching the line at χsolute = 0.20. Using 1/4 = 0.25 (dividing by the solvent moles instead of total moles) gives 150 torr; 40 torr is the vapor-pressure LOWERING, not the vapor pressure; 200 torr is pure solvent.
x: This divides by the solvent moles. Use the total moles.
40 torr is how much the pressure drops, not the vapor pressure.
200 torr is pure solvent.

q: Four aqueous solutions at 25 °C are listed in the table. Assuming complete dissociation of the ionic solutes, which solution has the HIGHEST osmotic pressure?
h: Π = i M R T. At the same temperature, compare i × M (the total particle concentration), not the molarity alone.
w: Effective particle concentrations: I 0.100 × 1 = 0.100 M; II 0.070 × 2 = 0.140 M; III 0.050 × 3 = 0.150 M; IV 0.045 × 4 = 0.180 M. Solution IV wins even though it has the LOWEST molarity, because K3PO4 releases four ions per formula unit. Picking I because 0.100 M is the biggest number ignores dissociation.
x: 0.100 M is the biggest number, but sucrose doesn't dissociate.
III gives 0.150 M particles. Another gives more.
II gives 0.140 M particles. Another gives more.

q: The table gives the measured boiling-point elevation of four 0.100 m aqueous solutions. How many ions does one formula unit of the unknown salt X release when it dissolves?
h: ΔT<sub>b</sub> = i K<sub>b</sub> m. Use the sucrose row (i = 1) to find K<sub>b</sub> m, then see how many times larger X's elevation is.
w: Sucrose (i = 1) gives 0.051 °C, so Kb m ≈ 0.051 °C. X gives 0.205 °C → i = 0.205/0.051 ≈ 4 ions per formula unit (like K3PO4 or AlCl3). Comparing X with NaCl instead of sucrose (0.205/0.102 = 2) only tells you X makes twice as many ions as NaCl — that is still 4, not 2.
x: This compares X with NaCl. Compare with sucrose (i = 1).
Compare X's elevation with sucrose's, since sucrose has i = 1.
This is too many ions. Compare X only with sucrose, which has i = 1.

q: The mass spectrum of a pure element is shown; each peak is labeled with its percent abundance. Which element is it?
h: Weighted average: Σ(mass × fractional abundance). Then find the element with that average atomic mass on the periodic table.
w: Using the peak positions: (28)(0.9223) + (29)(0.0467) + (30)(0.0310) = 28.11 u (28.09 u with exact isotope masses) → silicon. Aluminum (26.98) lies below every peak and phosphorus (30.97) above every peak, so neither can be a weighted average of these masses; nickel (58.69) is roughly the SUM of two peaks, not an average.
x: Aluminum's mass is below every peak.
Phosphorus's mass is above every peak.
Nickel's mass is about the sum of two peaks, not an average.

q: Rubidium's two natural isotopes appear as the bars in this mass spectrum, with the percent abundance printed above each bar; their exact masses are tabulated. Use the data to compute rubidium's average atomic mass.
h: Average atomic mass is a weighted average: each isotope's mass times its fractional abundance, added together.
w: (84.912)(0.7217) + (86.909)(0.2783) = 61.28 + 24.19 = 85.47 u. 85.91 u is the simple (unweighted) average of the two masses; 86.35 u swaps the abundances; 86.00 u is the average of the mass numbers 85 and 87.
x: This is the simple average. It ignores the abundances.
This swaps the abundances.
This averages the mass numbers 85 and 87.

q: The table lists the protons (p<sup>+</sup>), neutrons (n<sup>0</sup>) and electrons (e<sup>−</sup>) in four atomic species. Which one is a NEGATIVE ion of an isotope of oxygen?
h: The element is set by the number of protons; the charge by protons minus electrons. Oxygen has 8 protons.
w: Species I has 8 protons (oxygen) and 10 electrons, so its charge is 8 − 10 = −2: an O2− ion of oxygen-18 (8 + 10 = 18). II is a neutral oxygen-16 atom; III has 10 protons, so it is neon, not oxygen, even though it has 10 electrons like I; IV has 8 protons but only 6 electrons, making it a 2+ CATION.
x: II is a neutral oxygen atom.
III has 10 protons, so it's neon.
IV has fewer electrons than protons, so it's a cation.

q: Protons, neutrons and electrons are tabulated for species I–IV. Which pair of entries are ISOTOPES of one element?
h: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Electron count does not matter for this.
w: Species I and II both have 17 protons (chlorine) with 18 and 20 neutrons: Cl-35 and Cl-37 (II happens to be the Cl− ion, which does not change the element). II and III have the same MASS NUMBER (37) but different elements; III and IV share 18 electrons (isoelectronic), not the same element; I and IV differ in protons.
x: II and III have the same mass number but are different elements.
III and IV have the same electrons but different elements.
I and IV have different numbers of protons.

q: The boxes show molecules of two different compounds formed by nitrogen and oxygen. Which law do the two compounds illustrate, and what is the ratio of the mass of oxygen per gram of nitrogen in compound II to that in compound I?
h: Count O atoms per N atom in each compound. When two compounds of the same elements are compared, their mass ratios are small whole numbers.
w: Compound I is NO (1 O per N) and compound II is NO2 (2 O per N). For a fixed mass of nitrogen, II has twice the oxygen: 2 : 1. Two different compounds of the same two elements with oxygen masses in a small whole-number ratio is the law of multiple proportions. The law of definite proportions describes a SINGLE compound's fixed composition.
x: The law of definite proportions is about a single compound.
Count the O atoms per N: 1 and 2, not 2 and 3.
Conservation of mass is about a reaction keeping its total mass. Here two compounds are compared, and they do not have the same O per N.

q: In an oil-drop experiment, the charges measured on four different drops are listed. What is the best value for the charge of a single electron from these data?
h: Every drop carries a whole number of electrons, so the electron charge is the largest value that divides evenly into ALL the measured charges.
w: The charges are 2, 3, 5 and 4 times 1.6 × 10−19 C, the greatest common factor. 3.2 × 10−19 C is simply the SMALLEST drop charge, but 4.8 is not a whole-number multiple of it (1.5×), so it cannot be the unit charge; 5.6 × 10−19 C is the average of the four values, which has no physical meaning here.
x: 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ is the smallest drop, but 4.8 isn't a whole-number multiple of it.
This is the largest charge measured. The charge of one electron must divide evenly into every drop, including the smaller ones.
The average has no meaning here. Find the common factor.

q: The bar chart gives the mass percent composition of a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
h: Treat the percents as grams in a 100 g sample, convert each to moles with its atomic mass, then divide all by the smallest.
w: 40.0 g C ÷ 12.01 = 3.33 mol; 6.7 g H ÷ 1.008 = 6.65 mol; 53.3 g O ÷ 16.00 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by 3.33 gives C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1 → CH2O. CHO comes from treating the near-equal C and O PERCENTS as equal atom counts and assuming one H because its percent is small; mass percent must be converted to moles first.
x: Similar mass percents don't mean equal atoms. Convert to moles.
Convert each percent to moles and divide by the smallest. Then recheck the C to O ratio.
Recheck the hydrogen. Divide its mass by 1.008 g/mol, then by the smallest mole value.

q: An iron oxide has the composition shown in the bar chart. What is its empirical formula?
h: Convert each percent to moles (÷ atomic mass). Iron atoms are heavy, so a large mass percent does not mean more atoms.
w: 69.9 ÷ 55.85 = 1.25 mol Fe; 30.1 ÷ 16.00 = 1.88 mol O. O/Fe = 1.50 → multiply by 2: Fe2O3. FeO is the trap for students who see that iron is 'about two-thirds of the mass' and think the atoms are roughly equal — the mole ratio, not the mass ratio, sets the formula. FeO3 would require 46% O; Fe3O4 27.6% O.
x: FeO would be only 22.3% O. Convert each mass percent to moles before comparing.
Fe₃O₄ has an O : Fe mole ratio of 1.33 and would be only 27.6% O, below the 30.1% in the chart. Convert each mass percent to moles and compare the ratio.
FeO₃ would be 46% O, far more than the chart shows; it puts three O per Fe. Convert each mass percent to moles: there are only 1.5 O for each Fe.

q: A hydrocarbon is burned completely in excess oxygen and the products are collected (table). What is the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon?
h: All the carbon ends up in CO<sub>2</sub> and all the hydrogen in H<sub>2</sub>O. Each H<sub>2</sub>O carries TWO hydrogen atoms.
w: mol C = 1.4971 g ÷ 44.01 = 0.03402 mol; mol H = 2 × (0.8172 g ÷ 18.016) = 0.09072 mol. H/C = 2.667 = 8/3 → C3H8. Forgetting the factor of 2 for H2O gives H/C = 1.33 → C3H4. The sample mass (0.5000 g) checks the result: 0.03402 mol C × 12.01 + 0.09072 mol H × 1.008 = 0.500 g, so no oxygen was in the compound.
x: This forgets that each H₂O has 2 H atoms.
C₂H₅ has an H to C ratio of 2.5. Recheck the moles of C from the CO₂ mass and the moles of H from the H₂O mass.
CH₃ has an H to C ratio of 3. Recheck the moles of C from the CO₂ mass and the moles of H from the H₂O mass.

q: The table relates mass, moles and number of molecules for three gases; two entries for ammonia are missing. How many NH<sub>3</sub> molecules are in the 8.52 g sample?
h: grams → moles (÷ molar mass of NH<sub>3</sub>, 17.03 g mol⁻¹) → molecules (× 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>). Compare with the completed rows.
w: 8.52 g ÷ 17.03 g mol⁻¹ = 0.500 mol NH3; 0.500 mol × 6.022 × 1023 = 3.01 × 1023 molecules — the same count as the 0.500 mol of water in the first row. 5.13 × 1024 multiplies grams directly by Avogadro's number, skipping the molar mass; 1.51 × 1023 is the CO2 row (0.250 mol), not ammonia.
x: This multiplies grams by Avogadro's number. Convert to moles first.
1.51×10²³ is the CO₂ row, not ammonia.
Recheck the moles of NH₃ using its molar mass, 17.03 g/mol.

q: A hydrate of magnesium sulfate, MgSO<sub>4</sub>·xH<sub>2</sub>O, has the mass composition shown. What is x? (MgSO<sub>4</sub>: 120.37 g mol⁻¹; H<sub>2</sub>O: 18.02 g mol⁻¹)
h: Per 100 g: convert the mass of MgSO<sub>4</sub> and the mass of water to moles separately, then take the ratio mol H<sub>2</sub>O : mol MgSO<sub>4</sub>.
w: 48.8 g ÷ 120.37 g mol⁻¹ = 0.405 mol MgSO4; 51.2 g ÷ 18.02 g mol⁻¹ = 2.84 mol H2O. 2.84/0.405 = 7.0 → x = 7 (epsom salt). The near-equal MASS percents tempt students to answer x = 1, but one water molecule is almost seven times lighter than one MgSO4 unit.
x: Similar mass percents don't mean equal molecules. One water is much lighter than one MgSO₄.
Convert both the MgSO₄ mass and the water mass to moles, then recheck the ratio of water to MgSO₄.
Recheck the mole ratio of water to MgSO₄; 6 is not what the percentages give.

q: Four solutions of sodium chloride are described in the table. Which solution contains the GREATEST number of moles of NaCl?
h: moles = molarity × volume in LITERS. Neither the largest volume nor the highest molarity alone decides it.
w: I: 0.250 L × 0.100 M = 0.0250 mol; II: 0.0500 L × 0.600 M = 0.0300 mol; III: 1.00 L × 0.0200 M = 0.0200 mol; IV: 0.100 L × 0.250 M = 0.0250 mol. The biggest volume (III) has the FEWEST moles because it is so dilute; the most concentrated (II) wins despite its small volume.
x: III has the biggest volume but is so dilute it has the fewest moles.
Solution I has 0.250 L × 0.100 M = 0.0250 mol. Moles depend on volume times molarity together, and another solution's product is larger.
Solution IV has 0.100 L × 0.250 M = 0.0250 mol. Multiply volume (in L) by molarity for every solution; another one has a larger product.

q: The thermal conductivity of a plastic is 0.60 W m<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>. What is this value in mW cm<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>?
h: Convert the numerator prefix (W → mW, ×1000) and the denominator unit (per m → per cm, 1 m = 100 cm) separately.
w: 0.60 W m−1 × (1000 mW / 1 W) × (1 m / 100 cm) = 6.0 mW cm−1 K−1. 0.060 inverts both factors (÷1000, ×100); 6.0×104 multiplies by 100 instead of dividing because the meter is in the denominator; 60 is off by a factor of 10 (1 m is 100 cm, not 10 cm).
x: This flips both conversion factors.
This multiplies by 100. Since m is in the denominator, divide by 100.
Check both factors: W to mW multiplies by 1000, and since m is in the denominator, 1 m = 100 cm divides by 100.

q: A student records the two masses in the table. What mass of liquid should be reported?
h: In subtraction the answer keeps the fewest DECIMAL PLACES of the data, not the fewest significant figures.
w: 48.113 g − 35.60 g = 12.513 g, but 35.60 g is known only to the hundredths place, so the result is rounded to 12.51 g. 12.513 g keeps a digit that is not justified; 12.5 g and 13 g round off digits that the hundredths-place data justify.
x: This keeps 3 decimal places, but 35.60 g has only 2.
This rounds to the tenths place, but both masses are known at least to the hundredths place.
This rounds to whole grams, but both masses are known at least to the hundredths place.

q: Chlorous acid is a weak acid used in some disinfectant formulations. What is its formula?
h: An -ous acid comes from the -ite anion; an -ic acid from the -ate anion. Chlorite is ClO−2.
w: -ous ↔ -ite: chlorous acid contains the chlorite ion, ClO−2, so the acid is HClO2. HClO is hypochlorous acid, HClO3 is chloric acid (from chlorate) and HClO4 is perchloric acid.
x: HClO is hypochlorous acid.
HClO₃ is chloric acid, from the chlorate ion. The -ic acids come from -ate ions; an -ous acid comes from the -ite ion, which has one fewer O.
HClO₄ is perchloric acid.

q: Sodium thiosulfate has the formula Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. What is the formula of calcium thiosulfate?
h: Two Na<sup>+</sup> balance one thiosulfate ion, so find its charge first, then balance it with Ca<sup>2+</sup>.
w: Two Na+ (+2 total) balance one S2O2−3 ion. One Ca2+ balances one S2O2−3, giving CaS2O3. Ca2S2O3 copies the sodium subscript; Ca(S2O3)2 treats thiosulfate as a 1− ion.
x: This copies sodium's subscript. Ca²⁺ needs only one thiosulfate.
This treats thiosulfate as a 1− ion. It's 2−.
This doubles the oxygens. The thiosulfate ion stays S₂O₃²⁻.

q: In the name sulfur hexafluoride, what does the prefix hexa- tell you?
c: Six fluorine atoms are covalently bonded to one sulfur atom.
Sulfur has lost six electrons to form S<sup>6+</sup> ions.
The molecule has a six-sided (hexagonal) planar shape.
The compound contains six sulfur atoms per fluorine atom.
h: Greek prefixes in molecular (covalent) names count atoms of the element they are attached to.
w: Prefixes in covalent names count atoms: hexa- means six F atoms bonded to one S atom, SF6. The name says nothing about ions (a molecular compound has none), and prefixes never describe geometry.
x: SF₆ is molecular. There are no ions.
Prefixes count atoms. They don't describe shape.
Hexa- counts fluorine atoms, not sulfur atoms.

q: Boxes I–IV are particle-level views of four gas samples (two kinds of atoms: gray and white). Which box contains a pure compound?
h: A compound is a pure substance whose particles are all identical AND contain more than one kind of atom.
w: Box III holds only one kind of particle, each made of two different atoms: a compound. Box I is an element (identical diatomic molecules of one atom type). Box II mixes two elements, and box IV mixes a compound with an element, so both are mixtures.
x: Box I has only one kind of atom, so it's an element.
Box II mixes two elements.
Box IV mixes a compound with an element.

q: An ion has a charge of 2− and contains 18 electrons. What is the atomic number of the element?
h: A negative ion has MORE electrons than protons. Atomic number = number of protons.
w: A 2− charge means two extra electrons, so protons = 18 − 2 = 16 (sulfur, S2−). Answering 18 ignores the charge; 20 adds the two electrons instead of subtracting (that would be a 2+ ion).
x: This ignores the 2− charge.
This adds 2. A 2− ion has 2 extra electrons, so subtract.
This subtracts only 1. A 2− charge means 2 extra electrons.

q: Four atoms are identified below by name and mass number. Which one has the largest number of neutrons in its nucleus?
h: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. The largest mass number does not guarantee the most neutrons.
w: Argon-40: 40 − 18 = 22 neutrons. Calcium-40 has 40 − 20 = 20, potassium-39 has 39 − 19 = 20 and chlorine-37 has 37 − 17 = 20. Ca-40 is tempting because it has the same mass number and more protons, but more protons means fewer neutrons for the same mass number.
x: Ca-40 has 40 − 20 = 20 neutrons.
K-39 has 39 − 19 = 20 neutrons.
Cl-37 has 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.

q: Which statement about atomic structure is correct?
c: The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.
The atomic number of an element equals the number of neutrons in one of its atoms.
The nucleus of an atom contains both protons and electrons.
In a neutral atom the number of neutrons equals the number of electrons.
h: Z counts protons; A counts protons + neutrons; electrons sit outside the nucleus and equal protons in a neutral atom.
w: Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Atomic number Z counts protons (not neutrons); electrons are outside the nucleus; neutrality links electrons to protons, and the neutron count is unrelated.
x: The atomic number counts protons, not neutrons.
Electrons are outside the nucleus.
The neutron count has nothing to do with the electron count.

q: Silver has two stable isotopes, <sup>107</sup>Ag and <sup>109</sup>Ag, and its average atomic mass is 107.87 u. Which statement is correct?
c: The two isotopes are equally abundant.
h: The weighted average sits closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope.
w: 107.87 is closer to 107 than to 109, so 107Ag is the more abundant isotope (about 52%). Equal abundances would give an average of about 108.0; an average near 109 would require mostly 109Ag.
x: 107.87 is closer to 107, so ¹⁰⁷Ag is the larger share.
Equal amounts would give an average near 108.0.
Mostly ¹⁰⁹Ag would put the average near 109.

q: Gallium has two natural isotopes. The more abundant one, <sup>69</sup>Ga (mass 68.9256 u), makes up 60.11% of gallium atoms, and the average atomic mass of gallium is 69.72 u. What is the other isotope?
h: average = (fraction<sub>1</sub>)(mass<sub>1</sub>) + (fraction<sub>2</sub>)(mass<sub>2</sub>); the second fraction is 1 − 0.6011. Solve for mass<sub>2</sub>.
w: 69.72 = 0.6011(68.9256) + 0.3989(m), so m = (69.72 − 41.43)/0.3989 = 70.9 u → 71Ga. 70Ga would put the average at about 69.3 u; choosing a mass below 68.9 cannot raise the average above the 69Ga mass.
x: ⁷⁰Ga would put the average around 69.3 u.
⁷²Ga would push the average up to about 70.1 u.
A mass below 68.9 can't raise the average above ⁶⁹Ga's mass.

q: Natural boron is 19.9% <sup>10</sup>B and 80.1% <sup>11</sup>B. Each box holds ten boron atoms. Which box best represents a natural sample of boron?
h: Convert the percentages to atoms out of ten: about 2 of one isotope and 8 of the other. Then check which isotope is which.
w: 19.9% of 10 atoms ≈ 2 atoms of 10B and 80.1% ≈ 8 atoms of 11B: box I. Box II reverses the isotopes, box III shows a 50 : 50 sample, and box IV shows only 11B.
x: Box II reverses the two isotopes.
Box III shows a 50:50 mix.
Box IV shows only B-11 and ignores the 19.9% of B-10. With ten atoms, about 2 should be B-10 and about 8 should be B-11.

q: Which element exists as diatomic molecules under ordinary conditions?
h: Seven elements exist as diatomic molecules: hydrogen, the halogens and two gases that make up most of air. Noble gases are monatomic.
w: Nitrogen exists as N2. Neon, like all noble gases, is monatomic. Sulfur and phosphorus are molecular nonmetals but form S8 rings and P4 tetrahedra, not diatomic molecules.
x: Neon is a noble gas, so it exists as single atoms.
Sulfur is a molecular nonmetal, but its atoms join into S₈ rings, not two-atom molecules. The diatomic elements are H, N, O and the halogens.
Phosphorus forms P₄ molecules.

q: Moving down one column of the periodic table, the elements change from nonmetal to metalloid to metal. Which group shows this pattern?
h: The metal–nonmetal staircase cuts through the p block; groups it crosses contain all three element types.
w: Group 14: carbon is a nonmetal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals. Groups 1 and 2 are entirely metals (hydrogen aside); group 17 is entirely nonmetals.
x: Group 1 is all metals (hydrogen aside).
Every element in group 2, from Be to Ra, is a metal, so there is no change from nonmetal to metalloid going down. Look for the group that starts with a nonmetal at the top.
Group 17 is all nonmetals.

q: A reagent label says "contains a transition metal." For which of these compounds would that label be accurate?
h: Transition metals are the d-block elements in groups 3–12.
w: Manganese (group 7) is a d-block transition metal. Aluminum (group 13) and tin (group 14) are main-group metals, and strontium (group 2) is an alkaline earth metal.
x: Aluminum is a main-group metal (group 13).
Tin is a main-group metal (group 14).
Strontium is an alkaline earth metal (group 2).

q: An element M forms an ionic oxide with the formula MO. What is the formula of the phosphate of M?
h: Use the oxide (O2−) to find the charge on M, then balance that charge against PO3−4.
w: In MO one O2− is balanced by one M, so M is M2+. Three M2+ (+6) balance two PO3−4 (−6): M3(PO4)2. MPO4 would need M3+; M2(PO4)3 cannot balance at all (two M would have to supply +9); it copies the 2 : 3 pattern of an oxide such as M2O3.
x: MPO₄ balances only if M is M³⁺ (to cancel one PO₄³⁻). But MO shows one M balancing one O²⁻, so M is M²⁺; balance +2 ions against −3 ions.
In M₂(PO₄)₃, two M ions would have to balance a 9− charge, which no whole-number charge can do. Find the charge on M from MO first.
M(PO₄)₂ gives +2 and −6, so the charges don't balance.

q: In the Bohr model the electron of a hydrogen atom travels in a fixed circular orbit. In the modern quantum-mechanical model, what replaces this orbit?
c: An orbital: a region of space where there is a high probability of finding the electron
An elliptical orbit whose shape depends on the energy level
A continuous ring of negative charge spread evenly around the nucleus
A set of orbits of any radius, because the energy is no longer quantized
h: Modern theory gives up exact electron paths (uncertainty principle) but keeps quantized energies.
w: Quantum mechanics describes the electron by a wave function; its square gives the probability of finding the electron, an orbital, not a path. Energies remain quantized, so the orbits do not become arbitrary, and the electron is not a smeared ring of charge.
x: The quantum model has no orbits at all, elliptical or not.
An orbital isn't a ring of charge. It's a probability region.
Energies are still quantized.

q: An element is in period 4, group 15 of the periodic table. What is the electron configuration of its valence electrons?
h: Period number = n of the valence shell; group 15 is the third column of the p block.
w: Period 4 puts the valence electrons in n = 4; group 15 means five valence electrons, 4s2 plus three in 4p: 4s24p3 (arsenic). The filled 3d10 is part of the core, not the valence shell; 3s23p3 is phosphorus in period 3.
x: 3d¹⁰ is part of the core, not the valence shell.
3s² 3p³ is phosphorus, in period 3.
4s² 4p⁵ has seven valence electrons, which is group 17 (bromine). Group 15 has five valence electrons, so only three go into 4p.

q: The 4f subshell is made up of seven orbitals. At most, how many electrons can ONE of those orbitals hold?
h: Think about what the Pauli exclusion principle says about the spins of electrons that share one orbital.
w: Any one orbital, whatever its shape, holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli exclusion principle). 14 is the capacity of the whole 4f SUBSHELL (7 orbitals × 2); 7 is the number of f orbitals.
x: 14 is the capacity of the whole 4f subshell.
7 is the number of f orbitals.
No single orbital holds 4 electrons. Ask how many different spin directions two electrons in one orbital can have.

q: The species O<sup>2−</sup>, F<sup>−</sup>, Ne and Na<sup>+</sup> all contain 10 electrons. From which one does it take the MOST energy to remove an electron?
h: Same electron count, different nuclear charge: more protons pull the same 10 electrons more tightly.
w: All four have the same electrons, so the one with the most protons, Na+ (Z = 11), holds them most tightly and has the highest ionization energy. O2− (Z = 8) loses an electron most easily; its extra electrons are only weakly held. Ne is neutral but has fewer protons than Na+.
x: O²⁻ has the fewest protons, so it loses an electron most easily.
F⁻ has fewer protons than another choice.
Ne has fewer protons than Na⁺.

q: Exactly 6.022×10<sup>23</sup> molecules of oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub>, are sealed in a flask. Which statement about this sample is correct?
c: It contains 1.00 mol of O<sub>2</sub> molecules and 2.00 mol of oxygen atoms.
It contains 1.00 mol of O<sub>2</sub> molecules and 1.00 mol of oxygen atoms.
It contains 0.500 mol of O<sub>2</sub> molecules and 1.00 mol of oxygen atoms.
It contains 1.00 mol of O<sub>2</sub> molecules and has a mass of 16.00 g.
h: Avogadro's number counts whatever particle you name. Each O<sub>2</sub> molecule contains two atoms.
w: 6.022×1023 molecules is exactly 1.00 mol of O2; each molecule has two atoms, so there are 2.00 mol of O atoms. Counting 1.00 mol of atoms (or 0.500 mol of molecules) treats the number as atoms; the mass is 1.00 mol × 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 32.00 g, not 16.00 g.
x: Each O₂ molecule contains two oxygen atoms. Recount the moles of atoms.
6.022×10²³ molecules is 1.00 mol of molecules, not 0.500.
1.00 mol of O₂ weighs 32.00 g.

q: Each of these samples contains Avogadro's number of particles. Which one weighs the most?
h: Equal numbers of particles: compare molar masses. A molecule's mass is the sum of its atoms' masses.
w: Molar masses: CO2 44.01, Ar 39.95, H2O 18.02, He 4.003 g mol⁻¹. One mole of CO2 weighs the most. Argon is tempting because a single Ar atom is heavier than any atom in CO2, but each CO2 molecule totals 44 u.
x: Ar (39.95 g/mol) is lighter than CO₂ (44.01 g/mol).
A mole of H₂O is only 18.02 g; it has three atoms, but they are light. With the same number of particles, the heaviest mole is the one with the largest molar mass.
Helium has the smallest molar mass here, only 4.003 g/mol. Equal moles means equal particles, so the sample with the largest molar mass weighs the most.

q: A tablet contains 2.50×10<sup>22</sup> molecules of aspirin, C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub>. What mass of carbon does the tablet contain?
h: molecules → moles of aspirin (÷ N<sub>A</sub>) → moles of C (×9) → grams of C (×12.01).
w: 2.50×1022 ÷ 6.022×1023 = 0.0415 mol aspirin; × 9 = 0.374 mol C; × 12.01 g mol⁻¹ = 4.49 g. 0.499 g forgets the 9 carbons per molecule; 0.374 is the number of moles of C, not grams; 7.48 g is the mass of the whole aspirin sample.
x: This forgets the 9 carbons per molecule.
0.374 is the moles of C, not grams.
This is the mass of the whole aspirin sample.

q: A bottle holds 2.0 mol of aluminum sulfate, Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>. How many moles of oxygen ATOMS does the bottle contain?
h: Multiply the subscripts inside and outside the parentheses to count O atoms per formula unit.
w: Each Al2(SO4)3 has 3 × 4 = 12 O atoms, so 2.0 mol × 12 = 24 mol O. 12 mol is the count for one mole; 8.0 mol uses only the 4 inside the parentheses (4 × 2.0); 6.0 mol uses only the 3 outside (3 × 2.0).
x: 12 mol is the count for one mole of the compound.
This uses only the 4 inside the parentheses. The 3 outside multiplies every atom in SO₄.
This uses only the 3 outside the parentheses.

q: Mass spectrometry shows that a single molecule of an unknown gas weighs 7.31×10<sup>−23</sup> g. What molar mass does this correspond to?
h: A mole is 6.022×10<sup>23</sup> molecules, so multiply the mass of one molecule by Avogadro's number.
w: 7.31×10−23 g/molecule × 6.022×1023 molecules/mol = 44.0 g mol−1 (CO2 or N2O, for example). Dividing by NA gives 1.21×10−46; 22.0 and 88.0 halve or double the correct value.
x: Recheck the conversion: the molar mass is the mass of one molecule times the number of molecules in a mole.
Recheck the conversion: multiply the mass of one molecule by Avogadro's number, and nothing else.
This divides by Avogadro's number. Multiply instead.

q: A compound of sulfur and fluorine has the formula SFn. A sample containing 3.01×1021 molecules has a mass of 0.730 g. What is n?
h: Convert molecules to moles, divide mass by moles to get the molar mass, then subtract the mass of S and divide by 19.00.
w: 3.01×1021 ÷ 6.022×1023 = 5.00×10−3 mol; 0.730 g ÷ 5.00×10−3 mol = 146 g mol⁻¹. (146 − 32.07)/19.00 = 6.0, so n = 6 (SF6). SF4 would have a molar mass of 108 g mol⁻¹, giving only 0.540 g for this many molecules.
x: SF₄ is 108 g/mol, which would weigh only 0.540 g.
SF₈ would be 184 g/mol. Find the molar mass from the sample mass and the number of moles, then compare.
SF₂ would be 70.07 g/mol, so 5.00×10⁻³ mol would weigh only 0.350 g, not 0.730 g. Find the molar mass (g ÷ mol) and solve for n.

q: Oxygen makes up a different fraction of the mass of each of these compounds. In which one is that fraction the largest?
h: Percent by mass depends on what the oxygen is combined with, not just on how many O atoms there are.
w: H2O: 16.00/18.02 = 88.8% O. CO2 is 72.7%, NO2 69.6% and SO2 50.0%. The dioxides have more O atoms, but each is paired with a heavier atom than hydrogen, so oxygen is a smaller fraction of the mass.
x: CO₂ is only 72.7% O by mass. Having two O atoms doesn't guarantee the largest fraction; the 12.01 g of carbon is much heavier than the partner atoms in another choice.
NO₂ is only 69.6% O by mass. The nitrogen (14.01 g) dilutes the oxygen's share; the largest fraction comes from pairing O with the lightest possible partner.
SO₂ is only 50.0% O by mass, because the sulfur atom (32.07 g) weighs as much as both oxygens. More O atoms don't help when the partner atom is heavy.

q: A 5.00 g sample of glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, is 40.0% carbon by mass. What is the mass percent of carbon in a 25.0 g sample of glucose?
h: Mass percent is a ratio set by the formula (law of definite composition); it does not depend on sample size.
w: Every sample of a pure compound has the same composition, so the 25.0 g sample is also 40.0% C (it simply contains 10.0 g of C instead of 2.00 g). 8.00% divides the percent by 5 and 200% multiplies it by 5, as if percent scaled with mass.
x: Percent composition doesn't change with sample size.
Percent composition doesn't change with sample size.
60% is the part that isn't carbon.

q: An oxide of phosphorus is 56.4% P and 43.6% O by mass, and each molecule contains four phosphorus atoms. What is the molar mass of the compound?
h: Find the empirical formula from the percentages, then scale it so the molecule has four P atoms.
w: Per 100 g: 1.821 mol P and 2.725 mol O, ratio O/P = 1.50, so the empirical formula is P2O3. Four P atoms per molecule means P4O6: 4(30.97) + 6(16.00) = 220 g mol−1. 110 is the empirical-formula mass; 284 is P4O10, which is only 43.6% P.
x: 110 g/mol is the empirical formula's mass.
284 g/mol is P₄O₁₀, which is only 43.6% P, not 56.4%. Work out the P : O mole ratio from the percents (1 : 1.5) before scaling up to four P atoms.
142 g/mol is P₂O₅, which doesn't match.

q: Analysis shows that a cylinder of propane, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, holds 4.032 g of hydrogen. How many moles of carbon atoms are in the cylinder?
h: Convert the hydrogen mass to moles of H atoms, then use the 3 C : 8 H ratio in the formula.
w: 4.032 g H ÷ 1.008 g mol⁻¹ = 4.000 mol H; × (3 mol C / 8 mol H) = 1.500 mol C. 4.000 mol is the moles of H itself; 0.5000 mol divides by 8 but forgets to multiply by 3; 10.67 mol inverts the ratio.
x: 4.000 mol is the moles of H, not C.
This divides by 8 but forgets to multiply by 3.
This flips the C:H ratio.

q: In a reaction mixture containing two reactants, the limiting reactant is the one that
c: is completely consumed, so it fixes how much product can form.
is present in the smaller number of moles at the start of the reaction.
has the smaller coefficient in the balanced chemical equation.
is present in the smaller mass at the start of the reaction.
h: Limiting means it runs out first. Compare amounts AFTER dividing by the coefficients, not raw moles or masses.
w: The limiting reactant is consumed completely, so the amount of product is fixed by it. The reactant with fewer moles (or less mass) is not necessarily limiting if its coefficient is also smaller; the coefficient alone says nothing without the amounts.
x: Fewer moles isn't enough. The coefficients matter too.
A coefficient alone doesn't decide it. You need the amounts too.
Less mass isn't enough. Compare moles and coefficients.

q: How many moles of O<sub>2</sub> are needed to burn 0.600 mol of propane completely by the reaction shown?
h: Use the coefficients as a mole ratio: 5 mol O<sub>2</sub> per 1 mol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>.
w: 0.600 mol C3H8 × (5 mol O2 / 1 mol C3H8) = 3.00 mol O2. 0.120 mol inverts the ratio; 1.80 and 2.40 mol use the CO2 (3) or H2O (4) coefficient instead of the O2 coefficient.
x: 0.120 mol comes from dividing 0.600 by 5, which inverts the mole ratio. Each mole of propane needs 5 mol O₂, so the O₂ amount must be larger than 0.600 mol.
This uses CO₂'s coefficient (3).
This uses H₂O's coefficient (4).

q: In a blast furnace, 0.450 mol of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is reduced by excess carbon monoxide as shown. How many grams of iron result?
h: Moles Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → moles Fe with the 1 : 2 ratio, then multiply by the molar mass of Fe (not Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>).
w: 0.450 mol Fe2O3 × (2 mol Fe / 1 mol Fe2O3) × 55.85 g mol⁻¹ = 50.3 g Fe. 25.1 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio; 75.4 g uses the CO coefficient; 71.9 g multiplies by the molar mass of Fe2O3.
x: This uses a 1:1 ratio. Each Fe₂O₃ makes 2 Fe.
This uses CO's coefficient (3).
This uses Fe₂O₃'s molar mass. Use Fe's.

q: Automobile airbags inflate when sodium azide decomposes as shown. How many molecules of N<sub>2</sub> are produced from 1.30 g of NaN<sub>3</sub>?
h: grams → moles NaN<sub>3</sub> → moles N<sub>2</sub> (3 : 2) → molecules (× N<sub>A</sub>).
w: 1.30 g ÷ 65.01 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol NaN3; × 3/2 = 0.0300 mol N2; × 6.022×1023 = 1.81×1022 molecules. 1.20×1022 uses a 1 : 1 ratio; 8.03×1021 inverts the ratio; 3.61×1022 counts N atoms rather than N2 molecules.
x: This uses a 1:1 ratio. Use 3 N₂ per 2 NaN₃.
8.03×10²¹ uses 2 N₂ per 3 NaN₃, which inverts the ratio. The equation makes 3 N₂ for every 2 NaN₃, so there are more N₂ molecules than NaN₃ units.
This counts N atoms, not N₂ molecules.

q: 0.40 mol of aluminum is mixed with 0.90 mol of chlorine gas and the reaction shown goes to completion. What amount of the excess reactant remains?
h: Find how much Cl<sub>2</sub> the 0.40 mol Al actually needs (2 : 3), then subtract from 0.90 mol.
w: 0.40 mol Al needs 0.40 × 3/2 = 0.60 mol Cl2; only 0.60 of the 0.90 mol reacts, leaving 0.30 mol Cl2. 0.50 mol subtracts the moles of Al directly (ignores the ratio); 0.60 mol is the amount of Cl2 consumed, not left over; Al is limiting, so none remains.
x: This subtracts the moles of Al directly, ignoring the ratio.
0.60 mol is the Cl₂ used up, not left over.
Al runs out first, so no Al is left.

q: Equal numbers of moles of CH<sub>4</sub>, O<sub>2</sub> and He are sealed in a chamber and the combustion shown goes to completion. The amount of which substance determines how much CO<sub>2</sub> forms?
h: Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest quotient marks the limiting reactant. Helium does not react.
w: Each mole of CH4 needs 2 mol O2, so with equal moles the O2 runs out first and limits the CO2. CH4 is left over; helium is an inert bystander and affects nothing.
x: Compare moles ÷ coefficient for each reactant. CH₄ is not the one that runs out.
Helium is an inert noble gas and doesn't react at all, so it can't limit the product. Compare moles ÷ coefficient for CH₄ and O₂.
Equal moles do not mean equal consumption; check the coefficients.

q: 4,000 molecules of NH<sub>3</sub> and 5,000 molecules of O<sub>2</sub> react completely according to the equation shown. How many molecules in total are present afterward?
h: Check whether the amounts are in the exact 4 : 5 ratio, then count the product molecules formed. Molecules are not conserved, atoms are.
w: 4,000 : 5,000 is exactly 4 : 5, so both reactants are used up: 4,000 NO + 6,000 H2O = 10,000 molecules. 9,000 assumes the number of molecules is conserved (only atoms are); 4,000 and 6,000 count a single product.
x: The number of molecules isn't conserved. Only atoms are.
4,000 counts only the NO.
6,000 counts only the H₂O.

q: An open beaker of 1.0 M KCl solution is left on the bench for a week and some of the water evaporates. Which statement describes the solution afterward?
c: The moles of KCl are unchanged and the molarity has increased.
The moles of KCl have decreased and the molarity has decreased.
The moles of KCl are unchanged and the molarity is still 1.0 M.
The moles of KCl have increased and the molarity has increased.
h: Only water (solvent) leaves. Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution.
w: Evaporation removes solvent only, so the moles of KCl stay the same while the volume shrinks, raising the molarity. Solute cannot leave or appear; the molarity changes because the denominator changes.
x: KCl is a nonvolatile ionic solid, so it can't evaporate; only water leaves. With the same moles in less volume, the molarity can't go down.
The volume shrank, so the molarity went up.
Nothing added KCl to the beaker; evaporation removes only water, so the moles of solute stay fixed. The molarity rises only because the volume shrinks.

q: Which procedure correctly prepares 250.0 mL of 0.100 M NaCl (58.44 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)?
c: Weigh 1.46 g NaCl, dissolve it in water, and add water until the total volume is 250.0 mL.
Weigh 1.46 g NaCl and add 250.0 mL of water.
Weigh 5.84 g NaCl, dissolve it in water, and add water until the total volume is 250.0 mL.
Weigh 5.84 g NaCl and add 250.0 mL of water.
h: Moles = M × V(L); molarity is per liter of SOLUTION, so dilute to the final volume rather than adding a fixed volume of water.
w: 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.2500 L = 0.0250 mol × 58.44 g mol⁻¹ = 1.46 g, dissolved and diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL. Adding 250.0 mL of water gives a slightly larger total volume and a lower concentration; 5.84 g uses 1.000 L instead of 0.2500 L.
x: Adding 250.0 mL of water makes the total volume too big.
5.84 g is for 1 L, not 0.2500 L.
5.84 g is for 1 L, and adding 250.0 mL of water makes the volume too big.

q: What volume of solution is needed to make a 0.250 M solution of KNO<sub>3</sub> (101.10 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) from 15.0 g of the solid?
h: Convert grams to moles, then V = moles ÷ molarity.
w: 15.0 g ÷ 101.10 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1484 mol; V = 0.1484 mol ÷ 0.250 mol L⁻¹ = 0.593 L. 0.0371 L multiplies moles by molarity instead of dividing; 60.0 L skips the molar-mass conversion.
x: This multiplies moles by molarity. Divide instead.
This divides molarity by moles (upside down).
This skips converting grams to moles.

q: A 40.0 mL portion of 0.200 M AgNO<sub>3</sub> is treated with 0.150 M Na<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> until all of the silver has precipitated (equation shown). How many milliliters of the chromate solution are used?
h: Moles AgNO<sub>3</sub> = M × V; convert to moles Na<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> with the 2 : 1 ratio; then V = n ÷ M.
w: 0.0400 L × 0.200 M = 0.00800 mol AgNO3 × (1 mol Na2CrO4 / 2 mol AgNO3) = 0.00400 mol; ÷ 0.150 M = 26.7 mL. 53.3 mL assumes a 1 : 1 ratio; 107 mL inverts the ratio.
x: This uses a 1:1 ratio. Each CrO₄²⁻ takes 2 Ag⁺.
107 mL comes from multiplying the Ag⁺ moles by 2, which inverts the ratio. Each CrO₄²⁻ precipitates 2 Ag⁺, so you need half as many moles of chromate as silver.
This divides by 2 twice. Apply the 2:1 ratio only once.

q: A student combines three 1.0 M solutions in one beaker: NaBr, K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and Ba(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. A white solid appears. What is it?
h: List every cation–anion pairing possible in the mixture and apply the solubility rules.
w: The ions present are Na+, K+, Ba2+, Br−, SO2−4 and NO−3. Group 1 salts and nitrates are soluble, and bromides are soluble except with Ag+, Pb2+ and Hg2+2; sulfate with Ba2+ is insoluble, so BaSO4 precipitates.
x: Bromides are soluble except with Ag⁺, Pb²⁺ and Hg₂²⁺.
Sodium compounds are always soluble.
Potassium compounds and nitrates are always soluble.

q: Ba<sup>2+</sup>, Ag<sup>+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> are all dissolved in one solution, and three reagents are available: HCl, Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and NaOH. Using the table, choose the sequence of additions that removes the cations one at a time, each as its own precipitate.
h: Each reagent added must precipitate exactly ONE of the cations still in solution. Check every reagent against all remaining ions.
w: Cl− precipitates only Ag+ (AgCl), leaving Ba2+ and Cu2+; sulfate then removes only Ba2+ (BaSO4; CuSO4 is soluble); finally OH− precipitates Cu(OH)2: HCl, Na2SO4, NaOH. Adding NaOH or Na2SO4 first would precipitate two cations at once (Ag+ forms insoluble hydroxide and slightly soluble sulfate).

head: Anion
Insoluble with
rows: all except group 1, Ba<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup>

x: Sulfate first would precipitate Ba²⁺ and some Ag⁺ together.
NaOH first would precipitate Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺ together.
NaOH first would precipitate Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺ together.

q: Four acid–base reactions are listed. When each is rewritten as a net ionic equation, which one simplifies to H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + OH<sup>−</sup>(aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O(l)?
h: Only strong acids, strong soluble bases and soluble salts are written as separate ions.
w: HNO3 + KOH: both are strong and fully dissociated, and KNO3 is soluble, so K+ and NO−3 cancel, leaving H+ + OH− → H2O. HF is a weak acid (written as HF), Mg(OH)2 is an insoluble solid, and NH3 is a weak base with no OH− in its equation.
x: HF is a weak acid, so it stays as HF.
Mg(OH)₂ is an insoluble solid, so it stays whole.
NH₃ is a weak base. No OH⁻ appears in its equation.

q: Methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is a weak base. Which best describes the particles in an aqueous solution of methylamine?
c: Mostly CH3NH2 molecules and water, with a small number of CH3NH+3 and OH− ions
Only CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> molecules and water molecules
CH3NH+3 and OH− ions and water, with essentially no CH3NH2 molecules
CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup> and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions and water
h: A weak base accepts a proton from water to a small extent: a few ions form, but most molecules stay intact.
w: A weak base ionizes only partially: CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH+3 + OH− lies far to the left, so mostly molecules with a few ions. No ions at all would be a nonelectrolyte; complete ionization describes a strong base; a base accepts H+, so CH3NH− and H3O+ do not form.
x: A weak base forms a few ions, not none.
A weak base stays mostly as molecules.
A base accepts H⁺. It doesn't form CH₃NH⁻ and H₃O⁺.

q: Nitrogen appears in each reaction below. In which one does nitrogen GAIN electrons, that is, undergo reduction?
h: Assign oxidation numbers to N before and after. Reduction = decrease in oxidation number (gain of electrons).
w: In N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3, nitrogen goes from 0 to −3: reduced. N2 → NO is 0 → +2 (oxidized); NH3 → NO is −3 → +2 (oxidized); NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl leaves N at −3, an acid–base reaction with no electron transfer.
x: N goes from 0 to +2, which is oxidation.
N stays at −3. No electrons are transferred.
N goes from −3 to +2, which is oxidation.

q: One-gram samples of lead and aluminum, both at 20 °C, are dropped into a large bath of boiling water and left until nothing changes. Which statement is correct?
c: Aluminum absorbs more energy than lead, and the two reach the same final temperature.
Lead absorbs more energy than aluminum, and the two reach the same final temperature.
The two absorb the same energy, but lead reaches a higher final temperature.
The two absorb the same energy, but aluminum reaches a higher final temperature.
h: At thermal equilibrium every object is at the bath temperature. q = mcΔT with equal m and equal ΔT.
w: Both end at 100 °C, so ΔT is the same and the sample with the larger specific heat, aluminum (0.897 vs 0.128 J g−1 °C−1), absorbs about 7 times more energy. Equal-energy answers confuse 'same final temperature' with 'same heat'.
x: Lead's specific heat is smaller, so it absorbs less energy.
They reach the same temperature, but they absorb different amounts of energy.
They reach the same temperature, but they absorb different amounts of energy.

q: To identify a metal, a student heats a 28.0 g piece to 98.0 °C and transfers it into an insulated cup holding 50.0 g of water at 22.0 °C. The water and metal settle at 25.5 °C. What specific heat does this give for the metal?
h: Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water. Use each object's OWN ΔT; the metal's ΔT is 98.0 − 25.5.
w: qwater = (50.0 g)(4.184 J g−1 °C−1)(3.5 °C) = 732 J. cmetal = 732 J ÷ [(28.0 g)(72.5 °C)] = 0.361 J g−1 °C−1. 0.0862 omits the specific heat of water; 2.77 inverts the ratio; 7.47 uses the metal's 72.5 °C drop as the water's temperature change too.
x: This leaves out water's specific heat.
2.77 divides (mass × ΔT) of the metal by the heat, which inverts the formula. Specific heat is c = q ÷ (m × ΔT), with the 732 J of heat on top.
This uses the metal's 72.5 °C drop for the water too.

q: A hot iron horseshoe is plunged into a bucket of cool water inside an insulated container, and the two reach the same temperature. Assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings, which statement is correct?
c: The energy lost by the iron equals the energy gained by the water.
The iron loses more energy than the water gains because the iron was much hotter.
The water gains more energy than the iron loses because water has a higher specific heat.
The iron and the water each lose energy until they reach equilibrium.
h: Energy is conserved: q<sub>iron</sub> + q<sub>water</sub> = 0. Specific heat and temperature difference affect the ΔT values, not the energy balance.
w: With no losses, every joule the iron gives up goes into the water: qlost = qgained. The higher specific heat of water means its temperature changes less, not that it gains more energy; the water gains energy, it does not lose it.
x: With no losses, energy lost equals energy gained.
Water's higher specific heat means a smaller temperature change, not more energy.
The water gains energy. It doesn't lose it.

q: A student mixes 50.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl with 50.0 mL of 1.0 M NaOH in a foam cup and records a temperature rise ΔT<sub>1</sub>. She repeats the experiment with 25.0 mL of each solution and records ΔT<sub>2</sub>. If no heat is lost, how are the two related?
h: Halving the volumes halves the heat released AND halves the mass that absorbs it. ΔT = q/(mc).
w: Half as many moles react, so half as much heat is released, but it warms half as much solution: ΔT = q/(mc) is unchanged, so ΔT2 = ΔT1. Choosing ½ ΔT1 considers only the smaller q and forgets the smaller mass.
x: Halving the volumes halves the heat released, but what else is halved?
Halving the volumes halves the heat released, but what else is halved?
Halving the volumes halves the heat released, but what else is halved?

q: A welding torch burns 0.400 mol of acetylene by the reaction shown and releases 519.6 kJ of heat. What is ΔH for the equation as written, which consumes 2 mol of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>?
h: Find kJ per mole of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>, then multiply by the 2 in the equation. Heat released means ΔH is negative.
w: 519.6 kJ ÷ 0.400 mol = 1299 kJ per mol C2H2; the equation consumes 2 mol, so ΔH = −2 × 1299 = −2598 kJ. −1299 kJ forgets the coefficient 2; a positive sign would mean heat absorbed; −208 kJ multiplies instead of dividing by the moles.
x: This forgets the coefficient 2.
Heat is released, so ΔH is negative.
This multiplies by the moles instead of dividing.

q: A 0.500 g pellet of benzoic acid is burned in a bomb calorimeter and the temperature rises by 2.65 °C. Using the data in the table, what is the heat capacity of the calorimeter?
h: q<sub>released</sub> = (moles burned)(|ΔH<sub>comb</sub>|). The calorimeter absorbs it all: C = q/ΔT.
w: 0.500 g ÷ 122.12 g mol⁻¹ = 0.00409 mol × 3227 kJ mol⁻¹ = 13.21 kJ; C = 13.21 kJ ÷ 2.65 °C = 4.99 kJ °C−1. 609 treats 3227 kJ as per gram; 1218 forgets the sample size entirely; 0.201 inverts C.
x: This treats 3227 kJ as per gram. It's per mole.
This forgets the sample size.
This flips C. C = heat ÷ ΔT.

q: Which equation represents the reaction whose enthalpy change is the standard enthalpy of formation, ΔH°<sub>f</sub>, of liquid methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH(l)?
c: C(s, graphite) + 2 H<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½ O<sub>2</sub>(g) → CH<sub>3</sub>OH(l)
h: Formation: exactly 1 mol of product from its ELEMENTS in their standard states (H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, graphite).
w: C(graphite) + 2 H2 + ½ O2 → CH3OH(l) makes one mole from the elements as they exist at 25 °C. CO is a compound, not an element; isolated gaseous atoms are not the standard states of the elements; the equation that forms 2 mol of CH3OH has that coefficient, so its ΔH is 2ΔH°f.
x: CO is a compound, not an element.
Separate gas atoms aren't the standard states of the elements.
This forms 2 mol, so its ΔH is 2 × ΔH°f.

q: Let x stand for ΔH°f of ammonia gas. In terms of x, what is ΔH° for decomposing two moles of ammonia into its elements, 2 NH3(g) → N2(g) + 3 H2(g)?
h: Write the formation reaction of NH<sub>3</sub>, then see how the target reaction is related: reversed and doubled.
w: Formation: ½ N2 + 3/2 H2 → NH3, ΔH = x. The target is that reaction reversed (sign flips) and multiplied by 2: −2x. 2x forgets to flip the sign on reversal; −x forgets the factor of 2.
x: Reversing the reaction flips the sign.
This forgets the factor of 2.
This halves instead of doubling.

q: Using the two equations shown, which expression gives the standard enthalpy of formation of hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(l)?
h: Target: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) → H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>(l). Halve equation 1 and reverse equation 2 so the H<sub>2</sub>O cancels.
w: ½ × (1): H2 + ½ O2 → H2O, ½ΔH1. Reverse (2): H2O + ½ O2 → H2O2, −ΔH2. Adding gives H2 + O2 → H2O2, so ΔH°f = ½ ΔH1 − ΔH2. Adding +ΔH2 forgets the sign change on reversing; ΔH1 − ΔH2 forgets to halve equation 1.
x: Reversing equation 2 flips its sign.
This forgets to halve equation 1.
This has the overall sign reversed.

q: Sulfur trioxide can be made from sulfur in two stages (table). Combine the two equations to obtain ΔH° for the overall reaction shown.
h: Double equation 1 and reverse equation 2 (change its sign) so that 2 SO<sub>2</sub> cancels.
w: 2 × (−296.8) = −593.6 kJ for 2 S + 2 O2 → 2 SO2; reversing equation 2 gives 2 SO2 + O2 → 2 SO3, −197.8 kJ. Sum: −791.4 kJ. −395.8 doubles equation 1 but adds equation 2 without reversing it; −99.0 neither doubles nor reverses; −593.6 ignores equation 2.
x: This adds equation 2 as written. Equation 2 must be reversed so SO₂ cancels, and reversing it changes the sign of its ΔH°.
This neither doubles nor reverses.
−593.6 kJ is just equation 1 doubled; it leaves out equation 2, so SO₂ never becomes SO₃. Add equation 2 (reversed, with its sign changed) so SO₂ cancels.

q: Ethanol burns according to the equation shown, with ΔH° = −1367 kJ. Using the enthalpies of formation in the table, what is ΔH°<sub>f</sub> of ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH(l)?
h: ΔH°<sub>rxn</sub> = Σ ΔH°<sub>f</sub>(products) − Σ ΔH°<sub>f</sub>(reactants); O<sub>2</sub> contributes zero. Solve for the one unknown.
w: −1367 = [2(−393.5) + 3(−285.8)] − [ΔH°f(ethanol) + 0]; the products sum to −1644.4 kJ, so ΔH°f(ethanol) = −1644.4 + 1367 = −277.4 kJ mol−1. −3011.4 adds ΔH°rxn instead of subtracting; −1644.4 is just the product sum.
x: This adds ΔH°rxn instead of subtracting it.
Check the rearrangement. The products together are more negative than ΔH°rxn, so ethanol's ΔH°f must come out negative.
This is just the products' sum.

q: Compare the two enthalpies of formation in the table. Making NaF from sodium and fluorine is ____ making NaCl from sodium and chlorine.
h: Both values are negative (exothermic). Compare how far below zero each one lies.
w: Both reactions release heat (negative ΔH°f); −576.6 kJ releases more than −411.2 kJ, so NaF formation is more exothermic. 'Less exothermic' treats the smaller (more negative) number as less heat released; neither process is endothermic.
x: A more negative ΔH°f means more heat is released per mole formed. Compare −576.6 with −411.2 again.
Both are negative, so both are exothermic.
Both are negative, so both are exothermic.

q: Which list places the ionic solids KBr, MgO, KCl and CaO in order from the weakest to the strongest lattice energy?
h: Lattice energy ∝ (q<sub>+</sub>q<sub>−</sub>)/r. Sort by ion charges first, then by ion size within the same charges.
w: The 2+/2− oxides far exceed the 1+/1− salts. Among the 1+/1− pair, the smaller Cl− gives KCl a larger lattice energy than KBr; among the oxides, the smaller Mg2+ puts MgO above CaO: KBr < KCl < CaO < MgO. Putting KCl below KBr or MgO below CaO reverses the size effect, and the fully reversed list ranks strongest first.
x: KCl's smaller Cl⁻ gives it a larger lattice energy than KBr.
MgO's smaller Mg²⁺ gives it a larger lattice energy than CaO.
This list runs from strongest to weakest, the reverse of what was asked. Higher ion charges (2+/2−) and smaller ions give larger lattice energies, so those belong at the end.

q: Using the electronegativities in the table, how is the bond between nitrogen and hydrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> best described?
h: ΔEN below about 0.4 is nonpolar covalent, roughly 0.4–1.7 polar covalent, above about 1.7 ionic.
w: ΔEN = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9: electrons are shared unequally, a polar covalent bond with N partially negative. The difference is too small for ionic character and too large to call nonpolar; metallic bonding occurs between metal atoms only.
x: A difference of 0.9 is too big to be nonpolar.
A difference of 0.9 is too small to be ionic.
Metallic bonding happens only between metal atoms.

q: Which description of the bonding in sodium hydroxide, NaOH, is correct?
c: An ionic bond between Na<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup>, and a covalent bond between O and H
Covalent bonds between Na and O and between O and H
Ionic bonds between Na and O and between O and H
A covalent bond between Na and O and an ionic bond between O and H
h: A metal with a polyatomic ion is ionic; the atoms INSIDE the polyatomic ion are held together covalently.
w: NaOH is an ionic compound of Na+ and the hydroxide ion; within OH− the O–H bond is covalent (two nonmetals sharing electrons). Na–O is not covalent (metal + nonmetal, large ΔEN), and O–H is not ionic.
x: Na–O isn't covalent (metal + nonmetal).
O–H isn't ionic (two nonmetals sharing).
This swaps the bond types. Na–O is a metal–nonmetal pair with a big electronegativity difference (ionic), while O–H is two nonmetals sharing electrons (covalent).

q: What holds a crystal of potassium bromide, KBr, together?
c: Electrostatic attraction between K<sup>+</sup> ions and Br<sup>−</sup> ions
Shared pairs of electrons between K and Br atoms
A sea of mobile electrons surrounding K and Br atoms
Dipole–dipole attractions between neighboring KBr molecules
h: Metal + nonmetal: electrons are transferred, and the resulting ions attract each other in a lattice.
w: Ionic bonding is the attraction between oppositely charged ions, K+ and Br−, extending throughout the crystal. Shared pairs describe covalent bonds; an electron sea describes metals; there are no KBr 'molecules' in the solid.
x: Shared pairs describe covalent bonds.
A sea of electrons describes metals.
There are no KBr molecules in the solid.

q: The carbonate ion, CO2−3, has three equivalent resonance structures. Using the bond enthalpies in the table, what is the best estimate of the energy of one carbon–oxygen bond in carbonate?
h: Resonance averages the bonds: each C–O is one-third double and two-thirds single (bond order 1⅓).
w: Across the three structures each C–O position is single in two and double in one, so its energy ≈ (358 + 358 + 799)/3 = 505 kJ mol−1, between a single and a double bond. 358 and 799 treat the bond as purely single or double; 1515 is the total for all three bonds.
x: 358 treats the bond as purely single.
799 treats the bond as purely double.
1515 is the total for all three bonds.

q: Four balloons at 1.00 atm and 300 K are each filled with a different gas. Which balloon holds the densest gas?
h: At the same P and T, equal volumes hold equal moles, so density tracks molar mass.
w: d = PM/RT: at fixed P and T the densest gas has the largest molar mass. Cl2 (70.90 g mol⁻¹) beats CO2 (44.01), Ar (39.95) and N2 (28.02). Argon is tempting because its atoms are heavy, but each Cl2 molecule is heavier still.
x: CO₂ (44 g/mol) is lighter than Cl₂.
Ar (40 g/mol) is lighter than Cl₂.
N₂ (28 g/mol) is lighter than Cl₂.

q: A fixed amount of ideal gas has its pressure doubled while its absolute temperature is halved. What happens to its volume?
c: It becomes one-quarter of the original volume.
It becomes half of the original volume.
It becomes four times the original volume.
h: V ∝ T/P for a fixed amount of gas. Apply both changes.
w: V = nRT/P. Doubling P halves V, and halving T halves it again: V becomes ¼ of the original. 'Half' applies only one of the two changes; 'the same' would require P and T to change in the same direction by the same factor.
x: This applies only one of the two changes.
Both changes shrink the volume, so it doesn't stay the same.
This is upside down. Both changes make V smaller.

q: A 5.00 g sample of CaCO<sub>3</sub> (100.09 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is heated and decomposes as shown. The CO<sub>2</sub> collected occupies 0.952 L at 25 °C and 1.00 atm. What is the percent yield?
h: Theoretical moles of CO<sub>2</sub> from the mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub>; actual moles from PV = nRT (T in kelvin). Yield = actual/theoretical.
w: Theoretical: 5.00 ÷ 100.09 = 0.0500 mol CO2. Actual: n = PV/RT = (1.00)(0.952)/[(0.08206)(298 K)] = 0.0389 mol. Yield = 0.0389/0.0500 = 77.9%. 85.1% uses 22.4 L mol⁻¹, which applies only at 0 °C; 128% inverts the ratio; 43.6% divides the 5.00 g by the molar mass of CaO instead of CaCO3.
x: 22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C.
128% divides the theoretical moles (0.0500) by the actual moles (0.0389), which inverts the ratio. Percent yield is actual ÷ theoretical × 100, so it can't exceed 100% here.
This uses CaO's molar mass. Use CaCO₃'s.

q: A rigid container of gas is heated. According to kinetic molecular theory, why does the pressure increase?
c: The molecules move faster, so they strike the walls more often and each collision exerts more force.
The molecules expand and take up a larger share of the container's volume.
Attractions between the molecules weaken, releasing more molecules to hit the walls.
Heating creates additional gas molecules, so there are more collisions.
h: Pressure comes from wall collisions. Think about how the speed of the molecules affects both the rate and the force of those collisions.
w: Higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy and speed: more frequent and more forceful collisions with the walls, so P rises. Ideal-gas molecules have negligible volume and no attractions, and heating does not create molecules.
x: Ideal gas molecules don't expand.
Ideal gas molecules have no attractions.
Heating doesn't create molecules.

q: At room temperature chlorine, Cl<sub>2</sub>, is a gas but iodine, I<sub>2</sub>, is a solid. What is the best explanation?
c: I<sub>2</sub> has more electrons and is more polarizable, so its dispersion forces are stronger.
The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond, so I<sub>2</sub> is harder to pull apart.
I<sub>2</sub> molecules are polar and attract one another by dipole–dipole forces.
I<sub>2</sub> molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another.
h: Both are nonpolar diatomics with only dispersion forces; compare their size and electron count. Melting breaks intermolecular forces, not bonds.
w: Both molecules are nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act; the larger, more polarizable I2 has much stronger dispersion forces and is a solid. The I–I bond is actually weaker than Cl–Cl, and bond strength is irrelevant to the phase anyway; neither molecule is polar or hydrogen-bonds.
x: The I–I bond is actually weaker, and bonds don't decide the phase anyway.
I₂ is nonpolar: two identical atoms share the electrons equally, so there is no dipole. The only attraction between I₂ molecules is London dispersion.
I₂ has no H atoms, so it can't hydrogen bond.

q: Liquid X has stronger intermolecular forces than liquid Y. At the same temperature, compared with Y, liquid X has
c: a higher enthalpy of vaporization and a lower vapor pressure.
a higher enthalpy of vaporization and a higher vapor pressure.
a lower enthalpy of vaporization and a lower vapor pressure.
a lower enthalpy of vaporization and a higher vapor pressure.
h: Stronger attractions make escaping into the vapor harder: more energy per mole and fewer molecules in the gas phase.
w: Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to vaporize (higher ΔHvap) and let fewer molecules escape, giving a lower vapor pressure. Pairing a high ΔHvap with a high vapor pressure confuses 'hard to vaporize' with 'lots of vapor'.
x: Stronger forces mean fewer molecules escape, so the vapor pressure is lower.
Stronger forces mean a higher ΔH_vap.
This describes the liquid with weaker forces. Stronger attractions take more energy to overcome (higher ΔH_vap) and let fewer molecules escape (lower vapor pressure).

q: A chemist describes an unknown as soft and waxy, melting at 53 °C, a nonconductor whether solid or molten, insoluble in water yet soluble in hexane. What type of solid is it?
h: Low melting point plus no conductivity even when melted points to discrete neutral molecules held by weak forces.
w: A low melting point, no mobile ions or electrons in any state, and solubility in a nonpolar solvent all fit a molecular solid held together by intermolecular forces. An ionic solid conducts when molten and melts high; a metal conducts; a network solid melts extremely high and is insoluble in everything.
x: Ionic solids melt high and conduct when molten.
Metals conduct electricity.
Network solids melt extremely high.

q: Formaldehyde, H<sub>2</sub>C=O, is used to preserve tissue samples. What are the hybridizations of the carbon atom and of the oxygen atom?
h: Count electron groups on each atom, including the oxygen: bonded atoms + lone pairs, with a double bond counted once.
w: C has 3 groups (C=O and two C–H) → sp2. O has 1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs = 3 groups → sp2. So C sp2, O sp2. The unhybridized 2p orbital left on each atom forms the C=O π bond.
x: O has only 3 groups (1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs), so it is sp<sup>2</sup>. Counting the double bond as two groups gives sp<sup>3</sup>.
sp<sup>3</sup> needs 4 groups. C has 3 (the double bond counts once), and so does O.
sp needs only 2 groups. C has 3 and O has 3.

q: In acetonitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>–C≡N, what are the hybridizations of the carbon bonded to nitrogen and of the nitrogen atom?
h: Count groups on the end nitrogen too: 1 bonded atom + its lone pair. A triple bond is one group.
w: The nitrile carbon has 2 groups (C–C and C≡N) → sp. The nitrogen has 1 bonded atom + 1 lone pair = 2 groups → sp. So C sp, N sp; each atom keeps two unhybridized 2p orbitals for the two π bonds.
x: N has 1 bonded atom + 1 lone pair = 2 groups, so it is sp, not sp³. A triple bond counts as one group.
N has 2 groups (the triple bond counts once, plus 1 lone pair), so it is sp.
The nitrile carbon has only 2 groups (C–C and C≡N), so it is sp.

q: Acetone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, is a common solvent and is found in the breath during ketosis. Which describes the C=O double bond?
c: one σ bond (C sp<sup>2</sup> – O sp<sup>2</sup>) and one π bond (C 2p – O 2p)
one σ bond (C sp<sup>2</sup> – O sp<sup>3</sup>) and one π bond (C 2p – O 2p)
two σ bonds, both C sp<sup>2</sup> – O sp<sup>2</sup>
one σ bond (C 2p – O 2p) and one π bond (C sp<sup>2</sup> – O sp<sup>2</sup>)
h: A double bond is one σ plus one π. σ = head-on overlap of hybrids; π = side-by-side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals.
w: C has 3 groups and O has 3 groups (1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs), so both are sp2. The σ bond is C sp2 – O sp2 and the π bond is C 2p – O 2p.
x: O has 3 groups (1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs), so it is sp<sup>2</sup>, not sp<sup>3</sup>.
Only one σ bond can form along the C–O axis. The second bond of a double bond is π.
These are swapped. Hybrids overlap head-on to make the σ bond; the 2p orbitals overlap side by side to make the π bond.

q: Which describes the C≡N triple bond in hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N?
c: one σ bond (C sp – N sp) and two π bonds (C 2p – N 2p)
one σ bond (C sp – N sp) and one π bond (C 2p – N 2p)
one σ bond (C sp – N sp<sup>3</sup>) and two π bonds (C 2p – N 2p)
three σ bonds, all C sp – N sp
h: A triple bond is one σ plus two π. Find the hybridization of C and of N by counting groups on each.
w: C has 2 groups (C–H and C≡N) → sp. N has 1 bonded atom + 1 lone pair = 2 groups → sp. The σ bond is C sp – N sp; the two π bonds come from the two unhybridized 2p orbitals on each atom, at 90° to each other.
x: A triple bond has two π bonds, not one.
N has 2 groups (1 bonded atom + 1 lone pair), so it is sp, not sp³.
Only one σ bond fits along the C–N axis. The other two bonds are π.

q: In CO<sub>2</sub> (O=C=O), what is the hybridization of each oxygen atom, and which orbitals overlap to form each C=O π bond?
c: O is sp<sup>2</sup>; each π bond is C 2p – O 2p
O is sp<sup>3</sup>; each π bond is C 2p – O 2p
O is sp; each π bond is C sp – O sp
O is sp<sup>2</sup>; each π bond is C sp – O sp<sup>2</sup>
h: Count groups on an oxygen (1 bonded atom + its lone pairs). π bonds never use hybrid orbitals.
w: Each O has 1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs = 3 groups → sp2. The central C is sp, so it keeps two unhybridized 2p orbitals, one for each π bond: C 2p – O 2p. The two π bonds are at 90° to each other.
x: O has 3 groups (1 bonded atom + 2 lone pairs), so it is sp<sup>2</sup>. Counting the double bond as two groups gives sp<sup>3</sup>.
π bonds use unhybridized p orbitals, not sp hybrids. And O has 3 groups, so it is sp².
π bonds come from side-by-side p orbitals. Hybrid orbitals (C sp, O sp²) form σ bonds and hold lone pairs.

q: Urea, (NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, is how the body gets rid of excess nitrogen. Which orbitals overlap to form the π bond of its C=O group?
h: π bonds form from side-by-side overlap of orbitals that were left out of hybridization.
w: Both C and O are sp2 (3 groups each). Each keeps one unhybridized 2p orbital, and these overlap side by side to form the π bond: C 2p and O 2p. The sp2 hybrids form the C=O σ bond.
x: The sp<sup>2</sup> hybrids form the C=O σ bond (head-on). The π bond uses the leftover 2p orbitals.
An sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid makes σ bonds, not π. The carbon's π orbital is its unhybridized 2p.
The oxygen is sp<sup>2</sup> (3 groups), and its π orbital is the unhybridized 2p, not a hybrid.

q:
A sealed, rigid steel container of an ideal gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K. Which statements are true?
I. The pressure of the gas doubles.
II. The root-mean-square speed of the molecules doubles.
III. The average kinetic energy of the molecules doubles.
h: In a rigid container n and V stay fixed. Compare how pressure, average kinetic energy and molecular speed each depend on the Kelvin temperature.
w: At constant n and V, P is proportional to T, so doubling the Kelvin temperature doubles P (I true). Average kinetic energy is proportional to T, so it also doubles (III true). The rms speed is √(3RT/M), so it rises only by √2, about 1.41 times (II false). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement II is false: rms speed depends on √T, so doubling T raises the speed by only about 1.41 times.
Statement III is also true: average kinetic energy is directly proportional to the Kelvin temperature.
Statement I is true: with n and V fixed, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature.

q:
The rigid flask shown holds a mixture of N2 and H2 at a total pressure of 4.0 atm. Which statements are true?
I. The partial pressure of H2 is 3.0 atm.
II. If helium is pumped into the flask at constant temperature, the partial pressure of N2 does not change.
III. The N2 molecules have a greater average kinetic energy than the H2 molecules.
h: Count molecules to get mole fractions. A gas's partial pressure depends only on its own moles, the volume and the temperature.
w: The flask holds 6 H2 and 2 N2 molecules, so χ(H2) = 6/8 and P(H2) = 0.75 × 4.0 atm = 3.0 atm (I true). Adding He raises the total pressure, but n(N2), V and T are unchanged, so P(N2) = n(N2)RT/V stays 1.0 atm (II true). At the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy; the heavier N2 simply moves more slowly (III false). The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is true: P(N₂) = n(N₂)RT/V, and none of those change when helium is added to a rigid flask.
Statement III is false: at the same temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy. Heavier molecules just move slower.
Statement I is true: 6 of the 8 molecules are H₂, and 6/8 of 4.0 atm is 3.0 atm.

q:
Which comparisons of lattice energy (in magnitude) are correct?
I. MgO has a larger lattice energy than NaF.
II. NaCl has a larger lattice energy than NaI.
III. CaO has a larger lattice energy than KCl.
h: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ion charges and shrinks as the distance between ion centers grows. Charge matters most.
w: MgO (2+, 2−) beats NaF (1+, 1−) because of its larger ion charges (I correct). Cl− is smaller than I−, so the ions in NaCl are closer together and attract more strongly than in NaI (II correct). CaO has 2+ and 2− ions while KCl has 1+ and 1− ions, so CaO has the larger lattice energy (III correct). The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III is also correct: Ca²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges, while K⁺ and Cl⁻ carry single charges.
Statement II is also correct: Cl⁻ is smaller than I⁻, so the ions in NaCl sit closer together.
Statement I is correct: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have twice the charges of Na⁺ and F⁻, which outweighs small size differences.

q:
The nitrate ion, NO3−, is described by three equivalent resonance structures, each with one N=O double bond and two N–O single bonds. Which statements about nitrate are true?
I. The ion switches rapidly back and forth among the three structures.
II. All three nitrogen–oxygen bonds in the real ion have the same length.
III. In each of the three structures, the nitrogen atom has a formal charge of +1.
h: Resonance structures are not real molecules that take turns existing. For formal charge, count the nitrogen's bonds and lone pairs in one structure.
w: The real ion is a single blend (hybrid) of the three structures; it does not flip between them (I false). Because every N–O bond is the same blend of one double and two single bonds, all three have the same length, with bond order 1⅓ (II true). In each structure N has four bonds and no lone pairs, so its formal charge is 5 − 0 − 4 = +1 (III true). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III is true: nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and in each structure it has 4 bonds and no lone pairs, giving 5 − 4 = +1.
Statement I is false: resonance structures do not take turns. The real ion is one hybrid structure all the time.
Statement I is false: the ion does not flip between structures. It is a single average of all three.

q:
Which statements describe trends across period 3 from sodium to chlorine?
I. Atomic radius decreases.
II. The effective nuclear charge felt by the valence electrons increases.
III. Metallic character increases.
h: Across a period, protons are added while the valence electrons stay in the same shell.
w: Moving from Na to Cl, each element adds a proton, but the added electron goes into the same n = 3 shell and shields poorly, so Zeff rises (II true). The valence electrons are pulled in more tightly, so atoms get smaller (I true). Holding electrons more tightly makes atoms less likely to lose them, so metallic character decreases: Na is a metal, Cl a nonmetal (III false). The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true: each step adds a proton while the new electron enters the same shell, so the pull on valence electrons grows.
Statement III is false: the period starts with the metal sodium and ends with the nonmetal chlorine, so metallic character falls.
Statement I is true: the stronger pull from the nucleus draws the n = 3 electrons closer, so atoms shrink across the period.

q:
Which statements about ionization energies are true?
I. The first ionization energy of Mg is greater than that of Al.
II. The first ionization energy of S is greater than that of P.
III. The second ionization energy of Na is greater than that of Mg.
h: Ask which electron is removed in each case: from a filled s subshell, from a p subshell, from a paired orbital, or from a noble-gas core.
w: Al's outermost electron is a lone 3p electron, higher in energy than Mg's 3s electrons, so Mg has the larger IE1 (I true). In S the fourth 3p electron is paired in an orbital, and the electron repulsion makes it easier to remove than any of P's unpaired 3p electrons, so S has the smaller IE1 (II false). Na's second electron comes from the 2p core, while Mg's second electron is still a 3s valence electron, so Na's IE2 is far larger (III true). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: removing a second electron from Na means breaking into the neon core, which takes much more energy.
Statement II is false: sulfur's paired 3p electron is pushed by its partner, so it comes off more easily than phosphorus's unpaired 3p electrons.
Statement I is true: aluminum's single 3p electron is higher in energy and easier to remove than magnesium's 3s electrons.

q:
Light shining on a clean metal surface ejects electrons. Which statements about this photoelectric effect are true?
I. Making the light brighter, at the same frequency, raises the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons.
II. Light of any frequency will eject electrons if it is bright enough.
III. Using light of a higher frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons.
h: Each electron is ejected by one photon. Brightness sets the number of photons, while frequency sets the energy of each photon.
w: The energy of one photon is E = hν, and the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is hν minus the work function, so a higher frequency gives faster electrons (III true). Brighter light means more photons of the same energy, so more electrons come off but none of them faster (I false). Below the threshold frequency each photon has too little energy, and no brightness can make up for it (II false). The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is false: brighter light gives more electrons, but each photon still has the same energy, so the electrons are not faster.
Statement II is false: below the threshold frequency no electrons come off, however bright the light is.
Statement II is false: a photon below the threshold frequency cannot free an electron, and adding more such photons does not help.

q:
Natural gas burns in a furnace, an exothermic reaction at constant pressure. Taking the reacting chemicals as the system, which statements are true?
I. The products have a greater enthalpy than the reactants.
II. q for the system is negative.
III. The surroundings become colder.
h: Exothermic means heat leaves the system. Think about where that heat goes.
w: In an exothermic reaction heat flows out of the system, so q (and ΔH) for the system is negative (II true). Since heat is released, the products have LESS enthalpy than the reactants (I false). The released heat goes into the surroundings, which get warmer, not colder (III false). The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is false: in an exothermic reaction the products end up lower in enthalpy, because energy has left as heat.
Statement III is false: the heat released by the system flows into the surroundings and warms them.
