Statement III is false: heat leaves the system and enters the surroundings, so they warm up.

q:
The enthalpy change for the reaction shown is ΔH° = −572 kJ. Which statements are true?
I. For H2(g) + ½ O2(g) → H2O(l), ΔH° = −286 kJ.
II. For 2 H2O(l) → 2 H2(g) + O2(g), ΔH° = +572 kJ.
III. For 2 H2(g) + O2(g) → 2 H2O(g), ΔH° = −572 kJ.
h: ΔH scales with the coefficients and changes sign when the equation is reversed. Also check the physical state of each product.
w: Halving every coefficient halves ΔH, giving −286 kJ (I true). Reversing the equation reverses the sign, giving +572 kJ (II true). Making water vapor instead of liquid water releases less heat, because the heat of condensation is not given off, so ΔH° for that reaction is less negative than −572 kJ (III false). The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement I is true: ΔH is an extensive quantity, so cutting all coefficients in half cuts ΔH in half.
Statement III is false: forming H₂O(g) instead of H₂O(l) skips the condensation step, so less heat is released.
Statement II is true and statement III is false: reversing a reaction flips the sign of ΔH, and the state of the product matters.

q:
A closed flask holds liquid water in equilibrium with its vapor at 25 °C. Which changes would increase the equilibrium vapor pressure of the water?
I. Raising the temperature to 35 °C.
II. Adding more liquid water to the flask.
III. Moving the water to a larger closed flask, with some liquid still present.
h: Equilibrium vapor pressure is a property of the liquid at a given temperature. It does not depend on how much liquid or space there is.
w: Vapor pressure depends only on the substance and its temperature. At a higher temperature more molecules have enough energy to escape, so the vapor pressure rises (I true). Adding liquid or giving the vapor more room changes how much liquid or vapor there is, but once equilibrium returns the pressure of the vapor is the same as before (II and III false). The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false: extra liquid does not change how easily molecules escape from the surface, so the equilibrium vapor pressure stays the same.
Statement III is false: in a larger flask more liquid evaporates until the vapor pressure returns to the same value at 25 °C.
Statement II is false: the amount of liquid does not matter, only the temperature sets the equilibrium vapor pressure.

q:
Which statements about phase diagrams are true?
I. At the triple point, the solid, liquid and gas phases can all exist together at equilibrium.
II. Above its critical temperature, a substance cannot be turned into a liquid by raising the pressure.
III. Because the solid–liquid line of water slopes to the left, squeezing ice that is just below 0 °C can melt it.
h: Recall what the triple point and the critical point mark, and which unusual feature water's phase diagram has.
w: The triple point is the one temperature and pressure where all three phases coexist (I true). Above the critical temperature the liquid and gas can no longer be told apart, so no pressure produces a separate liquid (II true). Water's melting line has a negative slope because liquid water is denser than ice, so higher pressure lowers the melting point and can melt ice just below 0 °C (III true). The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III is also true: liquid water is denser than ice, so pressure favors the liquid and lowers the melting point.
Statement II is also true: beyond the critical point, raising the pressure never produces a separate liquid phase.
Statement II is also true: above the critical temperature the gas and liquid merge, so pressure alone cannot form a separate liquid.

q:
Two aqueous solutions are compared at the same temperature: 0.10 m CaCl2 and 0.10 m glucose (C6H12O6). Assume CaCl2 dissociates completely. Which statements are true?
I. The CaCl2 solution has the lower freezing point.
II. The CaCl2 solution has the lower boiling point.
III. The glucose solution has the higher vapor pressure.
h: Colligative effects depend on the number of dissolved particles. Count the particles that one formula unit of each solute gives.
w: Each CaCl2 gives 3 ions (i = 3), so its solution has 0.30 m of particles versus 0.10 m for glucose. More particles lower the freezing point more (I true) and lower the vapor pressure more, so the glucose solution has the higher vapor pressure (III true). More particles RAISE the boiling point more, so the CaCl2 solution has the higher boiling point, not the lower one (II false). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true: the glucose solution has fewer dissolved particles, so its vapor pressure is lowered less.
Statement II is false: dissolved particles raise the boiling point, and CaCl₂ gives three times as many particles.
Statement II is false: more dissolved particles mean a higher boiling point, not a lower one.

q:
Equal volumes of 0.10 M aqueous solutions are mixed in each of these pairs. Which mixtures form a precipitate?
I. KNO3 and Na2SO4
II. AgNO3 and NaBr
III. Pb(NO3)2 and KI
h: Swap partners in each pair and use the solubility rules to check whether either new combination is insoluble.
w: Silver halides other than AgF are insoluble, so AgNO3 and NaBr form solid AgBr (II yes). Lead(II) iodide is insoluble, so Pb(NO3)2 and KI form yellow PbI2 (III yes). In pair I the possible new products are K2SO4 and NaNO3, and all nitrates and all alkali metal salts are soluble, so nothing forms (I no). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III also gives a solid: lead(II) iodide is one of the insoluble iodides.
Statement II also gives a solid: silver bromide is insoluble, like silver chloride.
Mixture I gives no solid: every possible product is a nitrate or a sodium or potassium salt, and all of those dissolve.

q:
Which statements are correct according to molecular orbital theory?
I. N2+ has a higher bond order than N2.
II. He2 has a bond order of ½.
III. O2+ has a shorter bond than O2.
h: Bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons). Note whether each removed electron comes from a bonding or an antibonding orbital.
w: N2 has bond order 3; removing an electron takes it from the bonding σ2p orbital, so N2+ has bond order 2.5, which is lower (I false). He2 has 2 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons, so its bond order is 0 (II false; ½ is the value for He2+). O2 has bond order 2; removing an electron from a π* antibonding orbital raises the bond order of O2+ to 2.5, so its bond is shorter (III correct). The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is incorrect: the electron removed from N₂ comes from a bonding orbital, so the bond order drops from 3 to 2.5.
Statement II is incorrect: He₂ has two bonding and two antibonding electrons, so its bond order is zero. The value ½ belongs to He₂⁺.
Statement II is incorrect: count the electrons in He₂. Equal numbers of bonding and antibonding electrons give no bond.

q: Two molecules of a compound of nitrogen and oxygen are broken down completely into N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>. The box shows ALL of the molecules that form. What are the molecular formula and the empirical formula of the compound?
h: Count the N and O atoms in the box and share them equally between the two original molecules. The empirical formula is the smallest whole-number ratio of the atoms.
w: The box holds 2 N2 and 4 O2, which is 4 N atoms and 8 O atoms. These came from 2 molecules, so each molecule had 2 N and 4 O: the molecular formula is N2O4. The ratio 2 : 4 reduces to 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is NO2. The answer is molecular N2O4; empirical NO2. N4O8 puts every atom in the box into one molecule, and NO2 as the molecular formula ignores that only two molecules were broken down.
x: These two are swapped. The empirical formula is the reduced ratio, so it can never have larger subscripts than the molecular formula.
This puts all the atoms in the box into one molecule, but the box came from two molecules. Also, an empirical formula must be fully reduced.
NO₂ is the reduced ratio, but the box came from only two molecules. Count how many N atoms each one must have held.

q: A sample of a hydrocarbon burns completely in excess O<sub>2</sub>. The box shows ALL of the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O molecules that formed (leftover O<sub>2</sub> is not shown). What is the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon?
h: Every C atom in the CO<sub>2</sub> and every H atom in the H<sub>2</sub>O came from the hydrocarbon. Count atoms, not molecules, then reduce the ratio.
w: There are 4 CO2 (4 C atoms) and 5 H2O (10 H atoms), so C : H = 4 : 10 = 2 : 5, giving C2H5. C4H5 counts one H per water molecule instead of two; C4H10 has the right ratio but is not reduced to an empirical formula. The O in the products came from O2, not from the hydrocarbon.
x: Each H₂O molecule carries two H atoms. Count H atoms, not water molecules.
This ratio is right, but an empirical formula must be reduced to the smallest whole numbers.
A hydrocarbon contains only C and H. The O atoms in the products came from the O₂.

q: Methane burns according to the equation shown. The Before box shows the reaction mixture. Which box (I–IV) shows the contents after the reaction goes to completion?
h: Find the limiting reactant first: each CH<sub>4</sub> needs 2 O<sub>2</sub>. Then check that every kind of atom is conserved.
w: Before: 3 CH4 and 4 O2. The 4 O2 can burn only 2 CH4, so O2 is limiting: 2 CO2 and 4 H2O form and 1 CH4 is left over, as in box III. Box I burns all 3 CH4, which needs 6 O2 (it has more O atoms than the Before box). Box II leaves O2 over even though O2 runs out first (and it has lost a C atom), and box IV loses H and O atoms.
x: Count O atoms in box I and in the Before box. Burning all the CH₄ would need more O₂ than is there.
Box II has O₂ left over, but compare how much O₂ each CH₄ needs with how much is present.
Count H atoms in box IV and in the Before box. Atoms must be conserved.

q: The two solutions shown, CaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) and Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>(aq), are mixed, and Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(s) precipitates until one of its ions is used up. Which ions are still dissolved after the reaction is complete?
h: Each formula unit of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> uses 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup> and 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>. Which ion runs out first, and which ions never react?
w: The boxes hold 4 Ca2+, 8 Cl−, 6 Na+ and 2 PO43−. The 2 PO43− take 3 Ca2+ to make one Ca3(PO4)2, so 1 Ca2+ is left, and the spectators Na+ and Cl− all stay dissolved: 1 Ca2+, 6 Na+ and 8 Cl− (charges balance: 2 + 6 = 8). Using a 1 : 1 ratio leaves 2 Ca2+, which does not balance the charge.
x: Phosphate runs out before all the calcium can react. Check how many Ca²⁺ ions 2 PO₄³⁻ can take.
This uses a 1 : 1 ratio of Ca²⁺ to PO₄³⁻. The solid's formula has 3 Ca for every 2 PO₄. Also check that the charges balance.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions. They do not go into the solid.

q: Four rigid containers have the SAME volume. Each holds the gas shown at the temperature in its caption. Which container has the HIGHEST pressure?
h: For an ideal gas at fixed volume, P is proportional to n × T. Count molecules (not atoms) and use kelvin temperatures.
w: P ∝ nT. I: 9 × 200 = 1800; II: 4 × 300 = 1200; III: 5 × 400 = 2000; IV: 3 × 600 = 1800. Container III is highest. Container I has the most particles and IV the highest temperature, but neither product is the largest. Counting atoms instead of molecules would wrongly favor IV (9 atoms in 3 CO2).
x: Container I has the most particles, but its temperature is the lowest. Multiply molecules by temperature.
Container II has few molecules at a moderate temperature. Compare n × T for every container.
Count molecules, not atoms. Three CO₂ molecules are only 3 gas particles, even at 600 K.

q: The rigid container shown holds N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> at a total pressure of 1.80 atm. The gases react completely by the equation shown, and the container is returned to the original temperature. What is the total pressure afterward?
h: At constant V and T, total pressure is proportional to the total number of gas molecules. Find the limiting reactant and count every molecule left, including leftover reactant.
w: Before: 3 N2 + 6 H2 = 9 molecules. The 6 H2 react with 2 N2 to give 4 NH3, leaving 1 N2: 5 molecules. P = (5/9)(1.80 atm) = 1.00 atm. 0.800 atm counts only the NH3, 1.20 atm assumes all 3 N2 react, and 1.80 atm assumes the pressure cannot change because mass is conserved.
x: Mass is conserved, but the number of gas molecules changes. Pressure depends on the number of molecules.
This counts only the NH₃. Leftover reactant also pushes on the walls.
This assumes all the N₂ reacts. Check whether there is enough H₂ for that.

q: Three sealed flasks at the SAME temperature each contain a different pure liquid, A, B or C, in equilibrium with its vapor. Each box shows the vapor molecules in an equal volume of the space above the liquid. Which ranks the liquids from WEAKEST to STRONGEST intermolecular forces?
h: More molecules in the same volume of vapor means a higher vapor pressure. How does vapor pressure depend on the forces holding molecules in the liquid?
w: The vapor boxes hold 8 (A), 3 (B) and 5 (C) molecules, so vapor pressure is A > C > B. Molecules escape most easily from the liquid with the weakest attractions, so the IMF order is A < C < B. Reversing this treats a high vapor pressure as a sign of strong forces.
x: This is reversed. Many molecules in the vapor means the liquid holds its molecules weakly.
Recount the vapor molecules above B and C.
Recount the vapor molecules above A and C.

q: Pure water is boiling at 100 °C. Which box best represents the contents of a bubble that forms inside the boiling water?
h: Boiling is a physical change. Are any bonds inside the water molecules broken?
w: Boiling separates whole H2O molecules from one another, so the bubble is filled with water vapor, box II. Box I (H2 and O2) and box III (separate H and O atoms) would require breaking O–H bonds, which is a chemical change such as electrolysis. Box IV is air, but the bubbles form from the water itself.
x: H₂ and O₂ form only if water decomposes, which is a chemical change. Boiling is physical.
Breaking water into separate atoms takes far more energy than boiling supplies.
Dissolved air can make a few bubbles in warm water, but the bubbles in boiling water come from the water itself.

q: Boxes X and Y each show the sugar molecules in 1.0 mL of a sugar solution (water not shown). Equal volumes of X and Y are mixed. Which box (I–IV) best represents 1.0 mL of the mixture?
h: Suppose you mix 1.0 mL of each. How many sugar molecules are present, and in what total volume?
w: 1.0 mL of X (8 molecules) plus 1.0 mL of Y (4 molecules) gives 12 molecules in 2.0 mL, or 6 molecules per 1.0 mL: box III. Box I adds the molecules but forgets that the volume also doubled. Boxes II and IV keep the concentration of one of the original solutions, but the mixture must lie between them.
x: This adds the molecules but forgets the volume doubled too.
This is solution Y unchanged. Mixing with the more concentrated X must raise the concentration.
This is solution X unchanged. Mixing with the more dilute Y must lower the concentration.

q: Each box shows the solute particles dissolved in the same mass of water in four different dilute solutions (water not shown). The ionic solutes dissociate completely. Which solution has the LOWEST freezing point?
h: Freezing-point depression depends on the total number of dissolved particles, not on what kind of particles they are.
w: Count every dissolved particle: I has 10 glucose molecules; II has 3 Na+ + 3 Cl− = 6; III has 3 Mg2+ + 6 Cl− = 9; IV has 4 K+ + 4 Cl− = 8. The most particles give the largest depression, so I freezes lowest. MgCl2 gives the most ions per formula unit, but box III still holds fewer particles than box I.
x: Count all the dissolved particles in each box, not just whether the solute is ionic.
MgCl₂ gives the most ions per formula unit, but count the total particles in each box.
Count the total particles in each box and compare.

q: Boxes I–IV show particle views of four samples made of two kinds of atoms, A and B. Which box represents a mixture of an element and a compound?
h: An element's molecules contain only one kind of atom. A compound's molecules contain two or more kinds bonded together.
w: Box III holds A2 molecules (an element) mixed with AB molecules (a compound). Box I is a mixture of two elements (A2 and B2), box II is a single pure compound (AB), and box IV is a mixture of two compounds (AB and AB2).
x: Both kinds of molecules in box I contain only one kind of atom, so both are elements.
Box II has only one kind of molecule, so it is a pure substance, not a mixture.
Every molecule in box IV contains both A and B, so all of them are compounds.

q: The box shows a representative sample of Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules made from the two natural isotopes of chlorine, <sup>35</sup>Cl (34.97 u) and <sup>37</sup>Cl (36.97 u). Based on this sample, what is the average atomic mass of chlorine?
h: Count the individual atoms of each isotope (not the molecules), find each isotope's fraction, and take a weighted average.
w: The 10 molecules contain 20 atoms: 15 35Cl and 5 37Cl, so the fractions are 0.75 and 0.25. Average = 0.75(34.97) + 0.25(36.97) = 35.47 u. 35.97 u is a simple average that ignores abundance, 36.47 u swaps the fractions, and 70.94 u is the average mass of a Cl2 molecule, not a Cl atom.
x: This is a simple average. The two isotopes are not equally common in the box.
This gives the larger weight to the rarer isotope. Recount which isotope is more common.
This is the average mass of a Cl₂ molecule. The question asks for one Cl atom.

q:
Which statements about exact numbers and significant figures are true?
I. The measurement 0.00450 g has five significant figures.
II. A count of 32 students in a classroom is an exact number.
III. The relation 1 in = 2.54 cm is exact, so it does not limit the significant figures in a conversion.
h: Leading zeros only locate the decimal point. Counted numbers and defined relations are exact.
w: Statement I is false: leading zeros are not significant, so 0.00450 g has three significant figures (4, 5 and the trailing 0). Statement II is true because a count of objects has no uncertainty. Statement III is true because the inch is defined as exactly 2.54 cm. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement II was judged false. Counting whole objects such as students gives an exact number with no uncertainty.
Statement I was judged true. Leading zeros only place the decimal point, so they are not significant.
Statement I was judged true. Count only the digits from the first nonzero digit onward.

q:
A piece of copper is cut in half. Which properties are intensive (the same for each half as for the whole piece)?
I. Temperature
II. Volume
III. Heat released when the piece cools by 10 °C
h: An intensive property does not depend on how much of the sample you have.
w: Temperature does not change when the piece is divided, so I is intensive. Volume (II) is halved, and the heat released on cooling by 10 °C (III) is also halved because q = mcΔT depends on mass. Both are extensive, so the answer is I only.
x: Statement II was judged intensive, but each half has half the volume of the whole piece.
Statement III was judged intensive, but q = mcΔT, so half the mass releases half the heat.
Statement I was judged extensive, but each half has the same temperature as the whole piece.

q:
A metal cube is 2.00 cm on each edge and has a mass of 21.6 g. Which statements are true?
I. The density of the metal is 2.70 g cm−3.
II. The cube sinks in water (density 1.00 g cm−3).
III. A 5.40 g piece of the same metal has a volume of 0.500 cm3.
h: Find the cube's volume from its edge length first, then use d = m/V for every statement.
w: The volume is (2.00 cm)3 = 8.00 cm3, so d = 21.6 g ÷ 8.00 cm3 = 2.70 g cm−3 (I true). The metal is denser than water, so the cube sinks (II true). A 5.40 g piece has V = 5.40 g ÷ 2.70 g cm−3 = 2.00 cm3, not 0.500 cm3 (III false: 0.500 comes from dividing density by mass). The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II was judged false. An object denser than water sinks in it.
Statement I was judged false. The volume of a cube is the edge length cubed, 8.00 cm³ here.
Statement III was judged true. Volume is mass divided by density, not density divided by mass.

q:
Rank these temperatures from lowest to highest.
I. 300 K
II. 25 °C
III. 80 °F
h: Convert all three to the same scale. K = °C + 273.15 and °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9.
w: 25 °C = 298.15 K. 80 °F = (80 − 32) × 5/9 = 26.7 °C = 299.8 K. 300 K is 26.85 °C, the warmest of the three. So the order is II < III < I. Comparing the raw numbers without converting gives the wrong order.
x: 80 °F is 26.7 °C, which is warmer than 25 °C.
The numbers cannot be compared until they are on the same scale. Convert each one to kelvins.
300 K is 26.85 °C, which is slightly warmer than 80 °F (26.7 °C).

q:
Which statements correctly describe what early experiments showed about atoms?
I. Thomson's cathode-ray experiments showed that atoms contain small, negatively charged particles (electrons).
II. Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed that an atom's positive charge and most of its mass are in a tiny nucleus.
III. Millikan's oil-drop experiment showed that electrons move in orbits of fixed energy.
h: Match each scientist to what the experiment measured. One of them measured a charge, not an energy.
w: I is true: cathode rays are streams of electrons, negative particles present in all atoms. II is true: the rare large-angle deflections showed a small, dense, positive nucleus. III is false: Millikan measured the charge of the electron. Fixed electron energy levels came from Bohr's model of hydrogen. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II was judged false. The few alpha particles that bounced back showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
Statement I was judged false. Thomson showed that cathode rays are negative particles present in all atoms.
Statement III was judged true. Millikan measured the charge on the electron, and fixed energy levels came from Bohr's model.

q:
Which species are isoelectronic with a neon atom (have 10 electrons)?
I. O2−
II. K+
III. Al3+
h: Count electrons as the atomic number minus the charge.
w: O2− has 8 + 2 = 10 electrons and Al3+ has 13 − 3 = 10 electrons, so I and III are isoelectronic with Ne. K+ has 19 − 1 = 18 electrons, like argon. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III was judged false. Al has 13 electrons, and Al³⁺ has lost 3 of them.
Statement I was judged false. O has 8 electrons, and O²⁻ has gained 2 more.
Statement II was judged true. K has 19 electrons, so K⁺ has 18, the same as argon.

q:
Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, and its average atomic mass is 35.45 u. Which statements are true?
I. The two isotopes have the same number of neutrons.
II. Neutral atoms of both isotopes have 17 electrons.
III. 37Cl is more abundant in nature than 35Cl.
h: Isotopes share an atomic number. The average atomic mass lies closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope.
w: I is false: 35Cl has 18 neutrons and 37Cl has 20. II is true: both have 17 protons, so their neutral atoms have 17 electrons. III is false: 35.45 u is much closer to 35 than to 37, so 35Cl is more abundant (about 76%). The answer is II only.
x: Statement I was judged true. Neutrons equal the mass number minus 17, so the two isotopes differ in neutron count.
Statement III was judged true. The average mass, 35.45 u, sits much closer to 35 than to 37.
Statement II was judged false. Both isotopes are chlorine with 17 protons, so neutral atoms have 17 electrons.

q:
Which formula–name pairs are correct?
I. Cu2O, copper(II) oxide
II. FeCl3, iron(III) chloride
III. Na2SO3, sodium sulfate
h: Work out the metal's charge from the anion's charge, and recall that the −ite and −ate anions differ by one oxygen.
w: I is wrong: in Cu2O, two Cu ions balance one O2−, so each copper is +1 and the name is copper(I) oxide. II is right: three Cl− ions require Fe3+. III is wrong: SO32− is sulfite, so Na2SO3 is sodium sulfite (sulfate is SO42−). The answer is II only.
x: Pair I was judged correct. Two Cu ions balance one O²⁻, so each copper is +1, not +2.
Pair III was judged correct. SO₃²⁻ is sulfite, the ion with one fewer oxygen than sulfate.
Pair I was judged correct. In Cu₂O each copper must be +1 to balance a single O²⁻.

q:
Consider a 1.00 mol sample of H2O and a 1.00 mol sample of CO2. Which statements are true?
I. The two samples contain the same number of molecules.
II. The two samples have the same mass.
III. The two samples contain the same number of oxygen atoms.
h: A mole is a fixed number of particles, but each kind of molecule has its own molar mass and its own atom count.
w: I is true: each sample has 6.022 × 1023 molecules. II is false: 1.00 mol H2O is 18.0 g but 1.00 mol CO2 is 44.0 g. III is false: each CO2 has two O atoms, so the CO2 sample holds 2.00 mol O and the H2O sample holds 1.00 mol O. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II was judged true. Equal moles have equal mass only when the molar masses match, and 18.0 g/mol differs from 44.0 g/mol.
Statement III was judged true. Each CO₂ molecule carries two O atoms but each H₂O carries only one.
Statement I was judged false. One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

q:
Rank these compounds by mass percent of nitrogen, from lowest to highest.
I. N2O
II. NH3
III. NH4NO3
h: Mass percent N = (mass of N in one formula unit ÷ molar mass) × 100%.
w: NH4NO3: 28.02/80.05 = 35.0% N. N2O: 28.02/44.02 = 63.7% N. NH3: 14.01/17.03 = 82.2% N. The order is III < I < II. Counting N atoms alone misleads: NH4NO3 has two N atoms but a large molar mass.
x: N₂O is 63.7% N, which is more than NH₄NO₃ at 35.0% N.
NH₃ has only one N atom, but its small molar mass makes its mass percent of N the largest of the three.
Ranking by the number of N atoms ignores molar mass. Compute each percent.

q:
A compound has the empirical formula CH2O and a molar mass of 180.2 g mol−1. Which statements are true?
I. Its molecular formula is C6H12O6.
II. Its mass percent of carbon equals that of formaldehyde, CH2O.
III. Hydrogen makes up a larger mass percent of the compound than oxygen does, because there are more H atoms than O atoms.
h: Divide the molar mass by the empirical-formula mass. Mass percent depends on mass, not on atom count.
w: CH2O has a formula mass of 30.03 g mol−1, and 180.2/30.03 = 6, so the formula is C6H12O6 (I true). A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so its percent composition is identical: 40.0% C (II true). III is false: H is only 6.7% by mass and O is 53.3%, because each O atom (16.00 u) is much heavier than an H atom (1.008 u). The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II was judged false. Multiplying every subscript by the same number leaves the percent composition unchanged.
Statement III was judged true. Each O atom is about 16 times heavier than an H atom, so O makes up more of the mass.
Statement I was judged false. 180.2 divided by 30.03 is 6, so multiply each subscript by 6.

q:
A student prepares 250.0 mL of 0.200 M Na2SO4(aq). Which statements are true?
I. The solution contains 0.0500 mol Na2SO4.
II. The concentration of Na+ ions is 0.200 M.
III. Diluting the solution with water to 500.0 mL gives 0.100 M Na2SO4.
h: Moles = molarity × volume in liters. Each formula unit of Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> releases two Na<sup>+</sup> ions.
w: I: 0.2500 L × 0.200 mol L−1 = 0.0500 mol (true). II is false: each Na2SO4 gives 2 Na+, so [Na+] = 0.400 M. III: M1V1 = M2V2 gives (0.200 M)(250.0 mL)/(500.0 mL) = 0.100 M (true). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III was judged false. Doubling the volume with water halves the concentration.
Statement I was judged false. Moles equal molarity times volume in liters, 0.2500 L here.
Statement II was judged true. Each Na₂SO₄ releases two Na⁺ ions, so [Na⁺] is twice the salt concentration.

q:
Which substances are strong electrolytes when dissolved in water?
I. HNO3
II. NH3
III. CH3COOH (acetic acid)
h: A strong electrolyte breaks apart completely into ions. Only a few acids, the strong acids, do this.
w: HNO3 is a strong acid that ionizes completely (I true). NH3 is a weak base and acetic acid is a weak acid. Each forms only a few ions, so II and III are weak electrolytes. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II was judged strong. NH₃ is a weak base that makes only a few ions in water.
Statement III was judged strong. Acetic acid is a weak acid, mostly present as whole molecules in water.
Statement III was judged strong. Acetic acid ionizes only slightly, so its solution conducts weakly.

q:
For the reaction Mg(s) + 2 Ag+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + 2 Ag(s), which statements are true?
I. Mg is oxidized.
II. Ag+ is the reducing agent.
III. Two electrons are transferred in the equation as written.
h: Track oxidation numbers. The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.
w: Mg goes from 0 to +2, so it is oxidized (I true) and loses 2 electrons. Each Ag+ gains one electron, so the two Ag+ ions gain the 2 electrons that Mg lost (III true). Ag+ is reduced, which makes it the oxidizing agent, not the reducing agent (II false). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III was judged false. One Mg atom loses 2 electrons, and the two Ag⁺ ions gain them.
Statement II was judged true. Ag⁺ gains electrons, so it is reduced and acts as the oxidizing agent.
Statement I was judged false. Mg goes from 0 to +2, so it loses electrons.

q:
In which species does sulfur have an oxidation number of +6?
I. SO2
II. Na2S2O3
III. SO3
h: Give O −2 and Na +1, then solve for sulfur so the charges sum to zero.
w: SO2: S + 2(−2) = 0, so S = +4. Na2S2O3: 2(+1) + 2S + 3(−2) = 0, so each S = +2. SO3: S + 3(−2) = 0, so S = +6. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I was judged +6. Two O atoms at −2 each give −4, so S in SO₂ is +4.
Statement II was judged +6. Two S atoms share the charge, so solve 2(+1) + 2x + 3(−2) = 0.
Statement III was judged not +6. In SO₃, three O atoms at −2 give −6, which S must balance.

q:
Which reactions are oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions?
I. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
II. CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)
III. Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)
h: Assign oxidation numbers to every element on both sides. In a redox reaction at least one element's oxidation number changes.
w: In I (neutralization) and II (decomposition of a carbonate), every element keeps its oxidation number (H +1, Cl −1, Na +1, O −2, Ca +2, C +4). In III, Zn goes from 0 to +2 and H goes from +1 to 0, so III is a redox reaction. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I was judged redox. In a neutralization, H, O, Na and Cl all keep their oxidation numbers.
Statement II was judged redox. Ca stays +2, C stays +4 and O stays −2 when CaCO₃ decomposes.
Statement III was judged not redox. Zn starts as the element (0) and ends as Zn²⁺.

q:
A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M H2SO4 is titrated to the equivalence point with 0.200 M NaOH. Which statements are true?
I. 25.0 mL of the NaOH solution is needed.
II. The salt in the flask at the equivalence point is Na2SO4.
III. The moles of NaOH added equal twice the moles of H2SO4.
h: Write the balanced equation first. Sulfuric acid has two acidic hydrogens.
w: H2SO4 + 2 NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2 H2O. Moles of acid = 0.0250 L × 0.100 M = 0.00250 mol, so 0.00500 mol NaOH is needed, twice the moles of acid (III true). That is 0.00500 mol ÷ 0.200 M = 0.0250 L = 25.0 mL (I true). The salt formed is Na2SO4 (II true). The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III was judged false. Each H₂SO₄ gives two H⁺, so it needs two OH⁻.
Statement I was judged false. Use the 1 : 2 mole ratio before dividing by the NaOH molarity.
Statement I was judged false. The acid needs 0.00500 mol NaOH, so find the volume of 0.200 M NaOH that holds that amount.

q:
Samples of 100.0 g of water (c = 4.184 J g−1 °C−1) and 100.0 g of iron (c = 0.449 J g−1 °C−1) each absorb 1.00 kJ of heat. Which statements are true?
I. The temperature of the iron rises more than that of the water.
II. The temperature of the water rises by about 2.4 °C.
III. Because both absorb the same heat, both have the same temperature change.
h: Use q = mcΔT and solve for ΔT for each sample.
w: ΔT = q/(mc). Water: 1000 J ÷ (100.0 g × 4.184 J g−1 °C−1) = 2.39 °C (II true). Iron: 1000 J ÷ (100.0 g × 0.449 J g−1 °C−1) = 22.3 °C, so iron warms much more (I true). III is false: equal heat gives equal ΔT only if m × c is the same, and iron's specific heat is much smaller. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement I was judged false. A smaller specific heat means a larger temperature change for the same heat.
Statement III was judged true. ΔT depends on the specific heat, which differs a lot here.
Statement I was judged false. Compute ΔT for iron with c = 0.449 J/(g·°C).

q:
Which of these are state functions?
I. The heat, q, absorbed by a system
II. The work, w, done on a system
III. The enthalpy, H, of a system
h: A state function depends only on the present state of the system, not on the path taken to reach it.
w: Enthalpy depends only on the state of the system, so ΔH is the same for any path (III true). The amounts of heat and work exchanged depend on how the change is carried out, so q and w are path functions (I and II false). Only their sum, ΔE = q + w, is a state function. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I was judged a state function. The heat exchanged depends on the path, even when the start and end are the same.
Statement II was judged a state function. Work depends on how the change is carried out.
Statement I was judged a state function. Heat is energy in transit along a particular path.

q:
50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl and 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH are mixed in a foam coffee-cup calorimeter, and the temperature rises by 6.7 °C. Which changes would give a LARGER temperature rise?
I. Using 100.0 mL of each solution instead of 50.0 mL
II. Using 2.00 M HCl and 2.00 M NaOH (still 50.0 mL of each)
III. Using a metal cup instead of a foam cup
h: ΔT = q/(mc). Ask how each change affects both the heat released and the mass of solution that must be warmed.
w: Doubling both concentrations doubles the moles that react in the same 100 mL of solution, so twice the heat warms the same mass and ΔT is about 13 °C (II true). Doubling both volumes doubles the heat but also doubles the mass of solution to warm, so ΔT stays about 6.7 °C (I false). A metal cup conducts heat away to the room, so ΔT would be smaller (III false). The answer is II only.
x: Statement I was judged to raise ΔT. Twice the volume releases twice the heat but also has twice the mass to warm.
Statement III was judged to raise ΔT. A metal cup lets heat escape to the room.
Statement I was judged to raise ΔT. The heat per gram of solution stays the same when both volumes double.

q:
Which processes are endothermic?
I. Liquid water freezing
II. Liquid ethanol evaporating
III. Breaking the Cl–Cl bond in Cl2(g) to form two Cl atoms
h: Melting, evaporating and breaking bonds all need energy. Their reverse processes release it.
w: Freezing releases heat (it is the reverse of melting), so I is exothermic. Evaporation needs energy to separate the molecules (II endothermic), and breaking any chemical bond requires energy (III endothermic). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III was judged exothermic. Energy must always be added to break a chemical bond.
Statement I was judged endothermic. Water releases heat as it freezes.
Statement I was judged endothermic. Freezing is the reverse of melting, so heat flows out.

q:
Compare red light with violet light. Which statements about red light are true?
I. Each photon of red light has more energy than a photon of violet light.
II. Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light.
III. In a vacuum, red light travels at the same speed as violet light.
h: All light moves at the same speed c in a vacuum. Photon energy is E = hc/λ.
w: Red light (about 700 nm) has a longer wavelength than violet light (about 400 nm), so II is true. Since E = hc/λ, the longer wavelength means LESS energy per photon, so I is false. All electromagnetic radiation travels at c = 3.00 × 108 m s−1 in a vacuum (III true). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I was judged true. A longer wavelength means a lower frequency and less energy per photon.
Statement III was judged false. Every color of light travels at the same speed c in a vacuum.
Statement I was judged true. Photon energy falls as wavelength grows, E = hc/λ.

q:
Which sets of quantum numbers (n, ℓ, mℓ) describe an allowed orbital?
I. (3, 3, 0)
II. (3, 2, −2)
III. (4, 0, 0)
h: ℓ can be any whole number from 0 up to n − 1, and m<sub>ℓ</sub> any whole number from −ℓ to +ℓ.
w: I is not allowed because ℓ must be less than n (for n = 3, ℓ = 0, 1 or 2). II is a 3d orbital: ℓ = 2 allows mℓ = −2 through +2. III is the 4s orbital (ℓ = 0, mℓ = 0). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III was judged not allowed. ℓ = 0 is allowed for any n, and then mℓ must be 0.
Statement I was judged allowed. ℓ can go only up to n − 1.
Statement I was judged allowed. For n = 3 the largest ℓ is 2.

q:
Which statements about a 4f subshell are true?
I. Its orbitals have ℓ = 3.
II. It contains seven orbitals.
III. It can hold up to 14 electrons.
h: For an f subshell, find ℓ, then count the allowed m<sub>ℓ</sub> values and allow two electrons per orbital.
w: The letter f means ℓ = 3 (I true). mℓ runs from −3 to +3, giving 2ℓ + 1 = 7 orbitals (II true). Each orbital holds two electrons, so the subshell holds 14 (III true). The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III was judged false. Seven orbitals with two electrons each hold 14 electrons.
Statement I was judged false. The letters s, p, d and f stand for ℓ = 0, 1, 2 and 3.
Statement II was judged false. The mℓ values −3 through +3 make seven orbitals.

q:
Rank these kinds of electromagnetic radiation by the energy of one photon, from lowest to highest.
I. Visible light
II. X-rays
III. Microwaves
h: Photon energy rises as frequency rises and as wavelength gets shorter.
w: Microwaves have wavelengths of centimeters, visible light about 400 to 700 nm and X-rays about 0.01 to 10 nm. Shorter wavelength means more energy per photon (E = hc/λ), so the order is III < I < II.
x: This is the order of wavelength from shortest to longest. Energy runs the opposite way.
Microwaves have much longer wavelengths than visible light, so their photons carry less energy.
X-rays have the shortest wavelength of the three, so their photons have the most energy.

q:
Which comparisons of size are correct?
I. Fe3+ is smaller than Fe2+.
II. Se2− is larger than Br−.
III. A magnesium atom is larger than a sodium atom.
h: For ions of one element, compare how many electrons the same nucleus holds. For isoelectronic species and for atoms in one period, compare the nuclear charges.
w: I is true: Fe3+ has one fewer electron than Fe2+ held by the same 26 protons, so it is pulled in more tightly. II is true: Se2− and Br− both have 36 electrons, but Se has only 34 protons to Br's 35, so Se2− is larger. III is false: Mg has one more proton than Na in the same n = 3 shell, so Mg is smaller. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true. Se²⁻ and Br⁻ have the same 36 electrons, and Se has fewer protons to hold them.
Statement III is false. Mg has a larger nuclear charge than Na with its valence electrons in the same shell, so Mg is smaller.
Statement III is false. Atoms get smaller from left to right across a period, so Mg is smaller than Na.

q:
Arrange these atoms in order of increasing first ionization energy.
I. N
II. F
III. O
h: Ionization energy generally rises across period 2, but there is one well-known exception among these three. Think about a half-filled versus a paired 2p subshell.
w: First ionization energy rises across period 2 as the nuclear charge grows, so F is highest (1681 kJ/mol). Oxygen (1314 kJ/mol) is lower than nitrogen (1402 kJ/mol) because O's fourth 2p electron is paired, and repulsion within that orbital makes it easier to remove. The order is O < N < F, which is III < I < II.
x: This follows the general trend but misses the exception. Oxygen's paired 2p electron is easier to remove than any of nitrogen's half-filled 2p electrons.
Fluorine has the largest nuclear charge of the three in the same shell, so its ionization energy is the highest, not the lowest.
Fluorine holds its electrons most strongly of the three, so it cannot come in the middle of the order.

q:
Which statements are true?
I. Removing an electron from a gaseous Cl− ion takes more energy than removing an electron from a gaseous Cl atom.
II. Argon has the most negative (most exothermic) electron affinity of the period 3 elements.
III. The first ionization energy of potassium is lower than that of sodium.
h: Removing an electron from Cl<sup>−</sup> is the reverse of adding one to Cl. For argon, ask where an added electron would have to go.
w: I is false: removing the electron from Cl− takes only 349 kJ/mol (the reverse of chlorine's electron affinity), far less than the 1251 kJ/mol needed for a neutral Cl atom, because the extra electron is repelled by the others. II is false: an electron added to argon must enter the 4s orbital, far from the nucleus, so argon's electron affinity is not negative. Chlorine has the most negative value in period 3. III is true: potassium's valence electron is in n = 4, farther from the nucleus than sodium's n = 3 electron. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is false. An anion holds its extra electron loosely because of electron repulsion, so removing it takes much less energy than ionizing the neutral atom.
Statement II is false. Argon has a full n = 3 shell, so an added electron would sit in a new, higher shell and is not held.
Statement II is false. A noble gas does not release energy when it gains an electron.

q:
Which statements correctly explain periodic trends in atomic radius?
I. Atoms get larger across a period because each element has more electrons than the one before it.
II. Atoms get larger down a group because the valence electrons are in shells with larger n.
III. Atoms get smaller across a period because the added protons are only partly shielded by the electrons added to the same shell.
h: First decide which direction each trend actually goes. Then ask whether the stated reason is the real cause.
w: I is false: atoms get smaller, not larger, across a period. Electrons added to the same shell shield each other poorly, so the rising effective nuclear charge pulls the shell inward (III true). II is true: each step down a group adds a new principal shell, so the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. Atomic radius decreases across a period even though electrons are added.
Statement II is true. A larger n means the valence electrons are on average farther from the nucleus.
Statement I is false. Across a period the atoms shrink, so it cannot be explained by atoms getting larger.

q:
Which molecules are polar?
I. BF3
II. NF3
III. SO2
h: Draw each Lewis structure and check for lone pairs on the central atom. Polar bonds only make a polar molecule when the shape keeps the bond dipoles from canceling.
w: BF3 is trigonal planar with no lone pair on boron, so its three B–F dipoles cancel and it is nonpolar (I false). NF3 is trigonal pyramidal because of the lone pair on N, so its dipoles do not cancel (II polar). SO2 is bent because of the lone pair on S, so it is polar (III polar). The answer is II and III only.
x: BF₃ is the one to recheck. Boron has no lone pair, so the molecule is flat and symmetric and its bond dipoles cancel.
NF₃ is polar too. Nitrogen has a lone pair, so the molecule is a pyramid and the N to F dipoles do not cancel.
BF₃ is nonpolar. Its three equal bond dipoles point 120° apart in a plane and add to zero.

q:
In which species does the central atom have MORE than eight valence electrons around it in the Lewis structure?
I. ICl4−
II. NH4+
III. BCl3
h: Count the bonding pairs and lone pairs on each central atom. Only atoms in period 3 and below can go beyond an octet.
w: In ICl4−, iodine has four bonds and two lone pairs, 12 electrons, an expanded octet (I yes). In NH4+, nitrogen has four bonds and no lone pairs, exactly 8 electrons (II no). In BCl3, boron has three bonds and only 6 electrons, fewer than an octet (III no). The answer is I only.
x: Recheck NH₄⁺. Nitrogen has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, which is exactly eight electrons.
Recheck BCl₃. Boron has only three bonding pairs, which is fewer than eight electrons, not more.
Recheck ICl₄⁻. Iodine has four bonds plus two lone pairs, which is more than eight electrons.

q:
Which statements about molecular shapes are true?
I. XeF2 is linear.
II. SF4 is tetrahedral.
III. ClF3 is T-shaped.
h: Count all electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) on the central atom first. Lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramid go to the equatorial positions.
w: XeF2 has 5 electron groups (2 bonds, 3 lone pairs); the three lone pairs fill the equatorial positions, leaving a linear molecule (I true). SF4 has 5 electron groups (4 bonds, 1 lone pair), so it is seesaw, not tetrahedral (II false). ClF3 has 5 electron groups (3 bonds, 2 lone pairs), so it is T-shaped (III true). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. ClF₃ has three bonds and two equatorial lone pairs, which gives a T shape.
Statement II is false. Sulfur in SF₄ also has a lone pair, so there are five electron groups and the shape is a seesaw.
Statement I is true. The three lone pairs on Xe sit around the equator, so the two F atoms are 180° apart.

q:
Arrange the carbon–oxygen bonds in these species from SHORTEST to LONGEST.
I. CO32−
II. CO
III. CO2
h: Find the C–O bond order in each species, averaging over resonance structures where needed. Higher bond order means a shorter bond.
w: CO has a triple bond (bond order 3). Each C=O in CO2 is a double bond (bond order 2). The three equivalent bonds in carbonate each have bond order 1⅓ from resonance. Higher bond order gives a shorter bond, so CO < CO2 < CO32−, which is II < III < I.
x: This is the order from longest to shortest. A higher bond order makes a shorter bond.
CO has a triple bond, which is shorter than the double bonds in CO₂.
The bonds in carbonate are partial double bonds (order 1⅓), so they are longer than the full double bonds in CO₂.

q:
Which statements about covalent bonds are true?
I. A C=C double bond is stronger than a C–C single bond, but less than twice as strong.
II. The H–F bond is more polar than the H–Cl bond.
III. For bonds between the same kinds of atoms, a longer bond is generally a stronger bond.
h: Think about what a π bond adds compared with a σ bond. Compare electronegativity differences, and how bond order affects both length and strength.
w: I is true: C=C is about 614 kJ/mol and C–C about 348 kJ/mol; the π bond adds less than a σ bond does, so the double bond is less than twice as strong. II is true: F is more electronegative than Cl, so the H–F bond has the larger electronegativity difference. III is false: for the same pair of atoms, higher bond order gives a shorter and stronger bond, so a longer bond is weaker. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement I is true. The π bond in C=C is weaker than the σ bond, so the double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong.
Statement III is false. Going from single to double to triple, bonds get shorter and stronger together.
Statement III is false. A longer bond between the same two atoms is a weaker bond.

q:
According to molecular orbital theory, which of these diatomic species are paramagnetic?
I. N2
II. B2
III. C2
h: For B<sub>2</sub>, C<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>, the π<sub>2p</sub> orbitals lie below σ<sub>2p</sub>. Fill the valence electrons and look for unpaired ones.
w: B2 has 6 valence electrons: (σ2s)2(σ*2s)2(π2p)2, with the two π electrons in separate orbitals, so it is paramagnetic. C2 has 8: the two π2p orbitals are completely filled, so it is diamagnetic. N2 has 10: π2p and σ2p are both filled, so it is diamagnetic. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is wrong. N₂ fills the π2p and σ2p orbitals completely, so all its electrons are paired.
Statement III is wrong. In C₂ the four π2p electrons exactly fill both π2p orbitals, so none are unpaired.
N₂ has all of its electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic.

q:
Which statements about ethene (ethylene), H2C=CH2, are true?
I. Each carbon atom is sp2 hybridized.
II. The π bond forms from the overlap of two sp2 hybrid orbitals.
III. The molecule has five σ bonds and one π bond.
h: Each carbon has three electron groups. Ask which orbitals are left over after the hybrids are made, and count every bond, including the C–H bonds.
w: Each carbon has three electron groups (two C–H and one C=C), so it is sp2 (I true). The σ bonds come from sp2 hybrids, but the π bond comes from side-by-side overlap of the unhybridized 2p orbitals (II false). There are four C–H σ bonds plus one C–C σ bond, five σ in all, and one π bond (III true). The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. Count the four C to H bonds plus the σ part of the double bond.
Statement II is false. The π bond uses the unhybridized p orbital left on each carbon, not hybrid orbitals.
Statement II is false. Hybrid orbitals point along the bond axis and form σ bonds. π bonds come from leftover p orbitals.

q:
In which species is the central atom sp3 hybridized?
I. BF3
II. CO32−
III. H3O+
h: Count electron groups (bonds plus lone pairs) on the central atom. A double bond counts as one group.
w: BF3: boron has 3 bonds and no lone pair, 3 groups, so sp2. CO32−: carbon has 3 groups (one double bond counts once), so sp2. H3O+: oxygen has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair, 4 groups, so sp3. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is misjudged. Boron in BF₃ has only three electron groups and no lone pair, so it is sp².
Statement II is misjudged. The C=O double bond counts as one electron group, so carbon has three groups and is sp².
Recheck BF₃. Three electron groups means sp², not sp³.

q:
Which statements are correct according to molecular orbital theory?
I. The peroxide ion, O22−, has a bond order of 2.
II. F2 has a bond order of 1.
III. Adding an electron to O2 to form O2− makes the O–O bond longer.
h: For O<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub>, extra electrons go into the π*<sub>2p</sub> antibonding orbitals. Bond order = ½(bonding − antibonding electrons).
w: O2 (12 valence electrons) has bond order 2. Each added electron enters π*2p, so O2− has bond order 1.5 and a longer bond (III true), and O22− has bond order 1 (I false). F2 (14 valence electrons) has 8 bonding and 6 antibonding, bond order 1 (II true). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. The added electron goes into an antibonding orbital, which lowers the bond order and lengthens the bond.
Statement I is false. Peroxide has two more antibonding electrons than O₂, which lowers the bond order below 2.
Statement I is false. O₂²⁻ has 8 bonding and 6 antibonding valence electrons.

q:
A sample of an ideal gas is at 1.0 atm and 27 °C. Which changes, each made with the amount of gas held constant, would DOUBLE its volume?
I. Heating the gas from 27 °C to 54 °C at constant pressure.
II. Lowering the pressure to 0.50 atm at constant temperature.
III. Doubling both the pressure and the Kelvin temperature.
h: Use V = nRT/P with T in kelvins. Convert both Celsius temperatures before comparing them.
w: I: 27 °C is 300 K and 54 °C is 327 K, so V rises only by 327/300, about 9% (does not double). II: halving P at constant T doubles V (Boyle's law). III: doubling both P and T leaves T/P, and so V, unchanged. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I does not double the volume. Gas laws use kelvins, and 300 K to 327 K is only about a 9% increase.
Statement III does not change the volume. Doubling P halves V and doubling T doubles V, so the effects cancel.
Statement I does not double the volume. Doubling a Celsius temperature does not double the Kelvin temperature.

q:
A rigid container holds equal numbers of moles of He and CH4 at 25 °C. Which statements are true?
I. Helium atoms effuse through a tiny hole twice as fast as CH4 molecules.
II. The CH4 molecules have a greater average kinetic energy than the He atoms.
III. The partial pressure of CH4 is four times the partial pressure of He.
h: Graham's law compares effusion rates using the square root of the molar masses. Average kinetic energy and partial pressure depend on different things than mass.
w: I is true: rate(He)/rate(CH4) = √(16.04/4.00) = 2.00. II is false: average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so both gases have the same value at 25 °C. III is false: partial pressure depends on the number of moles, not the mass, so equal moles give equal partial pressures. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. At the same temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy. Heavier molecules just move more slowly.
Statement III is false. Partial pressure is set by moles, and the moles of the two gases are equal.
Statement I is true. √(16/4) = 2, so helium effuses twice as fast.

q:
Which statements help explain why real gases do not behave exactly like ideal gases?
I. Gas molecules take up some volume of their own, which matters when the gas is compressed to high pressure.
II. Attractions between molecules make the measured pressure lower than the ideal-gas value.
III. Deviations from ideal behavior are largest at high pressure and low temperature.
h: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law for two things the kinetic molecular theory ignores. Think about when molecules are crowded together and moving slowly.
w: I is true: molecular volume is ignored by the ideal model and becomes significant when molecules are crowded at high pressure (the b term). II is true: attractions pull molecules back as they approach the wall, so they hit it less hard and the pressure is lower than ideal (the a term). III is true: high pressure crowds the molecules and low temperature lets attractions matter more, so deviations are largest there. The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement III is true as well. Crowding at high pressure and slow motion at low temperature both make the ideal model fail.
Statement II is true as well. Attractions between molecules soften their collisions with the wall and lower the pressure.
Statement I is true as well. At high pressure the molecules' own volume is no longer a tiny part of the container volume.

q:
Three 1.0 L flasks at 25 °C each contain 2.0 g of a different gas. Arrange the flasks in order of INCREASING pressure.
I. H2
II. He
III. CH4
h: At the same V and T, pressure is proportional to moles. Convert each 2.0 g to moles.
w: Moles: H2 2.0/2.02 ≈ 0.99 mol, He 2.0/4.00 = 0.50 mol, CH4 2.0/16.04 ≈ 0.12 mol. At equal V and T, P is proportional to n, so the order of increasing pressure is CH4 < He < H2, which is III < II < I.
x: This is the order of molar mass. Equal masses of a lighter gas mean more moles, and more moles mean more pressure.
Helium has the higher molar mass of these two (4.00 vs 2.02 g/mol), so 2.0 g of it is fewer moles than 2.0 g of H₂.
H₂ has the smallest molar mass, so 2.0 g of it is the most moles of the three.

q:
In which pure liquids do the molecules hydrogen bond to one another?
I. methanol, CH3OH
II. dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3
III. hydrogen fluoride, HF
h: A molecule can hydrogen bond to its own kind only if it has an H atom bonded directly to N, O or F.
w: Methanol has an O–H group, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other (I yes). HF has H bonded directly to F (III yes). Dimethyl ether has an O atom, but all of its H atoms are bonded to carbon, so it has no H to donate and cannot hydrogen bond to itself (II no). The answer is I and III only.
x: Recheck methanol. Its O to H group can donate a hydrogen bond to the O of a neighboring molecule.
Recheck dimethyl ether. Its H atoms are all on carbon, so it has no H to donate to a neighbor.
Dimethyl ether is the one to recheck. An O atom alone is not enough, the H must be bonded to N, O or F.

q:
Which statements about boiling are true?
I. A liquid always boils when its vapor pressure reaches 760 torr, no matter what the external pressure is.
II. Water boils below 100 °C on a high mountain.
III. Of two liquids, the one with stronger intermolecular forces usually has the higher normal boiling point.
h: Boiling happens when the vapor pressure of the liquid matches the pressure pushing down on it.
w: I is false: a liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure, which is 760 torr only at sea level. II is true: on a mountain the air pressure is lower, so water's vapor pressure reaches it at a lower temperature. III is true: stronger intermolecular forces lower the vapor pressure, so a higher temperature is needed to reach 1 atm. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. The boiling point depends on the external pressure, and 760 torr is only the pressure at sea level.
Statement II is true. Lower air pressure on a mountain means water boils at a lower temperature.
Statement I is false. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals whatever the external pressure is.

q:
Heat is added at a steady rate to a sample of ice at −20 °C until it becomes steam at 120 °C. Which statements are true?
I. The temperature stays constant while the ice melts.
II. Melting the ice takes longer than boiling the water.
III. While the water is boiling, the added energy raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
h: On a heating curve, flat sections are phase changes. Compare ΔH<sub>fus</sub> (6.01 kJ/mol) with ΔH<sub>vap</sub> (40.7 kJ/mol) for water.
w: I is true: during melting the added heat breaks intermolecular attractions, so the temperature stays at 0 °C. II is false: ΔHvap (40.7 kJ/mol) is almost seven times ΔHfus (6.01 kJ/mol), so at a steady heating rate boiling takes much longer. III is false: during boiling the temperature, and so the average kinetic energy, stays constant; the energy goes into separating molecules (raising potential energy). The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. Vaporizing water takes far more energy per mole than melting ice, so the boiling plateau is longer.
Statement III is false. Temperature does not change during boiling, so the average kinetic energy does not change either.
Statement II is false. ΔHvap is much larger than ΔHfus, so boiling takes longer than melting.

q:
Which statements about solids are true?
I. Diamond is a molecular solid held together by dispersion forces.
II. Solid NaCl does not conduct electricity, but molten NaCl does.
III. Metals conduct electricity because they contain anions that are free to move.
h: Match each solid with the particles it is made of and the forces between them. Conduction needs charged particles that can move.
w: I is false: diamond is a covalent network solid, with every carbon joined to four others by covalent bonds, which is why it is so hard and melts so high. II is true: the ions in solid NaCl are locked in the lattice, but in the melt they can move and carry current. III is false: metals conduct because their valence electrons are delocalized and mobile, not because of moving anions. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is false. Diamond is a network of covalent bonds, not separate molecules held by dispersion forces.
Statement III is false. In a metal the charge carriers are delocalized electrons, and there are no anions.
Statement I is false. Diamond's extreme hardness comes from a continuous network of covalent bonds.

q:
Which changes would increase the solubility of CO2 gas in water?
I. Warming the water.
II. Stirring the water faster.
III. Raising the partial pressure of CO2 above the water.
h: Solubility is how much dissolves at equilibrium, not how fast it dissolves. Think about Henry's law and why warm soda goes flat.
w: I: gases become less soluble in water as temperature rises, so warming lowers the solubility. II: stirring only speeds up how fast the gas dissolves; it does not change how much can dissolve at equilibrium. III: by Henry's law, the solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure, so raising P(CO2) increases it. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is misjudged. Gas solubility in water decreases when the water is warmed, which is why warm soda goes flat.
Statement II is misjudged. Stirring changes the rate of dissolving, not the amount that can dissolve at equilibrium.
Warming the water does the opposite. Gases are less soluble in warmer water.

q:
Which statements about dissolving an ionic solid in water are true?
I. Water molecules around a cation point their oxygen atoms toward it.
II. A salt with a positive (endothermic) enthalpy of solution can still dissolve on its own.
III. Dissolving an ionic solid in water is always exothermic.
h: Think about which end of a water molecule carries the partial negative charge. Remember that a cold pack works by dissolving a salt.
w: I is true: oxygen carries the partial negative charge of water, so it faces the positive cation. II is true: salts such as NH4NO3 dissolve endothermically (the basis of cold packs); the increase in dispersal (entropy) of the ions drives the process. III is false: the enthalpy of solution is the balance of lattice energy and hydration energy and can be either positive or negative. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true. Cold packs dissolve a salt that absorbs heat, and it still dissolves on its own.
Statement I is also true. The partially negative O end of water is attracted to a positive ion.
Statement III is false. Some salts, like NH₄NO₃, absorb heat when they dissolve.

q:
Which aqueous solutions have a LOWER freezing point than 0.20 m glucose? Assume the ionic solutes dissociate completely.
I. 0.15 m NaCl
II. 0.050 m CaCl2
III. 0.10 m Na2SO4
h: Freezing-point depression depends on the total molality of dissolved particles, i × m. Compare each with glucose's 0.20 m of particles.
w: Particle molality (i × m): glucose 1 × 0.20 = 0.20 m. NaCl 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 m (I lower freezing point). CaCl2 3 × 0.050 = 0.15 m, which is less than 0.20 m, so its freezing point is higher than glucose's (II no). Na2SO4 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 m (III lower freezing point). The answer is I and III only.
x: Recheck Na₂SO₄. It gives 3 ions per formula unit, so 0.10 m makes 0.30 m of particles.
Recheck NaCl. It gives 2 ions per formula unit, so 0.15 m makes 0.30 m of particles.
Recheck CaCl₂. Its 3 ions times 0.050 m is only 0.15 m of particles, fewer than glucose's 0.20 m.

q:
Which pairs of liquids mix completely (are miscible) in all proportions?
I. ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and water
II. hexane, C6H14, and octane, C8H18
III. acetone, (CH3)2CO, and water
h: Like dissolves like: liquids mix well when the attractions between unlike molecules are similar to the attractions within each liquid.
w: I: ethanol and water both hydrogen bond, so they mix in all proportions. II: hexane and octane are both nonpolar and held by dispersion forces only, so they mix in all proportions. III: acetone is small and polar and its C=O oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water, so it mixes with water in all proportions. The answer is I, II and III.
x: Statement II is true as well. Two nonpolar hydrocarbons have the same kind of forces, so they mix freely.
Statement II is true as well. Hexane and octane are both nonpolar, so like dissolves like.
Statement I is true as well. Ethanol's O to H group hydrogen bonds with water.

q: Each drawing shows the nucleus (protons and neutrons) and the electrons of one particle. Which two particles have the same mass number?
h: Mass number counts only the particles in the nucleus: protons plus neutrons. Electrons are not counted.
w: Particle II has 2 protons + 1 neutron and particle III has 1 proton + 2 neutrons, so both have mass number 3 (II is helium-3, III is hydrogen-3). I and III are isotopes (same proton count) but their mass numbers are 2 and 3. II and IV are both helium, with mass numbers 3 and 4. I and II each have one neutron, but their mass numbers are 2 and 3.
x: These two have the same number of protons, so they are isotopes with different mass numbers (2 and 3).
These are the same element, but one nucleus holds 3 particles and the other holds 4.
These have the same number of neutrons, not the same total of protons plus neutrons.

q: The drawing shows the nucleus and the electrons of one particle. Which symbol represents this particle?
h: The number of protons fixes the element. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Charge = protons − electrons.
w: The nucleus holds 2 protons (helium) and 1 neutron, so the mass number is 3. There is only 1 electron, so the charge is 2 − 1 = +1: 32He+. A 1− charge would need more electrons than protons, using the electron count as the atomic number gives H, and a mass number of 1 counts only the neutron.
x: A negative ion has more electrons than protons. Compare the counts in the drawing.
The atomic number is the number of protons, not the number of electrons.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, not neutrons alone.

q:
Each Lewis symbol is meant to show the monatomic ion that the element forms in ionic compounds. Which are drawn correctly?
I. calcium ion
II. bromide ion
III. aluminum ion
h: A main-group cation loses all of its valence electrons. A main-group anion gains electrons until it has eight valence electrons.
w: I is correct: Ca loses its two valence electrons, so Ca2+ shows no dots. II is correct: Br has 7 valence electrons and gains 1, so Br− shows 8 dots. III is wrong: Al3+ has lost all three valence electrons, so it should show no dots, not 8. I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct. Bromine has 7 valence electrons and gains one, giving 8 dots and a 1− charge.
Statement III is wrong. Aluminum loses its three valence electrons, so Al³⁺ should show no dots.
Statement III is wrong. The 8 dots around a 3+ cation do not fit an atom that lost its valence electrons.

q: Which Lewis symbol correctly represents the phosphide ion?
h: Phosphorus is in group 15. Decide whether it gains or loses electrons, and how many valence electrons the ion ends up with.
w: P has 5 valence electrons and gains 3 to reach an octet, so the phosphide ion shows 8 dots and a 3− charge. Gaining electrons makes the charge negative, not positive, and 6 dots or no dots do not match 5 + 3 = 8 valence electrons.
x: Gaining electrons gives a negative charge. A 3+ ion would have lost electrons.
Phosphorus starts with 5 valence electrons. Adding 3 gives more than 6.
An anion keeps its valence electrons and gains more. No dots fits a cation that lost them all.

q: Elements X and Y are marked on the outline of the periodic table. What is the formula of the ionic compound they form?
h: Find each element's group. Group 2 metals form 2+ ions and group 15 nonmetals form 3− ions. The total charge must be zero.
w: X is in group 2 (X2+) and Y is in group 15 (Y3−). Three X2+ (+6) balance two Y3− (−6): X3Y2. X2Y3 swaps the charges, XY would need equal and opposite charges, and XY2 treats Y as a 1− ion.
x: This swaps the subscripts. Check which element forms the 2+ ion and which forms the 3− ion.
A 1 to 1 formula needs charges of equal size. These two ions have charges of different size.
This treats Y as a 1− ion. Y is in group 15, not group 17.

q:
Elements A, B and C are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Which statements are true?
I. A is an alkali metal.
II. B is a main-group element.
III. C is a metalloid.
h: Group 1 (except H) holds the alkali metals. Groups 3–12 are transition metals. Metalloids sit along the stair-step line between B and At.
w: I is true: A is in group 1, period 4 (potassium), an alkali metal. II is false: B is in group 8 (iron), a transition metal, not a main-group element. III is false: C is in group 17 (chlorine), a nonmetal halogen. I only.
x: Statement II is false. B sits in the middle block (groups 3–12), so it is a transition metal.
Statement III is false. C is in group 17, which holds nonmetals, not metalloids.
Statement II is false because B is a transition metal, and statement III is false because C is a halogen.

q: Four elements are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Which marked element is a metal that is NOT a transition metal?
h: Transition metals fill groups 3–12. Main-group metals lie to the left of the metalloid stair-step line in groups 1, 2 and 13–16.
w: A is in period 5, group 14 (tin), a main-group metal below the metalloid line. B is in group 8 (iron), a transition metal. C is in period 4, group 14 (germanium), a metalloid. D is in period 3, group 15 (phosphorus), a nonmetal.
x: B is in groups 3–12, so it is a transition metal.
C sits on the stair-step line, so it is a metalloid, not a true metal.
D is above and to the right of the stair-step line, so it is a nonmetal.

q: Each marked element forms one common monatomic ion. Which element's common ion has the same electron configuration as krypton?
h: Krypton has 36 electrons. Find each element's usual ion charge from its group, then count the ion's electrons.
w: A is rubidium (period 5, group 1), and Rb+ has 37 − 1 = 36 electrons, the krypton configuration. B is calcium: Ca2+ has 18 electrons (argon). C is iodine: I− has 54 (xenon). D is sulfur: S2− has 18 (argon).
x: B is in group 2 of period 4. Its 2+ ion loses the 4s electrons and matches the noble gas of period 3.
C is in group 17 of period 5. Its 1− ion gains an electron and matches the noble gas of period 5.
D is in group 16 of period 3. Its 2− ion matches the noble gas at the end of period 3.

q: The box shows a representative portion of an ionic solid made of metal ions and nitride ions, N<sup>3−</sup>. Which metal could form this compound?
h: Count each kind of ion. The total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge.
w: The box holds 6 metal ions and 4 nitride ions, a 3 : 2 ratio. Four N3− carry −12, so each of the 6 metal ions is +2: a group 2 metal such as calcium (Ca3N2). K+ would need a 3 : 1 ratio, Al3+ a 1 : 1 ratio, and Sn4+ a 3 : 4 ratio.
x: A 1+ ion would need three metal ions for every nitride ion. Recount the ratio in the box.
A 3+ ion would pair one to one with N³⁻. The box has more metal ions than nitride ions.
A 4+ ion would need more nitride ions than metal ions. The box shows the reverse.

q: Water molecules are not shown. Which box best represents an aqueous solution of sodium phosphate, Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Sodium phosphate separates into Na<sup>+</sup> ions and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> ions. The polyatomic ion stays in one piece.
w: Each Na3PO4 releases 3 Na+ and 1 intact PO43−. Box I shows 6 Na+ and 2 PO43−, the 3 : 1 ratio. Box II has a 1 : 1 ratio, box III breaks phosphate into separate P and O atoms, and box IV has a 2 : 1 ratio, as if phosphate were 2−.
x: This 1 to 1 ratio would fit a phosphate ion with a 1− charge. Phosphate is 3−.
The atoms of a polyatomic ion stay bonded together in water.
This 2 to 1 ratio would fit a 2− anion. Phosphate carries a larger charge.

q:
Boxes I–III each show a sample of a pure substance. Which statements are true?
I. Box II contains a compound because each molecule has three atoms.
II. Boxes I and II show two allotropes of oxygen.
III. The atoms in box III are isotopes of the atoms in box I.
h: A compound needs two or more different elements. Allotropes are different forms of one element, and isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
w: I is false: box II (O3, ozone) has only oxygen atoms, so it is an element, not a compound. II is true: O2 and O3 are allotropes, different molecular forms of oxygen. III is true: 16O and 18O have the same 8 protons but different neutron counts. II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. Every atom in box II is oxygen, so O₃ is an element.
Statement III is also true. ¹⁶O and ¹⁸O are both oxygen with different numbers of neutrons.
Statement I is false. A compound must contain more than one element.

q:
Three species are listed in the table. Which statements are true?
I. Species 1 and species 2 are isotopes of the same element.
II. Species 1 and species 3 have the same number of neutrons.
III. Species 2 and species 3 have the same number of electrons.
h: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Electrons = atomic number − charge.
w: I is true: both have 26 protons (iron). II is false: species 1 has 54 − 26 = 28 neutrons and species 3 has 54 − 24 = 30. III is true: Fe2+ has 26 − 2 = 24 electrons and neutral Cr has 24. I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. Count electrons as atomic number minus charge for each species.
Statement II is false. Equal mass numbers do not mean equal neutrons when the atomic numbers differ.
Statement II is false. Subtract each atomic number from 54 and compare.

q: Element X exists as X<sub>2</sub> molecules and has only two isotopes, of mass 50 u and 52 u. The mass spectrum of X<sub>2</sub> shows the three peaks graphed, with heights relative to the tallest peak. What percent of X atoms are the mass-50 isotope?
h: Mass 100 is two light atoms, 102 one of each, 104 two heavy. With light fraction p, the peaks are p² : 2p(1 − p) : (1 − p)².
w: The heights 100 : 50 : 6.25 match p² : 2p(1 − p) : (1 − p)². The ratio of the first two peaks gives p² ÷ 2p(1 − p) = 2, so p = 0.80, or 80%. Check: 0.64 : 0.32 : 0.04 = 100 : 50 : 6.25. 64% is the share of molecules in the tallest peak, 67% ignores the mass-104 peak, and 50% would give peaks in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.
x: 64% is the fraction of molecules made of two light atoms, not the fraction of light atoms.
This compares only the first two peaks as if each held one isotope. Each X₂ peak contains two atoms.
Equal amounts of the two isotopes would make the middle peak the tallest.

q: The box shows a representative sample of magnesium atoms, with the three natural isotopes drawn in different colors. Based on this sample, what is the average atomic mass of magnesium?
h: Count the atoms of each isotope, turn each count into a fraction of the total, and take the weighted average of the masses.
w: The box has 20 atoms: 16 24Mg, 2 25Mg and 2 26Mg. Average = (16 × 23.985 + 2 × 24.986 + 2 × 25.983) ÷ 20 = 24.28 u. 24.98 u is a simple average of the three masses, 25.68 u gives the 16 atoms to the heaviest isotope, and 23.99 u ignores the minor isotopes.
x: This is a simple average of the three masses. The isotopes are not equally common in the box.
This gives the largest weight to the heaviest isotope. Recount which color is most common.
This uses only the most common isotope. The other two also add to the average.

q: Rank the species in the table by number of neutrons, fewest first.
h: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. The charge changes electrons, not neutrons.
w: Neutrons: I = 82 − 34 = 48, II = 81 − 35 = 46, III = 83 − 36 = 47. So II < III < I. Ordering by mass number gives II < I < III, and ordering by atomic number gives I < II < III. The 2− charge on species I changes its electrons, not its neutrons.
x: This orders the species by mass number. Subtract the atomic number from each first.
This orders the species by atomic number. Neutrons are mass number minus atomic number.
This has the order backward. The question asks for the fewest neutrons first.

q: Four elements are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Which two marked elements should have the most similar chemical properties?
h: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.
w: J and L are both in group 1 (sodium and rubidium), so each has one valence electron and they react in similar ways. J, K and M are all in period 3, and elements in the same period have different numbers of valence electrons. K and L are in different groups and periods.
x: J and K are neighbors in the same period, but they have different numbers of valence electrons.
J and M are in the same period at opposite ends. One is a reactive metal and the other a nonmetal.
K and L are in different groups, so they have different numbers of valence electrons.

q: The Lewis structures show the ions in a compound of chlorine with a period 3 metal, M. Which element is M?
h: Read the charge on M. A main-group metal's ion charge equals the number of valence electrons it lost.
w: Each chloride ion is 1−, and two of them balance M2+. A 2+ ion in period 3 comes from group 2: magnesium (MgCl2). Sodium forms 1+ ions, aluminum forms 3+ ions, and calcium is in period 4.
x: Sodium is in group 1 and forms 1+ ions.
Aluminum is in group 13 and forms 3+ ions.
Calcium forms 2+ ions, but it is in period 4.

q: An ion contains 50 protons, 70 neutrons and 48 electrons. Which symbol represents it?
h: Protons set the element and the atomic number. Add protons and neutrons for the mass number. Compare protons with electrons for the charge.
w: 50 protons is tin, the mass number is 50 + 70 = 120, and 50 − 48 = +2: 12050Sn2+. Two fewer electrons than protons gives a positive charge, the mass number is not the neutron count, and the electron count does not set the element.
x: There are fewer electrons than protons, so the charge is positive.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together.
The element is set by the number of protons, not electrons.

q:
Rank these species by number of electrons, fewest first.
I. Ca2+
II. Se2−
III. Ti
h: Start from each atomic number. Subtract electrons for a positive charge and add them for a negative charge.
w: Ca2+: 20 − 2 = 18. Ti: 22. Se2−: 34 + 2 = 36. So I < III < II. The other orders come from adding electrons to the cation, removing them from the anion, or ranking by atomic number alone.
x: Ca²⁺ has lost two electrons. Recount it and compare with Ti.
Se²⁻ has gained two electrons, so it has more than 34.
A 2− ion has more electrons than its atom. Recount Se²⁻.

q: The diagram shows the 4s and 3d orbitals of a ground-state transition-metal ion with a 2+ charge. Which ion is it?
h: Count the d electrons. A period 4 transition metal loses its 4s electrons first, so the neutral atom had 2 more valence electrons than the ion shows.
w: The diagram shows 7 electrons in 3d and none in 4s. Adding back the two 4s electrons gives a neutral atom with [Ar]4s23d7, cobalt, so the ion is Co2+. Mn2+ is 3d5, Fe2+ is 3d6 and Ni2+ is 3d8.
x: Mn has 7 valence electrons as an atom, but its 2+ ion keeps only five 3d electrons.
Ni²⁺ keeps eight 3d electrons. Recount the arrows.
Fe²⁺ keeps six 3d electrons. Recount the arrows.

q:
Each diagram shows the 4s and 3d electrons of the ion named. Which diagrams show the ground state correctly?
I. Ti2+
II. Cu+
III. Ni2+
h: When a period 4 transition metal forms a cation, the 4s electrons leave before any 3d electrons.
w: I is wrong: Ti is [Ar]4s23d2, so Ti2+ should be 3d2 with an empty 4s, not 4s2 with an empty 3d. II is right: Cu is [Ar]4s13d10, and Cu+ loses the 4s electron to give 3d10. III is wrong: Ni2+ should be 3d8 with an empty 4s, not 4s23d6. II only.
x: Diagram I is wrong. Ti²⁺ should lose its 4s electrons, not its 3d electrons.
Diagram III is wrong. Ni²⁺ should have an empty 4s and eight 3d electrons.
Diagrams I and III both remove 3d electrons and keep 4s. The 4s electrons leave first.

q: The energy-level diagram shows every electron of a neutral atom. What does the diagram represent?
c: an excited state of a magnesium atom
the ground state of an aluminum atom
the ground state of a magnesium atom
an excited state of a sodium atom
