h: Count all the arrows to find the element. Then ask whether a lower-energy orbital is left partly empty while a higher one is used.
w: The diagram holds 12 electrons, so the atom is magnesium. In the ground state both 3s electrons would be paired in 3s, but here one sits in 3p, so this is an excited state of a magnesium atom. Aluminum has 13 electrons and sodium has 11.
x: Aluminum has 13 electrons. Count the arrows again.
In the ground state, 3s fills completely before any electron enters 3p.
Sodium has 11 electrons. Count the arrows again.

q: The diagram shows the only four energy levels of a hypothetical atom. If electrons can drop from any level to any lower level, how many different lines can appear in the emission spectrum?
h: Each line comes from one pair of levels, with the electron moving down. Count the pairs.
w: Every pair of levels gives one downward drop: from the top level there are 3, from the next 2 and from the next 1, so 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 lines. The gaps (2, 4, 6, 11, 15 and 17 × 10−19 J) are all different, so each line has its own wavelength. 3 counts only drops to the next level down, 4 is the number of levels, and 12 counts upward jumps too, which are absorption.
x: Drops can skip levels. Count jumps between any two levels, not just neighbors.
That is the number of levels, not the number of pairs of levels.
Upward jumps absorb light. The emission spectrum includes only downward drops.

q: The diagram shows energy levels of a hypothetical atom. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted in the transition shown by the arrow? (h = 6.626 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s, c = 2.998 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>)
h: The photon carries the energy difference between the two levels. Then use λ = hc/E.
w: The arrow drops from −9.00 to −16.00 × 10−19 J, so Ephoton = 7.00 × 10−19 J. λ = hc/E = (6.626 × 10−34)(2.998 × 108) ÷ (7.00 × 10−19) = 2.84 × 10−7 m = 284 nm. 221 nm uses the upper level's energy alone, 124 nm uses the lower level's energy alone, and 79.5 nm adds the two energies.
x: This uses only the starting level's energy. The photon energy is the gap between the levels.
This uses only the final level's energy. The photon energy is the gap between the levels.
This adds the two level energies. The photon carries their difference.

q: Three lines in the visible emission spectrum of an element are labeled I, II and III. Rank the photon energies of these lines, lowest first.
h: E = hc/λ, so photon energy goes down as wavelength goes up.
w: Line I is at 640 nm, III at 530 nm and II at 425 nm. The longest wavelength has the lowest energy, so I < III < II. The reverse order assumes energy rises with wavelength, and the others follow the labels instead of the positions.
x: This ranks by wavelength. Photon energy is inversely related to wavelength.
This follows the label numbers, not where the lines sit on the wavelength scale.
Line III is not the longest wavelength. Read each line's position on the scale.

q: The diagram shows four ultraviolet lines in the emission spectrum of hydrogen. All four come from electrons falling to n = 1. Which line comes from the n = 4 → n = 1 transition? (E<sub>n</sub> = −2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J/n<sup>2</sup>)
h: Find ΔE for the drop from n = 4 to n = 1, then λ = hc/ΔE. A bigger drop releases more energy and gives a shorter wavelength.
w: ΔE = 2.18 × 10−18 J (1 − 1/16) = 2.04 × 10−18 J, and λ = hc/ΔE = 97.2 nm. In order of decreasing wavelength the lines come from n = 2 (121.5 nm), n = 3 (102.5 nm), n = 4 (97.2 nm) and n = 5 (94.9 nm).
x: 121.5 nm is the smallest drop of the series, the one from n = 2.
102.5 nm is the drop from n = 3.
94.9 nm is a larger drop than n = 4 → n = 1, the one from n = 5.

q: Four elements are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Which marked element has exactly two unpaired electrons in its ground-state atom?
h: Write each valence configuration from the element's position, then apply Hund's rule to the partly filled subshell.
w: A is silicon, 3s23p2: the two 3p electrons sit in separate orbitals, so A has 2 unpaired electrons. B is phosphorus, 3p3, with 3. C is calcium, 4s2, with 0. D is manganese, 3d5, with 5.
x: B has three p electrons, each in its own orbital.
C has only a filled s subshell, so all its electrons are paired.
D has five d electrons, one in each d orbital.

q: Elements I, II and III are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Rank them by first ionization energy, lowest first.
h: Ionization energy falls down a group. Across a period it rises, but watch for the first element whose removed p electron is paired.
w: III (phosphorus) is below I, so it has the lowest value. I is nitrogen (2p3, half-filled) and II is oxygen (2p4); oxygen's fourth 2p electron is paired, and the repulsion makes it easier to remove, so O < N. Order: III < II < I (P 1012, O 1314, N 1402 kJ mol−1).
x: This follows the simple left to right trend. Oxygen's paired 2p electron makes its value lower than nitrogen's.
This is backward. Moving down a group lowers the ionization energy.
Phosphorus is one period lower, so its electron is held less tightly than oxygen's.

q: The bar graph shows the first six ionization energies of a period 3 element X. In which group of the periodic table is X?
h: Look for the huge jump. Electrons before the jump are valence electrons, and the electron after it comes from the core.
w: IE1 to IE5 rise gradually, then IE6 jumps from about 6300 to 21,300 kJ mol−1. So X has five valence electrons and the sixth comes from the n = 2 core: Group 15 (phosphorus). Group 16 counts the jump bar itself, and the smaller rises after IE3 and IE4 are not the core jump.
x: This counts the sixth bar as a valence electron. That bar is the first core electron.
The rise from IE₃ to IE₄ is small compared with the jump after IE₅.
The rise from IE₄ to IE₅ is small compared with the jump after IE₅.

q: The table lists four sets of quantum numbers. Which set could describe a valence electron of a ground-state bromine atom?
h: Bromine's valence electrons are in 4s and 4p. Check that each set is allowed and points to one of those subshells.
w: Set 1 (n = 4, ℓ = 1) is a 4p electron, and Br is [Ar]4s23d104p5. Set 2 is a 4d electron, and 4d is empty in Br. Set 3 is a 3p electron, which is a core electron. Set 4 is not allowed, because mℓ cannot be 1 when ℓ = 0.
x: Set 2 has ℓ = 2 in the fourth shell, a 4d orbital. No electrons are there in ground-state Br.
Set 3 is in the third shell, which is part of bromine's core.
Check mℓ. When ℓ = 0 the only allowed mℓ value is 0.

q:
Which statements about effective nuclear charge (Zeff) are true?
I. In a neon atom, a 1s electron feels a larger Zeff than a 2p electron.
II. Core electrons shield valence electrons better than electrons in the same shell shield each other.
III. The Zeff felt by valence electrons increases from Li to F.
h: Z<sub>eff</sub> is the nuclear charge minus the shielding by electrons that sit, on average, between the electron and the nucleus.
w: I is true: the 1s electron sits inside the n = 2 electrons and is barely shielded. II is true: core electrons lie between the nucleus and the valence shell, while same-shell electrons shield each other poorly. III is true: across period 2 each step adds a proton but only a poorly shielding same-shell electron. I, II and III.
x: Statement III is also true. Each step from Li to F adds a proton while the core stays the same.
Statement I is also true. Few electrons sit between a 1s electron and the nucleus.
Statement II is also true. Core electrons lie between the nucleus and the valence shell.

q:
The table gives the energies of the four lowest levels of the hydrogen atom. Which statements are true?
I. The energy gap between n = 2 and n = 3 is larger than the gap between n = 3 and n = 4.
II. An electron in the n = 1 level has the highest energy.
III. Removing the electron from n = 2 takes one fourth of the energy needed to remove it from n = 1.
h: E<sub>n</sub> = −2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J/n<sup>2</sup>. Ionization takes the electron from its level up to E = 0.
w: I is true: the levels crowd together as n rises (3.03 vs 1.06 × 10−19 J). II is false: n = 1 is the lowest, most negative energy. III is true: ionizing from n takes 2.18 × 10−18 J/n2, so n = 2 needs 1/4 as much as n = 1. I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. The ionization energy from level n is proportional to 1/n².
Statement II is false. The n = 1 level is the lowest point on the diagram.
Statement II is false. The n = 1 level has the most negative energy.

q:
Elements A, B and C are marked on the outline of the periodic table. Which statements are true?
I. C is more electronegative than A.
II. B has a larger atomic radius than A.
III. C has a larger atomic radius than B.
h: Electronegativity rises toward the upper right of the table. Atomic radius grows down a group and shrinks across a period.
w: I is false: A (oxygen) is up and to the right of C (aluminum), so A is far more electronegative. II is true: B (sulfur) is below A in group 16, with one more shell. III is true: C is left of B in period 3, where Zeff is lower, so C is larger. II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. C is a metal far to the lower left of A.
Statement II is also true. B is one period below A in the same group.
Statement I is false. Electronegativity is highest toward the upper right, where A sits.

q: The graph shows the atomic (covalent) radii of the elements from Z = 1 to 20, with the noble gases left out. Four points are labeled P–S. Which labeled element has the highest first ionization energy?
h: The smaller the atom, the closer its valence electrons are to the nucleus and the harder they are to remove.
w: Q (Z = 9, fluorine) has the smallest radius of the four, so its valence electrons are held most tightly and its first ionization energy is highest. P (Li), R (Na) and S (K) are the large group 1 atoms at the start of each period, which have the lowest ionization energies.
x: P is at the start of period 2, where atoms are large and lose an electron easily.
R is a large group 1 atom. Its valence electron is far from the nucleus.
S is the largest atom on the graph, so it has the lowest ionization energy.

q:
Rank these ground-state ions by number of unpaired electrons, fewest first.
I. Cr3+
II. Co3+
III. Cu2+
h: Remove the 4s electrons first, then fill the five 3d orbitals one electron at a time before pairing.
w: Cr3+ is 3d3 (3 unpaired), Co3+ is 3d6 (4 unpaired: one pair and four singles), and Cu2+ is 3d9 (1 unpaired). So III < I < II. Ranking by atomic number or counting all d electrons gives a different order.
x: This follows atomic number. Cu²⁺ has nine 3d electrons, so only one is unpaired.
Co³⁺ has six 3d electrons, which leaves four unpaired, more than Cr³⁺.
Cu²⁺ has only one unpaired electron, fewer than Cr³⁺.

q: The top spectrum is the emission spectrum of a gas mixture. Below it are the emission spectra of elements A, B and C. Which elements are in the mixture?
h: Each element gives its own set of lines wherever it is. An element is present only if every one of its lines appears in the mixture.
w: All three A lines (450, 520, 610 nm) and all three C lines (405, 590, 650 nm) appear in the mixture, but none of the B lines (470, 560, 680 nm) do. The mixture contains A and C only.
x: Some mixture lines are not A lines. Another element must be present too.
None of B's lines appear in the mixture spectrum.
B's lines are missing from the mixture, so B cannot be present.

q: The bars show the SECOND ionization energies of the period 3 elements in order (bar 1 = Na, bar 8 = Ar). What best explains why the bar for sodium is far taller than the others?
c: Na<sup>+</sup> has a noble-gas core, so its next electron comes from n = 2.
Na has the largest atomic radius in period 3.
Na has the smallest nuclear charge in period 3.
Na<sup>+</sup> has a half-filled 3s subshell that resists losing an electron.
h: Write the configuration of each element's 1+ ion and ask where the second electron must come from.
w: After sodium loses its single 3s electron, Na+ is [Ne], so the second electron must come from the n = 2 shell, much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded: a core electron. A large radius or a small nuclear charge would make ionization easier, not harder, and Na+ has no 3s electrons at all.
x: A large radius makes electrons easier to remove, which would lower the bar.
A smaller nuclear charge would make the electron easier to remove, not harder.
Na⁺ has lost its only 3s electron, so its 3s subshell is empty.

q: A ground-state hydrogen atom absorbs a 97.2 nm photon, which raises its electron to n = 4. The atom then returns to n = 1 by emitting exactly two photons. Which pair of wavelengths could those two photons have? The diagram shows levels n = 2 to 4. The n = 1 level, at −21.8 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J, is far below the graph.
h: The two emitted photon energies must add up to the energy absorbed. The path must go 4 → some level → 1.
w: With two photons, the electron goes 4 → 3 → 1 or 4 → 2 → 1. The 4 → 3 drop gives 1875 nm and the 3 → 1 drop gives 102.6 nm, so 1875 nm and 102.6 nm works. 656 + 121.6 nm is the path 3 → 2 → 1, which starts at n = 3. 434 + 121.6 nm is 5 → 2 → 1, and 1282 + 102.6 nm is 5 → 3 → 1, both starting at n = 5.
x: 656 nm is the 3 → 2 drop, so this path starts at n = 3, not n = 4.
434 nm is the 5 → 2 drop, so this path starts at n = 5, not n = 4.
1282 nm is the 5 → 3 drop, so this path starts at n = 5, not n = 4.

q: How many electrons in a ground-state iron atom (Z = 26) have the quantum number ℓ = 2?
h: ℓ = 2 means a d orbital. Write the configuration and count the d electrons.
w: Fe is 1s22s22p63s23p64s23d6. Only the 3d electrons have ℓ = 2, so there are 6. 2 counts the 4s electrons, 8 counts all valence electrons (4s + 3d), and 10 is the capacity of a d subshell.
x: The 4s electrons have ℓ = 0, not ℓ = 2.
This adds the 4s electrons, which have ℓ = 0.
10 is how many a d subshell can hold, not how many iron has.

q: Each box shows a sample of a different gas: box I holds water vapor (H<sub>2</sub>O), box II carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>), box III oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) and box IV ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>). Which box contains the greatest mass of gas?
h: Count the molecules in each box, then weigh them: number of molecules × molar mass of the molecule.
w: Mass is proportional to (number of molecules) × (molar mass). Box I: 6 × 18.02 = 108 u. Box II: 3 × 44.01 = 132 u. Box III: 4 × 32.00 = 128 u. Box IV: 7 × 17.03 = 119 u. So box II is heaviest even though it has the fewest molecules. Box IV has the most molecules and the most atoms, but NH3 molecules are light.
x: Box IV has the most molecules and the most atoms, but each NH₃ molecule weighs only 17 u. Multiply the count by the molar mass.
Box III is close. Multiply 4 by 32.00 and compare it with the other boxes again.
Box I has many atoms, but most of them are light H atoms. Weigh each box with molar masses.

q: The box shows a sample of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>. Each drawn molecule stands for 0.250 mol of NH<sub>3</sub>. What mass of hydrogen does the sample contain?
h: Count the molecules to get moles of NH<sub>3</sub>, then use the formula: each NH<sub>3</sub> carries three H atoms.
w: 6 molecules × 0.250 mol = 1.50 mol NH3. Each mole of NH3 holds 3 mol H, so 4.50 mol H × 1.008 g mol−1 = 4.54 g. 1.51 g counts only one H per molecule, 3.02 g counts two, and 25.5 g is the mass of the whole NH3 sample.
x: This uses one H atom per molecule. Look at how many H atoms each NH₃ carries.
This is the mass of all the NH₃, nitrogen included. Only the hydrogen is asked for.
This counts two H atoms per molecule. Count the H atoms on one molecule in the drawing again.

q: Glycine, the simplest amino acid, is drawn below with every atom shown. What is the mass percent of nitrogen in glycine?
h: Read the molecular formula from the drawing first (count every C, H, N and O), then divide the mass of N by the molar mass.
w: The drawing shows C2H5NO2: 2(12.01) + 5(1.008) + 14.01 + 2(16.00) = 75.07 g mol−1. %N = 14.01/75.07 × 100 = 18.66%. Leaving out the H atoms gives 20.01%, 10.00% is the fraction of atoms that are N, and 42.63% is the percent oxygen.
x: This molar mass leaves out the five H atoms. Count them in the drawing and include them.
This is 1 N out of 10 atoms. Mass percent must weigh each atom by its atomic mass.
This is the mass percent of oxygen, not nitrogen.

q: Succinic acid, an intermediate in cellular respiration, is drawn below. What is its empirical formula?
h: Count each kind of atom to get the molecular formula, then divide all the subscripts by their largest common factor.
w: The drawing has 4 C, 6 H and 4 O, so the molecular formula is C4H6O4. Dividing by 2 gives C2H3O2. C4H6O4 is the molecular formula, not the simplest ratio. C2H2O2 misses the two O–H hydrogens.
x: This is the molecular formula. An empirical formula is the smallest whole number ratio.
This misses the H atoms bonded to oxygen. Count every H in the drawing.
CH₂O has the right 1 to 1 ratio of C to O, but it has 2 H per C. The drawing has 6 H for 4 C, only 1.5 H per C.

q:
Box I contains oxygen, O2, and box II contains ozone, O3. Which statements about the two samples are true?
I. They contain the same number of oxygen atoms.
II. They have the same mass.
III. They contain the same number of moles of molecules.
h: Count molecules and atoms in each box. The mass of a sample depends only on which atoms it holds.
w: Box I has 6 O2 = 12 O atoms, and box II has 4 O3 = 12 O atoms, so I is true. Both samples are 12 oxygen atoms, so they have the same mass, and II is true. III is false: 6 molecules is not the same amount as 4 molecules. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true. Both samples are made of the same 12 oxygen atoms, so their masses match.
Statement III is false. Box I has 6 molecules and box II has only 4.
Statement I is true. Count the atoms: each box holds 12 O atoms.

q: Samples of different masses of one oxide of sulfur were analyzed. The graph shows the mass of oxygen in each sample against the mass of the sample. What is the formula of the oxide?
h: The slope of the line is the mass fraction of oxygen. Compare it with the mass percent of O in each formula.
w: The line passes through (10.0 g, 6.0 g), so the oxide is 60% O by mass. SO3: 48.00/80.06 = 60.0% O. SO2 is 50.0% O, S2O3 42.8% and SO 33.3%. The oxide is SO3.
x: SO₂ is 50% oxygen by mass. Read the oxygen mass at 10 g on the graph again.
S₂O₃ is under 43% oxygen by mass, below what the line shows.
SO is only about one third oxygen by mass, far below the line.

q: The graph shows the mass of samples of a pure gas against the number of molecules in each sample. Which gas is it?
h: Read one point, convert the number of molecules to moles with Avogadro's number, then divide mass by moles.
w: At 6.0 × 1022 molecules the mass is 6.4 g. Moles = 6.0 × 1022 / 6.022 × 1023 = 0.0996 mol, so M = 6.4 g / 0.0996 mol ≈ 64 g mol−1, which is SO2 (64.06). CO2 (44.01) and O2 (32.00) would give lower lines, and Cl2 (70.90) a higher one.
x: CO₂ is 44 g per mole, so its line would reach only about 4.4 g at 6 × 10²² molecules.
Cl₂ is about 71 g per mole, so its line would sit above this one.
O₂ is 32 g per mole, half of what this line gives.

q: Urea, drawn below, is a common nitrogen fertilizer. What mass of nitrogen is in a 25.0 kg bag of pure urea?
h: Read the formula from the drawing, find the mass fraction of N (count every N atom), and multiply by the mass of the bag.
w: Urea is CH4N2O, 60.06 g mol−1, with 2 × 14.01 = 28.02 g N per mole. Mass of N = 25.0 kg × 28.02/60.06 = 11.7 kg. 5.83 kg counts only one N atom, 6.25 kg uses the fraction of atoms (2 of 8), and 13.3 kg is the mass of everything except nitrogen.
x: This counts one N atom. The drawing shows two NH₂ groups.
This uses 2 N out of 8 atoms. Mass percent must use atomic masses, not atom counts.
This is the mass of the C, H and O in the bag, the part that is not nitrogen.

q: Three samples of chromium were heated in oxygen until each was completely converted to the same chromium oxide. The results are in the table. What is the empirical formula of the oxide?
h: The mass of oxygen is the oxide mass minus the chromium mass. Convert both to moles and find the whole number ratio.
w: Trial 2: O = 3.800 − 2.600 = 1.200 g. Cr: 2.600/52.00 = 0.05000 mol. O: 1.200/16.00 = 0.07500 mol. The ratio O:Cr = 1.500, so multiply by 2: Cr2O3. Every trial gives the same ratio. A ratio of 1.5 cannot be rounded to 1 (CrO) or 2 (CrO2), and Cr3O2 inverts it.
x: This rounds an O to Cr ratio of 1.5 down to 1. A ratio of 1.5 must be multiplied to get whole numbers.
This rounds an O to Cr ratio of 1.5 up to 2. Multiply by a small whole number instead of rounding.
This inverts the ratio. There are more moles of O than moles of Cr.

q: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) has the mass composition shown in the table. What is its empirical formula?
h: Assume a 100 g sample, convert each mass to moles, and divide by the smallest. If a ratio ends in .33 or .67, multiply everything by 3.
w: In 100 g: C 40.92/12.01 = 3.407 mol, H 4.58/1.008 = 4.54 mol, O 54.50/16.00 = 3.406 mol. Dividing by 3.406 gives C 1.000 : H 1.333 : O 1.000. Multiplying by 3 gives C3H4O3. CHO rounds 1.33 to 1, and C6H8O6 is the molecular formula, which is twice the empirical one.
x: This rounds an H ratio of 1.33 down to 1. That ratio is too far from a whole number to round.
Doubling gives 2 : 2.67 : 2, which is still not whole numbers. Try a different multiplier.
This is the molecular formula of vitamin C. Its subscripts can still be divided by a common factor.

q: Ammonium dichromate, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, is used in the classic "volcano" demonstration. What is its molar mass?
h: The subscript after the parentheses multiplies every atom inside them. Count N, H, Cr and O separately.
w: One formula unit holds 2 N, 8 H, 2 Cr and 7 O: 2(14.01) + 8(1.008) + 2(52.00) + 7(16.00) = 252.08 g mol−1. 234.04 counts only one NH4, 200.08 counts only one Cr, and 156.08 counts only one O.
x: This counts one NH₄ group. The subscript 2 outside the parentheses doubles the N and the H.
This counts one Cr atom. The formula has Cr₂.
This counts one O atom. The formula has seven.

q: A flask holds 8.00 g of methane, CH<sub>4</sub>. What mass of oxygen gas, O<sub>2</sub>, contains the same number of molecules?
h: Equal numbers of molecules means equal moles. Find the moles of CH<sub>4</sub>, then the mass of that many moles of O<sub>2</sub>.
w: 8.00 g / 16.04 g mol−1 = 0.499 mol CH4. The same number of O2 molecules is 0.499 mol × 32.00 g mol−1 = 16.0 g. 8.00 g would be equal masses, not equal molecules, and 39.9 g would match the number of atoms.
x: Equal masses of different substances contain different numbers of molecules.
This matches the number of atoms (5 per CH₄, 2 per O₂), not the number of molecules.
This inverts the molar mass ratio. An O₂ molecule is heavier than a CH₄ molecule.

q:
Rank these sulfur compounds by mass percent of sulfur, from lowest to highest.
I. FeS2 (pyrite)
II. SO2
III. CuS
h: Work out mass of S divided by molar mass for each. The number of S atoms in the formula matters, and so does how heavy the partner atoms are.
w: FeS2: 64.14/119.99 = 53.5% S. SO2: 32.07/64.07 = 50.1% S. CuS: 32.07/95.62 = 33.5% S. So III < II < I. SO2 and FeS2 are close, so each must be calculated.
x: CuS does not have the highest percent sulfur, because copper is much heavier than sulfur.
This is the reverse order. Calculate the mass percent of S for each formula.
FeS₂ has two S atoms per formula, which lifts it above SO₂.

q: Which compound has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O?
h: Count the atoms in each structure to get its molecular formula, then reduce it to the simplest whole number ratio.
w: Acetic acid has 2 C, 4 H and 2 O: C2H4O2, which reduces to CH2O, so the answer is acetic acid. Ethanol is C2H6O, acetone is C3H6O and formic acid is CH2O2. None of these reduce to CH2O.
x: This structure has 2 C, 6 H and 1 O. That ratio does not reduce to CH₂O.
This structure has 3 C but only 1 O, so C and O are not 1 to 1.
This structure has one C and two O atoms, so C and O are not 1 to 1.

q:
Ethylene glycol, the main ingredient in antifreeze, is drawn below. Which statements are true?
I. Its empirical formula is CH3O.
II. One mole of it contains 6.022 × 1023 oxygen atoms.
III. Its mass percent of carbon equals that of methanol, CH3OH.
h: Get the molecular formula from the drawing. Two compounds have the same mass percents only if they share an empirical formula.
w: The drawing shows C2H6O2. I is true: it reduces to CH3O. II is false: each molecule has 2 O atoms, so a mole has 1.204 × 1024 O atoms. III is false: ethylene glycol is 38.7% C, but methanol (CH4O, a different empirical formula) is 37.5% C. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. Each molecule has two O atoms, so one mole has twice Avogadro's number of O atoms.
Statement III is false. Methanol is CH₄O, which is not the same empirical formula, so its percent carbon differs.
Statement II is false. Each molecule carries two O atoms, not one.

q: Glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has a molar mass of 180.16 g mol<sup>−1</sup>. What is the mass of a single glucose molecule?
h: One mole is 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> molecules. Divide the mass of a mole by the number of molecules in it.
w: Mass of one molecule = 180.16 g / 6.022 × 1023 = 2.992 × 10−22 g. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1.085 × 1026 g, which is far too large for one molecule, and 1.661 × 10−24 g is the mass of 1 atomic mass unit.
x: This multiplies by Avogadro's number. One molecule must weigh far less than a mole of molecules.
This is the mass of a whole mole of glucose molecules.
This is the mass of one atomic mass unit. A glucose molecule is 180 u.

q: The first box holds 2 molecules of oxygen, O<sub>2</sub>. Boxes I–IV hold helium atoms. Which helium box has the same mass as the O<sub>2</sub> box?
h: Find the mass of the O<sub>2</sub> box in atomic mass units, then work out how many He atoms (4.00 u each) have that mass.
w: Two O2 molecules weigh 2 × 32.00 = 64.00 u. Each He atom is 4.00 u, so 64.00/4.00 = 16 He atoms are needed, which is box IV. Box I has the same number of particles, box II the same number of atoms, and box III uses 16 u for each O2 molecule instead of 32 u.
x: This box has the same number of particles. Each O₂ molecule is eight times heavier than a He atom.
This box matches the number of atoms, but an O atom is four times as heavy as a He atom.
This treats each O₂ molecule as 16 u. An O₂ molecule has two O atoms, so it is 32 u.

q: The box shows the ions in a sample of solid aluminum sulfate, Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (342.14 g mol<sup>−1</sup>). Each drawn ion stands for 0.0100 mol of that ion. What is the mass of the sample?
h: Find the moles of Al<sup>3+</sup> from the drawing. Each formula unit of Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> releases two Al<sup>3+</sup> ions.
w: There are 4 Al3+ (0.0400 mol) and 6 SO42− (0.0600 mol). Each formula unit has 2 Al3+ and 3 SO42−, so there are 0.0200 mol Al2(SO4)3. Mass = 0.0200 × 342.14 = 6.84 g. 34.2 g treats all 10 ions as formula units, and 13.7 g treats each Al3+ as a formula unit.
x: This treats all 10 ions as 10 formula units. Five ions make up one formula unit.
This treats each Al³⁺ ion as a whole formula unit. Each unit holds two Al³⁺ ions.
This counts only 0.0100 mol of compound. Use the ion counts to find how many formula units there are.

q: The boxes show a reaction mixture of A<sub>2</sub> and B<sub>2</sub> molecules before and after the reaction. Which balanced equation, with the smallest whole-number coefficients, represents the reaction?
h: Molecules that appear unchanged in both boxes did not react. Count only what was used up and what was made, then reduce.
w: Before: 5 A2 and 3 B2. After: 4 A2B plus 1 A2 and 1 B2 left over. So 4 A2 + 2 B2 made 4 A2B, which reduces to 2 A2 + B2 → 2 A2B. Leftover molecules are not part of the equation, and A2 + B2 → A2B is not balanced for A.
x: Leftover A₂ and B₂ molecules did not react, so they do not belong in the equation.
This is not balanced. Count the A atoms on each side.
These coefficients can still be divided by a common factor.

q: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with chlorine as shown. The Before box shows the starting mixture. Which box (I–IV) shows the contents after the reaction goes to completion?
h: Find the limiting reactant from the 2 : 1 mole ratio. At completion it is gone, and every atom from the Before box must still be present.
w: 6 NO need only 3 Cl2, and 5 Cl2 are present, so NO is limiting. 6 NO + 3 Cl2 → 6 NOCl, leaving 2 Cl2: box III. Box I still has both reactants, so the reaction is not complete. Box II shows lone Cl atoms, but leftover chlorine stays as Cl2. Box IV has 16 Cl atoms but only 10 were present.
x: This box still contains both NO and Cl₂, so the reaction has not gone to completion.
Leftover chlorine stays as Cl₂ molecules. It does not split into separate atoms.
Count the Cl atoms. This box has more chlorine than the Before box.

q: Hydrogen sulfide burns as shown. The box shows a mixture of H<sub>2</sub>S and O<sub>2</sub>. What would have to be added to the box so that both reactants are completely used up with nothing left over?
h: Count each reactant. Find how much of each the other one needs using the 2 : 3 ratio, and see which one is short.
w: The box holds 4 H2S and 9 O2. 4 H2S need only 6 O2, so O2 is in excess. 9 O2 need 9 × 2/3 = 6 H2S, so 2 more H2S molecules must be added. 6 is the total H2S needed, not the number to add, and 5 assumes a 1 : 1 ratio.
x: Six is the total number of H₂S molecules needed. Some are already in the box.
This assumes H₂S and O₂ react 1 to 1. Use the coefficients 2 and 3.
O₂ is already in excess here. Adding more of it leaves even more unused.

q: Potassium chlorate decomposes on heating as shown. What mass of O<sub>2</sub> forms when 5.00 g of KClO<sub>3</sub> decomposes completely?
h: Grams of KClO<sub>3</sub> → moles of KClO<sub>3</sub> → moles of O<sub>2</sub> (use the 2 : 3 ratio) → grams of O<sub>2</sub>.
w: 5.00 g / 122.55 g mol−1 = 0.04080 mol KClO3. × (3 mol O2 / 2 mol KClO3) = 0.06120 mol O2. × 32.00 g mol−1 = 1.96 g. 1.31 g uses a 1 : 1 ratio, 0.870 g turns the ratio upside down, and 3.92 g uses 3 mol O2 for every mole of KClO3.
x: This uses a 1 to 1 mole ratio. The equation shows 3 O₂ for every 2 KClO₃.
This turns the mole ratio upside down. More moles of O₂ form than moles of KClO₃ used.
This takes 3 mol O₂ from each mole of KClO₃. The coefficients give 3 O₂ per 2 KClO₃.

q: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol as shown. A batch starting with 100.0 g of glucose yields 40.0 g of ethanol. What is the percent yield?
h: First find the theoretical yield of ethanol in grams from the glucose. Percent yield = actual/theoretical × 100.
w: 100.0 g / 180.16 g mol−1 = 0.5551 mol glucose → 1.110 mol ethanol × 46.07 g mol−1 = 51.14 g (theoretical). Percent yield = 40.0/51.14 × 100 = 78.2%. 40.0% compares masses of different substances, 156% uses a 1 : 1 ratio, and 128% divides theoretical by actual.
x: This compares grams of ethanol with grams of glucose directly. Find the theoretical yield of ethanol first.
A yield above 100% is a warning sign. Check the mole ratio of ethanol to glucose.
This divides the theoretical yield by the actual yield. The actual yield goes on top.

q: In a series of experiments, 2.00 g of zinc is heated with different masses of sulfur, and the mass of ZnS formed is measured (graph). Zn + S → ZnS. In the experiment at point B, which reactant is limiting, and what is left over?
c: Zn is limiting, and about 0.52 g of S is left
S is limiting, and about 0.52 g of Zn is left
Zn is limiting, and about 1.50 g of S is left
Neither, both reactants are used up exactly
h: On the rising part of the graph, adding more S makes more ZnS. On the flat part, adding S makes no more product. Where does the line level off?
w: The mass of ZnS stops rising at about 0.98 g of S (2.00 g Zn / 65.39 g mol−1 = 0.0306 mol needs 0.0306 mol × 32.07 = 0.98 g S). At point B, 1.50 g of S was added, so Zn is limiting and about 0.52 g of S is left (1.50 − 0.98). S is the limiting reactant only on the rising part, such as point A.
x: On the flat part adding more sulfur makes no more ZnS, so sulfur is not what limits the product there.
Only part of the sulfur at point B reacts. Find where the graph levels off.
At point B more sulfur was added than the zinc can use. The exact match is where the graph levels off.

q: A solution of a metal ion M<sup>n+</sup> and a NaOH solution, both 0.100 M, are mixed in different proportions. The total volume is always 12.0 mL. The precipitate M(OH)<sub>n</sub> is collected and weighed (graph). What is the value of n?

x.label: Volume of 0.100 M NaOH (mL); the rest is 0.100 M M<sup>n+</sup>

h: The most precipitate forms when the two ions are mixed in exactly the ratio of the formula. Read the volumes of the two solutions at the peak.
w: The peak is at 9.0 mL of NaOH, which leaves 3.0 mL of the Mn+ solution. Both are 0.100 M, so the mole ratio OH− : Mn+ = 9.0 : 3.0 = 3 : 1. The formula is M(OH)3, so n = 3. A ratio of 1 or 2 would put the peak at 6.0 mL or 8.0 mL of NaOH.
x: A 1 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 6 mL of each solution. Read where this peak is.
A 2 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 8 mL of NaOH. Read the peak on the graph again.
A 4 to 1 ratio would put the peak at 9.6 mL of NaOH. Read the peak on the graph again.

q: Ammonia gas passed over hot copper(II) oxide reduces it to copper metal (skeleton equation below). When the equation is balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the coefficient of CuO?
h: Start with N: N<sub>2</sub> needs two NH<sub>3</sub>. Then balance H with water, O with CuO, and Cu last.
w: N2 needs 2 NH3, whose 6 H make 3 H2O. Three O atoms require 3 CuO, which give 3 Cu: 2 NH3 + 3 CuO → 3 Cu + N2 + 3 H2O. Check: N 2 = 2, H 6 = 6, Cu 3 = 3, O 3 = 3.
x: Two is the coefficient of NH₃. Balance H with water and then match the O atoms with CuO.
With one CuO there is only one O atom, but the H atoms from ammonia need more water than that.
These are not the smallest whole numbers. Check whether the whole set can be halved.

q: Acetone, drawn below, burns completely in oxygen to give CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. How many moles of O<sub>2</sub> are needed to burn 0.250 mol of acetone?
h: Read the formula from the drawing and write the balanced combustion equation. Don't forget the oxygen atom already in acetone.
w: Acetone is C3H6O: C3H6O + 4 O2 → 3 CO2 + 3 H2O (O: 1 + 8 = 6 + 3). 0.250 mol × 4 = 1.00 mol O2. 1.13 mol ignores the O atom in acetone, and 0.750 mol is the amount of CO2 (or H2O) formed.
x: This leaves out the oxygen atom that acetone already contains. Count it when balancing O.
This is the amount of CO₂ produced, not the O₂ consumed.
This divides by the coefficient instead of multiplying. More O₂ is needed than acetone.

q: 5.00 g of iron and 8.00 g of chlorine react as shown until one reactant is used up. What mass of the excess reactant remains?
h: Convert both masses to moles. Find which one runs out first using the 2 : 3 ratio, then find how much of the other one reacts.
w: Fe: 5.00/55.85 = 0.0895 mol. Cl2: 8.00/70.90 = 0.1128 mol. All the Fe would need 0.134 mol Cl2, more than is present, so Cl2 is limiting. Fe used = 0.1128 × 2/3 = 0.0752 mol = 4.20 g, so 0.80 g of Fe remains. 4.20 g is the iron that reacts, and 3.00 g of Cl2 assumes the smaller mass runs out.
x: This treats iron as limiting. Check whether there is enough Cl₂ for all of the iron.
Subtracting the masses does not find the limiting reactant. Compare moles using the coefficients.
This is the mass of iron that reacts. The question asks what is left.

q:
The box shows a mixture of P4 molecules (four P atoms each) and Cl2 molecules that react as shown until one reactant is used up. Which statements are true?
I. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.
II. The total number of molecules in the box is the same after the reaction.
III. The total mass of the box contents is the same after the reaction.
h: Count the molecules of each reactant and use the 1 : 6 ratio. Then count the molecules after the reaction and think about what happens to atoms.
w: The box has 2 P4 and 6 Cl2. Two P4 would need 12 Cl2, so I is true: Cl2 runs out. 6 Cl2 + 1 P4 → 4 PCl3, leaving 1 P4, so there are 5 molecules after versus 8 before, and II is false. III is true because atoms are conserved, so mass is conserved. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. Every atom is still in the box, so the mass cannot change.
Statement II is false. Count the molecules before and after.
Statement I is true. Two P₄ molecules would need twelve Cl₂ molecules.

q:
A student burns a strip of magnesium in a crucible open to the air, so O2 is always in excess. Which statements are true?
I. Using more O2 would increase the theoretical yield of MgO.
II. Using a longer strip of Mg would increase the theoretical yield of MgO.
III. If some MgO smoke escapes, the percent yield is lowered.
h: The theoretical yield depends only on the amount of the limiting reactant. The percent yield compares what is collected with that amount.
w: Mg is the limiting reactant. I is false: more of an excess reactant does not change the theoretical yield. II is true: more Mg means more MgO can form. III is true: lost product lowers the actual yield, so the percent yield drops (the theoretical yield is unchanged). The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I is false. O₂ is already in excess, so adding more cannot raise the theoretical yield.
Statement III is also true. Product that escapes is not weighed, so the actual yield falls.
Statement I is false. Extra excess reactant does not change how much product can form.

q:
Each fuel below burns completely to CO2 and H2O. Rank them by the mass of CO2 produced per gram of fuel burned, from least to most.
I. methane, CH4
II. ethane, C2H6
III. propane, C3H8
h: Every C atom in the fuel ends up in one CO<sub>2</sub>. Compare the mass fraction of carbon in each fuel.
w: Grams of CO2 per gram = (number of C × 44.01)/molar mass. CH4: 44.01/16.04 = 2.74. C2H6: 88.02/30.07 = 2.93. C3H8: 132.03/44.10 = 2.99. So I < II < III: the larger the fuel, the higher its fraction of carbon.
x: This is the reverse. Methane has the most hydrogen per carbon, so it has the lowest fraction of carbon.
Ethane has a higher fraction of carbon than methane, so it gives more CO₂ per gram.
Propane has a higher fraction of carbon than ethane. Work out grams of CO₂ per gram for each.

q: A sample of cobalt(II) chloride hydrate, CoCl<sub>2</sub>·nH<sub>2</sub>O, is heated in a crucible until all the water is driven off. The data are shown. What is n? (CoCl<sub>2</sub>: 129.83 g mol<sup>−1</sup>; H<sub>2</sub>O: 18.02 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Find the mass of the hydrate, the anhydrous residue and the water lost. Convert the water and the CoCl<sub>2</sub> to moles and take their ratio.
w: Hydrate = 20.832 − 18.452 = 2.380 g. CoCl2 = 19.752 − 18.452 = 1.300 g, which is 0.01001 mol. Water lost = 2.380 − 1.300 = 1.080 g, which is 0.05993 mol. n = 0.05993/0.01001 = 5.99, so n = 6. 13 treats the whole hydrate mass as water, and 1 compares grams instead of moles.
x: This treats the whole hydrate mass as water. Subtract the residue to get the water lost.
This compares the masses of water and CoCl₂ directly. Convert both to moles first.
4 does not fit the data. Convert the water lost (1.080 g) and the CoCl₂ left (1.300 g) to moles, then divide.

q: A mixture of 2.00 mol of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and 5.40 mol of carbon reacts as shown. What is the theoretical yield of iron?
h: Find how much Fe each reactant could make on its own. The smaller amount is the theoretical yield.
w: From Fe2O3: 2.00 × 2 = 4.00 mol Fe. From C: 5.40 × 2/3 = 3.60 mol Fe. Carbon is limiting, so the theoretical yield is 3.60 mol. 4.00 mol would need 6.00 mol C, which is not available.
x: This is what Fe₂O₃ alone could make, but there is not enough carbon for all of it.
This uses a 1 to 1 ratio of C to Fe. The coefficients are 3 and 2.
This turns the C to Fe ratio upside down. Three C atoms give two Fe atoms.

q: Nitrogen reacts with fluorine as shown. Which box (I–IV) contains N<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> in exactly the right ratio for both to be used up completely?
h: The coefficients say one N<sub>2</sub> molecule for every three F<sub>2</sub> molecules.
w: Box II has 2 N2 and 6 F2, a 1 : 3 ratio, so it makes 4 NF3 with nothing left: box II. Box I (1 : 1) leaves N2 over, box III (3 : 1) has the ratio upside down, and box IV (1 : 6) leaves F2 over.
x: Equal numbers of molecules do not match a 1 to 3 ratio. N₂ would be left over.
This box has the ratio upside down, with more N₂ than F₂.
One N₂ uses only three F₂, so F₂ would be left over.

q: Calcium carbide is made in two steps, shown below. What maximum mass of CaC<sub>2</sub> can be made from 50.0 g of CaCO<sub>3</sub> if carbon is in excess? (CaCO<sub>3</sub>: 100.09 g mol<sup>−1</sup>; CaC<sub>2</sub>: 64.10 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Follow the calcium: one CaCO<sub>3</sub> gives one CaO, which gives one CaC<sub>2</sub>. The coefficient of carbon does not matter here.
w: 50.0 g / 100.09 g mol−1 = 0.4996 mol CaCO3 → 0.4996 mol CaO → 0.4996 mol CaC2. Mass = 0.4996 × 64.10 = 32.0 g. 10.7 g and 96.1 g wrongly bring in the coefficient 3 on carbon, and 64.1 g is the mass of one full mole.
x: This divides by the 3 on carbon. Carbon is in excess, so it does not set the ratio of CaC₂ to CaCO₃.
This multiplies by the 3 on carbon. Each CaO gives one CaC₂.
This is the mass of one mole of CaC₂. Only about half a mole of CaCO₃ is used.

q: Chlorine and fluorine react to form chlorine trifluoride. The boxes show the mixture before the reaction and after it has stopped. What is the percent yield of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
h: Work out how many ClF<sub>3</sub> molecules could form if the reaction went to completion, then compare with how many did form.
w: 3 Cl2 and 9 F2 are in the exact 1 : 3 ratio, so 6 ClF3 could form. Only 4 formed, with 1 Cl2 and 3 F2 left. Percent yield = 4/6 × 100 = 66.7%. 44.4% divides by the 9 F2, 133% divides by the 3 Cl2, and 50.0% is the share of molecules in the After box that are ClF3.
x: This divides by the number of F₂ molecules. Compare with the most ClF₃ that could form.
A yield over 100% is impossible. Each Cl₂ can make two ClF₃.
This is the fraction of molecules after the reaction that are product, not the percent yield.

q: Which statement correctly describes the balanced equation for the combustion of ethane?
c: 2 mol of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 mol of O<sub>2</sub>.
2 g of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 g of O<sub>2</sub>.
The products weigh more than the reactants, since 10 mol form from 9 mol.
2 molecules of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> react with 7 atoms of oxygen.
h: Coefficients count particles (molecules or moles), not grams.
w: Coefficients give the ratio of molecules or moles, so 2 mol of C2H6 react with 7 mol of O2. They are not mass ratios. Mass is always conserved even though the number of moles changes (9 → 10). The 7 counts O2 molecules, which is 14 O atoms.
x: Coefficients count moles or molecules, not grams. The two gases have different molar masses.
Mass is conserved in every reaction. Moles of molecules are not.
The coefficient 7 counts O₂ molecules, and each one has two O atoms.

q: Substances A and B react to form a single product, C. In each trial in the table the reaction goes until one reactant is used up. Which equation fits the data?
h: In trial 1, B is plentiful, so A must run out. In trial 2, A is plentiful, so B must run out. Each tells you one coefficient.
w: Trial 1: if A limits, 1.00 mol A gives 0.500 mol C, so 2 A per C. Trial 2: if B limits, 1.50 mol B gives 0.500 mol C, so 3 B per C. Trial 3 checks it: 2.00 mol A and 3.00 mol B are used up exactly and give 1.00 mol C. The equation is 2 A + 3 B → C. 2 A + 10 B → C assumes all of B reacts in trial 1, but then trial 2 could make only 0.15 mol C.
x: These coefficients are swapped. In trial 2, find how many moles of B make 0.500 mol C.
This assumes all 5.00 mol of B reacts in trial 1. Test it on trial 2, where it predicts far less C.
With a 1 to 1 to 1 ratio, trial 1 would give 1.00 mol C. Compare that with the table.

q: Solutions of MgCl<sub>2</sub> and NaOH were mixed, and Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>(s) formed by the reaction shown. The box shows everything present after the reaction stopped (water not shown). Each cluster of one Mg<sup>2+</sup> with two OH<sup>−</sup> is one unit of the solid. How many formula units of each reactant were mixed?
h: Atoms and ions are conserved. Count every Mg²⁺, Cl⁻, Na⁺ and OH⁻ in the box, both in the solid and dissolved.
w: The box holds 3 Mg(OH)2 units plus 1 dissolved Mg2+, 6 Na+ and 8 Cl−. Total Mg2+ = 4 and Cl− = 8, which is 4 MgCl2. Total OH− = 6 (all in the solid) and Na+ = 6, which is 6 NaOH. So 4 MgCl2 and 6 NaOH were mixed, and MgCl2 was in excess (1 Mg2+ is left over). Answers with 3 MgCl2 miss the leftover Mg2+, and 8 NaOH would need 8 Na+.
x: This counts only the Mg²⁺ in the solid. One Mg²⁺ ion is still dissolved, and it came from the reactants too.
The number of NaOH units equals the number of Na⁺ ions, not the number of Cl⁻ ions. Count the Na⁺ again.
Each Mg(OH)₂ unit contains two OH⁻ ions, and each OH⁻ came from one NaOH.

q: The two boxes show the ions in a sample of HCl(aq) and a sample of Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub>(aq) (water not shown, except water formed by reaction). The samples are mixed and react completely. Which box (I–IV) best represents the mixture after reaction?
h: H⁺ and OH⁻ combine one to one to make H₂O. Find which ion runs out first and what is left over. Spectator ions stay dissolved.
w: The HCl sample has 4 H+ and 4 Cl−; the Ba(OH)2 sample has 3 Ba2+ and 6 OH−. The net reaction is H+ + OH− → H2O, so 4 H+ react with 4 OH− to make 4 H2O, and 2 OH− are left. Ba2+ and Cl− are spectators. Box I shows 3 Ba2+, 4 Cl−, 2 OH− and 4 H2O. Box II shows no reaction, box III leaves H+ instead of OH−, and box IV makes more water than there was H+ to make it.
x: Box II shows the ions just mixed, with no reaction. H⁺ and OH⁻ cannot stay together in large numbers because they combine to form water.
Box III leaves H⁺ over. Compare the 4 H⁺ with the 6 OH⁻ to see which ion is used up first.
Box IV shows 6 water molecules, but only 4 H⁺ ions were present to make water. Hydrogen atoms are not conserved there.

q:
Dichromate ion oxidizes iron(II) ion in acid by the reaction shown. Which statements are true?
I. Fe2+ is the reducing agent.
II. Each chromium atom gains three electrons.
III. H+ is oxidized.
h: Assign oxidation numbers to Cr, Fe and H on both sides. The reducing agent is the species that is oxidized.
w: Fe goes from +2 to +3, so Fe2+ loses electrons, is oxidized, and is the reducing agent: I is true. Cr goes from +6 in Cr2O72− to +3 in Cr3+, a gain of 3 electrons per Cr atom (6 per dichromate ion, matching the 6 Fe2+): II is true. H stays +1 in H+ and in H2O, so III is false. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is true as well. Find the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ and compare it with Cr³⁺.
Statement III is false. Hydrogen is +1 in H⁺ and still +1 in H₂O, so it is neither oxidized nor reduced.
Statement III is false. H⁺ supplies hydrogen for the water but its oxidation number does not change.

q: Phosphoric acid, a weak acid, is completely neutralized by sodium hydroxide as shown. What is the net ionic equation?
h: A weak acid is mostly un-ionized in water, so it is written as a molecule. Strong bases and soluble salts are written as ions.
w: NaOH and Na3PO4 are strong electrolytes and split into ions, while H3PO4 is weak and stays as a molecule. Canceling the 3 Na+ spectators gives H3PO4(aq) + 3 OH−(aq) → PO43−(aq) + 3 H2O(l). Writing 3 H+ treats the acid as strong, the single-OH− equation is only the first step of the neutralization, and the Na+ equation describes no reaction at all.
x: This treats phosphoric acid as a strong acid that is fully ionized. A weak acid is written as the intact molecule.
This removes only one H⁺. The equation shows complete neutralization with three NaOH.
Na⁺ and PO₄³⁻ stay dissolved as ions on both sides, so this is not a reaction that takes place.

q: A 0.500 g sample of lawn fertilizer is dissolved in water, and excess BaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) is added. All of the sulfate precipitates as BaSO<sub>4</sub> by the reaction shown, and the dried solid weighs 0.7015 g. If all of the sulfate came from (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, what is the mass percent of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the fertilizer?
h: Convert the mass of BaSO₄ to moles. One mole of BaSO₄ comes from one mole of (NH₄)₂SO₄.
w: mol BaSO4 = 0.7015 g ÷ 233.39 g mol−1 = 3.006×10−3 mol = mol (NH4)2SO4. Mass = 3.006×10−3 mol × 132.14 g mol−1 = 0.3972 g, and 0.3972 g ÷ 0.500 g × 100% = 79.4%. 57.7% is the percent of sulfate ion alone, 39.7% divides by 1 g instead of the sample mass, and 140.% compares the mass of the precipitate itself with the sample.
x: This is the mass percent of the sulfate ion only. The question asks for the whole ammonium sulfate compound.
Divide by the actual sample mass, 0.500 g, when finding the percent.
A percent over 100 cannot be right. The precipitate is BaSO₄, which must be converted to the mass of ammonium sulfate first.

q: A 25.00 mL sample of an iron(II) solution is titrated with 0.02000 M KMnO<sub>4</sub> in acid by the reaction shown. The purple color first stays after 18.40 mL is added. What is the molarity of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the sample?
h: Find the moles of MnO₄⁻ used, then use the mole ratio in the balanced equation. Each MnO₄⁻ reacts with more than one Fe²⁺.
w: mol MnO4− = 0.01840 L × 0.02000 M = 3.680×10−4 mol. From the equation, 5 Fe2+ react per MnO4−: 5 × 3.680×10−4 = 1.840×10−3 mol Fe2+. [Fe2+] = 1.840×10−3 mol ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.07360 M. 0.01472 M ignores the 5 : 1 ratio, 0.002944 M divides by 5 instead of multiplying, and 0.1359 M swaps the two volumes.
x: This uses a 1 : 1 ratio. Check the coefficients of Fe²⁺ and MnO₄⁻ in the equation.
This divides by the ratio instead of multiplying. Each MnO₄⁻ consumes several Fe²⁺ ions, so there are more moles of Fe²⁺ than of MnO₄⁻.
The two volumes are swapped. The permanganate volume goes with the permanganate molarity, and the Fe²⁺ moles are divided by the sample volume.

f.text: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>(aq) + 5 Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 8 H<sup>+</sup>(aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 5 Fe<sup>3+</sup>(aq) + 4 H<sub>2</sub>O(l)

q: 15.0 g of aluminum nitrate, Al(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, is dissolved in water and diluted to 250.0 mL. What is the concentration of nitrate ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, in the solution?
h: First find the molarity of the salt. Then use the formula: count how many NO₃⁻ ions each formula unit releases.
w: mol Al(NO3)3 = 15.0 g ÷ 213.01 g mol−1 = 0.0704 mol, so the salt is 0.0704 mol ÷ 0.2500 L = 0.282 M. Each formula unit gives 3 NO3−, so [NO3−] = 3 × 0.282 M = 0.845 M. 0.282 M is the salt concentration, 1.13 M counts the Al3+ as well, and 0.0704 is the number of moles, not a concentration.
x: This is the concentration of the salt. Each Al(NO₃)₃ releases more than one nitrate ion.
This counts all four ions from each formula unit. Only the nitrate ions are asked for.
This is the number of moles of salt. Molarity also requires dividing by the volume in liters.

q: A student needs 500.0 mL of 0.150 M HCl and has a stock bottle of 6.00 M HCl. Which procedure is correct?
c: Add 12.5 mL of the stock acid to some water in a 500-mL volumetric flask, then add water to the mark.
Add 12.5 mL of the stock acid to 500.0 mL of water.
Add 75.0 mL of the stock acid to some water in a 500-mL volumetric flask, then add water to the mark.
Add 12.5 mL of water to 487.5 mL of the stock acid.
h: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. The final volume of the solution, not the volume of water added, must be 500.0 mL.
w: V1 = (0.150 M × 500.0 mL) ÷ 6.00 M = 12.5 mL of stock. Diluting it to a final volume of 500.0 mL in a volumetric flask (acid added to water) gives 12.5 mL of stock diluted to the mark. Adding it to 500.0 mL of water makes 512.5 mL, too dilute. 75.0 mL is millimoles of HCl, not a volume of stock, and the last procedure swaps the acid and water.
x: Adding to 500.0 mL of water makes a total volume larger than 500.0 mL, so the solution is a little too dilute.
75.0 is the number of millimoles of HCl needed. It must be divided by the stock molarity to give a volume.
This uses mostly concentrated acid, so the result is far more concentrated than 0.150 M. The stock and water amounts are swapped.

q: Sulfur is recovered from natural gas by the reaction shown. Which statement is correct?
c: H<sub>2</sub>S is the reducing agent and SO<sub>2</sub> is the oxidizing agent.
SO<sub>2</sub> is the reducing agent and H<sub>2</sub>S is the oxidizing agent.
S is the oxidizing agent and H<sub>2</sub>O is the reducing agent.
It is not a redox reaction because sulfur is both a reactant and a product.
h: Find the oxidation number of S in H₂S, in SO₂ and in elemental S. The reducing agent is the reactant that is oxidized.
w: S rises from −2 in H2S to 0 in S, so H2S is oxidized and is the reducing agent. S falls from +4 in SO2 to 0, so SO2 is reduced and is the oxidizing agent: H2S is the reducing agent and SO2 is the oxidizing agent. Agents are always reactants, so products such as S and H2O cannot be the agents. The reaction is redox because oxidation numbers change.
x: The roles are reversed. The oxidation number of S in SO₂ goes down, which means SO₂ gains electrons.
Oxidizing and reducing agents are reactants. S and H₂O are products of the reaction.
Oxidation numbers of sulfur change from −2 and +4 to 0, so electrons are transferred.

q:
Household bleach is made by bubbling chlorine into sodium hydroxide solution, as shown. Which statements are true?
I. Chlorine changes from 0 to −1 in Cl− and from 0 to +1 in ClO−.
II. OH− is the oxidizing agent.
III. Cl2 is both the oxidizing agent and the reducing agent.
h: Assign oxidation numbers to every atom on both sides, including O and H in OH⁻ and H₂O.
w: In Cl2 chlorine is 0; it becomes −1 in Cl− and +1 in ClO− (O is −2): I is true. O stays −2 and H stays +1 in OH−, ClO− and H2O, so OH− is not reduced and is not the oxidizing agent: II is false. Some Cl atoms are reduced and others oxidized, so Cl2 is both agents (a disproportionation): III is true. The answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is true as well. One Cl atom of each Cl₂ gains an electron and the other loses one.
Statement II is false. Oxygen is −2 and hydrogen is +1 in OH⁻ and in both products, so OH⁻ gains no electrons.
Statement II is false. The oxidizing agent must be reduced, and the atoms in OH⁻ keep their oxidation numbers.

q: The box shows copper atoms from a piece of copper wire in a silver nitrate solution, before any reaction (water not shown). The reaction shown runs until every Ag<sup>+</sup> ion has reacted. What is in the beaker afterward, besides the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> ions?
c: 3 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and 1 Cu atom
6 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and no Cu atoms
4 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 6 Ag atoms and no Cu atoms
3 Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, 3 Ag atoms and 1 Cu atom
h: Count the Ag⁺ ions and the Cu atoms. Each Cu atom gives up two electrons, enough to reduce two Ag⁺ ions.
w: The box has 6 Ag+, 6 NO3− and 4 Cu atoms. By the equation, 6 Ag+ need 3 Cu atoms, producing 3 Cu2+ and 6 Ag atoms, and 1 Cu atom is left over: 3 Cu2+, 6 Ag and 1 Cu. Six Cu2+ uses a 1 : 1 ratio, four Cu2+ assumes all the copper reacts, and 3 Ag atoms loses silver.
x: This uses one Cu for every Ag⁺. A Cu atom loses two electrons, and each Ag⁺ gains only one.
Not all of the copper is needed. Six Ag⁺ ions can accept electrons from only some of the Cu atoms.
Silver atoms are conserved. Every Ag⁺ ion that reacts becomes one Ag atom.

q: The box shows the ions in a sample of calcium hydroxide solution (water not shown). How many formula units of sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, are needed to neutralize this sample completely?
h: Count the OH⁻ ions. Each H₂SO₄ supplies two H⁺ ions, and each H⁺ neutralizes one OH⁻.
w: The box holds 4 Ca2+ and 8 OH−. Neutralization needs 8 H+, and each H2SO4 provides 2, so 4 H2SO4 are needed (Ca(OH)2 + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + 2 H2O). 8 treats the acid as monoprotic, 2 matches H2SO4 to half the Ca2+, and 16 doubles instead of halving.
x: This gives one acid unit per OH⁻. Sulfuric acid is diprotic, so each unit neutralizes two OH⁻ ions.
Each Ca²⁺ comes with two OH⁻. Count the OH⁻ ions, not just the calcium ions.
This multiplies by two instead of dividing. Each H₂SO₄ supplies two H⁺, so fewer acid units are needed than OH⁻ ions.

q: 30.0 mL of 0.200 M FeCl<sub>3</sub> is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.300 M NaOH, and Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> (106.87 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) precipitates by the reaction shown. What is the maximum mass of Fe(OH)<sub>3</sub> that can form?
h: Find the moles of Fe³⁺ and of OH⁻. Three OH⁻ are needed for each Fe³⁺, so check which reactant runs out first.
w: mol FeCl3 = 0.0300 L × 0.200 M = 0.00600 mol; mol NaOH = 0.0500 L × 0.300 M = 0.0150 mol. Using all the Fe3+ would need 0.0180 mol OH−, more than is present, so NaOH is limiting. mol Fe(OH)3 = 0.0150 ÷ 3 = 0.00500 mol, and 0.00500 mol × 106.87 g mol−1 = 0.534 g. 0.641 g assumes FeCl3 is limiting, 1.60 g ignores the 3 : 1 ratio, and 0.674 g uses the formula Fe(OH)2.
x: This assumes FeCl₃ runs out first. Check whether there is enough NaOH to react with all of the Fe³⁺.
This uses a 1 : 1 ratio of NaOH to Fe(OH)₃. The equation shows three NaOH per Fe(OH)₃.
This divides the OH⁻ by 2 as if the product were Fe(OH)₂. Iron is +3 here.

q: What volume of water must be ADDED to 40.0 mL of 2.50 M NaOH to make a solution that is 0.800 M? Assume the volumes are additive.
h: Use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ to find the final volume, then compare it with the starting volume.
w: V2 = (2.50 M × 40.0 mL) ÷ 0.800 M = 125 mL. This is the final volume; the water added is 125 mL − 40.0 mL = 85.0 mL. 125 mL is the final volume, 12.8 mL inverts the ratio of concentrations, and 165 mL adds the starting volume instead of subtracting it.
x: This is the total volume after dilution. The question asks how much water is added to the 40.0 mL already present.
The concentrations are inverted. A more dilute solution needs a larger final volume than the starting 40.0 mL.
The starting 40.0 mL is already part of the final volume, so it should not be added again.

q:
Which of these net ionic equations are balanced for both mass and charge?
I. Zn(s) + Ag+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Ag(s)
II. Cu(s) + 2 Fe3+(aq) → Cu2+(aq) + 2 Fe2+(aq)
III. 2 Al(s) + 6 H+(aq) → 2 Al3+(aq) + 3 H2(g)
h: Count the atoms of each element on both sides, then add up the ionic charges on each side. Both must match.
w: I has matching atoms, but the charge is +1 on the left and +2 on the right, so it is not balanced (it needs 2 Ag+ and 2 Ag). II has a total charge of +6 on each side (2 × 3 = 6; 2 + 2 × 2 = 6) and matching atoms. III has 2 Al and 6 H on each side and a charge of +6 on each side. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement I fails the charge check. The left side has a charge of +1 and the right side +2.
Statement I is not balanced for charge, even though the atoms match. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained.
Statement II is balanced too. Add the charges: 2 Fe³⁺ gives +6, and Cu²⁺ plus 2 Fe²⁺ gives +6.

q: 0.100 M Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is added a little at a time to 25.0 mL of a KI solution, and the dried PbI<sub>2</sub> precipitate is weighed after each addition (graph). What was the concentration of KI in the original solution?
h: The graph levels off when all of the I⁻ has precipitated. Read that volume and use the 1 : 2 ratio of Pb²⁺ to I⁻.
w: The mass stops rising at 15.0 mL, so all of the I− is used up there. mol Pb2+ = 0.0150 L × 0.100 M = 1.50×10−3 mol, and 2 I− react per Pb2+, so mol I− = 3.00×10−3 mol. [KI] = 3.00×10−3 mol ÷ 0.0250 L = 0.120 M. 0.0600 M ignores the 1 : 2 ratio, 0.0750 M divides by the combined 40.0 mL, and 0.333 M swaps the two volumes.
x: This uses a 1 : 1 ratio. Each Pb²⁺ removes two I⁻ ions from solution.
The KI concentration refers to the original 25.0 mL sample, not to the combined volume after mixing.
The volumes are swapped. The 15.0 mL goes with the Pb(NO₃)₂ concentration.

q: In the Ostwald process, ammonia is burned over a platinum catalyst as shown. Which element is oxidized, and how does its oxidation number change?
h: Assign oxidation numbers with H = +1 and O = −2 in compounds and 0 in elements. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.
w: In NH3, N is −3 (three H at +1); in NO, N is +2 (O at −2). The increase means N is oxidized, from −3 to +2. Oxygen goes from 0 to −2, which is reduction. N cannot be +3 in NH3, and H stays +1 in both NH3 and H2O.
x: Oxygen gains electrons as it goes from 0 to −2, which is reduction, not oxidation.
In NH₃ each H is +1, so N must be negative to make the molecule neutral.
Hydrogen is +1 in NH₃ and still +1 in H₂O, so its oxidation number does not change.

q: Which ions are spectator ions when aqueous barium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid as shown?
h: Write the complete ionic equation. Spectators appear unchanged, as dissolved ions, on both sides.
w: Complete ionic: Ba2+ + 2 OH− + 2 H+ + SO42− → BaSO4(s) + 2 H2O(l). Ba2+ and SO42− leave solution as the insoluble solid, and H+ and OH− become water, so no ions are spectators; the net ionic equation is the same as the complete ionic equation.
x: BaSO₄ is insoluble, so Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ leave the solution as a solid. They are not spectators.
H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water, so they take part in the reaction.
Ba²⁺ ends up in solid BaSO₄ and OH⁻ ends up in water, so both react.

q: The heating curve shows 0.500 mol of a pure substance heated at constant pressure. What is the molar enthalpy of vaporization of the substance?
h: Vaporization happens on the flat part at the boiling point. The heat absorbed is the length of that plateau along the heat axis.
w: The upper plateau (boiling, 80 °C) runs from 12 kJ to 32 kJ, so 20.0 kJ boils 0.500 mol. ΔHvap = 20.0 kJ ÷ 0.500 mol = 40.0 kJ mol−1. 20.0 kJ mol−1 forgets to divide by the moles, 4.0 kJ mol−1 uses the melting plateau, and 64.0 kJ mol−1 uses the total heat read at the end of the plateau.
x: 20.0 kJ is the heat for 0.500 mol. A molar value is per mole of substance.
This uses the lower plateau, where the substance melts rather than boils.
Only the heat absorbed along the boiling plateau counts, not the total heat added from the start.

q:
The heating curve shows a 50.0 g sample heated at a steady rate from a solid to a gas. Which statements are true?
I. The solid has a larger specific heat than the liquid.
II. More heat is needed to melt the sample than to boil it.
III. Between points B and C, the added heat separates the particles instead of raising their average kinetic energy.
h: On the sloped parts, a smaller temperature rise per kJ means a larger specific heat. On the flat parts, compare the lengths along the heat axis.
w: Solid (A→B) rises 30 °C over 1.5 kJ (20 °C per kJ); liquid (C→D) rises 40 °C over 4 kJ (10 °C per kJ). The liquid warms more slowly, so the liquid has the larger specific heat: I is false. Melting (B→C) takes 4 kJ but boiling (D→E) takes 12 kJ: II is false. On a plateau the temperature, and so the average kinetic energy, stays constant while the heat overcomes attractions: III is true. The answer is III only.
x: Statement I is false. The solid segment is steeper, so the solid warms faster per kJ and has the smaller specific heat.
Statement II is false. The boiling plateau D to E is much longer along the heat axis than the melting plateau B to C.
Statements I and II are both false. Compare the slopes of the sloped parts and the lengths of the two flat parts.

q: The energy diagram shows the path of a reaction, with the energy of each labeled point. Which description of the reaction is correct?
h: ΔH compares only the products with the reactants. The peak is the activation energy, not the enthalpy change.
w: ΔH = E(products) − E(reactants) = 40 kJ − 0 kJ = +40 kJ. The products are higher in energy than the reactants, so heat is absorbed: ΔH = +40 kJ; endothermic. +95 kJ is the activation energy of the forward reaction, +55 kJ is the activation energy of the reverse reaction, and −40 kJ has the sign backward.
x: 95 kJ is the height of the peak above the reactants. That is the activation energy, not ΔH.
The products sit above the reactants, so the system gains energy. Check the sign.
55 kJ is the drop from the peak to the products, which is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

q: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, 5.55 g of CaCl<sub>2</sub> (110.98 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is dissolved in 100.0 g of water at 2 min, and the temperature is recorded (graph). Using the highest temperature reached, a solution mass of 105.6 g and c = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>, what is ΔH for dissolving CaCl<sub>2</sub>?
h: Read ΔT from the starting temperature to the maximum. The heat gained by the solution was released by the dissolving salt.
w: ΔT = 30.0 °C − 21.0 °C = 9.0 °C. qsolution = (105.6 g)(4.18 J g−1 °C−1)(9.0 °C) = 3.97×103 J = 3.97 kJ. mol CaCl2 = 5.55 ÷ 110.98 = 0.0500 mol. ΔH = −3.97 kJ ÷ 0.0500 mol = −79.4 kJ mol−1; it is negative because the solution warmed. −75.2 uses only the 100.0 g of water, +79.4 has the wrong sign, and −3.97 is the heat in kJ, not per mole.
x: This uses only the mass of water. The stem gives the mass of the whole solution, which is what warms up.
The solution got warmer, so the dissolving released heat. Check the sign.
3.97 kJ is the total heat released. It still has to be divided by the moles of CaCl₂.

q: A 20.0 g ice cube at 0.0 °C is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 60.0 °C in an insulated cup. The ice melts completely. Using the data in the table, what is the final temperature?
h: Heat lost by the warm water = heat to melt the ice + heat to warm the melted ice from 0 °C to the final temperature.
w: Melting: 20.0 g × 334 J g−1 = 6680 J. Then (100.0)(4.184)(60.0 − T) = 6680 + (20.0)(4.184)(T − 0). 25104 − 418.4T = 6680 + 83.68T, so 18424 = 502.08T and T = 36.7 °C. 50.0 °C ignores the heat of fusion, 44.0 °C forgets to warm the melted ice, and 63.3 °C has a sign error (it is hotter than the hot water).
x: This treats the ice as water at 0 °C and ignores the heat needed to melt it.
After melting, the 20.0 g of cold water must also warm up to the final temperature, which takes more heat from the warm water.
The final temperature cannot be higher than the hottest thing in the cup. Check the signs in the heat balance.

q: A bomb calorimeter is calibrated with an electric heater and then used to burn naphthalene, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (128.17 g mol<sup>−1</sup>). Using the data in the table, what is the molar enthalpy of combustion of naphthalene? (Treat ΔE ≈ ΔH.)
h: The calibration run gives the heat capacity of the calorimeter (kJ per °C). Use it with the second temperature rise.
w: Ccal = 5.00 kJ ÷ 1.25 °C = 4.00 kJ °C−1. Heat released by the sample = 4.00 × 3.22 = 12.88 kJ for 0.320 g, which is 40.25 kJ g−1. Per mole: 40.25 × 128.17 = 5.16×103 kJ, released, so ΔHcomb = −5.16×103 kJ mol−1. −40.3 is per gram, −322 inverts the heat capacity, and the positive value has the wrong sign.
x: 40.3 kJ is the heat released per gram. Convert grams to moles with the molar mass.
The heat capacity is heat divided by temperature change, 5.00 kJ over 1.25 °C, not the reverse.
Combustion releases heat to the calorimeter, so ΔH for the reaction is negative.

q:
A gas in a cylinder with a movable piston absorbs 600 J of heat from a flame and expands, doing 250 J of work on the surroundings. Which statements are true?
I. q = +600 J
II. w = +250 J
III. ΔE of the gas = +850 J
h: Use ΔE = q + w, with each sign taken from the point of view of the gas. Work done BY the system is negative.
w: Heat flows into the gas, so q = +600 J: I is true. The gas does work on the surroundings, so it loses energy that way and w = −250 J: II is false. ΔE = q + w = +600 J − 250 J = +350 J, not +850 J: III is false. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. When the gas pushes the piston out, it does work on the surroundings, so w is negative.
Statement III is false. Expansion work removes energy from the gas, so ΔE is less than the heat absorbed.
Statements II and III are false. Work done by the gas carries a negative sign in ΔE = q + w.

q: The thermite reaction is shown. A mixture of 5.40 g of Al and 20.0 g of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> reacts until one reactant is used up. How much heat is released?
h: Find the limiting reactant first. ΔH is the heat for the moles shown in the equation: 2 mol Al with 1 mol Fe₂O₃.
w: mol Al = 5.40 ÷ 26.98 = 0.2001 mol; mol Fe2O3 = 20.0 ÷ 159.69 = 0.1252 mol. 0.2001 mol Al needs only 0.1001 mol Fe2O3, so Al is limiting. Heat = 0.2001 mol Al × (852 kJ ÷ 2 mol Al) = 85.3 kJ. 107 kJ assumes Fe2O3 is used up, 171 kJ ignores the 2 mol Al in the equation, and 852 kJ is the heat for the full equation as written.
x: This assumes Fe₂O₃ is used up. Check whether there is enough Al to react with all of it.
The 852 kJ is released for 2 mol of Al, so the heat per mole of Al is half of that.
852 kJ goes with 2 mol Al and 1 mol Fe₂O₃. The sample is much smaller than that.

f.text: 2 Al(s) + Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>(s) → Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>(s) + 2 Fe(s)   ΔH° = −852 kJ

q: Using the thermochemical equation shown, what is ΔH° for the reaction 3 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>(g) → 3 C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g)?
h: Reversing an equation changes the sign of ΔH. Multiplying the coefficients multiplies ΔH by the same factor.
w: The new reaction is the given one reversed (sign changes to +137 kJ) and tripled: 3 × (+137 kJ) = +411 kJ. −411 kJ triples but forgets to change the sign, +137 kJ reverses but forgets to triple, and +45.7 kJ divides by 3 instead of multiplying.
x: The reaction has been reversed, so the sign of ΔH must change as well.
Three moles react here, not one, so ΔH scales by the same factor.
The coefficients were multiplied by 3, so ΔH must be multiplied by 3, not divided.

q:
Use the three combustion reactions in the table to find the standard enthalpy of formation of propane:
3 C(s) + 4 H2(g) → C3H8(g)
h: C and H₂ are reactants in the target, so use equations 1 and 2 as written, scaled. C₃H₈ is a product in the target, so reverse equation 3.
w: 3 × (1): 3 C + 3 O2 → 3 CO2, 3(−393.5) = −1180.5 kJ. 4 × (2): 4 H2 + 2 O2 → 4 H2O, 4(−285.8) = −1143.2 kJ. Reverse (3): 3 CO2 + 4 H2O → C3H8 + 5 O2, +2220 kJ. Sum: −1180.5 − 1143.2 + 2220 = −104 kJ mol−1. The +104 value has the sign backward, −4.54×103 forgets to reverse equation 3, and +1.54×103 skips the 3 and 4 multipliers.
x: The sign is backward. Check that equation 3 is reversed and equations 1 and 2 are not.
Propane must be a product, so equation 3 has to be reversed and its sign changed.
Three C and four H₂ are needed, so equations 1 and 2 must be multiplied by 3 and 4.

q: Using the two equations shown, which expression gives the standard enthalpy of formation of methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH(l)?
h: Write the formation reaction: C(s) + 2 H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l). Then decide which given equations to scale or reverse.
w: Half of equation 2 gives C(s) + ½ O2(g) → CO(g), ½ ΔH°2. Adding equation 1 as written, CO(g) + 2 H2(g) → CH3OH(l), cancels CO and leaves C(s) + 2 H2(g) + ½ O2(g) → CH3OH(l). So ΔH°f = ΔH°1 + ½ ΔH°2. Using all of equation 2 makes 2 CO, reversing it is not needed, and halving equation 1 would make only ½ mol of methanol.
x: Equation 2 makes 2 mol CO, but only 1 mol CO is needed for 1 mol of methanol.
Equation 2 is already in the right direction, with C as a reactant and CO as a product, so it should not be reversed.
Equation 1 already makes exactly 1 mol of CH₃OH, so it should not be halved.

q: Iron ore is reduced in a blast furnace by the reaction shown. Using the standard enthalpies of formation in the table, what is ΔH° for the reaction?
h: ΔH° = Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants). Elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0.
w: Products: 2(0) + 3(−393.5) = −1180.5 kJ. Reactants: (−824.2) + 3(−110.5) = −1155.7 kJ. ΔH° = −1180.5 − (−1155.7) = −24.8 kJ. +24.8 kJ subtracts in the wrong order, +541.2 kJ ignores the coefficients of 3, and −356.3 kJ leaves out the CO.
x: This is reactants minus products. Subtract the reactant sum from the product sum.
The coefficients of 3 on CO and CO₂ must multiply their ΔH°f values.
CO is a compound, so its ΔH°f is not zero and must be included with the reactants.

q: Glucose burns as shown, with ΔH° = −2803 kJ. Using the enthalpies of formation in the table, what is ΔH°<sub>f</sub> of glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>(s)?
h: Write ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants) and solve for the one unknown. O₂ has ΔH°f = 0.
w: −2803 = [6(−393.5) + 6(−285.8)] − [ΔH°f(glucose) + 6(0)] = −4075.8 − ΔH°f(glucose). So ΔH°f(glucose) = −4075.8 + 2803 = −1273 kJ mol−1. +1273 has the sign flipped, −6879 adds −2803 instead of solving for the unknown, and +2124 ignores the coefficients of 6.
x: The sign is flipped. Solve the equation step by step, keeping track of the minus sign in front of the reactant term.
This adds the combustion enthalpy to the product sum. Glucose is a reactant, so its ΔH°f is subtracted, and you must solve for it.
There are 6 CO₂ and 6 H₂O in the equation, so their ΔH°f values must be multiplied by 6.

q: Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen, as drawn below (×3 and ×2 mark coefficients). Use the average bond enthalpies in the table to estimate ΔH for the reaction.
h: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Count every bond in each drawn molecule and multiply by its coefficient.
w: Broken: 1 N≡N + 3 H–H = 945 + 3(436) = 2253 kJ. Formed: 2 NH3 × 3 N–H = 6(391) = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ. +93 kJ subtracts in the wrong order, +1080 kJ forms only one NH3, and +208 kJ ignores all the coefficients.
x: This is formed minus broken. Energy is absorbed to break bonds and released when bonds form.
Two NH₃ molecules form, so six N–H bonds are made, not three.
This uses one molecule of each substance. Multiply the bonds in H₂ and NH₃ by their coefficients.

q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes as drawn below (×2 marks a coefficient of 2). Use the Lewis structures and the average bond enthalpies in the table to estimate ΔH.
h: Read each Lewis structure to see which bonds are single and which are double, then use ΔH ≈ Σ(broken) − Σ(formed).
w: Broken: 2 H2O2 × (2 O–H + 1 O–O) = 4(464) + 2(146) = 2148 kJ. Formed: 2 H2O × 2 O–H + 1 O=O = 4(464) + 498 = 2354 kJ. ΔH = 2148 − 2354 = −206 kJ. +206 kJ reverses the subtraction, −352 kJ ignores the coefficients of 2, and +498 kJ treats the O–O bond in H2O2 as a double bond.
x: This is formed minus broken. Breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it.
This uses one molecule of each substance. Two H₂O₂ and two H₂O appear in the equation.
The Lewis structure of H₂O₂ shows a single O–O bond, which is much weaker than O=O.

q:
Solid KOH dissolves in water in a coffee-cup calorimeter as shown, and the water gets warmer. Taking the dissolving KOH as the system, which statements are true?
I. The dissolving process absorbs heat from the water.
II. ΔH for dissolving KOH is negative.
III. q for the water is negative.
h: When the water warms, energy has moved into the water. Decide which way heat flowed for the system and for the water.
w: The water warms because the dissolving releases heat into it, so I is false. Heat leaves the system at constant pressure, so ΔH < 0: II is true. The water gains that heat, so qwater is positive, and III is false. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is false. A rising water temperature means the dissolving gave heat to the water, not that it took heat away.
Statement I is false. If the dissolving absorbed heat from the water, the water would get colder.
Statement III is false. The water gains heat, so its q is positive while the system's q is negative.

q: Rank the three fuels in the table by the heat released when ONE GRAM of each burns, from most to least.
h: The table gives heat per mole. Divide each value by the molar mass to get heat per gram.
w: Heat per gram = |ΔHcomb| ÷ molar mass: H2, 286 ÷ 2.016 = 142 kJ g−1; CH4, 890 ÷ 16.04 = 55.5 kJ g−1; C2H5OH, 1367 ÷ 46.07 = 29.7 kJ g−1. So H2 > CH4 > C2H5OH. The reverse order ranks the fuels per mole instead of per gram.
x: This ranks the fuels per mole. Ethanol releases the most per mole but is the heaviest molecule.
Hydrogen has by far the smallest molar mass, so each gram contains many moles. Recalculate its heat per gram.
Methane releases more per gram than ethanol, but check hydrogen. A gram of H₂ is almost half a mole.

q: The boxes show chlorine atoms combining into Cl<sub>2</sub> molecules at constant pressure. Which statement about this change is correct?
c: It is exothermic, because Cl–Cl bonds form and no bonds break.
It is endothermic, because energy is needed to form the Cl–Cl bonds.
ΔH is zero, because the same atoms are present before and after.
It is endothermic, because the number of particles decreases.
h: Compare the bonds in the two boxes. Breaking a bond always takes energy, and forming one always releases energy.
w: The Before box has 8 separate Cl atoms and the After box has 4 Cl2 molecules, so 4 Cl–Cl bonds form and none break. Bond formation releases energy, so ΔH < 0: it is exothermic. Forming bonds never requires energy, conserved atoms do not make ΔH zero, and a drop in the number of particles does not make a process endothermic.
x: Bond formation releases energy. It is bond breaking that requires energy.
Atoms are conserved in every chemical change, but the energy stored in bonds still changes.
The number of particles does not decide the sign of ΔH. Look at which bonds are made or broken.

q: How much heat is needed to warm 1.50 kg of water in a 0.800 kg copper pot from 20.0 °C to 100.0 °C? Use the specific heats in the table.
h: Both the water and the pot warm by the same ΔT. Add q = mcΔT for each, with masses in grams.
w: Water: 1500 g × 4.184 × 80.0 = 502,080 J. Copper: 800 g × 0.385 × 80.0 = 24,640 J. Total = 526,720 J = 527 kJ. 502 kJ leaves out the pot, 24.6 kJ is the pot alone, and 0.527 kJ uses kilograms with specific heats in J g−1 °C−1.
x: This warms only the water. The copper pot also rises by 80.0 °C and absorbs heat.
This is only the heat for the pot. The water absorbs most of the heat.
The specific heats are per gram, so the masses must be in grams, not kilograms.

q: Phosgene, COCl<sub>2</sub>, is a toxic gas used to make polycarbonate plastics. Carbon is the central atom. Which drawing is the best Lewis structure of phosgene?
h: Phosgene has 24 valence electrons. Check that every atom has an octet, then compare formal charges.
w: With a C=O double bond and two C–Cl single bonds, every atom has an octet and every formal charge is zero, so the structure with C=O and two C–Cl single bonds is best. Putting the double bond to Cl gives Cl a +1 and O a −1 formal charge, which is worse because the positive charge sits on an electronegative atom. With only single bonds carbon has just six electrons, and with a C≡O triple bond carbon has five bonds (ten electrons).
x: Every atom has an octet here, but Cl carries +1 and O carries −1. A structure with all formal charges zero is better.
