Carbon has only three bonds and no lone pair here, which leaves it six electrons. Carbon needs an octet.
Carbon makes five bonds in this drawing, which puts ten electrons around it. Carbon cannot exceed an octet.

q: Thionyl chloride, SOCl<sub>2</sub>, is drawn below with an S–O single bond and an octet on every atom (formal charges are not shown). What are the formal charges on the sulfur atom and on the oxygen atom in this structure?
h: Formal charge = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − (number of bonds). Sulfur and oxygen both have 6 valence electrons.
w: Sulfur: 6 − 2 (one lone pair) − 3 bonds = +1. Oxygen: 6 − 6 (three lone pairs) − 1 bond = −1. The charges sum to zero for the neutral molecule. +4 and −2 are oxidation numbers, which treat the bonds as fully ionic, and S −1, O +1 reverses the calculation.
x: Count the electrons each atom owns in the drawing. Sulfur owns 5 and oxygen owns 7, so neither is zero.
Those are oxidation numbers, which give all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom. Formal charge splits each bond evenly.
The signs are reversed. Oxygen owns 7 electrons here, one more than its 6 valence electrons.

q: Hydrazoic acid, HN<sub>3</sub>, has the Lewis structure drawn below. Which drawing is another valid resonance structure of HN<sub>3</sub>?
h: HN₃ has 16 valence electrons. A resonance structure keeps every atom in place, keeps the same electron total and gives each N no more than an octet.
w: Shifting the π pair of the left N=N bond onto the H-bearing N as a lone pair, and turning one lone pair of the end N into a third bond, gives H–N–N≡N, with formal charges −1, +1 and 0 on the three N atoms. It has 16 electrons and an octet on every N, so the structure with an N–N single bond and an N≡N triple bond is a valid resonance structure. The drawing with all formal charges zero gives the middle N five bonds (ten electrons). The other two have 18 and 14 electrons, so they describe ions, not HN3.
x: Count the electrons. This drawing has an extra lone pair, 18 electrons in all, so it is not HN₃.
Every formal charge is zero here, but the middle nitrogen has five bonds and ten electrons. Nitrogen cannot exceed an octet.
Count the electrons. A lone pair is missing, leaving 14 electrons and a nitrogen with only six.

q: Lewis structures of hydrogen cyanide (I), methanimine (II) and methylamine (III) are drawn below. Rank their carbon–nitrogen bonds from SHORTEST to LONGEST.
h: More shared electron pairs between the same two atoms pull them closer together.
w: Bond length falls as bond order rises. I has a C≡N triple bond, II a C=N double bond and III a C–N single bond, so the order is I < II < III. Reversing it ranks longest to shortest, and the bonds are not equal because the bond orders differ.
x: This is the order from longest to shortest. A triple bond is the shortest.
A triple bond is shorter than a double bond. Look at bond I again.
The three bonds have different bond orders, so their lengths differ.

q: The three-dimensional shapes of XeF<sub>4</sub> (I), AsF<sub>5</sub> (II) and TeCl<sub>4</sub> (III) are drawn below, with lone pairs on the central atoms. Which of these molecules are polar?
h: Every bond here is polar. Ask whether the bond dipoles point in opposing directions that cancel.
w: I (square planar) is nonpolar: its four Xe–F dipoles cancel in opposite pairs, and its two lone pairs sit opposite each other. II (trigonal bipyramidal, no lone pairs) is nonpolar: the axial dipoles cancel and the three equatorial dipoles cancel. III (seesaw) is polar: the equatorial lone pair leaves the Te–Cl dipoles unbalanced. The answer is III only.
x: Molecule I is nonpolar. In a square planar shape each Xe–F dipole is cancelled by the one opposite it.
Molecule II is nonpolar. A trigonal bipyramid with five identical ligands is symmetric.
Molecules I and II are both symmetric, so their bond dipoles cancel.

q: The shape of iodine pentafluoride, IF<sub>5</sub>, is drawn below, including the lone pair on iodine. What is the electron-group geometry around iodine, and what is the approximate angle between the top F and each of the four lower F atoms?
h: Count the electron groups on iodine, including the lone pair. Where does the lone pair push the four base fluorines?
w: Iodine has 5 bonds and 1 lone pair, 6 electron groups, so the electron-group geometry is octahedral and the molecular shape is square pyramidal. The top F is at 90° to the four base F atoms, and the lone pair below squeezes them up slightly, so the angle is slightly less than 90° (about 82°). Trigonal bipyramidal is for 5 groups, 109.5° is the tetrahedral angle, and 180° is the angle to the lone-pair position, which holds no atom.
x: That is the geometry for five electron groups. The lone pair on iodine is a sixth group.
Square pyramidal is the molecular shape, not the electron-group geometry, and 109.5° belongs to a tetrahedron.
The position 180° from the top F holds the lone pair, not a fluorine atom.

q: The shapes of CH<sub>4</sub> (I), NH<sub>3</sub> (II) and BF<sub>3</sub> (III) are drawn below. Rank the bond angles H–C–H, H–N–H and F–B–F from SMALLEST to LARGEST.
h: Start from the ideal angle for each number of electron groups, then let a lone pair push the bonds closer together.
w: BF3 has 3 electron groups (120°). CH4 has 4 bonding groups (109.5°). NH3 also has 4 groups, but its lone pair repels more strongly than a bond and squeezes the H–N–H angle to about 107°. So the order is II < I < III. Treating NH3 like CH4 misses the lone-pair effect.
x: NH₃ has a lone pair, which pushes its bonds closer than the 109.5° of CH₄.
This is close to the reverse. Three electron groups spread out the most.
NH₃ and CH₄ both have four electron groups, but NH₃'s lone pair makes its angle smaller.

q: Three sets of carbon orbitals are drawn below (blue = hybrid orbitals, yellow = unhybridized p orbitals). Which set does the carbon atom in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, use?
c: II, because each C=O double bond needs an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon
h: Count the electron groups on carbon in CO₂. Each group needs one hybrid orbital, and each π bond needs one leftover p orbital.
w: Carbon in CO2 has 2 electron groups (two double bonds, no lone pairs), so it needs two hybrid orbitals 180° apart: sp. Its two leftover p orbitals form the two C=O π bonds. That is set I. Set II (sp2) has three hybrids and only one p orbital, and set III (sp3) has none left for π bonds. The oxygen atoms, not the carbon, are sp2.
x: Set II has three hybrid orbitals, but carbon in CO₂ has only two electron groups.
Set III has no unhybridized p orbitals, so it could not make the two π bonds.
It is the oxygen atoms that are sp². Carbon has two double bonds and needs two p orbitals for π bonding.

q: The complete set of hybrid orbitals used by the central atom of a molecule is drawn below. Which molecule could it be?
h: Count the hybrid orbitals and note their arrangement. The central atom needs one hybrid orbital for each electron group, bonds and lone pairs alike.
w: Four hybrid orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron are an sp3 set, used by an atom with 4 electron groups. N in NH3 has 3 bonds and 1 lone pair = 4 groups. B in BF3 has 3 groups (sp2), C in CO2 has 2 (sp) and P in PCl5 has 5 (sp3d).
x: B in BF₃ has only three electron groups, so it needs three hybrid orbitals in a plane.
C in CO₂ has two electron groups, so it uses two hybrid orbitals 180° apart.
P in PCl₅ has five electron groups and needs five hybrid orbitals. Count the orbitals drawn.

q: Crotononitrile is drawn below with its carbon atoms labeled a–d. The orbitals drawn beside it are the hybrid orbitals (blue) and unhybridized p orbitals (yellow) of one of those carbons. Which carbon uses this orbital set?
h: Count the hybrid orbitals and the leftover p orbitals in the drawing, then match them to the σ bonds and π bonds of each carbon.
w: The drawing shows two hybrid orbitals 180° apart and two p orbitals: an sp carbon, which makes 2 σ bonds and 2 π bonds. That is carbon d, bonded to carbon c and triple-bonded to N. Carbons b and c each have a double bond and three σ bonds (sp2, one p orbital), and carbon a has four single bonds (sp3, no p orbital).
x: Carbon c is part of a C=C double bond. It needs three hybrid orbitals and only one p orbital.
Carbon a makes four single bonds. It uses four sp³ orbitals and has no leftover p orbital.
Carbon b is part of a C=C double bond. It needs three hybrid orbitals and only one p orbital.

q: Which orbital diagram correctly shows the five valence electrons of the nitrogen atom in NH<sub>3</sub> after hybridization?
h: Nitrogen in NH₃ has four electron groups (three bonds and one lone pair). Fill the hybrid orbitals by the Pauli principle and Hund's rule.
w: Four electron groups need four sp3 orbitals. Five electrons fill them as one lone pair plus three singly occupied orbitals that bond to the three H atoms: diagram I. Diagram II uses sp2 hybridization, which fits only three electron groups. III puts two parallel spins in one orbital (a Pauli violation), and IV pairs electrons while an orbital is still empty (a Hund's rule violation).
x: Nitrogen in NH₃ has four electron groups, not three, so sp² does not fit.
One sp³ orbital holds two electrons with the same spin. That breaks the Pauli principle.
Two pairs leave an orbital empty while others are doubly filled. Hund's rule spreads electrons out first, and N needs three half-filled orbitals to bond to three H.

q: Four molecular orbitals formed from 2p atomic orbitals are pictured below. Which one holds the highest-energy electrons (the HOMO) of N<sub>2</sub>?
h: For B₂, C₂ and N₂ the π2p orbitals lie below σ2p. Fill the 10 valence electrons of N₂ in order.
w: N2 has 10 valence electrons: σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2p4 σ2p2. Because π2p lies below σ2p in N2, the last two electrons go into the end-on bonding orbital, I (σ2p). II (π2p) is filled but lower in energy. III (π*2p) and IV (σ*2p) are empty in N2.
x: This π2p orbital is filled, but in N₂ it lies below σ2p.
This antibonding π* orbital is empty in N₂. It fills only in O₂ and F₂.
This σ* orbital is the highest MO of all and is empty in N₂.

q: The molecular orbital pictured below is formed from two side-by-side 2p orbitals of opposite phase. For which molecule is this type of orbital the highest occupied orbital?
h: Identify the orbital first: side-by-side overlap with a node between the nuclei. Then decide which species has enough electrons to reach it.
w: The picture is a π*2p antibonding orbital. It is occupied only after σ2s, σ*2s, π2p and σ2p are full (10 valence electrons). O2, with 12, puts its last two electrons there. N2 (10) stops at σ2p, while C2 (8) and B2 (6) stop at π2p.
x: N₂ has 10 valence electrons, and its last two fill σ2p. Its π* orbitals are empty.
C₂ has only 8 valence electrons, so its highest electrons are in π2p.
B₂ has only 6 valence electrons, so its highest electrons are in π2p.

q: The valence molecular orbital diagram of the C<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> ion is shown below. What are its bond order and its magnetic behavior?
h: Bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons). Look for any orbital holding a single electron.
w: C2− has 9 valence electrons: σ2s2 σ*2s2 π2p4 σ2p1. Bonding = 7, antibonding = 2, so bond order = ½(7 − 2) = 2.5. The single electron in σ2p makes the ion paramagnetic: 2.5, paramagnetic. A bond order of 3 forgets the σ*2s electrons, and 1.5 treats the ninth electron as antibonding.
x: An odd number of electrons always leaves one unpaired, so the ion cannot be diamagnetic.
This bond order ignores the two electrons in σ*2s, which cancel bonding.
The ninth electron goes into σ2p, a bonding orbital, so it raises the bond order.

q: Valence MO diagrams of N<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> and N<sub>2</sub><sup>2−</sup> are shown below. Rank the three species by nitrogen–nitrogen bond length, from SHORTEST to LONGEST.
h: Find where each added electron goes, then compute each bond order. Higher bond order means a shorter bond.
w: N2 (10 electrons) has bond order 3. The extra electrons of the ions go into π*2p antibonding orbitals: N2− has bond order ½(8 − 3) = 2.5 and N22− has ½(8 − 4) = 2. Lower bond order means a longer bond: N2 < N2− < N22−. Adding electrons does not strengthen the bond here because they enter antibonding orbitals.
x: This assumes added electrons strengthen the bond. They enter π* orbitals, which lowers the bond order.
N₂ has the highest bond order of the three, so its bond cannot be longer than N₂⁻.
The added electrons occupy antibonding π* orbitals, so the bond orders differ.

q:
The valence molecular orbital diagram for a hypothetical Ne2 molecule is shown below. Which statements are true?
I. The bond order of Ne2 is 0.
II. Ne2 would be diamagnetic.
III. Ne2 would have a stronger bond than F2.
h: Count bonding and antibonding electrons. Then look for any half-filled orbitals.
w: Statement I is true: Ne2 has 16 valence electrons, 8 bonding and 8 antibonding, so bond order = 0 (no stable molecule). Statement II is true: every orbital is filled, so all electrons are paired. Statement III is false: F2 has bond order 1, larger than 0. The answer is I and II only.
x: Statement II is also true. Every orbital in the diagram holds a pair of electrons.
Statement I is also true. Equal numbers of bonding and antibonding electrons give a bond order of zero.
Statement III is false. F₂ has a bond order of 1, while Ne₂ has none.

q: Rank the ionic solids NaCl, Na<sub>2</sub>O and MgO from the SMALLEST to the LARGEST magnitude of lattice energy.
h: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ion charges and with smaller ion sizes (Coulomb's law).
w: NaCl has only +1 and −1 ions, so it is smallest. Na2O has a 2− oxide ion, which raises the lattice energy above NaCl. MgO has both a 2+ and a 2− ion, and Mg2+ is smaller than Na+, so it is largest: NaCl < Na2O < MgO (about 790, 2480 and 3790 kJ mol−1).
x: This order is reversed. Larger ion charges give a larger lattice energy.
Na₂O contains the 2− oxide ion, which attracts Na⁺ more strongly than Cl⁻ does.
MgO has 2+ and 2− ions together. Na₂O has only one doubly charged ion.

q: Use the electronegativity values in the table. Rank the bonds C–S, P–Cl and Si–O from LEAST polar to MOST polar.
h: Bond polarity depends on the difference in electronegativity between the two bonded atoms, not on the atoms' sizes.
w: The differences are C–S: 2.58 − 2.55 = 0.03, P–Cl: 3.16 − 2.19 = 0.97 and Si–O: 3.44 − 1.90 = 1.54. So C–S < P–Cl < Si–O. The C–S bond is essentially nonpolar, while Si–O is strongly polar.
x: This order is reversed. The largest electronegativity difference gives the most polar bond.
Subtract the values. The C–S difference is only 0.03, the smallest of the three.
Subtract the values. Si–O has the largest difference, 1.54.

q: Nitrous acid has the atom connections H–O–N–O. Which drawing is its best Lewis structure?
h: HNO₂ has 18 valence electrons. Check the electron total and octets first, then prefer formal charges of zero.
w: With an N=O double bond to the end oxygen, every atom has an octet and every formal charge is zero, so H–O–N=O is the best structure. Putting the double bond between N and the OH oxygen also gives octets, but leaves +1 on that O and −1 on the end O. The all-single-bond drawing with 18 electrons leaves N with only six electrons, and the one with two lone pairs on N has 20 electrons.
x: Every atom has an octet here, but there are +1 and −1 formal charges. A structure with all zeros is better.
Nitrogen has only two bonds and one lone pair here, just six electrons. It needs an octet.
Count the electrons. This drawing has 20, two more than HNO₂ has.

q:
Two octet-rule resonance structures of sulfur dioxide are drawn below. Which statements are true?
I. An SO2 molecule switches back and forth between the two structures.
II. The two S–O bonds in SO2 have the same length.
III. Each S–O bond has a bond order of about 1.5.
h: Resonance structures are not separate molecules. The real molecule is one blend of them.
w: Statement I is false: the real molecule is a single resonance hybrid at all times, not a mixture that flips between forms. Statement II is true: averaging the two forms makes both S–O bonds identical. Statement III is true: each bond is single in one form and double in the other, an average of 1.5. The answer is II and III only.
x: Statement II is also true. In the hybrid both S–O bonds are the same.
Statement I is false. The molecule does not alternate. It is one blended structure.
Statement I is false. Resonance forms are not real structures that interconvert.

q: The shape of bromine trifluoride, BrF<sub>3</sub>, is drawn below with the lone pairs on bromine. What is the hybridization of the bromine atom?
h: Count all the electron groups around bromine: bonded atoms plus lone pairs.
w: Bromine has 3 bonds and 2 lone pairs, 5 electron groups in a trigonal bipyramid, so it is sp3d. sp2 counts only the three bonds, sp3 counts four groups, and sp3d2 is for six groups.
x: This counts only the three bonded atoms. The two lone pairs also need hybrid orbitals.
Bromine has five electron groups, not four. Count both lone pairs.
That set has six orbitals. Bromine here has five electron groups.

q: Polonium is the only element that crystallizes in the unit cell drawn below, with an edge length of 336 pm. What is the density of polonium? (Po: 209 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Count how many whole atoms belong to the cell (each corner atom is shared by 8 cells), then divide the mass of those atoms by the cell volume in cm³.
w: The cell is simple cubic: 8 corners × 1/8 = 1 atom. Mass = 209 g mol⁻¹ ÷ 6.022×1023 mol⁻¹ = 3.47×10−22 g. Volume = (3.36×10−8 cm)3 = 3.79×10−23 cm3. Density = 9.15 g cm−3. Using 2 atoms (bcc) or 4 atoms (fcc) doubles or quadruples the answer, and counting only one corner (1/8 atom) gives 1.14.
x: This answer uses 2 atoms per cell, which fits a body-centered cell. The drawing has no atom in the center.
This answer uses 4 atoms per cell, which fits a face-centered cell. The drawing has no atoms on the faces.
This answer counts only 1/8 of an atom. All eight corners contribute 1/8 each.

q: Magnesium oxide has the rock-salt unit cell drawn below. The larger O<sup>2−</sup> ions sit at the corners and face centers, and the smaller Mg<sup>2+</sup> ions sit at the edge centers and the body center. How many of each ion belong to one unit cell?
h: A corner is shared by 8 cells, a face by 2 and an edge by 4. The body center belongs to one cell only.
w: O2−: 8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2 = 4. Mg2+: 12 edges × 1/4 + 1 center = 4. So the cell holds 4 O2− and 4 Mg2+, a 1 : 1 ratio that matches the formula MgO. Counting every drawn sphere as whole gives 14 and 13, and counting only the body-center Mg2+ gives 1.
x: These are the numbers of spheres drawn. Most of them are shared with neighboring cells.
The body center is only one of the Mg²⁺ sites. The 12 edge-center ions each count as 1/4.
This swaps the two ions or treats the fcc ions as a single corner atom.

q: Cesium chloride has the unit cell drawn below: Cl<sup>−</sup> ions at the eight corners and one Cs<sup>+</sup> ion at the body center. What is the coordination number of Cs<sup>+</sup>, and how many CsCl formula units belong to one cell?
h: Count the Cl⁻ ions that touch the central Cs⁺. Then count the Cl⁻ that belong to this cell, sharing each corner among 8 cells.
w: The Cs+ at the center touches all 8 corner Cl− ions, so its coordination number is 8. The cell holds 8 × 1/8 = 1 Cl− and 1 Cs+: 8, and 1 formula unit. A coordination number of 6 belongs to the rock-salt structure, and 12 with 4 units to a face-centered cell of one kind of atom.
x: Nine spheres are drawn, but the 8 corner ions are each shared by 8 cells.
Six neighbors is the rock-salt (NaCl) arrangement. Count the corners around the center here.
Twelve neighbors and 4 per cell describe a face-centered cell. This cell has no ions on its faces.

q:
Three cubic unit cells of a metal are drawn below. Which statements are true?
I. Each corner atom is shared by eight unit cells.
II. Each atom in cell III touches eight nearest neighbors.
III. Of the three, cell I leaves the largest fraction of empty space.
h: Cell I is simple cubic, II is body-centered and III is face-centered. Think about how many neighbors touch an atom in each.
w: Statement I is true: a corner sits where eight cubes meet. Statement II is false: in the face-centered cell (III) each atom touches 12 neighbors; 8 is the body-centered value (cell II). Statement III is true: simple cubic (I) fills only about 52% of space, less than bcc (68%) or fcc (74%). So the answer is I and III only.
x: Statement III is also true. A simple cubic cell packs atoms least efficiently.
Statement II is false. Atoms in a face-centered cell have 12 nearest neighbors.
Statement II is false. Eight nearest neighbors fits the body-centered cell, not cell III.

q: Tungsten crystallizes in the unit cell drawn below, with edge length a = 316 pm. Atoms touch along the body diagonal. What is the atomic radius of tungsten?
h: Find the line along which atoms touch. In this cell it runs corner to center to the opposite corner, a length of a√3.
w: The cell is body-centered cubic, so atoms touch along the body diagonal: 4r = a√3. r = (316 pm)(1.732)/4 = 137 pm. 158 pm (a/2) assumes atoms touch along an edge (simple cubic), 112 pm (a√2/4) assumes they touch along a face diagonal (fcc), and 79.0 pm is a/4.
x: This assumes the corner atoms touch along an edge. In this cell the center atom keeps them apart.
This uses the face diagonal, which fits a face-centered cell. This cell has its extra atom in the body center.
This divides the edge by 4. The four radii lie along a longer line than the edge.

q: Aluminum atoms have a radius of 143 pm, and X-ray data show that the cubic unit cell of aluminum has an edge length of 404 pm. Which cell drawn below is the unit cell of aluminum?
c: none of them, because the edge is not a whole multiple of the radius
h: Divide the edge by the radius and compare with 2 (simple cubic), 4/√3 = 2.31 (body-centered) and 2√2 = 2.83 (face-centered).
w: a/r = 404/143 = 2.83 = 2√2, which is the face-centered cubic relation 4r = a√2. So the cell is III. A simple cubic cell (I) would need a = 2r = 286 pm, and a body-centered cell (II) would need a = 4r/√3 = 330 pm.
x: A simple cubic cell would have an edge of 2r, about 286 pm. That does not match 404 pm.
A body-centered cell would have an edge of 4r/√3, about 330 pm. That does not match 404 pm.
The edge does not have to be a whole multiple of r. Atoms can touch along a diagonal.

q: The phase diagram of a substance is drawn below. A sample is cooled at a constant pressure of 0.20 atm from point A (40 °C) to point B (−30 °C). Which phase change occurs along the way?
h: Follow the horizontal line from A to B. Which boundary does it cross, and is 0.20 atm above or below the triple point pressure?
w: Point A is in the gas region and point B in the solid region. At 0.20 atm, below the triple point pressure (0.40 atm), the path crosses only the solid–gas boundary, so the gas turns directly into solid: deposition. Condensation and freezing would happen only at pressures above the triple point, where the line passes through the liquid region. Sublimation is the reverse direction.
x: The path never enters the liquid region. At 0.20 atm the pressure is below the triple point.
Sublimation turns solid into gas. This sample goes the other way.
There is no liquid on this path, so nothing freezes.

q:
The phase diagram of a pure substance is drawn below; its triple point is at 2.0 atm and −40 °C. Which statements are true?
I. When the solid is warmed at 1.0 atm, it changes directly into a gas.
II. The solid is less dense than the liquid.
III. Compressing the solid at −35 °C from 5 atm to 6 atm melts it.
h: Check where the 1.0 atm line sits relative to the triple point, and which way the solid–liquid line leans.
w: Statement I is true: 1.0 atm is below the triple point pressure, so the 1.0 atm line crosses only the solid–gas curve (sublimation, near −49 °C). Statement II is false: the solid–liquid line leans to the right, so higher pressure favors the solid, which means the solid is denser than the liquid. Statement III is false: at −35 °C the points at 5 atm and 6 atm both lie left of the solid–liquid line, so the sample stays solid. The answer is I only.
x: Statement II is false. A solid–liquid line that leans right means pressure favors the solid, so the solid is denser.
Statement III is false. At −35 °C both 5 atm and 6 atm are in the solid region of this diagram.
Statements II and III both treat this substance like water. Its solid–liquid line leans the other way.

q: Use the phase diagram drawn below. What are the normal melting point and the normal boiling point of the substance?
c: melting point about −10 °C, boiling point about 40 °C
melting point about −20 °C, boiling point about 40 °C
melting point about −10 °C, boiling point about 54 °C
melting point about 0 °C, boiling point about 100 °C
h: "Normal" means at exactly 1 atm. Find where the 1 atm line crosses the solid–liquid line and the liquid–gas curve.
w: Along the 1 atm line, the solid–liquid boundary is crossed near −10 °C (normal melting point) and the liquid–gas curve near 40 °C (normal boiling point). −20 °C is the triple point temperature, which is at 0.10 atm, not 1 atm. 54 °C is where the liquid–gas curve reaches the top of the graph (1.5 atm). 0 °C and 100 °C are the values for water, not for this substance.
x: −20 °C is the triple point temperature. The triple point lies at 0.10 atm, not at 1 atm.
About 54 °C is where the liquid–gas curve meets 1.5 atm. Read the curve at the 1 atm line.
Those are water's values. Read this substance's own curves at 1 atm.

q: A 50.0 g sample of a pure solid is heated, and its temperature is plotted against the total heat added (graph below). What is the specific heat of the substance in its LIQUID state?
h: The liquid warms on the sloped segment between the two flat steps. Read the heat added and the temperature change on that segment only.
w: The liquid segment runs from 9 kJ to 15 kJ while the temperature rises from 10 °C to 60 °C. c = q/(mΔT) = 6000 J/(50.0 g × 50 °C) = 2.4 J g−1 °C−1. 2.0 is the solid's value (first segment), 4.8 wrongly includes the 6 kJ used to melt the solid, and 0.0024 leaves the heat in kJ.
x: This uses the first sloped segment, where the solid warms from −20 °C to 10 °C.
This includes the melting step. Heat absorbed on a flat step does not raise the temperature.
The heat was left in kilojoules. Convert to joules first.

q: A gaseous substance is cooled at a constant rate, giving the cooling curve below with segments A–E. What happens during segment D?
h: Flat steps on a cooling curve are phase changes. Which step is at the higher temperature, and does a cooling sample lose or gain heat?
w: Segment D is the second flat step (20 °C), after the liquid has cooled (C). There the liquid freezes and the sample releases heat, which is why the temperature can stay constant while heat is still being removed. Segment B (80 °C) is condensation. Melting is the reverse of freezing and needs heat to be absorbed.
x: Melting happens when heat is added. This sample is being cooled.
Freezing releases heat to the surroundings. A sample that loses heat cannot be absorbing it.
Condensation is the first flat step at the higher temperature.

q: Vapor-pressure curves for two pure liquids, 1 and 2, are shown below. What is the normal boiling point of the liquid with the STRONGER intermolecular forces?
h: Stronger attractions mean fewer molecules escape, so a lower vapor pressure at every temperature. The normal boiling point is where the vapor pressure reaches 760 torr.
w: Liquid 2 has the lower vapor pressure at every temperature, so its intermolecular forces are stronger. Its curve reaches 760 torr at about 90 °C. About 40 °C is the normal boiling point of liquid 1, the weaker-attraction liquid. About 72 °C is where liquid 2 reaches only 400 torr, and 100 °C is water's boiling point, not read from this graph.
x: That is where liquid 1 reaches 760 torr. Liquid 1 has the higher vapor pressure, so its attractions are weaker.
At that temperature liquid 2 has a vapor pressure of only about 400 torr. Boiling at 1 atm needs 760 torr.
That is water's normal boiling point. Read the curve where it crosses 760 torr.

q: A sealed flask held at 30 °C contains liquid 1 in equilibrium with its vapor (curves below). The flask's volume is then doubled at 30 °C, and some liquid is still present when equilibrium returns. What is the pressure of the vapor now?
h: Read the vapor pressure of liquid 1 at 30 °C. Does vapor pressure depend on how much space the vapor has, as long as liquid remains?
w: At 30 °C liquid 1 has a vapor pressure of about 520 torr. When the volume doubles, more liquid evaporates until the vapor again reaches the equilibrium vapor pressure, which depends only on temperature. So the pressure is still about 520 torr. Halving it to 260 torr applies Boyle's law to a gas with no liquid present, and about 60 torr is liquid 2's value.
x: Boyle's law applies only if no liquid is left to evaporate. Here liquid remains.
Expanding the space cannot raise the pressure. Equilibrium vapor pressure depends only on temperature.
That is the vapor pressure of liquid 2 at 30 °C, not liquid 1.

q: Curve 1 below is the speed distribution of CH<sub>4</sub> (16.0 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) at 300 K. Curve 2 is for a different gas at the same temperature. Which gas gives curve 2?
h: Read the speed at the peak of each curve. At the same temperature, the most probable speed is proportional to 1/√M.
w: Curve 1 peaks near 560 m s−1 and curve 2 near 280 m s−1, half as fast. Since u ∝ 1/√M, half the speed means 4 times the molar mass: 4 × 16.0 = 64 g mol−1, which is SO2. O2 (2 × 16) would peak at 560/√2 ≈ 395 m s−1, Ar near 350 m s−1 and Kr near 245 m s−1.
x: Twice the molar mass lowers the speed only by √2, to about 395 m/s. Curve 2 peaks lower than that.
Argon would peak near 350 m/s. Read curve 2's peak again.
Krypton is heavier than needed and would peak near 245 m/s.

q:
The speed distributions of N2 and He, both at 400 K, are drawn below as curves 1 and 2. Which statements are true?
I. The molecules of curve 2 have a greater average kinetic energy than those of curve 1.
II. The gas of curve 1 effuses through a pinhole more slowly than the gas of curve 2.
III. Raising the temperature of the gas of curve 1 would make its curve taller and narrower.
h: Both gases are at the same temperature. Which curve belongs to the heavier gas, and what does heating do to a speed distribution?
w: Statement I is false: at the same temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy; He atoms are faster only because they are lighter. Statement II is true: curve 1 peaks at the lower speed, so it is the heavier N2, which effuses more slowly. Statement III is false: heating shifts the curve to higher speeds and makes it lower and broader. The answer is II only.
x: Statement I is false. Average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, and both gases are at 400 K.
Statement III is false. Heating spreads the curve out, making it lower and broader.
Statements I and III are false. Same temperature means the same average kinetic energy, and heating flattens the curve.

q: Boxes I–III show equal volumes of the same gas at the same temperature (each sphere is one molecule). Rank the samples from MOST ideal to LEAST ideal behavior.
h: The ideal gas model assumes the molecules take up no space and do not attract one another. When does that work best?
w: Box I has 4 molecules, III has 9 and II has 18. The more crowded the sample (higher density, so higher pressure), the more the molecules' own volume and their attractions matter. So the order is I, III, II. Reversing it treats crowding as ideal, and since temperatures are equal the deviations are not the same.
x: This order is reversed. Crowded molecules feel more attraction and take up more of the space.
Box II is the most crowded, so it cannot sit in the middle. Count the molecules in each box.
The temperatures are equal, but the densities are not. Density affects how ideal a gas is.

q: Automobile airbags inflate with nitrogen made by the reaction below. What mass of sodium azide (65.01 g mol<sup>−1</sup>) is needed to fill a 65.0 L airbag at 1.10 atm and 30 °C?
h: Find moles of N₂ with PV = nRT (temperature in kelvins), then use the mole ratio from the equation.
w: n(N2) = PV/RT = (1.10 atm)(65.0 L)/[(0.08206 L atm mol−1 K−1)(303 K)] = 2.874 mol. NaN3: 2.874 × 2/3 = 1.916 mol × 65.01 g mol−1 = 125 g. 187 g skips the 2 : 3 mole ratio, 280. g inverts it, and 1.26 × 103 g uses 30 instead of 303 K.
x: This skips the mole ratio. Two NaN₃ make three N₂.
The mole ratio is upside down. Fewer moles of NaN₃ are needed than moles of N₂ made.
The temperature must be in kelvins, 303 K, not 30.

q: Two samples of the same gas are held at 1.00 atm, and their volumes are measured at several temperatures (lines A and B below, extended to zero volume). How many moles of gas are in sample B?
h: Pick a temperature where line B crosses a gridline and read its volume. Then use PV = nRT with the temperature in kelvins.
w: Line B reads 8.0 L at 100 °C (373 K). n = PV/RT = (1.00 atm)(8.0 L)/[(0.08206)(373 K)] = 0.261 mol. Line A, with twice the slope, holds twice as many moles (0.523 mol). 0.975 mol uses 100 instead of 373 K, and 3.83 inverts the equation.
x: That is sample A, the steeper line. Read line B.
The temperature must be in kelvins. Both lines reach zero volume at −273 °C.
The equation was inverted. n equals PV divided by RT.

q: The graph shows PV/nRT for H2, CH4 and CO2 at 400 K as the pressure rises (an ideal gas would stay at 1.0). Which curve is CO2?
c: none, because all three gases are ideal at 400 K
h: Values below 1.0 mean attractions pull the molecules together. Which of the three molecules has the most electrons and the strongest attractions?
w: CO2 has the most electrons and is the most polarizable, so its attractions are strongest and its PV/nRT drops furthest below 1. That is curve 2, which dips to about 0.64. Curve 1, with a smaller dip, is CH4. Curve 3 stays above 1 at all pressures because H2 has very weak attractions, so the molecules' own volume dominates.
x: Curve 1 dips only slightly below 1. A molecule with stronger attractions would dip further.
Curve 3 never drops below 1, so attractions barely matter for it. That fits the gas with the fewest electrons.
At these high pressures none of the curves stays at 1.0, so none of the gases is ideal here.

q: Gold crystallizes in the unit cell drawn below, and its density is 19.3 g cm<sup>−3</sup>. What is the atomic radius of gold? (Au: 196.97 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
h: Count the atoms per cell, get the cell volume from the density, then the edge from a cube root. Use the line along which the atoms touch.
w: The face-centered cell holds 8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2 = 4 atoms with a mass of 4 × 196.97/6.022×1023 = 1.308×10−21 g. Volume = 1.308×10−21 g ÷ 19.3 g cm−3 = 6.78×10−23 cm3, so a = 4.08×10−8 cm = 408 pm. Atoms touch along a face diagonal: 4r = a√2, so r = 144 pm. 408 pm is the edge itself, 204 pm assumes atoms touch along an edge, and 114 pm comes from counting only 2 atoms per cell.
x: That is the edge length of the cell. The radius is a fraction of it.
Half the edge assumes atoms touch along an edge. In this cell they touch along the face diagonal.
This counts 2 atoms per cell. Count the face atoms as halves and the corners as eighths.
